# THE COMPLETE WORKS OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA.

The life of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, most elegantly written by Gianfrancesco <note>also known as Giovanni Francesco Pico della Mirandola, the nephew of the author and a philosopher in his own right</note>, son of the illustrious Prince Galeotto Pico.

*Heptaplus*: On the sevenfold narration of the six days of Genesis. <note>A work of mystical exegesis where Pico attempts to reconcile the creation story in the Bible with Platonic and Neoplatonic philosophy.</note>

A prayer of deprecation to God in elegiac verse. <note>A poem seeking divine mercy and the turning away of judgment.</note>

An Apology concerning thirteen questions. <note>original: "Apologia tredecim quæstionum." This was Pico's formal defense of the thirteen "heretical" or "doubtful" theses among his 900 conclusions that were condemned by Pope Innocent VIII.</note>

A treatise on Being and the One, with certain objections and responses. <note>A work dedicated to Angelo Poliziano, attempting to harmonize the philosophies of Plato and Aristotle on the nature of existence.</note>

A most elegant Oration. <note>original: "Oratio quædam elegantissima." This is the famous "Oration on the Dignity of Man," originally intended as the introductory speech for his public debate on the 900 theses.</note>

Several letters of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola.

Testimonies of his life and teachings.

Twelve books of Disputations against Astrologers. <note>Pico's massive critique of judicial astrology, arguing for human free will against celestial determinism.</note>

A poem on the wood of the cross by Caecilius Cyprian, Bishop of Carthage.

In this volume, the following most distinguished men write letters:

--- Page 10 ---
<meta>This page begins the formal dedication of the volume. Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola, the author's nephew, addresses Ludovico Sforza, the Duke of Milan, establishing the biographical and moral purpose of the work that follows the table of contents from the previous page.</meta>

->Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola to Ludovico Maria Sforza Visconti, the Duke of Milan, sends heartiest greetings.<-

Most illustrious Prince, among those who have recorded the lives of famous men for future generations to read, some have done so to ensure that the names of those to whom they were bound by blood or owed their education would not be erased by the ravages of time <note>original: "edaci uetustate," literally "greedy old age" or "consuming antiquity"</note>, but rather be completely rescued from the injustice of being forgotten. This was the same kind of devotion that Pliny the Younger showed to his uncle, Pliny the Elder, and that Porphyry showed to his teacher, Plotinus. <note>Gianfrancesco is justifying his role as biographer by citing famous classical examples of students and relatives honoring their predecessors.</note>

Others, however, have achieved this same goal with even greater purpose: namely, they aimed not just at preserving the eternal memory of the deceased, but at providing a model of life for those who remain. Thus we find that Jerome recorded the life of Hilarion; Athanasius, that of Anthony; Sulpicius Severus, that of Martin; and Paulinus, that of Ambrose. <note>These are references to famous hagiographies: St. Jerome’s "Life of Hilarion," Athanasius’s "Life of St. Anthony," Sulpicius Severus’s "Life of St. Martin," and Paulinus’s "Life of St. Ambrose."</note> They committed these tireless studies, most upright characters, and most noble deeds to paper, so that the glory of God might spread throughout the world and guide men toward living well and blessedly—

<summary>This page is the opening of Gianfrancesco Pico's dedicatory preface to Ludovico Sforza, Duke of Milan. He explains that he is writing his uncle's biography not just out of family duty, but to provide a moral and spiritual example for others, following the tradition of great classical and Christian biographers.</summary>
<keywords>Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola, Ludovico Sforza, biography, moral examples, Pliny, Plotinus, St. Jerome, St. Athanasius, hagiography, Renaissance humanism</keywords>

--- Page 11 ---
<meta>This page transitions from the formal dedication to the Duke of Milan into the actual biography of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. The author, his nephew Gianfrancesco, begins by establishing his credibility and objectivity before detailing Pico's noble lineage, the specific date of his birth, and the miraculous omens that accompanied it.</meta>

# THE LIFE OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA, A MAN MOST ACCOMPLISHED IN EVERY BRANCH OF LEARNING, PUBLISHED BY GIANFRANCESCO, SON OF THE ILLUSTRIOUS PRINCE GALEOTTO PICO.

<note>A large decorative initial 'I' contains a floral design, marking the beginning of the narrative.</note>

Having begun to write the life of Giovanni Pico, my uncle, I consider it primarily necessary to state to my readers—lest they suspect that, because I was his brother’s son or his disciple, I might say anything to curry favor in the manner of flatterers—that nothing here is given to friendship, nothing to family, and nothing is repaid in false praise for the great benefits that truly stood out in my life through him. Indeed, my narrative is as far removed from adulation as it was from the necessity of flattering him. I have taken great care that readers do not judge me to be either lying or excessive in my praise. 

If I had committed to writing everything I had conceived of him, perhaps there would have been a danger that his excellent virtues themselves, or their defenders, could have accused me of being too sparse. This can be seen even from this argument: many of the most painstakingly written works of the learned men of our age, even from the foremost among them, have provided the most abundant testimony not only to what we are about to say, but while he still enjoyed this light <note>original: "hac luce," a common Latin metaphor for being alive</note> and after he exchanged it for a better one <note>A euphemism for death and the transition to the afterlife.</note>, they excelled me in proclamations of his character and teaching. I have ordered some of these to be added at the end of this book, after his own commentaries, so that a firmer faith might be applied by witnesses who are not of his own kin. 

Setting aside his paternal lineage <margin>Paternal lineage</margin>—although it is handed down in memory that it took its beginnings from the Emperor Constantine through his great-grandson Picus, from whom the surname of the entire family was derived—we shall take our starting point from the time of his birth itself. This is because he perhaps brought no less honor to the family than he received from it, and also because I have deemed it necessary to explain the particular gifts of his mind and the remaining sequence of his whole life and death, which I either drew from my own ears and eyes or received from most reliable witnesses. Rank and the famous deeds of ancestors are set aside in this account.

In the year 1463 after the Virgin’s birth, while Pope Pius II was presiding over the Church and Frederick III was holding the reins of the Roman Empire, his mother, Julia, from the noble family of the Boiardi <margin>Mother Julia; Gianfrancesco; Father Galeotto; Antonio Maria; brothers Alberto Pio</margin>, gave birth to Giovanni Francesco <note>The father's name was also Gianfrancesco.</note> as her last child. She had already given birth to Galeotto the elder (from whom I was born), Antonio Maria, and two sisters. One of these, having married Leonello, gave birth to Alberto Pio, one of the princes of Carpi, and is now the consort of Prince Rodolfo Gonzaga. The other, after the death of Prince Pino Ordelaffi of Forlì to whom she had long ago been married, entered into a second marriage with the Count of Montagnana. 

A portent of no small significance appeared before his birth. A circular flame was seen to stand above the wall of his mother’s bedroom and then soon vanished <margin>Portent of the flame</margin>, perhaps suggesting to us that he would be most similar to a circular figure <note>In Renaissance philosophy, the circle was the symbol of perfection, infinity, and the divine mind.</note> in the perfection of his intellect—which he would present among mortals at that same hour—and that he was to be celebrated for the excellence of his name throughout the entire globe. His mind was always destined to seek heavenly things like fire, and his fiery eloquence, in harmony with his inflamed mind, was destined to celebrate our God (who is a consuming fire <note>A reference to Deuteronomy 4:24 and Hebrews 12:29.</note>) with all its strength; yet, like that flame, it was destined to be hidden from the sight of men as soon as it vanished. 

Indeed, we read that unusual signs have sometimes preceded or followed the births of the most learned and holy men, as if the divine will were separating their cradles from the crowd of others and indicating that they were born for great achievements. <margin>Ambrose, Paulinus; Form and physical condition</margin> Thus, to omit others, a swarm of bees brushed against the mouth of the great Ambrose and entered into it; then, coming out and flying very high, it hid itself among the clouds and escaped the sight of his father and the others who were present. Paulinus, making much of this in his writings, argued that this portended for us the honeycombs of his works <note>St. Ambrose was famously called the "Honey-tongued Doctor" because of this legend, which symbolized his future eloquence.</note>.

A ii

<summary>Gianfrancesco Pico introduces the biography of his uncle, Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, asserting his objectivity and detailing Pico's noble birth in 1463. He describes a miraculous circular flame that appeared at Pico's birth, symbolizing his intellectual perfection and future fame.</summary>

### THE LIFE OF GIOVANNI PICO OF MIRANDOLA

...would announce these things, and would raise the minds of men from the earth toward the heavens. He was of **remarkable and noble form**: of a tall and lofty stature, with a soft complexion and a handsome face overall. His skin was fair, interspersed with a graceful redness; he had greyish and alert eyes, and blond, unaffected hair <note>original: "flauo & inaffectato capillitio." Blond hair was often idealized in Renaissance Italy as a sign of nobility or angelic nature.</note>. His teeth were also white and even. Under his mother’s authority, he was delivered to teachers and various disciplines. He cultivated the study of the **humanities** <note>The *studia humanitatis*, including grammar, rhetoric, poetry, history, and moral philosophy.</note> with such an ardent spirit that in a short time, 
<margin>A swift talent</margin> he was deservedly placed among the foremost poets and orators of that age. In learning, he was indeed most rapid, endowed with such a ready talent that he could recite poems he had heard only once from a reader, both in their direct and reverse order <note>The ability to recite text backward was a traditional Renaissance benchmark for a "prodigious memory."</note>, to the wondrous admiration of all. He retained them with a most tenacious memory, which is usually the opposite for others; for it often happens by nature that those who have a swift talent do not possess a strong memory, while those who learn with great labor become more tenacious in holding their teachers' lessons. 

When he reached his fourteenth year, by the command of his mother—who vehemently desired him to be initiated into the sacred rites <note>That is, to enter the priesthood or a career in the Church.</note>—he moved to Bologna for the sake of learning **Canon Law** <note>The legal system of the Catholic Church.</note>. After he had tasted this for two years, seeing that it consisted of nothing but unwilling traditions <note>original: "meris inuiti traditionib⁹." Pico famously found the study of legal precedents dry and "un-philosophical."</note>, he turned elsewhere, though not without producing some good fruit; for even then, as a boy and a tender youth, he compiled a certain **epitome** or brief summary from the letters of the Supreme Pontiffs which are called the **Decretals** <note>The collection of papal letters that formed the basis of Church law.</note>. 
<margin>As a boy he was skilled in Church law</margin> In this work, he concluded all the opinions of those sanctions as concisely as possible—a task of no small weight even for accomplished professors. 

But as a greedy explorer of the secrets of nature, he abandoned these well-trodden paths and devoted himself entirely to the contemplation of the intellect and to philosophy, both human and divine. For the sake of attaining this, he traveled through the literary gymnasiums <note>The universities and centers of learning.</note> not only of Italy but also of France, most scrupulously seeking out the celebrated teachers of that time in the manner of **Plato** and **Apollonius** <note>Apollonius of Tyana, a Greek Neopythagorean philosopher known for his extensive travels in search of wisdom.</note>. He spent such tireless labor on these studies that he was both considered and held to be a finished theologian and philosopher while still in the "blade" of his youth <note>original: "inherbis," a metaphor for being young/unripe.</note>. 

He had already spent seven years among these studies when, desirous of human praise and glory (for he did not yet burn with divine love, as will become clear), he moved to Rome. There, desiring to show how much envy would follow him from whisperers in the future, 
<margin>Nine hundred disputations proposed at Rome</margin> he proposed **nine hundred questions** <note>The famous "900 Theses" which Pico intended to debate publicly.</note> concerning logic, mathematics, natural things, and divine matters. These were drawn not only from the stores of the Latins and excerpted from the cabinets of the Greeks, but also unearthed from the mysteries of the **Hebrews**, tracked down from the secrets of the **Chaldeans**, and from the **Arabs**. He also wove into these questions much regarding the ancient and somewhat obscure philosophy of **Pythagoras**, **Trismegistus** <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary figure to whom the Hermetic writings are attributed.</note>, and **Orpheus**. He included much concerning the **Kabbalah**—that is, the secret reception of Hebrew dogmas—
<margin>Origen, Hilary</margin> which **Origen** and **Hilary** <note>Origen and Hilary of Poitiers, early Church Fathers who engaged with Jewish tradition.</note> among our own people primarily mention. He also included much concerning **natural magic**, which he taught was separated by a great distance from the impious and criminal kind <note>Pico was a pioneer in distinguishing "Natural Magic"—the study of the hidden powers of nature—from "Goetia" or demonic sorcery.</note>. This he proved most elegantly by the testimony of many. 

Nor were there lacking seventy-two new physical and metaphysical dogmas, his own inventions and meditations, adapted to elucidate any questions of philosophy. To these he annexed a new method of philosophizing through numbers. He posted all of these together in public places so they might be more easily publicized, promising that he would pay the expenses of those who traveled to Rome from remote regions for the sake of debating him. 

But due to the animosity of detractors (which always seeks the heights, just like fire), he was never able to ensure that a day for the debate was set. For this reason, he remained in Rome for a year, during which time those "vituperators" <note>Fault-finders or legalistic critics.</note> did not dare to attack him openly or in a free examination. Instead, corrupted by pestilential envy (as many have judged), they attempted to undermine him through tricks, "burrows," and hidden arrows. It was thought that he had stirred up this spite primarily because many who had long brooded over literary business—perhaps out of ambition or avarice—thought it would be a mark against them...

**THE LIFE OF GIOVANNI PICO OF MIRANDOLA**

If that young man—with the accumulated wealth of his ancestors and great learning, like a fertile field flourishing in the primary city of the world <note>Referring to Rome, where Pico intended to debate his theses.</note>—had not feared to put his learning and talent to the test concerning natural and divine matters, and many things that had not been accessible to our people for many centuries: And when his rivals realized that they could accomplish nothing against his learning with honest engines of argument, they brought into the open the engines of slander. They cried out that thirteen of the nine hundred questions were suspect regarding the true faith. To these critics, some perhaps joined themselves who—because those questions were unfamiliar to their ears—attacked them with more piety than perhaps erudition, under the pretext of religious zeal. Yet, not a few celebrated doctors of theology had previously approved those same questions as pious and pure, and had signed their names to them. Among that group was numbered **Bonfrancesco of Reggio**, 
<margin>Bonfrancesco, Bishop of Reggio</margin> 
the Bishop: a man distinguished by every kind of learning, the sharpest judgment, and gravity of character. He was serving at that time in Rome as the ambassador to the Supreme Pontiff for the Duke of Ferrara. Against him, however, those babblers <note>original: "Blaterones." A dismissive term for his vocal critics.</note> attempted nothing, fearing perhaps that his reputation could not be undermined by them, since he submitted whatever he handled to the correction of the Mother Church and the Pope. 

But Pico, not enduring this loss to his reputation, 
<margin>The Apology</margin> 
published an **Apology**. It was certainly a varied and elegant work, filled with the knowledge of many things worth knowing, yet it was composed by candlelight in only twenty nights. Through this publication, it was made clearer than light that his conclusions could indeed be understood in a Catholic sense, and that those who had previously barked against them <note>original: "adlatrauerant." A metaphor comparing his critics to barking dogs.</note> should be convicted of insolence and ignorance. Like a most Christian man, he committed the book itself and whatever he might write in the future to the judgment of the Mother Church and its most holy leader. For he was most firmly persuaded that this ought to be done, either expressly or silently, as if he were putting forward that saying of Augustine: <note>original: "Errare possum hæreticus esse non possum."</note> **"I can err, but I cannot be a heretic,"** since the former is a human trait, while the latter belongs to a perverse and obstinate will. 

But when 
<margin>Pope Innocent VIII</margin> 
**Innocent VIII**, the Supreme Pontiff, learned through the publication of the *Apology* that those conclusions—which had previously been besieged by slanders—were interpreted in a Catholic sense and relieved of the mark of crime; and when several people to whom the examination of the conclusions had been entrusted reported that traps could be set for the faithful if some of those questions (which lay about in a crude and unexplained manner of dispute) wandered about everywhere, he forbade the reading of the little book in which they were contained. All of these things are clearly seen through the Decree—which they call a *Brief*—of the Supreme Pontiff 
<margin>Alexander VI</margin> 
**Alexander VI**, under whom we now live. We have thought it right to deliver this Brief to the printers along with the *Apology* itself. 

Indeed, at the very end of the *Apology*, Pico had already done by whatever reasoning he could what the Pope later provided by his authority. He had entreated friends and enemies, the learned and the unlearned alike, 
<margin>Note</margin> 
to read the *Apology* but to pass over the little book of unexplained conclusions without reading it. This was because it contained many things that were not to be spread everywhere in the streets, but were undertaken to be disputed in secret gatherings among a few learned men. Following the custom of the Academies, he had considered these as scholastic exercises, and had proposed many impious dogmas of ancient philosophers—namely 
<margin>Alexander and Averroes</margin> 
**Alexander** <note>Likely Alexander of Aphrodisias, a commentator on Aristotle whose interpretations were sometimes seen as conflicting with Christian doctrine.</note> and **Averroes** <note>The influential Islamic philosopher whose "Commentary" on Aristotle was central to university life but often controversial for its views on the soul.</note> and many others. He had always asserted, professed, and preached, both publicly and privately, that these dogmas deviated no less from the paths of true and right philosophy than from the paths of faith. And in this manner, speaking of that little book of nine hundred conclusions, he concluded his apologetic work: "Therefore, let those who hate me not read them because they are mine; let those who love me not read them because from those things which are mine, they might think many things which are not truly ours."

<meta>This page continues the biography of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, picking up after the mention of his "Apology." It describes his spiritual transformation, his rejection of youthful vanities, and his deep immersion into sacred scripture and theology.</meta>

->**THE LIFE OF GIOVANNI PICO OF MIRANDOLA**<-

<margin>Conversion to God</margin> ...all those slanders falsely and malevolently imposed might correct his true errors. As he was wandering in the darkness—so that he might perceive how far he had strayed from the path of truth—a most splendid radiance <note>original: "splendidissimum iubar," a metaphor for divine illumination.</note> began to shine upon him. Previously, he had been both desirous of glory and inflamed by vain love, moved by feminine allurements. Indeed, many women, on account of his physical beauty and the grace of his face—to which were added great learning, vast wealth, and nobility of birth—burned with love for him. Not shrinking from their devotion, he had for a short time neglected the way of life and drifted into delights. But, awakened by that conflict, he restrained his mind which was dissolving in luxury and turned it toward Christ. He exchanged feminine flatteries for the joys of the heavenly fatherland. Neglecting the breeze of slight glory which he had once sought, he began to seek with his whole mind the glory of God and the utility of the Church. He so composed his character that, from then on, he could be approved even by the judgment of an enemy. And when he learned that a glorious reputation of him was flying through both neighboring and remote lands, many of the philosophers who were considered most learned flocked to him as if to a **marketplace of the good arts** <margin>Cicero</margin> <note>A reference to Cicero's "mercatura bonarum artium," describing a place where wisdom is traded like fine goods.</note>—either to provoke literary contests or because they possessed a more upright mental outlook—to hear and hold the healthy dogmas of right living. These were sought after all the more because they flowed from a man who was most learned and equally noble, and who had once followed the devious, winding paths of voluptuous softness. For those things seem to have the greatest weight in instilling moral discipline in the minds of listeners which are not only good by their own nature, but which proceed from a teacher who has turned to the paths of justice from the distorted and crooked track of lusts. 

<margin>Burned love poems</margin> He had played at love in elegiac verse, which, having composed in five books, he consigned to the flames for the sake of religion. He likewise played much with **Tuscan rhymes** <note>Poetry written in the Italian vernacular rather than Latin.</note> which he similarly consumed in the fire. <margin>Study of sacred letters</margin> Then, embracing sacred letters with the most burning zeal, he immediately offered—as if the first fruits of the harvest in the temple of God, being then in his twenty-eighth year—the **Heptaplus**, a work on the six days of Genesis and the day of rest. It was a work perfect in genius and elaborated with industry, most full of the sublime dogmas of the philosophers and the deepest mysteries of our Christian theology. It was connected by a sevenfold variety of narration and a sevenfold number of chapters assigned to each sevenfold exposition, fitting the name of the book perfectly. 

<margin>What the epistles of Paul declare about sacred letters</margin> Yet, because of the things unearthed from the bosom of nature and the difficult explanations of divine questions—as well as the most recondite meanings of the prophet and the elegance of the language—it does not offer itself everywhere to those unlearned in philosophy and eloquence. Rather, the use of that precious and rare furniture is prepared for few. Noticing this himself, he made a not ungraceful mention of this matter at the end of its preface. As soon as he tasted sacred letters, he rejoiced and exulted, finding not only true wisdom but also true eloquence. To omit many of the praises of the New Testament brought forward by him, he used to say that the **Epistles of Paul** surpassed the writings of all orators in eloquence, specifically citing the night-labors of **Tully** <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero.</note> and **Demosthenes**, the primary master of speaking. He said this not because Paul’s letters were, like theirs, "burned with curling irons" <note>original: "calamistris inustae," a classical metaphor for overly artificial or ornate rhetorical style.</note> or packed with makeup and curls scraped together from everywhere, but because they smelled of and tasted like true, solid eloquence, supported by true sentiments and true art. To put it briefly, they were not deliberately stuffed with the "wealth of the Egyptians" <note>A common patristic metaphor for using pagan learning/rhetoric to serve Christian truth.</note>. Furthermore, he proclaimed all the words <margin>Words of the Old Law</margin> of the Old Law to be full of the most consummate science and wisdom, which **Augustine**, <margin>Augustine</margin> among others, clearly showed in his book *On Christian Doctrine*.

These rules were certainly too brief and not fully explained, for he had intended to expand them into many chapters if he had lived. He also composed two prayers to God: <margin>Music cultivated</margin> one in Tuscan rhythms <note>original: "rhithmis hetruſcis." Pico wrote poetry in the Italian vernacular (Tuscan), which was common among humanists of his era.</note> and the other in elegiac meter. He did this so that when he was worn out by heavier studies, he could soothe his mind by singing to the lyre. Indeed, in the first years of his youth, he had so cultivated every kind of musical art that the melodies he devised and the harmonies he noted with their proper arrangements were held in high regard. We also saw many other things in his chests, although they were unorganized, from which I believe something useful could be compiled, especially an exposition of the Psalms.

<margin>Multifaceted letters</margin> Furthermore, about fifty letters emerged, published at various times—some familiar, some doctrinal, and some encouraging—along with the oration which he was to have delivered in Rome if the disputation had been allowed to take place. This oration reflects a most sharp genius and most abundant learning, remarkable for a youth who was not yet twenty-four years old. This is true of all his writings, which provide us with the richest testimony of his most fertile eloquence. 

<margin>An approved character of speaking</margin> He always used a style that was highly commendable—not artificial, but natural, multifaceted, and varying according to the subject. Although he used up (as they say) the whole "perfume-box" of Isocrates <note>original: "Iſocratis myrotheciōn." This is a classical metaphor, used by Cicero, referring to a storehouse of refined rhetorical ornaments.</note>, he nevertheless preserved a cleanliness of style and the ornaments of majestic decorum. 

<margin>Kinds of speaking</margin> Indeed, those celebrated "kinds of speaking"—of which Gellius lists three and Macrobius four—can be gathered from his works without great effort. <margin>Copious, Brief, Dry, Flowery, and Rich</margin> There one finds the **copious** style in which Cicero usually rules; the **brief** which is ascribed to Sallust; the **dry** given to Fronto; and the **rich and flowery** in which they say Pliny and Symmachus indulged. But perhaps Brutus would not have called this copiousness "weak," nor Sallust "immoderate." An orator with right judgment will easily perceive Fronto’s "dryness" moistened, Sallust’s "brevity" extended, and the flowery richness of Pliny carried into a wider field. Add to these the "milky fountain" of Livy—perhaps without that "Paduanism" <note>original: "patauinitate." A famous ancient criticism of Livy by Asinius Pollio, suggesting his Latin had a regional Paduan accent or style.</note>—with many little flowers of Apuleius added.

Truly, he did not exercise himself here in philosophy merely borrowed from the Greeks, nor in "Attic Nights" <note>Refers to the *Noctes Atticae* by Aulus Gellius, a collection of miscellaneous notes on grammar, philosophy, and history.</note>, nor in fictional "Saturnalia" <note>Refers to the *Saturnalia* by Macrobius, a work of Virgilian criticism and antiquarian lore.</note> fabricated almost entirely to praise Virgil’s *Aeneid*, nor in Roman history, nor in a mere natural history empty of the deepest and most difficult speculations. Rather, he labored over that admirable "fabric of the world" <note>likely referring to his work on the creation, the *Heptaplus*.</note> and wore himself out in attacking the enemies of the holy Catholic Church and in eliminating the influence of astrologers. He labored in examining theological questions and in the harmony of Aristotle and Plato; he applied himself to explaining the sacred words of Scripture and devoted his energy to advising and encouraging his friends. 

Truly, he was so far from affecting this eloquence of which we speak that he rather condemned those who, searching too scrupulously for "painted allurements," devoted all the powers of their genius to investigating the origins of words. All these things turned many people even more toward admiration of him, because he had been engaged long and most deeply among the writings of those who did not profess Latin letters filled with the "flowers of eloquence" <note>This refers to the Scholastic theologians, whom humanists often criticized for their "barbarous" or unpolished Latin style.</note>. Let the excessive lovers of antiquity bear this with an even mind; for although these things are stated concisely, they are perhaps more true for the fact that men more learned than I—Ermolao Barbaro, Battista the Carmelite, Marsilio Ficino, Matteo Bosso, and many other most learned and eloquent men—have declared them. 

<margin>Speed of reading</margin> He read through and excerpted from vast libraries of both Latin and Greek works with incredible speed; he passed over no commentaries unread, provided the opportunity was given. He had attained such a degree of knowledge concerning the ancient Doctors of the Church that it is difficult to believe, even for one who had spent his whole life doing nothing but unrolling their works. But concerning the "modern" theologians who used that style commonly called "Parisian" <note>original: "Parīſienſem." This refers to Scholasticism, the dialectical and logical method of theology associated with the University of Paris.</note>, such judgment resided in him that if anyone suddenly asked him to unravel some abstruse and poorly explained question of theirs, he would open it with such fertility of genius and unlock it with such skill that [it seemed]...

<meta>This page continues the biography of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, shifting from a list of his literary works to a description of his intellectual character, his respect for various philosophical schools, and his legendary skill—and eventual distaste—for public academic debate.</meta>

### THE LIFE OF GIOVANNI PICO OF MIRANDOLA

...he held all the sayings of that doctor <note>Referring back to Thomas Aquinas, mentioned in the following lines.</note> before his eyes and ready for use, and he had come to know all the schools of thought in the same way. He had examined every manuscript, yet you should not believe he was so devoted to any one of them (as is the custom among our men) that he looked down upon the others. For he himself had been so instructed and so inspired from his youth that he sought the truth within them all; he honored it with equal respect wherever it shone forth, and once found, he venerated it, stripped of any personal bias. What he actually thought of each individual who is considered famous throughout the world can be seen in the preface to his *Apology*, where he recounted the unique characteristics and specific praises of barbarian, Greek, and Latin philosophers. However, whenever mention was made of those philosophers or theologians who wrote in the French style of debating <note>original: "gallico more." This refers to the Scholastic method of the University of Paris, which focused on rigorous logical disputation.</note>, he was accustomed to praise Thomas Aquinas <margin>Thomas Aquinas</margin> above all others, as one who, more solid than the rest, rests upon the foundation of truth. He also names him the "splendor of our theology" in his *Heptaplus* <note>Pico's mystical seven-fold exposition on the six days of Genesis.</note>. Having been asked about this very frequently, even by myself, he gave the same answer. Nor should certain things contained in his *Apology* for the sake of debate persuade anyone to the contrary—namely, those points which were openly opposed to the opinions of Thomas. At that time, he was still a very young man and eager for glory; in that most celebrated city <note>Rome.</note>, in the manner of Gorgias of Leontini <margin>Gorgias of Leontini</margin> <note>Gorgias was a Greek Sophist famous for his claim that he could speak on any subject and win any argument.</note>, he sought the fame of his faction by defending whatever side was necessary. To this I add that out of ten thousand propositions, disagreeing with or even opposing three or four does not prove him an adversary. 

Furthermore, he was most skilled in disputation, and he spent frequent and very intense effort on literary contests while his fervor for them was high. If he were the one posing an objection, you could easily detect the sharpness and vigilance of Scotus <margin>Scotus's sharpness</margin> <note>John Duns Scotus, known as the "Subtle Doctor."</note>, the bite of Francis <note>Likely Francis of Meyronnes, a Scholastic known for his rigorous logic.</note>, and the abundance and multitude of Aureolus <margin>Aureolus</margin> <note>Peter Aureolus, a 14th-century Franciscan philosopher.</note>. Nor were there lacking those knots complicated by many twists, supported not so much by tickling cleverness as by gravity. If he were the one responding, you would have seen the strength and power of Thomas, and the breadth of Albert <note>Albertus Magnus, the teacher of Thomas Aquinas.</note>. 

Truly, he had long ago sent a farewell message to these conflicts, and he had grown to loathe that duty more and more every day. He declined it so much that even when Ercole d'Este, Duke of Ferrara <margin>Ercole d'Este</margin>, and his messengers asked him most urgently—requesting that while the general synod of the preaching friars <note>The Dominicans.</note> was being held in Ferrara, he would not be reluctant to debate—he resisted complying for a long time. Finally, however, nodding to the many requests of that prince, whose love for him was not small, he yielded. From this event, it was hard to tell whether he appeared more clever or more eloquent, more learned or more kind. From the mouth of the debater there always appeared such an alacrity of spirit that he seemed to be arguing about a pleasant and gentle matter rather than something bitter and difficult. Because of this, those in the audience who hung on his every word were moved to a wonderful love for him. 

But he had a frequent proverb <margin>Proverb</margin>: that this was the task of a dialectician, not a philosopher. He also said those disputations were beneficial which were practiced with a calm mind to track and search out the truth in private places with no judges present. But he said those held in public were most harmful, being done to show off learning or to catch the breeze of the common people and the applause of the unskilled. He judged it almost impossible for the desire for honor—which drives those wandering debaters—not to be joined by an inseparable bond to a desire for the shame and confusion of the person they are debating. He called this a lethal wound to the soul and a deadly poison to charity. He decided that he would have nothing at all to do with the little traps and quibbles of the sophists and those Suisethian trifles <margin>Sophistical quibbles; Suisethian</margin> which are called "calculations" <note>original: "Suiſſeticas quilquilias... calculationes." This refers to the works of Richard Swineshead, known as "The Calculator," whose highly technical mathematical logic was popular at Oxford but dismissed by humanists like Pico as trivial.</note>. These are mathematical commentaries applied to natural questions with more subtle—not to say more cranky—inventions. Even if he were learned in them and had read such writings (which perhaps Italy does not know in full, for no path of literature could be found so trackless and inaccessible that it had not been thoroughly explored by his footstep), he nevertheless seemed to hate and detest them. In my judgment, their value...

### THE LIFE OF GIOVANNI PICO OF MIRANDOLA

...observing the common practice <note>Referring to the academic disputations mentioned on the previous page.</note>: that in debating, men aimed more at bringing infamy upon their associates and undermining their memory than at finding the truth. He judged that such a pursuit contributed little or nothing to the tireless work of discovering the truth, to which he believed his efforts should be devoted. But lest I pursue this further and delay the reader, I shall be brief. One man might shine in eloquence, yet be disgraced by ignorance of the secrets of nature. Another might know foreign languages, but remain unlearned in the universal decrees of the philosophers. One might read the discoveries of the ancients, yet fail to compose any new doctrines. Knowledge might be sought by another only for the sake of human fame and glory, rather than for the benefit of the Christian republic, or for divine and human advancement. He, however, had embraced all these things with such equal zeal that it seemed as if they had flowed into him in troops and heaps. Nor was he like many who, though not excelling in any single thing, participate in all; rather, he had so perfected himself in all sciences that if you considered any one of them in him, you would have judged that he had chosen that specific one as his own particular specialty. These things were also the more admirable because he attained them by the force of his own genius and love of truth, almost as if without a teacher. Thus, we might say of him what Epicurus said of himself: that he had been his own master <note>original: "Se sibi ipsum... fuisse magistrum." Pico was famously proud of his independent study and diverse sources.</note>. I have found that five causes converged to produce such miraculous results in so short a span of time: <margin>Five causes of such wonderful effects.</margin> an incredible intellect, a most tenacious memory, and ample resources, by which he was aided in purchasing books in our own language, as well as in Greek and the "barbarian" languages <note>original: "barbarae linguae." In the Renaissance, this term referred to languages other than Latin and Greek, specifically Hebrew, Aramaic, and Arabic, which Pico studied deeply.</note>. Indeed, I recall from memory that he spent seven thousand gold coins <margin>Seven thousand gold coins spent in procuring books.</margin> in acquiring volumes of every kind of literature up to that day; finally, there was his constant and indefatigable study, and his contempt for earthly things. Therefore, if that ancient age of the Spartans had produced this man, he would—if we believe Aristotle—have been called a divine man.

But now, I think, the virtues of the intellect must be left behind, and those noble parts of his soul which concern his actions must be followed, and his most exacting character must be brought into public view. This is so that his soul, set aflame toward God, may become known; so that his riches, bestowed upon the needy, may be praised; and so that those who are at last devoted to the divine law may be prepared with an abundant occasion to give thanks to the Author of all good things. 

Three years before he departed this life, in order that he might live in deep peace, secure from wherever the scepters of power might fall and having set aside the cares of ruling, he transferred to me all the patrimony he possessed in Mirandola and Concordia <note>The ancestral territories of the Pico family.</note>—that is, a third part of them—I know not whether by gift or by sale. This deed was later confirmed by the generosity of the Emperor Maximilian <note>original: "Maximilianus Augustus." Maximilian I, Holy Roman Emperor.</note>, who is our King and Lord, and, so to speak, our immediate master (for we have recognized no other over the many centuries since Mirandola and Concordia were built, save for those who successively sit upon the royal or imperial throne of the Romans). Whatever money he had received from this transaction, <margin>Giving to the poor.</margin> he distributed partly to the poor, and partly spent on purchasing lands from which he and his household might be sustained; specifically, he had acquired for himself farms <note>original: "corbulas," likely referring to small agricultural plots or baskets of produce-bearing land.</note> in the territory of Ferrara for many thousands of gold coins. He likewise distributed many silver vessels and pieces of precious furniture for the use of the poor. He was content with a modest table, <margin>A modest table.</margin> though it retained something of his former elegance in terms of the dishes and silver vessels. Each day, he poured out prayers to God at the appointed hours. He always gave money to the poor whenever he encountered them; and not content with that, he gave a great mandate to Girolamo Benivieni <note>A Florentine poet and close friend of Pico who shared his interest in mystical philosophy and the reforms of Savonarola.</note>—a learned citizen of Florence whom he loved dearly for his great charity and integrity of character—to always assist the needy with his own money. He also provided for the marriage of young women, and ordered that whatever money was spent should be repaid to Benivieni as quickly as possible...

### THE LIFE OF GIOVANNI PICO OF MIRANDOLA

...[he had] shaken off the burden of the whole Christian commonwealth <note>original: "totius christianae rei publicae." In the Renaissance, this referred to the collective body of Christian nations and the Church.</note> from his shoulders. It was his deep conviction that this burden—though it prepares the greatest reward for those who undergo it, provided they embrace it unwillingly and only for the sake of obedience and helping others—was not for him. For a philosopher, he believed it was not a matter of praise to have accumulated riches, nor to have sought honors, but rather to have refused them. By refusing shadowy <note>original: "umbratilem," meaning fleeting or ghost-like glory.</note> glory, he attained the true glory which always accompanies virtues like an inseparable and devoted companion. 

He held human glory as almost nothing. He used to say often that fame is of some use to the living, but of no benefit at all to the dead. We have recognized that he valued his own learning <note>original: "doctrinam"</note> only insofar as it served the utility of the Church and contributed to the elimination and banishment of contrary errors. The most benevolent mind of the high-minded king <note>Charles VIII of France, who had entered Florence in 1494</note> and the distinguished virtues of the sick man demanded it. For Pico was both very well known to him by reputation and joined to him by a certain familiarity; indeed, when Pico had visited Paris in Gaul <note>France</note>, he had been honorably received by the king. Truly, just as he showed himself a wonder to the whole world and to many ages while he lived, so too it was decreed that his death should be celebrated no less remarkably. Therefore, I think those things should be related at present which I heard with my own ears while I was in Florence—having traveled there upon hearing of his illness, though I did not arrive in time—while in the sacred temple called Santa Reparata <note>The ancient cathedral of Florence, which stood on the site of the current Duomo</note>. There I heard Girolamo Savonarola of Ferrara, of the Order of Preachers <note>The Dominicans</note>, a man most learned in theology and most distinguished in fame and holiness, delivering sacred sermons to the Florentine people.

But first, it is my counsel to admonish those ignorant of sacred letters with the words of Apuleius <note>original: "Apulei uerbis." Savonarola quotes from the prologue of Apuleius's "Metamorphoses" to warn against skepticism regarding the supernatural.</note>: <margin>The words of Apuleius cited by Brother Jerome</margin> "Lest with dull ears and an obstinate heart they think those things to be lies which seem new to the hearing, or strange to the sight, or surely difficult beyond the reach of thought; which, if they investigate a little more deeply, they will find not only clearly proven but even very easy to accomplish." He, then, declaiming from the pulpit, suggested to all present the things I am about to say: "A secret must be opened to you, O Florence, which is indeed as true as that Gospel of John so frequent among you. I would have remained silent, certainly, but I am compelled to speak; He who can command me has ordered that I make these things public.

"I think there was none among you who did not know Giovanni Pico of Mirandola. He was heaped with great benefits and great graces from God, and endowed with manifold learning; perhaps to no mortal has such a celebrated genius fallen. The Church suffered a great loss in him. I would judge that, if a longer span of life had been granted to him, he would have excelled all who have died in the last eight hundred years because of the monuments of writing he would have left behind. He was accustomed to frequent my company and reveal his secrets, from which I knew he was summoned by God to a religious life by internal voices. Desiring to obey these inspirations, he had proposed more than once to comply. 

"But, ungrateful for divine benefits, or called away by his senses, he declined the labors (for he was of a delicate temperament), or perhaps thinking that religion did not need his work, he deferred until this time—not that I speak this as a truth, but as something conjectured and presumed by me. For this reason, for two years I threatened him with a scourge <note>A prophetic warning of divine punishment</note> if he should perform the work God had set for him to do negligently. I confess I prayed to God repeatedly that, being struck a little, he might finally take up the path shown to him from on high. I did not ask for this blow by which he was struck down; I did not think this had been decreed by God to that end: that he should leave this life and lose a portion of the distinguished crown prepared for him in heaven, and that he should not fully achieve the fame and celebrity of name which he would have held at the highest peak had he lived. 

"But the most kind Judge bore himself most mercifully toward him. And because of the large and most abundant alms <margin>Alms</margin> bestowed upon the poor by his hand, and the prayers which were poured out most insistently to God, it has come to pass that his soul does not yet exult in the Father's bosom above the heavens <margin>The state of his soul</margin>, nor is it consigned to the lower regions to be tortured with perpetual torments. But, handed over to the fire of Purgatory for a time, he pays temporary penalties. I say this most willingly in this place, so that those who knew him—and especially those who were heaped with his benefits—may help him with their prayers." 

The man of God asserted these and many other things with a clear voice, adding that it was not hidden from him that preachers of the word of God who mix in lies of this sort make themselves worthy of eternal punishment. He also added that for several days these things had been known to him in their entirety. But because of the words which the sick man had affirmed the Virgin <note>The Virgin Mary</note> had spoken to him, I <note>The narrator, Gianfrancesco Pico</note> stood wavering and feared for a long time lest he had been deceived by the works of demons, since the Virgin's promise seemed frustrated by his death. <margin>Two-fold death</margin> Nevertheless, it became known to me that the deceased had been deceived by an equivocation of "death." ...to receive the multitude of men when it is expedient for these most sacred laws of divinity to be revealed. We are taught this by the same Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century theologian whose works on the "Celestial Hierarchy" of angels were deeply influential to Pico's Neoplatonism.</note> in the book *On the Celestial Hierarchy*, so that through the first things that follow, those who are ignorant might be raised up toward the most majestic light. 

Those who doubt this are undoubtedly ignorant of divine literature, and are of an insolent and stubborn nature; for in those scriptures it is granted to see that future divine mysteries are revealed not only through good men, but sometimes even through wicked men and false prophets. This fact forbids us from withholding faith from this man <note>Girolamo Savonarola</note> who is so powerful in both learning and so many virtues, and who has already predicted many future things that have now come to pass. 

Furthermore, he has testified to this not in a dreamy or uncertain way, but has affirmed it with great conviction. Add to this that the philosophy of Aristotle does not cry out against these things, and the philosophy of Plato supports them. Although I would not accept any testimony as grave unless it were by the authority of the divine scriptures, yet to cite these external sources is sometimes not absurd, so that the arrows of the malevolent may be turned back upon their authors with greater force than they arrived. 

But we must now return to ourselves. We should not mourn so much that we have lost such a man, but rather give thanks to the King for whom all things live that we had him, and still have him. For he, having finished the duty of this mortal life and having long lived among the inhabitants of Kedar <note>original: "cedar," a biblical reference to Psalm 120:5, symbolizing life in a state of earthly exile or sorrow</note>—whom he had showered with no small light—is even now entering the inaccessible and infinite light of the heavenly homeland. There, in the presence of the ineffable divinity, he shall enjoy eternal life without end, while continuing to bring us aid day by day.

**The Epitaph of Mirandola.**

Here lies John of Mirandola. The rest is known
By both the Tagus and the Ganges, and perhaps even the Antipodes.
<note>The Tagus (in Spain/Portugal) and the Ganges (in India) represent the edges of the known world, while the "Antipodes" refers to people on the opposite side of the globe. The poem suggests Pico’s intellectual fame is universal.</note>

**A song by Caecilius Cyprian, Bishop of Carthage, concerning the wood of the Cross:**
<note>This poem is traditionally attributed to St. Cyprian, a 3rd-century martyr, though modern scholars often categorize it as "Pseudo-Cyprian." it uses rich metaphorical language to describe the Cross as a cosmic tree.</note>

There is a place which we believe to be the center of the whole world; 
The Jews call it Golgotha in their ancestral tongue. 
Here I remember that wood, cut from a sterile oak and planted, 
Bore healthy fruits. 
Yet it did not provide for those who established themselves as its cultivators; 
Rather, outsiders possessed the blessed fruits of the tree. 
This form rises from a single trunk, 
And soon extends its arms into twin branches, 
Just as the yardarms of a ship stretch out the heavy, full sails, 
<note>original: "antennæ carbaſa." Early Christians frequently compared the shape of a ship's mast and yardarm to the Cross.</note>
Or like when the yokes are removed from the oxen at the plow. 
What this tree bore from the first fallen, ripe seed, 
The earth conceived; soon thereafter—wonderful to tell!—
On the third light <note>The third day, referring to the Resurrection</note>, it raised a branch again, 
Tremendous to both the earth and those above, blessed with the fruit of life. 
But for twice twenty days <note>The 40 days between the Resurrection and the Ascension</note> that branch was strengthened, 
And it grew into the immense sky, and with its topmost peak 
It touched the heavens; and at last it added its holy head to the heights. 
While yet it put forth great branches of twelve-fold weight <note>Likely a reference to the twelve Apostles</note>, 
And spreading them out, reached across the whole world, 
So that to all nations it might provide sustenance and eternal life...

# THE SEVENFOLD EXPLANATION BY GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA ON THE SEVENFOLD NARRATION OF THE SIX DAYS OF GENESIS, DEDICATED TO LORENZO DE' MEDICI. INTRODUCTION.

**M**y emulation of your studies, Lorenzo de' Medici, moved me to review the secret volumes of Moses: since last winter, in what leisure was granted from the state, I noticed you spent your effort nowhere more or more willingly than in that reading. Then a private reason also invited me: since for another work of mine, long ago begun under your patronage but now growing in your name—in which I attempted to not only defend from all suspicion and slander the Davidic hymns <note>The Psalms of David.</note> translated by the Seventy <note>original: ".LXX."; refers to the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> and constantly sounding in the church, but also to illuminate them with the torches of interpretation—no treatment is found more useful, none more fruitful than those books; none again more consistent (or to speak more truly) more necessary. It happened, moreover, during these days that I was diligent in the work of the world's creation, those celebrated works of the six days. <margin>That the mysteries of all nature are in the Genesis of Moses.</margin> Great reasons present themselves for us to believe that the secrets of all nature are contained within them. For to omit the fact that our prophet <note>Moses.</note>, full of God and with the heavenly Spirit—the master of all truth—dictating, received all these things: have not the testimonies of our own people, his own, and finally the gentiles, declared him to be most learned in human wisdom and in all teachings and letters? <margin>Most learned Moses</margin> There exists among the Hebrews a book of that Solomon, surnamed "the Most Wise," titled *Wisdom*—not the one now in hands which is the work of Philo, but another composed in Jerusalem in what they call the more secret language, <margin>Why Moses appears unrefined and popular</margin> in which that man, an interpreter of the nature of things as is believed, confesses that he received all such discipline from the inner recesses of the Mosaic law. Likewise, as far as our own authors are concerned, both Luke and Philo, most weighty authors, say he was most learned in the universal doctrine of the Egyptians. Moreover, all the Greeks who were considered more divine—Pythagoras, Plato, Empedocles, and Democritus—used the Egyptians as teachers. <margin>Mysteries: Gymnosophists, Egyptians, Pythagoras</margin> That saying of the philosopher Numenius is well-known: that Plato is nothing other than an Attic Moses <note>original: "atticū Moſem"; This implies that Plato's philosophy was essentially the wisdom of Moses expressed in the Greek (Attic) language.</note>. But even Hermippus the Pythagorean attests that Pythagoras transferred many things from the Mosaic law into his own philosophy. But if, in the meantime, Moses appears in his books as unrefined and popular rather than as a philosopher or theologian or a master of some great wisdom: let us recall to mind that it was a celebrated practice of the ancient sages to write of divine matters either not at all or in a concealed manner. <margin>Philolaus, Pythagoreans</margin> Hence they were called "mysteries," for they are not mysteries if they are not hidden; this was observed by the Indians, by the Ethiopians (who are named for their nakedness <note>A reference to the Gymnosophists, or "naked philosophers," whom ancient writers located in India or Ethiopia.</note>), and by the Egyptians. The Sphinxes placed before their temples suggested this very thing. <margin>Lysis, Hipparchus</margin> Taught by them, Pythagoras became a master of silence; nor did he commit anything to writing except for a very few things which he entrusted to his daughter Damo as he was dying. For the "Golden Verses" that are circulated are not by Pythagoras, as is commonly believed even by the more learned, but by Philolaus. Thereafter, the Pythagoreans most religiously guarded that law of secrecy. Lysis complained that it was violated by Hipparchus. <margin>Ammonius, Origen, Plotinus, Herennius, Porphyry</margin> Finally, Porphyry is the authority that the disciples of Ammonius—Origen, Plotinus, and Herennius—swore to it. Our Plato similarly hid his dogmas in a shroud of winged enigmas and fables, with mathematical images and somewhat obscure signs of receding meanings, so that he himself said in his letters that no one would openly understand his opinion on divine matters from what he wrote; and he proved it in fact to those who did not believe it. Therefore, if for this reason we think the reading of Moses is, as it were, worn out <note>original: "exculcatā"; literally "trampled," meaning commonplace or trivial.</note>, because it contains nothing in the first...

...must not condemn them with a common or unrefined judgment, lest by the same example we condemn all the ancient philosophers as unrefined and ignorant—those whom we revere as the masters of all wisdom. We see this same practice observed in the Church. Jesus Christ, the image of the substance of God, did not write the Gospel, but preached it. Moreover, he preached to the crowds in parables, but privately to a few disciples, to whom it was given to know the mysteries of the kingdom of heaven <note>original: "mysteria regni cælorum"</note> openly and without figures. Nor did he tell everything even to those few, because they were not capable of receiving everything; and there were many things they could not carry until the coming Spirit taught them all truth. If the disciples of the Lord, though few and chosen from so many thousands, could not bear many things, how could the entire Israelite crowd—the tailors, cooks, butchers, shepherds, servants, and handmaids, to all of whom the Law was given to be read—have been able to bear the burden of all Mosaic or, rather, divine wisdom? 

Moses, indeed, on the height of the mountain—certainly that mountain where the Lord also often spoke to his disciples—was illuminated by the light of the divine sun, and his whole face shone in a wondrous manner. But because the people, with their owl-like and blinking eyes, could not endure the light, he spoke his words to them with a veiled face. Let us return to our own writers. Matthew was the first to write a Gospel; and as the prophet says, "hiding the words of God in his heart" <note>A reference to Psalm 119:11.</note> so that he might not sin, he followed the history of only those things which pertained to Christ’s humanity, lest the memory of his deeds fall into oblivion. Thus, in Ezekiel’s mystical vision, we understand Matthew through the figure of the Man <note>Ezekiel's vision of the four living creatures (Man, Lion, Ox, Eagle) was traditionally mapped to the four Evangelists.</note>. 

John, who more than all others revealed the secrets of divinity, was compelled to speak things he had long kept silent in his three published Gospels <note>Pico follows a tradition that John wrote his Gospel last to supplement the "Synoptic" Gospels.</note> many years after the Lord's cross. He did this to abolish the heresy of the Ebionites <note>The Ebionites were an early sect that regarded Jesus as a human prophet but not divine.</note>, who asserted that Christ was a man and not also God; he spoke of the eternal generation of the Son, yet briefly and obscurely. He began: "In the beginning was the Word" <note>original: "In principio erat verbum"</note>. Paul denies "solid food" to the Corinthians <note>1 Corinthians 3:2.</note> because they still lived by the laws of the flesh and not the spirit; yet he speaks "wisdom among the perfect." Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A 5th-century Christian Neoplatonist whose writings were then believed to be by a direct disciple of St. Paul.</note>, a disciple of Paul, writes that it was a holy and established custom in the churches not to communicate the more secret dogmas through letters, but only by voice to those who were rightly initiated.

I have pursued these matters at length because there are many who, judging by the "rough bark" of the words, despise and scorn the book of Moses as something common and trivial. To them, nothing is less credible than that he holds something more divine in retreat than what he promises on the surface. But if this has been sufficiently refuted, it is now easy to believe that he treated nature and the craftsmanship of the entire world—that is, if in any part of his work, like a farmer, he buried the treasures of all true philosophy. This was done primarily in this part where he philosophizes most loftily about the emanation of all things from God, concerning the degree, number, and order of the parts of the world. Therefore, there was a decree of the ancient Hebrews, which Jerome <note>St. Jerome, the translator of the Vulgate Bible.</note> also mentions, that no one should touch this account of the creation of the world unless they had reached a mature age.

I shall perhaps seem, therefore, to have done something worthwhile if, having lingered longer with more exact care and more laborious study (as much as my weakness allowed), I have searched out the understanding of the Mosaic reading. In the explanation of which, although I saw that many Latins and Greeks had labored—and furthermore, almost innumerable ancient and modern Chaldean and Hebrew interpreters—I did not even dare to think of writing or commenting anything new on this matter. However, I remembered that the Mosaic law cautioned that no one should reap his field entirely and completely, but should leave an untouched portion of it for the poor and needy, who might take sheaves and handfuls from there to sustain their hunger. When this came to mind, I began to survey the vast fields of the prophet with sharp eyes, to investigate whether the most learned interpreters—who were no less cultivators of the Law than its interpreters—had, according to the legal edict, left some untouched part for us, who are weaker, to reap. From this, I too...

...or to pluck a few ears of grain to place upon the altars of the Church as the first fruits of my labor, lest I be cast out from the privileges of the temple as if I were not a true Israelite or were entirely without a contribution <note>original: "asymbolus," a Greek-derived term meaning one who does not pay their share or bring a gift to a communal feast</note>. The matter has succeeded according to my wish—not that I have achieved anything they could not, but because they, following the law's command, did not wish to pave the way for the industry of those who came after them. Furthermore, such is the vastness and fertility of this field that no number of harvests could ever be equal to it. Although infinite and most capable labors have been exerted upon it with all their strength, we can still say that Gospel phrase: "The harvest is great, but the workers are few" <note>original: "Messis multa operarii pauci," quoting Matthew 9:37</note>. 

Therefore, whatever the most holy men—Ambrose and Augustine, as well as Strabo, Bede, and Remigius, and from the <margin>Latin interpreters.</margin> more recent ones, Giles and Albert—have written upon this book; and likewise among the Greeks—Philo, Origen, Basil, <margin>Greek interpreters.</margin> Theodoret, Apollinarius, Didymus, Diodorus, Severus, Eusebius, Josephus, Gennadius, and Chrysostom—we shall leave entirely untouched. It would be both rash and superfluous for a weak man to exert himself in that part of the field where the most robust minds have already labored. Likewise, concerning those things which either Jonetes, Onkelos <note>original: "Anchelos"</note>, or the elder Simeon handed down in the Chaldean language <note>Aramaic translations and paraphrases of the Bible known as Targums</note>, or those which the Hebrews wrote—the ancients such as Eleazar, Abba, Ioannes, Neonias, <margin>Chaldean interpreters.</margin> Isaac, and Joseph; or the more recent ones like Gersonides <note>Levi ben Gershom</note>, Saadia <note>Saadia Gaon</note>, the two Abrahams <note>likely Abraham ibn Ezra and Abraham bar Hiyya</note>, the two Moseses <note>Maimonides and Nachmanides</note>, Solomon <note>Rashi</note>, and <margin>Hebrew interpreters.</margin> Menahem—we shall make no mention of them at present. 

Instead, we shall bring forward, beyond all these, seven other expositions of our own invention and meditation. In these, we shall first take care to overcome, if we can, three difficulties with which all those who have undertaken to explain this book seem to have had a great and difficult struggle. The first <margin>Seven new expositions.</margin> difficulty is to ensure that nothing said by Moses seems either insufficient or lacking in learning and wisdom. Some have freed themselves from <margin>The first difficulty.</margin> this problem by claiming that he did not speak of everything, nor did he bring forward grand and sublime things, because he was speaking to a rude and unrefined people who were not capable of understanding everything. We might believe that the unrefined listeners were satisfied if the light of knowledge—which the wise would look into—were covered with thick words like a translucent horny shell, so that duller eyes would not be dazzled by it. He would thus have brought the light to benefit healthy eyes, yet brought it enclosed and veiled so as not to harm those with weak vision. For he neither ought to, nor could, nor would have wanted to help the learned any less than the unlearned. 

The second difficulty <margin>The second difficulty.</margin> is that the tenor of the interpretation must be consistent with itself, fitting together by its own merit, and as if by a single thread the whole series should be traced back to that sense from which it first proceeded, as if remembering its purpose. We should not, perhaps, introduce him as speaking of Ideas here, only to have him deal with elements in the next clause, or wish for him to speak of man. This is an arbitrary and violent kind of exposition. Yet, to avoid this in the explanation of this book has seemed to many—I will not say impossible—but certainly difficult and laborious to everyone. So great is the complexity, the ambiguity, and the variety of the entire reading. See how much labor it is, and how not easily done, to achieve what we have conceived in our mind (may we follow through with it!): that we might interpret this entire creation of the world <margin>How difficult it is to do what he attempts.</margin> not with just one, but with a seven-fold sense, starting each time from the beginning as a new work, in the order of a continuous and unmixed exposition, using none of the works of previous interpreters. 

The third difficulty <margin>The third difficulty.</margin> consists in this: that we do not make the Prophet—or rather the Divine Spirit through the Prophet—assert anything foreign, or monstrous, or alien to the nature of things as they are now observed, nor to the truth which our own scholars have received as discovered by the best philosophers. Why, however, seven expositions are brought forward by us, by what reasoning they were undertaken, what our plan was, and what necessity drove us to them—and indeed, what is entirely new in this which we are striving to bring forth—we shall make clear in the following chapter. In which, he who has written most perfectly on this <margin>The reasoning of the commentaries.</margin> matter—that is, on the creation of the world—in imitation of nature herself...

# HEPTAPLUS

...and as I am about to write, I will attempt to paint an Idea, proving in what follows that our prophet <note>referring to Moses</note> has not fallen away from that archetype in any respect. Instead, he has attained the Moiseide <note>the essence or law of Moses</note> in all its proportions, so that nothing else should be proposed as such an Idea other than himself. Because of his greatness, we can all more easily marvel at him than estimate his worth with due dignity. These works of ours, whatever these early fruits of our youth may be, are owed to you, most illustrious Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo de' Medici (1449–1492), the "Magnificent" ruler of Florence and Pico's patron</note>, either because they are mine—and I have long since given and vowed myself to you—or because you yourself provided for us that leisure of the Fiesole retreat <note>the Medici villa at Fiesole, a center for Neo-Platonic study</note> in which they were born. This work was also seasoned by the frequent visits and constant presence of your close friend Angelo Poliziano <margin>On nature</margin> <margin>Angelo Poliziano</margin> <note>a renowned Renaissance humanist and poet</note>, whose delightful and fertile genius, which previously brought forth various flowers of literature, now, as I judge, promises a solid and mature harvest of philosophy. It is also customary, when something festive or joyful happens to those we love or revere, not only to congratulate them with words but also to favor them with some gift, so as to share, so to speak, in their happiness and to testify to the joy of our own minds. This work of ours comes to you at an opportune time, as your son Giovanni <margin>Innocent VIII</margin> <note>Giovanni de' Medici, the future Pope Leo X, who was made a cardinal at a very young age</note> has been appointed at an age reached by no one before him to the highest college of the Christian orders by the Supreme Pontiff Innocent VIII. His own natural character, which promises all good things for itself, and your merits and authority, justly and deservedly demanded this for him. It remains for us to hope that he shows himself worthy of this dignity. This he will do if he holds the same man as the exemplar of his life—that is, of prudence and all virtue—whom he has as his father and the author of his dignity. Farewell.

## ANOTHER PROEM TO THE ENTIRE WORK

[Marginal notes:]
The grades and differences of the three worlds.
The Angelic world.
The Celestial world.
The Sublunary world.

[Main text:]
Antiquity figures three worlds. The highest of all is the ultra-mundane <note>beyond the physical world</note>, which theologians call the Angelic and philosophers call the Intellectual; Plato says in the *Phaedrus* that no one has sufficiently celebrated this realm according to its dignity. Next to this is the Celestial world; the last of all is this sublunary world which we inhabit. This is the world of darkness, while that other is the world of light; the heavens are tempered from both light and darkness. This world is characterized by water, because of its flowing and unstable substance; that higher world by fire, because of the brightness of its light and the sublimity of its place. The heavens, being of a middle nature, are therefore called by the Hebrews *shamayim* <note>original: "asciamaim," a pseudo-etymology combining the Hebrew "esh" (fire) and "mayim" (water)</note>, as if composed of fire and water, as we have said. Here there is the alternation of life and death; there, perpetual life and stable operation; in the heavens, there is stability of life but an alternation of positions and operations. This world is made of the decaying substance of bodies; that higher world is of the nature of the divine mind; the heavens are constituted of bodies, but incorruptible ones—of mind, but a mind bound to a body. The third world is moved by the second; the second is ruled by the first. Furthermore, there are many differences between them, which I do not intend to recount here, where we are merely skimming over these things rather than flooding the reader with them. I should not overlook that these three worlds were most evidently figured by Moses <margin>The three worlds figured in the Tabernacle of Moses.</margin> in the construction of that admirable Tabernacle of his. For he divided the Tabernacle into three parts, each of which could not more expressly represent the individual worlds we have mentioned. The first part, defended by no roof or shade, was exposed and vulnerable to rains, snows, sun, heat, and cold; it was a most evident likeness of our world—that is, the sublunary world. It was inhabited not only by clean and unclean men, sacred and profane, but also by animals of every kind; and because of the sacrifices and constant slaughters, there was a perpetual alternation of life and death. The remaining two parts were both covered and free on all sides from any external injury, just as both the Celestial and Super-celestial worlds are capable of neither injury nor insult. Both were likewise honored with the name of holiness, yet in such a way that the one which was more secret was called the "Holy of Holies," while the other was graced only with the title of "Holy." This is because although both the Celestial and Angelic worlds are holy, since above the moon after the fall of Lucifer no evil...
