...dwellings, nor is there or can there be a sample <note>original: "specimen"</note> of it; yet the angelic dwelling is held to be far holier and more divine than the celestial. But why do we pursue these more remote similarities? For if the final part of the tabernacle was common to men and beasts; and the second, which shone entirely with the splendor of gold, was illuminated by a candelabrum distinguished by seven lamps— <margin>What the Latin, Greek, and Hebrew interpreters intend to show</margin> which, as all the Latin, Greek, and Hebrew interpreters say, signifies the seven planets—then in the third part, the most sacred of all, were the winged cherubim. Does this not bring before our eyes the three worlds? This world, which both beasts and men inhabit; the celestial world, in which the planets glitter; and the super-celestial dwelling of the angels. 

<margin>What the tearing of the veil at Christ's death signifies</margin> We are also reminded here of a deeper evangelical mystery. For since the way to the super-celestial world and the company of angels has been opened for us through the cross and blood of Christ, therefore, at his death, the veil of the temple was torn. By this, the Holy of Holies—by which we said the angelic world is signified—was separated from the other parts. This was a sign that the entrance to the kingdom of God, to God himself who "flies upon the cherubim," is now open to man—an entrance that had been closed from the beginning by the laws of justice due to the sin of our first parent <note>referring to the Fall of Adam</note>. 

<margin>Three reasons why the world is one</margin> This is enough regarding the three worlds. Among these, it must first and foremost be observed—and upon this almost our entire intention depends—that these three worlds are one world. This is not only because they all relate back to one principle and to the same end, or because they are tempered by appropriate numbers and gathered by a certain harmonic kinship of nature and an orderly series of steps; but because whatever exists in all the worlds together is also contained in each individual one. <margin>Anaxagoras</margin> There is not one among them in which all things are not present that are in the others. I believe this was the opinion of Anaxagoras <note>Anaxagoras (c. 500–428 BCE) was a Pre-Socratic philosopher who famously taught that "everything is in everything."</note>, if we consider his view correctly explained thereafter by the <margin>Pythagoreans</margin> Pythagoreans and <margin>Platonists</margin> Platonists. 

<margin>An example of the proposed truth</margin> Truly, those things that are in the lower world are also in the superior ones, but of a better quality; likewise, those things that are in the superior worlds are seen in the lowest ones, but in a degenerate condition and with an "adulterated" nature, so to speak. Among us, heat is an elementary quality; in the celestial bodies, it is a warming power; in the angelic minds, it is the Idea of heat. Let me say something more specific. Among us, there is fire, which is an element. The Sun is fire in the heavens. In the ultra-mundane region, there is the Seraphic fire of the intellect <note>Pico plays on the Hebrew root of "Seraph," which means "burning ones."</note>. But see how they differ: the elemental fire burns; the celestial fire gives life; the super-celestial fire loves. 

There is water among us; there is water in the heavens, the moon, which is the mover and mistress of this world's foyer. There are also waters above the heavens, the cherubic seats. But see the disparity of condition in the same nature: the elemental moisture overwhelms the heat of life; the celestial moisture nourishes it; the super-celestial moisture understands <note>Pico associates the Cherubim with the "waters" above the firmament, linking them to the fullness of knowledge</note>. 

<margin>The ten spheres of the intellectual world</margin> In the first world <note>the Angelic world</note>, God, the primary Unity, presides over nine orders of angels as if over so many spheres, and being himself immobile, he moves them all toward himself. <margin>The ten spheres of the celestial world</margin> In the middle world, that is, the celestial, the Empyrean heaven <note>the highest, fiery heaven</note> similarly presides like a leader over an army of nine celestial spheres; and while each of these revolves with unceasing motion, that Empyrean remains immobile, mimicking God. 

<margin>The ten spheres of the elemental world</margin> In the elemental world, after prime matter which is its foundation, there are also nine spheres of corruptible forms. <margin>Body, Nature, Soul</margin> First, there are three spheres of bodies lacking life, which are the elements and their mixtures; then, between these, those that are mixed but imperfect, such as the impressions made in the heights <note>atmospheric phenomena like meteors or clouds</note>. Next, three of a vegetative nature, which is first divided into three genera: herbs, shrubs, and trees. Finally, three of the sensitive soul: one which is imperfect, such as is found in zoophytes <note><term>zoophytes</term>: organisms like corals or sponges that were historically thought to be halfway between plants and animals.</note>; or perfect, but within the limits of irrational imagination; or finally, that which is highest among the beasts, capable even of human-like instruction, which is a middle point between man and beast, just as the zoophyte is a middle point between beast and plant. 

But of these matters, more than is necessary has been said. Let us only add that the mutual containment of the worlds is also indicated in the Sacred Scriptures. For it is written in the Psalms: "Who creates the heavens in understanding" <note>Psalm 136:5</note>, and we read that the angels of God are spirits and his ministers are a "flame of burning fire" <note>Psalm 104:4</note>. Hence, celestial titles are often given to divine things, and even earthly titles; for now through the stars...

# **HEPTAPLUS**

...now by wheels and living creatures <note>original: "per rotas & animalia"; these are references to the prophetic vision of Ezekiel</note>, now by elements they represent them; hence also celestial names are often given to earthly things. For since all these worlds are bound by the chains of concord, they exchange their names as well as their natures with mutual generosity. From this principle (if anyone perhaps has not yet noticed this) the entire discipline of allegorical interpretation has flowed. Nor could the ancient fathers have properly represented some things by other figures unless they had been taught the hidden friendships and affinities, so to speak, of all nature. Otherwise, there would be no reason why they should have represented this thing by this <margin>The fourth world</margin> image and another by that, rather than the reverse. But being experts in all things and moved by that Spirit who not only knew but made all these things, they most aptly represented the natures of one world through those things which they knew corresponded to them in the other worlds. Therefore, the same knowledge (unless the same Spirit is also present) is needed by those who wish to correctly interpret their figures and allegorical senses.

Moreover, besides the three worlds we have described <note>The Angelic, Celestial, and Sublunary worlds described on the previous page</note>, there is a fourth world in which all those things found in the others are discovered: this is man himself. <margin>How man is a microcosm</margin> For this reason, as the Catholic doctors <note>theologians</note> say, man is designated in the Gospel by the name "every creature" <note>original: "omnis creaturae"; referencing Mark 16:15</note>; for although the Gospel is to be preached to men, and not to brutes or angels, yet Christ commanded that it be preached to "every creature." It is a common saying in the schools that man is a "microcosm" <note>original: "minorem mundum," literally "smaller world"</note>, in whom are seen a body mixed from the elements, the celestial spirit, the vegetative soul of plants, the senses of brutes, reason, the <margin>That Moses treated all these worlds</margin> angelic mind, and the likeness of God. If, therefore, we establish these four worlds, it is believable that Moses, when speaking sufficiently about "the world," discussed all of them. And since a writer portrays nature—if he is as skilled in nature as we believe this man <note>Moses</note> to be—it is <margin>That this scripture is an image of nature</margin> believable that his teaching about them was arranged no differently than the Almighty Artificer-God arranged them in themselves, so that this scripture of Moses might be an expressed image of the true world. This is just as we read he was also commanded on the mountain, where he learned these things, to make all things "according to the pattern shown to him on the mountain" <note>Exodus 25:40</note>. 

First, therefore—and this is the greatest point of all—as we have <margin>The root of the exposition</margin> shown that the things in all the worlds are contained in each one, Moses, as an emulator of nature's twofold quality, should never treat one of those worlds without treating all of them at once under the same words and the same context. From this, a fourfold exposition of the entire Mosaic reading immediately arises: first, we explain whatever is written there concerning the angelic and invisible world, making no mention of the others. Second, likewise everything regarding the celestial world; then this sublunary and corruptible world; fourth, the nature of man. For if the intelligible <note>the angelic or mental world</note> is never treated without the scripture also reminding us of the other worlds—since it, like man, contains all the lower natures within itself—then we certainly can, indeed we must, interpret every part concerning all of them. 

Again, just as the natures themselves are intermingled within each other, yet have obtained distinct and proper seats and certain peculiar laws; so too, if the same series of text discusses this fourfold nature in individual parts of the present work, it must be believed that the first <margin>The root of the fifth exposition</margin> part treats the first nature specifically, and so on in the same order for the rest. From this arises the necessity of a fifth exposition. To this is added that, by the same logic that these things are distinct, <margin>The root of the sixth exposition</margin> because there is no multitude that is not one, they are bound together by a certain "discordant concord" and tied by multiform chains. Since it is likely that Moses deals with this in the whole work, it now calls us, even against our will, to a sixth interpretation. In this, we shall show that there are fifteen modes by which we can understand one thing as being related or <margin>The root of the seventh exposition</margin> joined to another. These are expressed so sufficiently and clearly by the prophet <note>Moses</note> that Aristotle never wrote anything more clearly regarding the nature of things. Finally, just as the Sabbath—that is, rest—follows the six days of Genesis:

Thus far we have undertaken to explain Moses. We have divided the entire exposition into seven books or treatises, primarily to imitate Basil <note>Saint Basil the Great, author of the *Hexameron*, a series of homilies on the six days of creation.</note> and Augustine <note>Saint Augustine of Hippo, who wrote several commentaries on Genesis.</note>, and also because the reader's attention is refreshed by this frequent division, as if taking a break. Furthermore, since there are seven expositions arranged in seven books, and each book is divided into seven chapters, all things correspond to the seven days of creation. We have also acted by a most fitting logic: just as the seventh day in Moses is the Sabbath and a day of rest, so too every one of our expositions is always directed in the seventh chapter toward Christ—who is both the end of the Law and our Sabbath, our rest, and our happiness.

## THE FIRST EXPOSITION: ON THE ELEMENTAL WORLD.
### Chapter One of the First Book.

<note>A decorative initial "N" begins the first chapter of the first book.</note> Natural Philosophers <note>The term used for scientists or thinkers who studied the physical world and its laws before the modern era.</note> who discourse on the nature of corruptible things <note>Things that are subject to change, decay, and death, such as physical objects on Earth.</note> <margin>On the principles of corruptible things</margin> establish their principles in general as follows: there is a "crude matter" <note>original: "materiam rudem"; the underlying substance of the universe before it takes a specific shape or "form."</note> devoid of forms, which is indeed capable of receiving all forms but by its own nature is deprived of all of them. <margin>Matter</margin> Therefore, besides matter, they also make "privation" <note>original: "privationem"; the absence of a particular form or quality which matter is capable of having.</note> a principle of natural things. <margin>Privation</margin> Averroes <note>A 12th-century Andalusian philosopher whose interpretations of Aristotle were highly influential in the Renaissance.</note> added that matter is extended in a three-fold dimension of length, breadth, and depth—lest, forsooth, bodily things be said to come from an incorporeal subject. By the guidance and handling of the hand, he transforms it into various shapes according to the will of the handlers.

Since nature does nothing at random, but for the sake of achieving some good, the final cause <margin>Efficient cause</margin> immediately introduces itself. Indeed, the closest end of the acting cause is the *form* which it draws from the lap of matter. <margin>The End</margin> For it acts and turns with this plan: to lead that matter toward the perfect state of form. <margin>Form</margin> Hence, Aristotle established *form* as the third principle. This form, however, cannot be drawn out from the bosom of matter <margin>Dispositions of matter</margin> unless the matter is first affected and prepared with appropriate qualities. Around these qualities, the entire labor of the craftsman and the entire delay of the action is consumed, while the specific individual form itself shines forth instantly, as if it were the reward of the labor. The Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle, named for his habit of walking while teaching.</note> call the craftsman a "cause" rather than a "principle."

But the Platonists, always mindful of divine things, <margin>Natural causes are instruments of the divine</margin> want us to be reminded that natural acting causes—even if only those that act on bodies, shape them, and change them appear to us—are by no means the primary causes of what happens, but rather instruments of the divine art which they obey and serve. Just as a builder’s hand, even if it assembles, orders, and transforms all the material of the house—the wood, stones, and mortar—and even if nothing else seems responsible for the building of the house except those hands, we nevertheless know they are an instrument <margin>Organic and Exemplary Cause</margin> obedient and serving the art established in the architect's mind. The architect, having conceived of the house as a whole, arranges it bit by bit and unfolds it into the unfeeling matter. From this, it happens that they add two further causes: the organic <note>The instrument or tool used to make something.</note> and the exemplary <note>The mental model or "blueprint" in the mind of the creator.</note>.

Nor do the Peripatetics deny this; indeed, it is confirmed among those for whom that saying is common: "Every work of nature is a work of intelligence." These are the things said in general about corruptible things <note>Things subject to change and decay in the physical world.</note>; <margin>Explanation of the words of Moses</margin> Moses included all these in the work of the first day so that the most proven philosophers have said nothing more certain or more fitting concerning them.

### Chapter Two <margin>Heaven, Earth, Stoics</margin>

In the beginning, therefore, he established two causes: the agent and the material cause—that is, the cause which is in "act" and the cause which is in "potential." He calls the former "heaven" and the latter "earth." This interpretation is supported first by the authority of the Stoics, who called the acting cause "heaven" and the material cause "earth," as Varro writes (not to mention the Greeks). 

Reason also attests to this. For matter is the most lowly of all natures, just as earth is of all elements; <margin>Peripatetics</margin> they reside in an entirely similar proportion. As the Peripatetics prove, heaven is the agent to matter and earth. But this "earth"—that is, matter—was "empty and void," as Jerome translated it, or as the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> says, "invisible and uncomposed." <margin>The earth was empty and void.</margin> All these descriptions fit raw and formless matter, which, lacking all forms, is rightly called "empty and void," and is entirely uncomposed and invisible.

However, the Hebrew words *Tohu* and *Bohu* <margin>The Hebrews: *Tohu* and *Bohu*</margin> <note>Pico transliterates the Hebrew *Tohu wa-Bohu* (Genesis 1:2) as *Tou* and *Bou*.</note> read in this passage are explained differently by many Hebrews. *Tohu* they interpret as a crude thing, stunned and astonished. This is referred to by them as the dark and deformed face of matter, for the reason that when we fix our attention on knowing it, it leaves us astonished. <margin>Aristotle, Plato</margin> Because of this, Aristotle said it is known by "analogy" <note>original: *proportione*</note> and Plato by "bastard reasoning" <note>original: *notha ratione*; matter is difficult to perceive because it has no qualities of its own.</note>. 

But many explain *Bohu* from the force of the word as the beginning and rudiment of form. <margin>The beginning of form.</margin> For if we render it word for word, *Bohu* is as if we said "in it is" <note>original: *in eo est*</note> or "through it something is." If we follow this, we will understand that besides the potential of the subject, there is a "beginning form" within it. <margin>Albert, Ancient Simeon</margin> Not only Albertus [Magnus] and many Peripatetics believed this, but also the ancient Hebrews, as we clearly gather from the writings of the most ancient Simeon <note>Likely referring to Rabbi Simeon bar Yochai, the traditional author of the Zohar.</note>.

But how this beginning is to be accepted is declared by what follows: "and darkness <margin>Darkness, Abyss</margin> was upon the face of the abyss." He calls the earth—that is, matter extended in three dimensions to the deepest depths—the "Abyss." Upon this is "darkness," meaning *privation* <note>The absence of a form that ought to be present.</note>; a principle especially famous among the Peripatetics, for which no name is more fitting than "darkness." There is, however, a privation which differs from a mere negation, as the great Albertus most constantly maintains...

You will arrange these <margin>The dispositions of matter</margin> which we call the beginning of form; a subject on which the same philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> has discoursed copiously and subtly. Furthermore, if the earth lies beneath the waters and, being irrigated from there, brings forth what it will finally bear: do not the waters in this place signify the qualities and affections <margin>Light arises</margin> happening to matter? These, by their own flux and tractable nature, bear the likeness of waters. By these, so to speak, the moistened matter <margin>By God’s command light is made</margin> brings forth the form which it brings out into the light at the final moment of time. Over these waters, the Spirit of the Lord—that is, the power of the efficient cause, the Lord’s organ and instrument—is rightly said to be moved. While the Spirit turns and acts upon these, light arises—that is, the appearance and beauty of form, which is the driver and putter-to-flight of the darkness we mentioned (that is, of privation). <note>In philosophy, "privation" is the absence of a quality or form that should naturally be present.</note> This happens by the voice of God thus commanding: because natural causes do nothing that the order of divine art has not first prescribed. <margin>One day is made from evening and morning</margin> Then one day is made from evening and morning: when, from the nature of potentiality and act, a third substance—which we call the composite—has burst forth. The reason is now manifest why, according to this sense, he called it "one day" and not "the first day"; and rightly he saw the light, because it was good. <margin>Good light</margin> For the nature of form is nothing other than a faint image and shadowy likeness of the First Good. <margin>Epilogue</margin> Thus far, we have spoken generally of corruptible substance, such as everything that exists below the moon. Here we have seen both "heaven" and "earth"—that is, the nature which transforms and that which is transformed—and the same "earth"—that is, matter—void and empty of every species of substance, and likewise of every accidental form. We saw the darkness of privation sitting over it, extended into the triple-dimensioned abyss; these darknesses were not indeed internal to it (for privation is not the essence of matter, as Aristotle proves) but occupying its outermost face. <margin>Why darkness was over the face of the abyss</margin> We likewise saw the Spirit of the Lord moved over the waters—that is, the fluid dispositions of matter, present as if to the earth—not as the principal cause, but as the Spirit of the Lord, meaning the organ of the divine art, just as our vital spirit is the organ of the mind. And immediately, as the Spirit handled those waters and pervaded the subject at the command of God the craftsman, light arose—that is, the beauty and splendor of form.

### Chapter Three.

Since we descend in the right order from common and general things to specific ones, as Aristotle proves, Moses prepares to do the same. After he spoke of those things which are common to all elemental things, he divides the entire elemental substance into three parts on the second day. <margin>What we should understand by "waters" on the second day</margin> First, however, it must be understood that all material forms are designated by him here under the name of "waters," than which no term could be more fitting. For in this sphere of things that can be generated and corrupted, matter stands like a channel or a sea, while there is a perpetual and never-ending flow and ebb of waves: the coming and going of forms. <margin>Solomon</margin> "A generation passes away," as Solomon says, "and a generation arrives, but the earth stands forever." <note>A reference to Ecclesiastes 1:4.</note> For even among the Platonists <margin>Platonists are imitators of the Hebrews</margin> (who were always imitators of Hebrew teaching), these are called "generations" rather than "forms," because they can more truly be said to be "becoming" <note>original: "fieri"</note> than "being" <note>original: "esse"</note>. For this same reason it happened that, by the name used above—namely, "waters"—he called the qualities and accidental forms of matter; and here he has called the material substances themselves by the same name. <margin>Alexander</margin> He did this to remind us—not of what Alexander <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias, a 2nd-century commentator on Aristotle.</note> believed, that qualities themselves are the substantial forms of the elements—but of what the Platonists strongly confirm: that every species which exists in matter is to be referred to the condition of an "accident" rather than that of a true "substance." For that title is legitimately claimed only by those things which stand by themselves, leaning upon themselves, and are true by reason of what they are: unmixed with foreign things and not at all adulterated. <margin>Heraclitus the Poet</margin> Heraclitus called the substance of sensible things "the sea," and among the poets...

### Chapter Six.

<margin>Pythagoreans</margin> What follows concerning the production of animals and man is now manifest. For after plants come those mixed things which feel and move: although the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of the ancient philosopher Pythagoras, who believed all life was connected by a shared vital spirit; Pico notes they even attributed a "dull sense" to plants.</note> ascribe a dull sense even to plants: which we shall discuss with the help of a longer session in that concord we are bringing forth. ### Chapter Seven.

<margin>Christ is our happiness</margin> Just as man is the absolute consummation of all inferior things: so Christ is the absolute consummation of all men. For if, as the philosophers say, from that which is most perfect in every genus all perfection is derived to the others of the same order as if from a fountain: there is no doubt to anyone that the perfection of all goodness is derived from the man Christ into all men. To him alone, surely, was the Spirit given "not by measure," so that from his fullness we might all receive. See how undoubtedly this prerogative is owed to him as God and man: which also belongs to him by a peculiar and legitimate privilege insofar as he is man.

## SECOND EXPOSITION: CONCERNING THE CELESTIAL WORLD.

### PREFACE.

<note>A decorative initial 'S' is set within a square frame adorned with floral motifs, marking the start of the new exposition.</note>

<margin>Three reasons why Moses wrote figuratively</margin> Let us rise from the elements to the sky: from corruptible to incorruptible bodies: so that it may be clear to all that by the same words through which so many things of the elemental nature were shown to us, the highest doctrines concerning the celestial things were likewise encompassed by the prophet. When we revolve this in our mind with ourselves, there will be, besides those things we said in the prefaces, another reason ready at hand for us. Why, for instance, when Moses was about to speak of the acting cause and of matter, did he not call that "agent" and this "matter" in express words, but called them "heaven" and "earth"? And the dispositions of matter: not "qualities" as the philosophers say, but "waters"? And he called the form "light" rather than "form"? Likewise comets and lightning and others of that kind he did not name by their proper names, but as "constellations" and "stars": and so with the rest. In the introductions, it was brought forward by us that the ancient custom of writing great physical and divine things was secret and figurative; furthermore, the crudeness of the listeners was such that since they could not bear the brilliance of the Mosaic teaching, it was necessary to speak to them with a veiled face: lest those who were undertaking to be illuminated should be blinded by too much light. Now we have the opportunity for a third reason: because, namely, if he had named matter and form and qualities and the acting cause, those things could indeed <margin>The marvelous artifice of Moses; the most absolute kind of writing</margin> serve the treatments of the corruptible world: but not also the rest. Therefore, it is a novel and marvelous artifice of Moses—divine truly, not human industry—to use those expressions and so to arrange his discourse, that the same words, the same context, the same series of the whole scripture may aptly suit the figuring of the secrets of all worlds and of all nature. This is that in which the book of Moses surpasses all the learning, eloquence, and genius of the nations. This is that new thing, untouched until now, which we have attempted to bring forward: namely, that we might prove by the reality itself that this was done by Moses for our people. This is the idea, this is the model of the most absolute writer: not only because this kind of writing, as we demonstrated above, portrays and emulates nature...

### Chapter One.

Whatever exists after the unit is a number, perfected and completed by unity. <margin>Unity</margin> Unity alone, being altogether simple and perfect of itself, does not go out of itself; but in indivisible and solitary simplicity, it clings to itself, because it is sufficient unto itself, lacking nothing, and full of its own riches. Number <margin>Number</margin> by its nature, since it is a multitude, becomes simple by the benefit of unity to the extent that it is capable of simplicity; however, any number, the further it is from unity, always falls into a greater multitude, and there is more dissimilarity, more parts, and more composition within it. Yet no number is so close to unity that it is not a multitude, having an accidental unity and being one not by nature, but by composition. 

<margin>From mathematics, an ascent to divine things</margin> Let us transfer these things to divine matters in the Pythagorean manner. <note>Pico uses "mathematical" or Pythagorean logic—moving from the properties of numbers to the properties of spiritual beings—as a ladder to understand God.</note> God alone, who is from no one and from whom all things are, is the simplest and most indivisible essence. Whatever He has, He has from Himself: by the same reality that He exists, He knows, He wills, He is good, and He is just. Nor can we understand any thing by which He exists other than existence itself <note>original: "ipsum esse"; a core scholastic concept that in God, essence and existence are identical.</note> which He is. Other things are not "that"—that is, existence itself—but they exist by means of it. Therefore, an angel is not unity itself; otherwise he would be God, or there would be many gods, which cannot even be conceived. For what will be one, if even unity itself is not one? 

It remains, then, that an angel is a number. But if he is a number, he is a multitude that is one in another part of himself. Every number is imperfect insofar as it is a multitude, but perfect insofar as it is one. Therefore, whatever is imperfect in an angel, let us ascribe to the angelic multitude—which he has from the fact that he is a number, that is, a creature—and whatever is perfect, let us ascribe to the approaching unity which he has from the fact that he is joined to God. 

We find a twofold imperfection in the angel: First, because he is not existence itself, but rather an essence to which existence happens by participation so that he may be. Second, because he is not intellection <note>original: "intellectio"; the act of understanding.</note> itself, but it happens to him that he understands; though he is by his nature an intellect, he is merely capable of intelligence. The second depends on the first, since that which does not exist of itself certainly does not understand of itself, since nothing can exist where existence itself is not present. Both of these, therefore, happen to the angel insofar as he is a multitude. It remains that his resolution and completion come from the unity approaching from above. But God is Unity, from whom both being and life and all perfection are derived to the angel. 

Just as there is a twofold imperfection (a kind of double multitude), so let us understand a twofold approach of unity so that both may be perfected. The first is that by which there is a raw and unformed essence, devoid of life and being; this is the formless and empty earth <margin>Formless earth</margin> <note>original: "terra inanis et vacua"; Pico is interpreting the "earth" of Genesis 1:2 as the "prime matter" or raw essence of the angelic mind.</note> which God also created. You might not believe—as some have believed—that the formation of the essence belongs to the Creator, but not its creation. At the same time He created the earth, He also created heaven—that is, the act of that essence and the participated unity in the multitude, which is existence itself. Thus, the creation of heaven and earth is, as it were, the same creation, as a pair of embraces and of two natures coming together toward the same thing with a similar bond. Nor is it discordant with the ancients that we call "existence" <note>original: "ipsum esse"</note> the participation of divinity "Heaven"; for Xenophanes <margin>Xenophanes</margin> called the archetypal world a sphere, and the Saracens <note>Pico uses "Saracens" to refer to Islamic philosophers and theologians.</note>—and even our own people—call God a circle.

**Chapter Six**

Next follows the production of a multitude of inhabitants from the elements: the fish, birds, and beasts. These philosophers believed there were indeed some primary intellectual substances, but they denied that each of them (as theologians say) presided over a numerous multitude, just as generals lead legions. Therefore, when we think of the nine angelic orders, and each order has its own leader, let us imagine in our minds that leader and prince as a vast sphere, and the following army as the inhabitants and ornament of that sphere—just as we think of fish in the water, birds in the air, beasts on the earth, and the stars in the eighth sphere. **Chapter Seven**

Finally, he mentions Man—not because Man is an angel, but because he is the end and boundary of the angelic world. Just as when Moses dealt with corruptible nature, he also introduced Man into that nature—not as a part of it, but as its principle and head. Thus, the study of Man belongs to three worlds: to the world that is his own, and to both extremes—namely, the incorporeal and the elementary. He is so placed in the middle of these that he is established as the end of one and the beginning of the other. But I see a trap prepared for our interpretation, since it is added that Man is to rule over the fish of the sea, the birds, and the beasts. For if those things signify the angelic nature to us, how will it be true what is written—that Man rules over them—when both the philosophers know and the prophet testifies that Man was made "a little lower than the angels"? May he be present with us and break this trap, he who crushed Satan under our feet: <margin>Jesus Christ, the firstborn of every creature. Dionysius, Paul.</margin> Jesus Christ, the firstborn of every creature. He surely breaks the trap and unties or severs every knot. For not only in him, in whom the fullness of divinity dwelt bodily, was human nature so sublimated that the man Christ, insofar as he is man (if we believe Dionysius), teaches, illuminates, and perfects the angels; and as Paul says, he was made so much better than the angels as he has inherited a more excellent name than they. But also all of us, to whom power was given to become sons of God through the grace of which Christ is the giver, can be raised above angelic dignity.

->HEPTAPLUS<-

->THE FOURTH EXPOSITION ON THE WORLD, THAT IS, THE HUMAN WORLD, CONCERNING THE NATURE OF MAN. PREFACE TO THE FOURTH BOOK.<-

**A**fter we have shown that the Prophet <note>Pico refers to Moses, whom he considers the author of Genesis and a profound mystical philosopher.</note> has sufficiently treated all parts of the world and all nature—celestial, angelic, and perishable—it remains (if we are mindful of our promise) to interpret the entire reading once again regarding man. We shall prove by the facts themselves that there is no discourse in this entire work which does not encompass hidden meanings and the deepest truths concerning the nature of man, just as it did regarding the three worlds discussed above. Nor shall we have performed a less worthy task if we are diligent in explaining this fourth narration than we were in the previous ones. For how useful and how necessary self-knowledge is for man—beyond even the <margin>The Delphic Letter. Plato</margin> Delphic inscription <note>original: "litteram delphicam." This refers to the famous maxim *Gnothi Seauton* ("Know Thyself") inscribed on the Temple of Apollo at Delphi.</note>—was so demonstrated by Plato in the first *Alcibiades* that he left nothing for later writers to attempt to bring forth as new on this subject. Indeed, the ambition of one who, still ignorant of himself and still not knowing whether he can know anything at all, yet boldly affects the knowledge of things so far removed from himself, is wicked and reckless. 

Let us return, therefore, to ourselves, and let us see (as the prophet says) how many good things God has done for our soul. Lest, perhaps, if one is less diligent in recognizing what is within oneself, one might hear the Father saying in the Song of Songs: *If you do not know yourself, O most beautiful among women, go out and depart, following the tracks of your flocks.* <margin>The triple punishment of self-ignorance: Above self; From self; Behind self.</margin> You see what punishment awaits our ignorance of ourselves. For we must depart: namely, from the Father—a departure followed by disinheritance, and what could be more unhappy? Likewise, we must go out: certainly, out of ourselves. For the mind that does not see itself is not at home. He who goes out of himself is torn away from himself, and what could be more bitter? Thirdly, we must go following the tracks of our flocks: that is, after the tracks of the brutes within us—of which we shall say enough in the exposition—and what could be more miserable, more despicable, or more contemptible? To become, in effect, the foot-servants of the beasts over whom nature had appointed us the leaders. Therefore, walking not after the tracks of brutes but after the tracks of Moses, let us enter into ourselves; let us enter the inner chambers of the mind, with the Prophet himself unbolting the entrance for us, so that in ourselves we may happily recognize both all the worlds and the Father and our true homeland.

->Chapter one.<-

Before we arrange the exposition more accurately according to the words and order of the Prophet, it is necessary to say something in passing about the nature of man and to explain certain terms, so that the understanding of the entire meaning may then be more fitting. Man consists of a body and a rational soul. The rational soul is called "heaven." <margin>Rational soul. Aristotle. The Platonists. Plotinus.</margin> For Aristotle calls heaven a living being moved by itself; and our soul (as the Platonists prove) is a substance moving itself. Heaven is a circle; and the soul is likewise a circle; indeed, as Plotinus writes, heaven is a circle precisely because its soul is a circle. Heaven moves in a sphere. The rational soul, transferring itself from causes to effects and returning again from effects to causes, revolves in a circle of reasoning. If these points had to be explained individually for those who have not read them elsewhere, we would no longer be interpreters of Moses, but of Aristotle and Plato. <margin>Body. Spirit. Aristotle.</margin> The body is called "earth," since it is of an earthy and heavy substance. For this reason, Moses writes that man was made from the soil (*humus*), which gave him his name (*homo*). <note>A traditional etymological connection in Latin between *homo* (man) and *humus* (earth/ground).</note> But between the earthy body and the celestial substance of the soul, a middle bond was necessary to couple such distant natures together. Assigned to this task is that thin and spiritual little body which both physicians and philosophers call the <term>spirit <note>original: "spiritum." In Renaissance physiology, the 'spirit' was a subtle vapor that mediated between the immaterial soul and the physical flesh.</note></term>. Aristotle writes that this is of a more divine nature than the elements and corresponds in proportion to the heavens. Here it is called "light," a name that could not better suit the opinion of philosophers and physicians, whose common consensus is that it is a most lucid substance and rejoices in nothing more than in light.

### HEPTAPLUS

Nor would it be absurd for us to say that from that "sea," the five senses of the body—which we recognize as hearing, sight, taste, touch, and smell—flow like five Mediterranean seas, spreading out to enter the continent of the body. <margin>Plato</margin> This was clearly the opinion expressed in Plato’s *Theaetetus* <note>The *Theaetetus* is a Platonic dialogue concerning the nature of knowledge; Pico refers to the passage where Socrates suggests that the various senses must converge in a single power of the soul, like soldiers in a wooden horse.</note>. ->### JOHN PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA<-

...therefore let us ask <note>The transcription begins mid-word, likely "Quaeremus" (Let us ask/seek).</note> whether, among the affects by which we are moved, some belong more to the body, and others to the interior sense which the philosophers call **imagination** <note>original: "phantasiam"</note>. Those that impel us either toward food or toward lust seem to me to pertain to the body. For these were given to us by God both for the protection of the body which we nourish, and for the procreation of children, in whom we might survive when we ourselves perish. We abuse these very things, however, being lured more than is proper by the enticements of pleasure: through gluttony and through lust, *making provision for the flesh*, as <margin>Paul</margin> Paul says, *in its desires* <note>Romans 13:14: "But put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, to gratify its desires."</note>. In his words, it should be noted that he did not say "do not make provision for the flesh," but rather "do not do so in its desires"; for, clearly, we must use those things for necessity, not for pleasure—and much less should our happiness be placed in them. 

We may therefore understand these affects as the **beasts of burden and wild animals**, which are called the offspring of the earth rather than of the waters; for they are both fulfilled and excited through the members of this coarser body, and were provided for us by God for its health—even if they become a means of destruction for those who waste away in gluttony or are dissolved by lust. On the other hand, let us refer those affects to the "waters"—that is, the sense of the imagination—which can be called spiritual rather than fleshly offspring, and children of our thought rather than our body. Of this kind are those things which call us to honors, to anger, to vengeance, and to other affects related to these. These are necessary and useful to those who use them in moderation. For one must be angry, but within limits; and vengeance is often a work of justice; and every man must protect his own dignity; nor should honors be refused which are obtained through honorable arts. I say this so that, because God created these "brutes" which indicate the sensory appetites and blessed them once created, we do not believe—along with the <margin>Manicheans</margin> **Manicheans** <note>The Manicheans were a dualistic sect who believed the physical world and its passions were inherently evil, created by a malevolent deity.</note>—that they are evil by their very nature and were established by an evil principle rather than by the good God. All those things are therefore good and necessary to man; but we, exceeding the limit into ambition, fury, hot-temperedness, and pride, make them evil through our own fault, though that best of Beings had established them as the best of things.

->### Chapter Six<-

Let us see, however, how exactly it agrees with what we have said that man was subsequently made by God in His own image, so that he might rule over the fish, the birds, and the beasts which both the waters and the earth had produced. We have already discussed man above, but now for the first time we understand the "image of God" within him, from which comes his dominion and command over the brutes. For man was so established by nature that reason should rule the senses, and that by its law every fury and appetite, both of anger and of lust, should be restrained. But having obscured the image of God through the stain of sin, we have begun—wretched and unhappy as we are—to serve our own internal beasts. Like the <margin>Chaldean King</margin> **Chaldean King** <note>A reference to Nebuchadnezzar (Daniel 4), who was driven from men and ate grass like an ox until he acknowledged the sovereignty of God.</note>, we live among them and lie prostrate upon the ground, greedy for earthly things, forgetful of our fatherland, forgetful of our Father, forgetful of our kingdom, and of the privilege of our former dignity given to us. *For man, when he was in honor, did not understand; but was compared to the foolish beasts and became like them* <note>Psalm 49:20 (Vulgate Psalm 48:21).</note>.

->### Chapter Seven<-

But just as all of us in the first Adam, who obeyed Satan more than God, have degenerated from man to brute, being deformed in the flesh as his sons; so in the **newest Adam**, <margin>Jesus Christ</margin> <margin>The Newest Adam</margin> **Jesus Christ**, who fulfilled the will of the Father and by his blood overcame spiritual wickedness, we—all who are his sons according to the spirit—are reformed through grace and reborn from man into the adoption of the sons of God; if only the prince of darkness and of this world finds nothing in us, just as he found nothing in Him.

->### THE FIFTH EXPOSITION CONCERNING ALL THE WORLDS SEPARATELY IN CONSEQUENTIAL ORDER. PROLOGUE TO THE FIFTH BOOK.<-

# THE SEVENFOLD WORK
<note>original: "HEPTAPLVS"</note>

...he arranged his work in such a way that, although he discussed the same things everywhere under the same outward face and the same veil of words, he nevertheless assigned particular parts of his work to individual worlds in a sequential order. To demonstrate this, we shall begin by interpreting the first small part concerning the first world—that is, the **angelic world**. Then, we shall proceed through the remaining parts regarding the other worlds, wisely observing in Moses’s words that <margin>Homer’s chain; Platonic rings</margin> **golden Homeric chain** <note>The *Aurea Catena*, a classical metaphor for the hierarchy of being that links the divine to the material world.</note> and the **Platonic rings** <note>A reference to Plato’s *Ion*, where divine inspiration is compared to a magnet passing through a series of iron rings.</note> suspended from the living power of the Craftsman, as if from the true stone of indomitable Hercules.

### Chapter One

Since we are about to speak of the **angelic nature**, which is pure intellect, let us first conceive in our minds that intellects are like certain eyes. For what the eye is among bodily things, the mind is in the spiritual realm. Although the eye possesses some light within the mixture of its own innermost substance, it nevertheless requires external light to perform the duty of vision, by which it observes the colors and differences of things. Nor is it the case that, by its nature, it is not "sight" simply because it does not see except by the benefit of light. For the ears—not to mention inanimate things—and all other parts of the body are illuminated by light, yet they do not see. Therefore, that which has obtained the nature of seeing, and is "sight" by the very logic of its essence, is that which is able to see once light is received. 

Let us consider these same things in the intellects: Intellects are the **eyes**, intelligible truth is the **light**, and the intellect itself, being something of an intelligible nature, possesses some inner light by which it can see itself; but it cannot see other things. Instead, it requires forms and "Ideas" of things, by which—as if using certain rays of invisible light—intelligible truth is perceived without doubt. Nor should it be said, as we declared by the example of the eye, that they are not "intelligent" by nature, or that they obtained their intellectual property by accident, in the same condition as our own souls. From this error flows the opinion of those who think the name "intellect" is unworthy of God. For if we understand the intellect as an eye which sees not of itself, but by participation in light—since **God is Light** <note>original: "lux .n. est ueritas," for light is truth</note> (for light is truth) and vision is the action by which the eye reaches the light—God does not need this operation, for He is Light itself. He is as far removed from the ignorance of all things as the angels are, just as the nature of light is further from darkness than the eye is. 

But let us return to the angels. The eye—that is, <margin>Angels consist of act and potency; Averroes the Arab</margin> the intellectual substance—is not entirely simple; otherwise, it would not be open to the composition of incoming light. From this comes the common teaching that **angels consist of "act" and "potency"** <note>In Scholastic philosophy, "act" is the finished reality of a thing, while "potency" is its capacity to receive or become something more.</note>—though there is an anxious dispute over what that "act" is, what that "potency" is, and what the reason for their composition might be. Likewise, there is the question of what **Averroes the Arab** <note>Averroes (Ibn Rushd), a 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were central to Medieval and Renaissance thought.</note> intended when he said that both the intellect which is in act and the one which is in potency exist in all intellects beneath God. But for our purposes here, the common opinion suffices, however it is understood.

Moses reveals all these things to us on the **First Day**. For he divides the substance of the angel into **heaven and earth**: namely, the nature of "act" and the nature of "potency." Now, just as the same thing has different properties, so it has different names. Therefore, this same "act"—insofar as it is the virtue granting sight to the eye and the completion of potency—is called **"heaven,"** because it stands in the same relationship to potency as heaven does to the earth. On the other hand, insofar as it lacks light and cannot perform its own duty of intelligence by itself, it is symbolized by **"the waters"**: a body capable of receiving light, yet by its own nature not shining at all. There is also another reason for the likeness: because this act of potency (which he calls "earth") is as closely present to the earth as water is. 

But now let us meet the words of the Prophet: **"God created heaven and earth"**—the nature of act and the nature of potency, from which He fashions the angel. And indeed, the "earth"—that is, the potency—is **"void and empty"**: void of act and empty of light, which it does not receive except through the mediation of the "waters." And because opposites happen around the same thing, and it pertains to the same thing to host both light and darkness, he added: <margin>What the abyss is</margin> **"and darkness was over the face of the abyss."** He did not say "over the earth." For the **abyss** is nothing other (unless we misuse the word) than the depth of the waters. Over these waters the Spirit of the Lord was moved; the Spirit, certainly, which...

**GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA**

The Apostle James calls God the "Father of Lights" <note>original: *pater luminum*; a reference to James 1:17.</note>, from whom the light of intelligible forms immediately arises upon those angelic minds. Perhaps the <margin>The Saracens</margin> **Saracens** <note>A common Renaissance term for Muslims or followers of Islamic philosophy.</note> also understood this when they said that the angels were led by God from darkness into light and filled with eternal joy. For a pleasure follows from this understanding, than which none is greater, none truer, and none more lasting.

->### Chapter Two<-

Closest to this angelic world is the **celestial world**. Its primary property is that it serves as the interval between both worlds—that is, the intelligible world of which we have just spoken, and this sensible world which we inhabit. Nor can we more clearly indicate the essence of any median nature <note>A "median nature" is a substance that exists between two different levels of reality, sharing qualities of both.</note> than by expressing the extremes by which it is bounded, since a median nature tempers whatever qualities come from those extremes.

He [Moses] therefore opens up the greatest knowledge to us concerning the condition of heaven when he says that the sky was placed as a medium between **"waters and waters"**—that is, between angelic and corruptible substances—placed there not so much by its physical location as by the nature of its essence. We have already said that by "waters" we should understand the **forms** <note>In Aristotelian and Platonic philosophy, "form" is the organizing principle that gives matter its specific identity.</note> which are present to potentiality (which is like the "earth") and which bring essence to perfection.

Just as there is one "earth" of angels and another "earth" of elements (because the potentiality in both is different), so too the reason for the "waters"—that is, the forms—is different in each. Between these, the sky truly holds the middle ground, possessing divine life on one side and embodiment on the other; incorruptible substance here, visible substance there; the stability of essence here, and change of location there; on one side whatever is simple and uniform, and on the other whatever is varied, mixed, and dissimilar. This was the lot assigned by the disposing providence of the **Craftsman** <note>original: *opifex*; a term for God as the creator or architect of the universe.</note>.

->### Chapter Three<-

After this, he briefly advises us concerning the integrity, position, and order of the elements through the collection of the waters into one place and the laws prescribed for the sea so that it does not overwhelm the earth. For there is nothing that more clearly indicates that there are laws instilled in the elements by an **intelligent cause**—by which they are ruled and kept in their places, beyond the mere inclination of their bodily and brute nature—than these barriers of the waters.

By these barriers the ocean is restrained, whose impulse would otherwise carry it across the entire circumference of the earth, just as the element of fire rests upon the whole of the air. Yet, as if warned by the rod of a schoolmaster <note>Pico uses the term *paedagogus* (tutor/schoolmaster) to personify the divine laws governing nature.</note>, the sea draws back its foot and does not advance further than our safety and the life of all living things requires. This can be attributed neither to the necessity of matter (which would rather incline all elements equally toward a spherical shape), nor to the fortuitous collision of atoms—<margin>Epicurus</margin> such as **Epicurus** dreams of—nor to the "seminal force" of a mute nature—as <margin>Strato</margin> **Strato** <note>Strato of Lampsacus, a Greek Peripatetic philosopher who argued for a purely naturalistic explanation of the world.</note> says—which is ignorant of any purpose.

Rather, it must be referred to the **final cause** alone, which only a mind and intellectual providence can direct. Therefore, it happened that Moses, when about to treat the order of the elements, mentioned only this matter; and the prophets so often bring this forward as the most powerful argument for divine power and wisdom. Hence in the Proverbs: "When he fortified the depths with a certain law and circle." Hence that other saying: "He who surrounded the sea with its boundary." And in <margin>Jeremiah</margin> **Jeremiah**: "'Will you not then fear me?' says the Lord, 'I who have placed the sand as a boundary for the sea.'" And that other: "You have set a boundary which they shall not pass over, nor shall they cover the earth."

Since the entire constitution of the elements is organized so that living things especially may be mixed into it, for that reason, immediately after the ordering of the earth and waters and the firmament, he added the command for the earth to sprout plants—the treatment of which work otherwise belonged more properly to the fifth day.

->### Chapter Four<-

After he dealt with the celestial and elementary spheres, and consequently with the entire integrity of the bodily universe, it remained to speak of the inhabitants and citizens (so to speak) of this worldly city. First, he must deal with the celestial inhabitants as if with the senate and the prefects of the city, and then with the terrestrial ones as if with the commoners and the people. He therefore first makes mention of the celestial beings, which God placed in the firmament to be for signs and seasons, and to shine in the sky and illuminate the earth...

...and God as the foremost and most powerful avengers, and the gravest punishers of injuries received. From this, let us estimate what penalties and what punishments await the transgressors of the divine law. These are the Oracles, who (as the Oracle said) <note>original: "δαιμονες οι φοιτωσι περι χθονα και περι ποντον ακαματοι δαμνανται υπαι μαστιγι θειοιο"</note> demons who roam about the earth and about the sea and, being unwearied, are tamed under the whip of God. That is to say, they proceed around the earth and around the sea and, being hostile, are subdued under the lash of God. Against these, the heaven, the earth, and the unshakeable justice of the whole worldly republic strike with lightning and pursue. For they are guilty of violating the universe and of wounding the divine majesty, whose image they have defiled with the foulest stain of iniquity.

Hence it happened, perhaps, that among the prophets, when any command or prohibition is promulgated by God, heaven and earth are summoned as witnesses. This is surely because the transgression of that precept also violates them; and having received a common insult, they too—while they serve as God's ministers of punishment—will take their vengeance upon the wicked. Indeed, it altogether surpasses all madness to be led to believe that anyone placed in a city and decorated with the highest honors should be allowed to offend with impunity against the prince and against the whole republic (which has deserved the best from him), and not rather be handed over immediately to be tortured and tormented by lictors <note>Lictors were Roman civil servants who attended magistrates and carried out corporal or capital punishment; here, Pico uses them as a metaphor for divine executioners.</note> and executioners, or be overwhelmed with stones by the consensus of the entire people. 

<margin>Wicked demons. Paul. Orpheus.</margin> But there are executioners, and there are lictors in this republic of God: the wicked demons, assigned to the lowest ministry as punishment for an ancient crime. Hence that saying of **Paul**: *I have delivered him to Satan for the destruction of the flesh.* <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 5:5, where Paul discusses excommunication and spiritual discipline.</note> This designation of the "avenging demon" is also found in **Orpheus** <note>Pico often cites Orpheus as a representative of "ancient theology" (prisca theologia) that prefigured Christian truths.</note>, if by chance we trust our own writers less. 

Just as all creation hates and execrates the crimes of man, so his upright life and conduct is pleasing to all and satisfies all. For everything can be admitted (so to speak) into the participation of both his good and his evil, because they are implicated and joined to him by such a tight bond. Hence that Gospel saying: *If a sinner has repented, all the angels exult with joy.* Hence the fitting reason for that mystery which was hidden from the ages: that our nature, corrupted in the first **Adam** and cast down from its state, might be restored through the cross of **Christ**. Truly, for our sake the Son of God both becomes man and is fixed to the cross. For it was fitting that He who is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation in whom all things were founded, should be coupled by an ineffable union to the one who was made in the image of God—man—who is the bond of all creation and in whom all things are concluded. Nor was it right, if all nature was endangered along with man, that its loss should be neglected or repaired through any other than Him through whom all nature had been established.

# THE SIXTH EXPOSITION ON THE KINSHIP OF THE WORLDS WITH ONE ANOTHER AND OF ALL THINGS.
## PROLOGUE TO THE SIXTH BOOK.

<margin>Vestige of the Trinity. Triple unity in things.</margin> God is a unity so distinguished by a trinity that He does not depart from the simplicity of unity. There is a manifold vestige of the divine Trinity in the creature. We shall bring forward only this one vestige here—which, as far as I know, has been brought forward by no one else: that whatever unity we see in creatures, we find distributed in a triple manner. 

First, there is that unity in things by which each thing is "one" to itself, consisting of parts that cohere together. Second, there is that unity through which one creature is united to another, and through which finally all parts of the world are one single world. 

<margin>Father, Son, Spirit. The root of all ordered charity.</margin> The third and most principal unity of all is that by which the whole universe is one with its Maker, just as an army is one with its leader. This threefold union is present in every single thing through its one simple unity derived from that One which is both the first One and the Trinity at once: from the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. For the power of the Father, producing all things, bestows His unity on all; and the wisdom of the Son, rightly disposing all things, unites and couples all things to each other; and the love of the Spirit, converting all things back to God, joins the whole work to the Maker by the bond of charity <note>In this context, "charity" (caritas) refers to the divine love that holds the universe together.</note>. 

Just as God is more inward to us—and thus more "one" with us—than we are to ourselves; and conversely, as each thing is more closely joined to itself than to other parts of the world; so having been taught the order of universal charity, if the divine law of nature...

...of the seventh day, being at leisure for divine things, we shall speak of supernatural happiness.

### Chapter One.

This supreme happiness, as we have shown, is capable of a twofold nature: angelic and human. <margin>The angelic and human nature is capable of celestial happiness.</margin> The former is called heaven, the latter earth; for angels inhabit heaven, and we inhabit the earth. And concerning heaven there is no more to be said: for he <note>Moses, the presumed author of Genesis.</note> is writing the law not for angels, but for men. Descending therefore to men, he says: *The earth was void and empty, and darkness was over the face of the abyss.* <note>Genesis 1:2. Pico interprets the creation story as an allegory for human spiritual development.</note> God does not create emptiness; He does not create darkness. But the earth (he says) *was* void and there *was* darkness. He does not say these were created, but that they *were*. Why this was said will become clear once we know what this emptiness and what these darknesses are.

Human nature—which is called "earth" when compared to the angels—was, right from the beginning because it sinned immediately, void and empty of original justice; and its "face," that is, its reason, was covered by the darkness of sin. Nor did God make these things, but rather the malice of man, who willingly deprived himself of those goods with which God had enriched him. Thus the state of corrupted nature is described by the prophet; how it was then restored to its former dignity and prepared for supreme happiness by God—through Abraham, through Moses, through the prophets, and finally through His only-begotten Son—will be shown in what follows. 

Truly, even at the time when the waters were covered with darkness—infected, that is, with the ancient filth of the original stain <note>original: "notæ originalis" — referring to original sin.</note>—nevertheless the spirit of the Lord hovered over them. This is to be understood in two ways: both that men were ruled by the light of the divine countenance which is "signed upon us" <term>signed upon us: A reference to Psalm 4:6, often interpreted by theologians as the natural light of reason implanted by God.</term>, that is, by the light of natural intelligence; and that the human race was not then destitute of the care of divine providence, but the spirit of the Lord hovered over the waters—that spirit which (as the Apostle <margin>The Apostle</margin> <note>St. Paul.</note> says) *intercedes for us with groanings that cannot be described* <note>original: "intercedit pro nobis gemitibus inenarrabilibus" — Romans 8:26.</note>—and was then constantly considering how he might purge those waters from the poisons with which the ancient serpent had infected them.

And behold, immediately he commands light to arise: and light was made. This was Abraham <margin>Abraham</margin>, that most wise first founder of the true religion. The first to fulfill the law of nature and meditate on the divine law; the first to persuade men of the worship of one God against idols and the nations. The first who attempted both to drive away the darkness of error and to declare war on the evil demons who are called the "princes of darkness"; for which reason he is deservedly named "light." Because all the disciples of the Lord did this, they were all called by the Lord the "light of the world." This is the first light which shone upon the world, and it distinguished between the religion of demons and that of the true God, as if between light and darkness.

### Chapter Two.

After this followed the Law, which is deservedly called by the name "firmament," <margin>The Mosaic Law</margin> announcing to us at its very beginning the works of God's hands (as David sang: *And the firmament announces the works of his hands* <note>Psalm 19:1.</note>). The Law, therefore, given to Moses through an angel and confirmed by the word of God, discriminated even more than the previous light between the nations and the Israelites—that is, between impiety and piety—just as the "waters above the heavens" were divided from the "waters under the heavens." 

Moreover, the Jews are called "waters above the heavens" because they alone (as Jeremiah says) <margin>Jeremiah</margin> do not fear the signs of heaven <note>original: "signa cæli" — referring to astrological omens.</note> which the nations fear; they alone acknowledge, worship, and venerate not the stars or the sky, but the Author and Lord of the stars and the sky. The nations, on the other hand, are "waters under the heavens," since they adore and worship demons, the inhabitants of the misty air (which is the region above the waters), and they make the visible sky, the stars, and the planets their gods and lords.

->**JOHN PICO OF MIRANDOLA**<-

<margin>Jewish Doctrine</margin>
Weapons against the stony heart of the Hebrews, sought from their own armories, shall now be supplied. We will prove this first by the testimonies of the Jews themselves: that the coming of Christ is signified to us through the works of the fourth day. Second, we will show that the Messiah is represented to us by no thing more fittingly than by the sun. Finally, we will gather most evidently from the logic of time that Christ is not to come in the future, but that Jesus of Nazareth, the son of the Virgin, was indeed the Messiah promised to the Hebrews. Among the decrees of the ancient Hebrew discipline <note>Pico is referring to the Kabbalistic or rabbinic tradition.</note>, it is held that the six days of Genesis designate six thousand years of the world. Thus, what is said here regarding the works of the first day is a prophecy of those things that were to happen in the first millennium of the world; likewise, the works of the second day represent the second millennium, and so on, always preserving the same order of succession in both cases. 

<margin>Moses of Gerona</margin>
To this opinion, even among the more recent authors, Moses of Gerona <note>Also known as Nachmanides (1194–1270), a leading medieval Jewish scholar.</note>—a theologian of the highest celebrity among the Hebrews—bears witness. Saint Jerome also mentions this in his exposition of the Psalm inscribed to Moses <note>Psalm 90:4.</note>; indeed, this opinion seems to rest primarily on the foundation that "a thousand 
<margin>Saint Jerome</margin>
years are as one day in the sight of God," as the Prophet says. Therefore, if this doctrine is true, the fourth day 
<margin>A day of God is a thousand years</margin>
is a prophecy of those things which were to occur in the fourth millennium of the world. Come now, let us show according to the annals of the Hebrews and the very computation they approve, that Jesus appeared in the fourth millennium of the world. 

<margin>The time when Jesus appeared according to the annals of the Hebrews.</margin>
They calculate 1,556 years from Adam to the Flood; and 292 years from the Flood to Abraham. Thus, from Adam to Abraham, 1,848 years are collected. From the birth of Isaac to the destruction of the Second Temple (which occurred after the death of Christ), they count approximately 1,660 years—I do not cut this to the quick <note>Meaning he is using rounded or generally accepted figures rather than debating exact months.</note>. For they calculate 430 years from Isaac to the Departure from Egypt; nearly the same number from the Departure to the Temple built by Solomon; 410 years from Solomon to the destruction of the Temple by the Babylonians; and 420 years from the restoration of the Temple under Ezra to this final captivity under Titus. Therefore, if you collect all these together, you will calculate 3,508 years from the beginning of the world to Christ according to the very mind of the Hebrews. Thus, Christ arrived in the very middle of the fourth millennium, and within the boundaries of that same millennium—as if within the limits of the fourth day—the light of the Moon (that is, the Church) shone upon the whole world. Furthermore, an innumerable multitude of martyrs, apostles, and teachers, who all flourished within five hundred years after the death of Christ, illuminated the obscurity of the firmament (that is, the Old Law) and the shadows of our night.

But the Hebrews will say: "Suppose Jesus did arrive during these times. You still do not have proof that Jesus was the Christ unless you show that it was believed by our ancestors that Christ would come during that period." The matter stands well; they demand a fair thing, and we can easily provide what they justly require. For the Oracles of Elijah are maintained among them as manifest, common, and public knowledge. 
<margin>The Oracles of Elijah of the Talmudists</margin>
Without any figure or veil, they state expressly that the Messiah would come in the fourth millennium of the world. Lest these seem to be either invented by me or interpreted at my own whim, I shall bring forth the testimony of the Talmudists themselves, with whom we have this controversy. They make mention of these oracles and, compelled by the truth itself, they confess that the time predicted by Elijah for the coming of the Messiah has already passed. These are the words found in the section titled *Avodah Zarah* <note>The Talmudic tractate regarding "Idolatry."</note> in the chapter *Lifne Eidehen* <note>Original: "capite librẽ edeem," referring to the first chapter of Avodah Zarah.</note>: *Tanna debe Eliyahu: sheshet alaphim shanah havei ha-olam. Shene alaphim tohu; u-shene alaphim Torah; u-shene alaphim yemot ha-Mashiach; u-ba-avonoteinu she-rabu yatsu me-hen mah she-yatsu.* <note>Pico provides a Latin transliteration of the Hebrew text from the Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 97a and Avodah Zarah 9a.</note> Let us translate this into English, rendering it word for word: 

"The disciples of Elijah said: The world is to last six thousand years. Two thousand years of emptiness; two thousand years of the Law; two thousand years of the days of the Messiah. But because of our sins, which are many, there have passed from them those [years] which have passed." 

These are their words. Now, with these very words placed before the eyes of all, since I can no longer bring forth anything invented or arbitrary...

<meta>Pico continues his argument from the previous page, moving from the general concept of the six-millennia world-cycle to a specific "oracle" or prophecy attributed to Elijah. ### HEPTAPLUS

Let us examine and weigh the words of the oracle, and we shall immediately grasp our proposition. "The world," it says, "shall endure for six thousand years." We might interpret this to mean that after the cycles of six thousand years—as many of our own Christian writers have also believed—the consummation of the world will occur like a future Sabbath. Or, if we take the truer view that "no one knows 그날 [that day]," <note>A reference to Matthew 24:36.</note> let us understand it in this sense: that there is no prophecy in the Law concerning any time beyond that. But this does not pertain to the current question. Let us see what follows.

<margin>Hebrew interpreters</margin>
"Two thousand years void; two thousand years of the Law; then two thousand years of the Messiah." <note>This is the "Oracle of the House of Elijah," a famous chronological tradition found in the Babylonian Talmud (Sanhedrin 97a).</note> It calls the time "void" (as all Hebrew interpreters say) because it was the era before any law was given by God to men. But I see the Jew mocking and saying: "If there are two thousand years before the Law and two thousand of the Law, then the Messiah was not meant to come on the fourth day—that is, while the fourth millennium was passing—but rather on the fifth day, because he comes *after* the fourth millennium."

But the response is easy, provided by the spirited truth. For what is said by Elijah—"two thousand void, two thousand Law"—must not be understood as if the world would be without law for a full span of two thousand years, and similarly that the Law would remain for exactly two thousand years. Rather, it means that the era of the law of nature <note>The "void" period before the written Mosaic Law.</note> would reach into the second millennium, and the era of the Law would reach into the fourth. But before the second millennium was finished, the Law arrived; and before the fourth passes away, the Messiah shall be. 

I do not fashion this exposition for myself, nor did I see it in a dream. <margin>Elijah and the Talmudists</margin> Elijah himself teaches it to me, and the Talmudists <note>The compilers and scholars of the Talmud, the central text of Rabbinic Judaism.</note> themselves teach it. This shall soon be manifest to you, O Jewish asp <note>original: "Iudæa aspis." Pico uses the common (though harsh) medieval rhetorical trope of comparing those who reject his argument to the "deaf adder" of Psalm 58.</note>—unless you stop up your ears. 

Elijah says: "Two thousand void, and two thousand Law." Let us see in what sense the statement about the "void" was true; from that, let us learn the method of explaining what is said about the Law. 

<margin>How the beginning of the Law should be understood.</margin>
We must take the beginning of the Law either from Moses or from Abraham. It cannot be taken from Moses, for then the "void" would have lasted more than two thousand and three hundred years, or thereabouts—for there are almost that many years from Adam to Moses. Therefore, the beginning of the Law must be dated from Abraham, to whom the covenant of circumcision was given, which is the root and foundation of the entire ancient Law. From Adam to Abraham, however, if they consult their own histories, they find that a full span of two thousand years had not elapsed, but only one thousand eight hundred and forty-eight. Thus it happens that not *after* the second millennium, but *within* its boundaries, the fullness of the Law succeeded the "void." 

By the same reasoning, not *after* the fourth millennium, but while the fourth was passing, the evangelical fullness ought to succeed the "void" of the Law. If they shamelessly and obstinately persist in denying this, <margin>Talmudists</margin> let them hear their own Talmudists, who strongly reinforce our opinion. For they themselves confess that even then, when they were writing, the time predicted by Elijah for the coming of the Messiah had already passed; and they attribute this delay to their own sins. 

For if the words of Elijah were understood to mean that Christ was to come only *after* the fourth millennium, and not *within* the limits of that fourth, the Talmudists would neither have said, nor could they have said, that the time promised by the prophets for the Messiah had already passed. This is because at the time the Talmudic doctrine which we cited was written, four thousand years had not yet flowed from the beginning of the world. 

For Jesus appeared (as we showed above) three thousand five hundred and eight years after the beginning of the world, according to the Hebrew reckoning. <margin>The Jerusalem Talmud</margin> Moreover, the Jerusalem Talmud (as they themselves report) was written in the three-hundredth year after the death of Christ; and the Babylonian Talmud <margin>The Babylonian Talmud</margin> in the hundredth year after the Jerusalem one. Therefore, both were composed within the boundaries of the fourth millennium; and yet they both confess and lament that the time spoken of by Elijah regarding the coming Christ had passed. 

Where will they hide themselves here, or what lurking-places will they seek, so that they might utterly flee from or fail to see this Sun of ours, which shines throughout the universe despite their will? The Talmudists confess (even if they do not believe the ancients) that the times predicted by the prophets for the coming of Christ have passed. They confess that it was believed by the prophets that He would come during those very times in which we maintain Jesus arrived. Nor are their own teachers entirely untruthful when they say the Messiah did not come because of their sins. For indeed, He did not come *to them*, who did not recognize Him. Nor is the Messiah—that is, the redeemer and avenger of the most wretched captivity...
