### HEPTAPLUS

...namely, the fruits of vegetables and herbs. After the sun and the waters—with a fertility even greater than that of the earth—two kinds of living creatures were brought forth: birds and fish. The earth, no longer content with trees and shrubs, also produced great cattle and beasts of burden. 

Do you not see, even if I remain silent, <margin>Simeon</margin> that the word of the good Simeon has been fulfilled: that our Sun [Christ] should be a "light for the revelation of the nations and the glory of your people Israel"? <note>original: "lumen ad reuelationem gentium & gloriam plebis tuæ israel." This is the Nunc Dimittis from Luke 2:32, spoken by Simeon upon seeing the infant Jesus.</note> Do we not have before our very eyes—if we interpret it in no other way—both the calling of the nations and the transformation of the earthly Jerusalem and the shadowy Synagogue into the true Church and the eternal, heavenly city of God? 

Before the rising of the sun, the waters produce nothing. The earth produces something, but it is thin and meager. For before the coming of Christ, among the nations, there was no example of [true] life and no fruit of true religion. <margin>The Israelites worshipped the true religion</margin> Among the Israelites, there was indeed some hope of life, and they knew the way of light in part and worshipped the true religion, but it was in its beginning and imperfect until he should come who is the Way, the Truth, and the Life. <note>Pico identifies the "earth" before the Sun as the Hebrew people, who had some spiritual growth (plants), and the "waters" as the Gentiles, who remained barren until Christ's arrival.</note> 

And unless we return to this mystery, let someone bring me a reason why Moses divided the ornament and offspring of the earth in such a way that it brought forth some things before the sun and others after the sun. Why also do the waters produce nothing before the sun, while the earth produces something? Why are two kinds of living creatures produced from the waters, and only one kind from the earth? Why is the bird, an aerial animal, assigned to the waters? 

For (to address the first point), it is not enough to say, as some have said, that herbs and plants were brought out from the earth before the creation of the sun so that they would not appear to be created by its power. For by that same logic, it would have been much more necessary for the fish, the birds, and all the ornaments of the elements to be made before the sun, so that they would not be believed to have been made by its power. Moses would therefore have left behind a suspicion: even if the light of the sun were not needed to produce plants, as they are less perfect, it might still have been needed to produce animals, which are more perfect. For it follows that if the more perfect things had come into the light without its help, the less perfect things could also have been made without it. But the logic does not work in reverse: if the lowlier things were made without it—like plants, the most humble kind of living thing—it does not follow that the entire nature of animals of every kind could have been produced without its labor intervening. 

Therefore, the intention of the author is more truly investigated from the perspective we have stated. Likewise, if anyone says that animals "related to the waters" are simply those that dwell in the waters, he will see that one kind rather than two should have been referred to them, while two kinds should have been referred to the earth, because the home of birds is the earth rather than the water. And beyond all controversy, if we consider the nature of the animal, a bird is either a terrestrial or an aerial animal; <margin>The most profound reasons</margin> it is in no way aquatic. 

But hear the most profound reasons of all, which pull us, even against our will, toward the mysteries of Christ and the Church. And indeed, if all things (as <margin>Aristotle</margin> Aristotle says) harmonize with the truth, then all things must harmonize most of all with Christ, who is the Truth itself. <note>Pico references a common Aristotelian principle: "With a true view, all the data harmonize" (Nicomachean Ethics I.8).</note> He did not say to the Hebrews so often without cause or for no reason: "Search the scriptures, for it is they that bear witness to me," <note>John 5:39</note> asserting that so many things—indeed all things—in the Law, the Psalms, and the Prophets were predicted about himself. But we are often blind in the face of such great light, and we cannot consider the wonders of his Law unless he reveals them to our eyes.

Let us come, with his help, to the revelation of mysteries and figures. Two animals are produced from the waters, and one from the earth, because there was a greater fullness of believers from the Gentiles than from the Jews. However, even if the earth [the Jews] produces fewer things, it produces animals that are more perfect than those the waters [the Gentiles] produce: namely, cattle and all quadrupeds. Because even if more from the ethnic nations believed than from the Hebrews, those from the Hebrews were more perfect: from them came the Apostles, the founders of the whole religion. Likewise, the water produces two different kinds and a double nature...

### GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

This is because among the Gentiles, some are transferred to Christ from the service of demons, while others are moved from the law of nature. Every Hebrew is only a Hebrew, because he was not permitted to live within the boundaries of nature; to him was given the Law of God, which was peculiar to him and not shared with the other nations. For "He has not done so for any other nation, and his judgments he has not made manifest to them." <note>original: "Neq; enim fecit taliter omni nationi & iudicia ſua nō manifeſtauit eis." A quotation from Psalm 147:20.</note>

The fish, therefore, signify to us those who came to us from the worship of demons. This is not only because the waters (as we showed above) symbolize the impiety of the nations, but because the sacred scriptures often attest that wicked demons are signified by these animals that live in the waters, as **Jonathan the Chaldean** <margin>Jonathan the Chaldean</margin> <note>Pico is referring to *Targum Jonathan*, an ancient Aramaic translation and commentary on the Hebrew Bible. He frequently cites Jewish mystical and scholarly sources to support his Christian allegories.</note> confirms.

The birds signify those who have been moved from the institutions of nature to grace. The clear reason for this comes from what we wrote abundantly in the preface of this book concerning natural and supernatural happiness. We showed there that the sky is the clearest image of supernatural happiness, while natural happiness is a secondary and imaginary kind, rather than true happiness. Therefore, those who pursue this natural happiness by following the laws of nature are most fittingly denoted by birds—inhabitants not of the first and true sky, but of the air, which claims the name of "sky" for itself in a secondary and imaginary sense. This is why they are so frequently called "fowls of the sky" and "birds of the heaven" in the divine scriptures. 

Observe, however, with what deep wisdom it was arranged that birds should be referred to the water rather than the air. For those who lived according to nature were still considered part of the "peoples" <note>In Latin, *gentium* refers to the Gentiles or nations outside of Israel.</note> and the crowd. Indeed, they called themselves "nations" and lived among the nations—such as, perhaps, Socrates and many of the philosophers. For this reason, both types of converts were referred back to the waters in common. 

It is easy to show how well this exposition fits with evangelical and apostolic doctrine. The apostles who were converted from the Hebrews are figured by **Paul** <margin>Paul</margin> as terrestrial animals (oxen), and by our doctors in the **Gospel** <margin>Gospel</margin> commentary on the scene where the sellers are cast out of the temple. Moreover, **Christ** <margin>Christ</margin> calls the Israelites "sheep." But the apostles, to whom the conversion of the nations was commanded, were called "fishers" by the Lord. Their leader was Peter, who, in Rome—the mistress of nations—was destined to be a fisherman of the ocean, as it were, and of all other fish. Christ, however, who said he was not sent except to the sheep who had perished from the house of Israel, claimed for himself the name of "shepherd" rather than "fisherman."

### Chapter Six.

From this, the solution to the question that has long tormented the interpreters of this book becomes clear: Why was it not said on the second day, "and God saw that it was good"? <margin>Why it was not said on the second day "that it was good"</margin> If we say, as is usually said, that it was because the work of the waters was not completed on that day—but rather on the third, when the waters under the heaven flowed together into one place—this does not seem to fully satisfy the question. For the proper work of the second day is not the arrangement of the waters, but the arrangement of the firmament, which was fixed in the middle place between the waters. 

On that day, there was both the making of the firmament (when God said, "let there be a firmament") and the distinction of the waters (when he said, "and let it divide the waters from the waters"), which was quite complete. The collection of the waters called "the sea," the revelation of the dry land, and the production of plants belong entirely to the logic of a different work; thus, they were finished on another day, the third, to which they belonged. 

Therefore, we must seek the reason in a deeper mystery. The firmament (as we showed above) symbolizes the Law. Just as the firmament was unformed and not simply perfect until it was furnished with the sun, moon, and stars, so too the Law was not—as the **Manicheans** <margin>Manicheans</margin> <note>An ancient dualist sect that believed the material world was evil and that the Old Testament God/Law was inferior or malevolent. Pico rejects their view, arguing the Law was merely "incomplete" rather than "bad."</note> say—bad, but it was also not "simply good," which is to say, perfect, until...

### Chapter Seven.

<margin>What the power of baptism effects</margin>
Now, since the supreme benefit of the Word made flesh was that through the sacrament of baptism—by which the power of Christ is poured into us—we might be reborn as the children of God, born not of blood but of God; Moses finally indicates this to us when, after the sun has risen and been shown to the world, and after the fertility of the waters and the earth, he creates man in the image of God. This is not an earthly man, but a heavenly one. For after the Gentiles and Jews had turned to Christ, this one thing remained: that through the most holy washing, conforming themselves to the cross of the Lord, they might be reformed into the image of God. For if baptism makes us children of God, and the Son is the image of the Father, is it not the power of the entire Trinity working in baptism that says, "Let us make man in our image"? <note>original: "Faciamus hominem ad imaginem nostrā." If we are children, we are also heirs: "heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ." <note>A quotation from Romans 8:17.</note> But who are the children? It was written by **Paul** <margin>Paul</margin> that we cry out "Abba, Father" in the Holy Spirit. Those, therefore, who live by the Spirit, these are the children of God; these are the brothers of Christ; these are destined for the eternal inheritance, which they shall happily possess as the reward of both their faith and their well-spent lives in the heavenly Jerusalem.

->### EXPOSITION OF THE FIRST WORD, THAT IS, "IN THE BEGINNING"<-

# GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

...the words they form, which we read, display nothing but what is common and trivial. This arrangement of letters forms the "shell" <note>original: "corticem." For we cannot *learn* teachings and doctrines there; we can only *recognize* them.

I was pleased <margin>Pactolus</margin> to take a risk with the first word of the work, which among the Hebrews is *Bereshit* <note>original: "Bresit."</note> and among us is read as "In the beginning." Could I also, using the rules of the ancients, bring to light something from it worthy of knowledge? 

Therefore, beyond my hope and beyond my expectation, I found—what I myself did not believe even as I found it, and what others could not easily believe—the entire account of the creation of the world <margin>In the first</margin> and of all things revealed and explained in that single word. <margin>word</margin> I say a thing that is wondrous, unheard of, and incredible. But you will soon believe it if you pay attention, and the matter itself will prove me true. <margin>the entire</margin> That word among the Hebrews is written in this way: <margin>account of the</margin>

->[Hebrew: בראשית]<- <margin>whole world</margin>

From this word, therefore:
1. If we join the third letter to the first, it makes the word *Ab* <note>Father.</note>. <margin>to be</margin>
2. If we add the second letter to the first doubled, it makes *Bebar* <note>In the Son / Through the Son.</note>. <margin>contained</margin>
3. If we read all the letters except the first, it makes *Reshit* <note>Beginning.</note>. 
4. If we connect the fourth letter to the first and the last, it makes *Sciabat* <note>Sabbath / He rested.</note>. 
5. If we set the first three in the order they lie, it makes *Bara* <note>He created.</note>. 
6. If the first is omitted, the three following make *Rosc* <note>Head.</note>. 
7. If the first and second are omitted, the two following make *Es* <note>Fire.</note>. 
8. If the first three are omitted and we couple the fourth to the last, it makes *Seth* <note>Foundation.</note>. 
9. Conversely, if the second is joined to the first, it makes *Rab* <note>Great.</note>. 
10. If after the third we place the fifth and then the fourth, it makes *Hisc* <note>Man.</note>. 
11. If we join the first two to the last two, it makes *Berith* <note>Covenant.</note>. 
12. If we join the last to the first, it makes the final and twelfth word, which is *Thob* <note>Good.</note>—by changing the letter *thau* into *thet*, which is a most frequent occurrence among the Hebrews. 

Let us see, however, what these first signify in English <note>original: "latine" (Latin).</note>; then, what mysteries concerning the whole of nature are revealed through them to those not ignorant of philosophy. 
*   **Ab** signifies "Father." 
*   **Bebar** means "in the Son" and "through the Son" (for the preposition *Beth* signifies both). 
*   **Reshit** means "Beginning." 
*   **Sabath** means "Rest" and "End." 
*   **Bara** means "He created." 
*   **Ros** means "Head." 
*   **Es** means "Fire." 
*   **Seth** means "Foundation." 
*   **Rab** means "of the Great." 
*   **Hisc** means "of Man." 
*   **Berit** means "with a Covenant." 
*   **Tob** means "in/with Good." 

And if we weave the whole speech together in the following order, it will be of this sort: **"The Father, in the Son and through the Son, the beginning and the end (or rest), created the head, the fire, and the foundation of the great man with a good covenant."**

<summary>Pico demonstrates a Kabbalistic technique of rearranging the letters of the Bible's first word, "Bereshit," to extract twelve distinct words. He argues that this single word contains a hidden summary of the entire creation and the relationship between the Father, Son, and the structure of the universe.</summary>

# GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

...to see the good: this entire discourse leaps forth from the breakdown and recomposition of that first word <note>Pico refers to the Hebrew word *Bereshit* ("In the beginning"), the first word of Genesis. By rearranging its letters, he derives various Hebrew sentences that he then translates into the Latin/English arguments following.</note>. How deep and full of every doctrine its sense is cannot be obvious to everyone. But so that some things may be immediately open to all—though not everything—let us see what is signified by these words. It is known to all Christians what it means that the Father created in the Son and through the Son. Also, what it means that the Son is the beginning and the end of all: For he is the Alpha and Omega <note>original: "alpha & ω"</note> (as John writes <margin>John</margin>) and he called himself the "beginning": and we have demonstrated that he is the end of all things, so that they might be restored to their beginning. 

Other things are a little more obscure: what those words mean, namely "head of fire" and the "foundation of the great man"; what that "covenant" is and by what reasoning it is called "good." For it is not immediately obvious to everyone that the whole account of the four worlds <note>Pico’s system describes four levels of existence: the Intellectual (Angelic), the Celestial (Planetary), the Sublunary (Earthly/Corruptible), and the Human (the fourth world that unites the others).</note> of which we have treated is explained here: likewise their kinship and happiness, about which we most recently disputed. 

First, therefore, it must be noted that the world is called a "Great Man" by Moses. For if man is a "small world" <term>microcosm|The concept that the human being is a miniature map or reflection of the entire universe.</term>, then certainly the world is a "Great Man" <term>macrocosm|The universe viewed as a massive living organism or structure that mirrors human anatomy.</term>. Taking this opportunity, he most aptly figures the three worlds—the intellectual, the celestial, and the corruptible—through the three parts of man; simultaneously indicating by this figure that not only are all the worlds contained in man, but also briefly declaring <margin>Which part of man corresponds to which world</margin> which part of man corresponds to which world. 

Let us think, therefore, of three parts in man: the highest is the head; then that which extends from the neck to the navel; and the third, which extends from the navel to the feet. For these are also separated and distinguished in the human figure by a certain variety. But it is wonderful how beautifully and precisely, through an exact reasoning, they correspond in proportion to the three parts of the world. In the head is the brain, the source of knowledge <margin>Knowledge, Motion, Generation</margin>. In the chest is the heart, the source of life’s motion and heat. In the lower part are the genital members, the principle of generation. 

Likewise in the world, the highest part—which is the angelic or intellectual world—is the source of knowledge, because that nature was made for understanding. The middle part—which is the heavens—is the principle of life, motion, and heat, in which the sun rules like the heart in the chest. Below the moon is that which is known to all...

# Giovanni Pico della Mirandola’s Prayer to God. <margin>9</margin>

Gracious God, who must be revered in the highest majesty,
Who truly holds one divinity in a threefold power;
Whom, above the flaming walls <note>original: "flammantia mœnia." This is a classical allusion to Lucretius, here adapted to describe the boundary between the physical universe and the divine realm.</note> of the high world,
The blessed throng of the angelic choir serves;
Whose omnipotent right hand once created
This immense work, visible to our eyes;
You who turn the heavens, who guide the world with a nod,
By whose command the sent lightnings fall:
Spare, I pray, the wretched; wash away our filth, I pray,
Lest the just punishment of Your fury drive us headlong.
But if our debts were weighed on an equal scale,
And if the standard of Your judgment were severe,
Who could bear the horrendous scourge of the living
Avenger? And who could endure His heavy blows?
The very Machine of the World <note>original: "Machina." In Renaissance philosophy, the "Machine of the World" refers to the entire structured cosmos, functioning as a complex, divinely-ordered system.</note> would not withstand Your angry right hand—
That Machine not destined to perish until the final day.
What mind is not condemned from the origin of the first fault <note>A reference to Original Sin.</note>?
Or which has not been made guilty by its own crime?
Or surely You are He whose nature it is always to spare,
And who holds justice with equal mercy:
You who repay rewards far greater than our merits,
Just as You repay punishments lighter than the evils committed.
For Your mercy is greater than our faults,
And to give to those who are unworthy is a thing more worthy of God.
And He makes them worthy, if He deigns to love them—
He who makes worthy those whom He found unworthy.
Therefore, pitying us, I pray, look upon Your own with a peaceful face,
Whether You prefer us to be Your servants or, rather, the accused.
Truly the accused, if You look upon the crimes of our life—
The work of crimes from an all-too-ungrateful mind.
But if instead You see Your gifts in us—
Gifts ennobled by the most excellent blessings—
We are those whom Nature once made Your servants,
And whom Holy Grace soon made Your children.
But (alas!) the weight of such a fate oppresses the wretched:
Those whom Grace made children, Sin has made defendants.
Sin made them guilty, but let Grace conquer Sin,
So that Your honor may increase through our crime:
For whether Your wisdom or Your power might otherwise
Be able to reveal its wealth to the world,
A greater glory of Your goodness shines in our errors,
And that love shines out, to be loved above all things.

<summary>This page contains a Latin elegiac poem by Pico della Mirandola pleading for divine mercy. He argues that while human sin is great, God’s glory and grace are best demonstrated by forgiving the unworthy and transforming "servants" into "children."</summary>

<meta>This page concludes Giovanni Pico della Mirandola's "Prayer of Entreaty to God" and transitions into a formal dedication letter by Roberto Salviati. The prayer concludes with a plea for divine intimacy, moving from the terror of judgment described on the previous page to the hope of seeing God as a Father rather than a stern Master.</meta>

Who could bring down the Lord from high heaven,
And lift the limbs of the highest God onto a cross:
So that the blood and water from Your side <note>A reference to the Gospel of John 19:34, where blood and water flow from the side of the crucified Christ, symbolizing the sacraments of the Eucharist and Baptism.</note>
Might wash away the filth evilly contracted from our father’s seed. <note>original: "patrio de semine." Referring to the inheritance of Original Sin from Adam.</note>
Thus Your love and piety, O most gentle King,
Provides the material for such great goods to overcome our evils. <note>This echoes the theological concept of "O Felix Culpa" (O Happy Fault), suggesting that human sin allowed for the even greater glory of God's redemptive love.</note>
O love, O piety, so well-provided for our affairs!
O goodness, made the servant of Your own servant!
O love, O piety, poorly understood in our age;
O goodness, now nearly conquered by our own wickedness:
Grant, I pray, to this great love—which always preserves us—
That a matching fervor may exist within our hearts.
Grant that I may cast off the yoke and lay down the empire
Of Satan, whom I repent having served for so many years.
Grant, I pray, that the fires of a mad mind be extinguished,
And let Your love live within our breast:
So that when the spirit, having fulfilled the duty of mortal life,
Shall be led before its Lord,
Having gained the happy lot of the promised kingdom,
It may feel You to be not a Master, but a Father.

THE END.

### Roberto Salviati to Lorenzo de' Medici, Greetings.

Since I was born with such a character, most illustrious Lorenzo, and so fashioned by nature that nothing is more important to me than to love, cherish, and venerate those who are either excellent in talent or singular in learning: I could not help but love your friend Pico della Mirandola above all others and admire a man truly most worthy of all admiration. 

Since he recently dedicated to you a book on the sevenfold explanation of the six days of Genesis <note>This refers to the *Heptaplus*, the primary work contained in this volume.</note>—the first fruits of his studies—a work most excellent not only in my judgment but in the judgment of all, I wished to take pains so that it might be published in a corrected edition at my own expense. I did this doubting not that I would at once satisfy both my love for him and the public benefit of scholars. Added to this was my hope that I would do something not unpleasing to you if those physical and divine mysteries which he communicated to you privately were, through my efforts, finally made common to all people. Farewell.

# THE APOLOGY OF MIRANDOLA

**G**IOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA TO LORENZO DE' MEDICI:
I have dedicated my Apology <note>In the classical sense, an "Apology" is a formal defense of one's positions, not an expression of regret.</note> to you, Lorenzo de' Medici, not because I consider it a work (God is my witness) truly worthy of so great a man, but because it is yours by right, just as I realize I have long owed you everything I am. May you be most fully persuaded of this: that whatever I am or shall be in the future, it is yours, Lorenzo, and shall remain yours hereafter. I say less than I would wish, and these words are all too cold to sufficiently express what I feel—that is, with what love, what loyalty, and what respect I follow you, and have followed you for many years. I am moved by the many kindnesses you have shown me, which clearly testify to your most affectionate spirit, as well as by those rare and singular virtues of yours—not so much of fortune as of the mind—which your own modesty does not permit me to recount at present. I return to the Apology: I ask that you receive it with a cheerful countenance. It is indeed a small gift, but certainly no light testimony of my loyalty and respect toward you for all time. If it should happen that you touch upon this work while between the great affairs with which you are always occupied, remember that this was a hurried work rather than a polished one, and that the subject matter had to be chosen according to the judgment of others rather than my own. <note>Pico is referring to the fact that he was forced to write this defense because his "900 Theses" had been attacked by a papal commission.</note> I have not addressed it to you so that you might recognize in me some excellence of talent or learning—which I do not possess—but so that you may know (for I shall say it again) that whatever I am, I am most devoted to your greatness.

### THE APOLOGY OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA, COUNT OF CONCORDIA.

**W**hen I recently arrived in Rome to kiss the feet of the Supreme Pontiff Innocent VIII <margin>Innocent VIII, Supreme Pontiff.</margin>—whose name is most deservedly earned from the innocence of his life—and following my custom of never ceasing from my studies, I wished to do something worthy of the city of Rome, pleasing to a Christian Prince, and useful both to myself and to scholars. I therefore proposed nine hundred questions <note>Known as the *900 Theses*, these covered everything from logic and physics to magic and the Hebrew Kabbalah. Pico intended to pay for the travel of any scholar who wished to come to Rome to debate him.</note> concerning divine and natural matters, which I intended to answer in a public assembly of the most learned men. Hardly had these questions appeared in public when a manifold crowd of detractors arose among those who, even if they did not approve of my talent or learning, should have at least respected my zeal for the liberal arts. One could see various distastes, upturned noses, censures, and judgments from every side—as always happens when we attempt something new and unconventional. There were five principal flowers of criticism <note>original: "flores isti" — a sarcastic reference to the "blooms" of their arguments.</note> which different people cast against me.

Some, indeed, carped at philosophy and letters altogether, so that they might appear to be "wise-enoughs" <note>original: "scioli" — pseudo-intellectuals or those with a smattering of knowledge.</note>. Sometimes they added that Adam was cast out of paradise because he wished to make himself equal to the gods through the knowledge of good and evil; they argued that those who wish to know more than is proper should be banished from the court of Christ by a similar example. Others did not disapprove so much of philosophy itself as this specific style of disputing and the institution of publicly debating letters, barking <note>original: "oblatrantes"</note> that such displays were intended for the ostentation of talent and doctrine rather than the acquisition of erudition. <margin>The age of the author.</margin> Several called me bold and rash because, at my current age—having just reached my twenty-fourth year—I did not hesitate to propose a disputation in the most celebrated city, in the most ample assembly of learned men, regarding the highest points of philosophy, the sublime mysteries of Christian theology, and unknown disciplines. Many accused me of being superfluous and ambitious, and of acting beyond my strength, not so much because I was in Rome or because I was a youth, but because of the sheer number—that is, that I was going to dispute nine hundred questions. Among those who profess the study of wisdom—that is, theology—there were some who, perhaps not content with lighter insults, no longer called me merely bold or rash or boastful, but a magician, an impious man, and a new [heretic] in the Church of Christ...

    *   *Marginal note: Ruffin9* - Rufinus.
    *   *Scribit autē & ſapientiſſime Ruffinus eſſe quidē glorioſum Chriſti exēplo patiēter iniurias tolerare. At unā notā hæreſeos qui ferat uel diſſimulet nō eē chriſtianū* - Rufinus writes most wisely that it is indeed glorious to endure injuries patiently following the example of Christ; but he who bears or ignores the single mark of heresy is not a Christian.
    *   *Marginal note: Hieronymus* - Jerome.
    *   *& Hieronymus noſter quāta maxima pōt aī cōtētiōne clariffima exclamat uoce. Nolo in ſuſpitione hæreſeos quēq̄ eſſe patiētē.* - And our Jerome, with as much mental effort as possible, cries out with a most clear voice: "I do not wish anyone to be patient under suspicion of heresy."
    *   *Tacere ergo me nō uult Hieronymus & inuitū ocioſūq̄ hoīem pro ſua qua pōt auctoritate ad ſcribendū trahit & īpellit.* - Jerome, therefore, does not wish me to be silent, and he draws and impels me, an unwilling and idle man, toward writing by his great authority.
    *   *Quare ſi qui ſunt qui forte me tacere uellent: ſciāt ſibi nō mecū ſed cū Hieronymo eſſe cōtrouerſiā qui me tacere nō uult.* - Wherefore, if there are any who perhaps wish me to remain silent, let them know that their controversy is not with me, but with Jerome, who does not wish me to be silent.
    *   *Hieronymo nō audire quis pōt ſine flagitio?* - Who can fail to listen to Jerome without disgrace?
    *   *ipſo ergo ſuadēte imo cogente etiā breuē aggreſſus ſum aſcribere apologiā: nō ut quēq̄ lacerem uel accuſem: ſed ut a maximo quod mihi iniuria obiciē īpietatis crimine iure me excuſem.* - Therefore, at his persuasion, or rather his compulsion, I have undertaken to write even a brief apology; not so that I may tear apart or accuse anyone, but that I may justly excuse myself from the greatest crime of impiety which is unjustly cast upon me.
    *   *hoc quæſo patiātur obtrectatores mei eo animo quo ego iniquā illorū offenſam paſſus ſum ſemper.* - I ask that my detractors endure this with the same spirit with which I have always endured their unfair offense.
    *   *Patiant̄ inq̄ ut qui chriſtianus de chriſtianis ſum parētibus natus: qui uexillum Chriſti Ieſu in fronte gero: q̄ pro chriſti fide ēt obeā lubēs quaſi cū paulo hoc ipſis æquo aīo audiētibus exclamen uoce.* - Let them endure it, I say, as one who is a Christian born of Christian parents, who carries the banner of Christ Jesus on my forehead, and who would even gladly die for the faith of Christ, and like Paul, let me cry out with a voice while they listen with a calm mind.
    *   *Marginal note: Paulus* - Paul.
    *   *Nō magus nō iudæus ſum: nō yſmaelita nō hæreticus. ſed Ieſum colo & Ieſu crucē in corpe meo porto: per quē mihi mundus crucifixus eſt & ego mundo.* - I am no magician, no Jew, no Ishmaelite, no heretic. But I worship Jesus, and I carry the cross of Jesus in my body, through whom the world is crucified to me and I to the world.
    *   *Deniq̄ cū & ſanctitatis & ſapiē & id genus egregios titulos nec mihi arrogē nec illis derogē hunc unū mihi ipſi pro quo tuēdo etiā ſanguinē ultro effundā: quæſo nō demāt ut ſ. me poſſim dicere chriſtianū.* - Finally, while I neither claim for myself nor take away from them those distinguished titles of sanctity and wisdom and the like, I ask that they do not take away this one title for which I would even willingly shed my blood: namely, that I may call myself a Christian.
    *   *Quod ſi cōcedunt hæc eis nō ſcribo a quibus iam īpetraui quod tota noſtra cōtēdit apologia.* - If they concede this, I do not write for them, from whom I have already obtained what our entire apology strives for.
    *   *Aliis ſcribo qui eē me aut fuiſſe aliqn̄ hæreticū credūt uel ſuſpicant̄.* - I write for others who believe or suspect that I am or have been at some time a heretic.
    *   *Quāq̄ aut̄ principale propoſitū ē hoc ut ōndamus ab ortodoxo & catholico tramite nō me ſed illos deuiare qui me hæreticū calūniant̄: tn̄ poſtq̄ ſcribendū eſt: dicemus & aliqd de his quæ primo nobis obiecta ſunt: ne meo ſilentio quaſi culpa conſcia abuti poſſint n̄ri obtrectatores.* - However, although the principal purpose is this: to show that not I, but those who slander me as a heretic, deviate from the orthodox and catholic path; nevertheless, since I must write, we shall also say something about those things which were first charged against us, lest our detractors be able to misuse my silence as if it were a conscious guilt.

# APOLOGY

...proclaimed as a heresiarch <note>original: "hæreſiarchā". A term for the founder or leader of a heretical sect.</note>. I was (God is my witness) long in doubt as to whether I should refute these accusations or rather pass them over in silence. Two things especially moved me to keep silent: First, because I, abhorring contention and quarrels, have always loved peace of mind and the tranquility of that most quiet life which my studies provided me. Nor do I hate any task of writing more than one which is based on dispute and bitter altercation of any kind; for I have never considered it the part of a good man, nor of a philosopher, to return an injury or insult any more than to inflict one. The second reason was this very thing: that I was content with the judgment of the Supreme Pontiff <note>Pope Innocent VIII, who had initially suspended the debate on the Theses.</note> (whose memory I must always worthily celebrate) and with the judgment of many from the most holy apostolic senate <note>The College of Cardinals.</note>, whose kindness and most benevolent spirit toward me I can nor should ever forget. I seemed able easily to neglect the hatred and the insults of wicked men; and indeed, as far as other matters are concerned, I was of the opinion that I should consider them unworthy of a response at any time. But in this one charge of heresy brought against me, I feared that if I did not refute it, I would seem to acknowledge the crime through my silence.

<margin>Rufinus</margin> Moreover, Rufinus <note>Rufinus of Aquileia (c. 340–410 AD), a monk and historian known for his translations of Greek Church Fathers into Latin.</note> writes most wisely that it is indeed glorious to endure injuries patiently following the example of Christ; but he who bears or ignores the single mark of heresy is not a Christian.

<margin>Jerome</margin> And our Jerome <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the Church Father famous for translating the Bible into the Vulgate Latin.</note>, with as much mental effort as possible, cries out with a most clear voice: "I do not wish anyone to be patient under suspicion of heresy." Jerome, therefore, does not wish me to be silent, and he draws and impels me—an unwilling and idle man—toward writing by his great authority. Wherefore, if there are any who perhaps wish me to remain silent, let them know that their controversy is not with me, but with Jerome, who does not wish me to be silent. Who can fail to listen to Jerome without disgrace?

Therefore, at his persuasion, or rather his compulsion, I have undertaken to write even a brief apology; not so that I may tear apart or accuse anyone, but that I may justly excuse myself from the greatest crime of impiety which is unjustly cast upon me. I ask that my detractors endure this with the same spirit with which I have always endured their unfair offense. Let them endure it, I say, as one who is a Christian born of Christian parents, who carries the banner of Christ Jesus on my forehead, and who would even gladly die for the faith of Christ. Like Paul, let me cry out with a voice while they listen with a calm mind.

<margin>Paul</margin> "I am no magician, no Jew, no Ishmaelite <note>Used here historically to mean an outsider or non-believer.</note>, no heretic. But I worship Jesus, and I carry the cross of Jesus in my body, through whom the world is crucified to me and I to the world." <note>A paraphrase of Galatians 6:14-17.</note> Finally, while I neither claim for myself nor take away from them those distinguished titles of sanctity and wisdom and the like, I ask that they do not take away this one title for which I would even willingly shed my blood: namely, that I may call myself a Christian.

If they concede this, I do not write for them, from whom I have already obtained what our entire apology strives for. I write for others who believe or suspect that I am or have been at some time a heretic. However, although the principal purpose is this: to show that not I, but those who slander me as a heretic, deviate from the orthodox and catholic path; nevertheless, since I must write, we shall also say something about those things which were first charged against us, lest our detractors be able to misuse my silence as if it were a conscious guilt.

Moreover, many at first considered this philosophizing of mine to be a fault. To whom I shall answer nothing in this place, because it is my intention to plead the cause of philosophy separately in a special work. And entirely, if it is shameful to devote oneself to letters and to cultivate the fine arts and disciplines, I prefer to acknowledge this fault rather than to plead against it. Also to those who detest this manner of disputing and this practice of publicly debating about God, nature, and morals: I shall not say much, since this crime—if it is a crime—is common to me and to great men, indeed to the most esteemed philosophers of not only our age but almost all ages. To whom it was most certain that nothing was more helpful to them for attaining the knowledge of the truth they sought than to be in the habit of disputing...

<meta>Pico continues his defense, moving from general justification of his public debate to answering specific criticisms regarding his age and the unprecedented number of his theses (900). He argues that intellectual struggle is a form of training that benefits even the loser.</meta>

->GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA<-

...most frequent in exercise. For just as through gymnastics <margin>Gymnastics makes the strengths of the body firmer.</margin> the strengths of the body become firmer, so in this, as if it were a literary wrestling-ring, the strengths of the mind emerge far stronger and more vigorous. Nor would I believe that either the poets, by the celebrated arms of Pallas <note>original: "decantata Palladis arma." Pallas refers to Athena, the goddess of both wisdom and strategic war.</note>, or the Hebrews, when they say that iron is the symbol of the wise, meant anything else to us than that these most honorable kinds of contests are exceedingly necessary for obtaining wisdom.

Hence it happens perhaps that even the Chaldeans <margin>Chaldeans</margin> <note>The Chaldeans were ancient inhabitants of Mesopotamia famous for their developments in astronomy and astrology.</note> in the birth-chart of one who is to be a philosopher require that Mars should look upon Mercury in a <term>trine aspect</term> <note>An astrological term describing planets positioned 120 degrees apart, a placement thought to create a harmonious flow of energy. Here, Mars (war) energizes Mercury (intellect).</note>; as if to say that if you take away these meetings, these wars, all philosophy would be drowsy and sleepy. 

But as pertains to these things, as I said, I prefer to defend myself by the authorities and precedents of great men rather than by reasons. It is a matter of greater effort, however, to satisfy those who say that in age, genius, and learning I am unequal to so great a task; and that, according to Horace <margin>Horace</margin>, I have not consulted my shoulders as to what they can bear and what they refuse <note>A reference to Horace's *Ars Poetica*, advising writers to choose subjects suited to their abilities.</note>. Truly, here the mode of defense is difficult for me: if I say I am equal, I seem to incur the mark of an immodest man who thinks too much of himself; if I confess I am unequal, I seem to be marked as rash and ill-advised. I have fallen into heavy straits, since I cannot without fault promise of myself what I cannot also without fault fail to provide.

And indeed I could cite that passage of Job <margin>Job</margin> <note>Job 32:8: "But it is the spirit in a person... that gives them understanding."</note> that the spirit is in all people, and perhaps hear with Timothy <margin>Timothy</margin>: "Let no one despise your youth" <note>1 Timothy 4:12.</note>. But I shall say this more truly from my own conscience: there is nothing in us that is great or singular. I do not deny that I am perhaps studious and desirous of the <term>good arts</term> <note>The "liberal arts," the traditional curriculum of a humanist education.</note>. Yet I neither claim nor arrogate to myself the name of a learned man. For as my friend Hermolaus <margin>Hermolaus</margin> <note>Hermolao Barbaro (1454–1493), a famous Venetian scholar and close friend of Pico.</note> once wrote—that delight of the Roman tongue, the splendor and glory of our age—he cannot but be unlearned who believes himself learned. 

Therefore, the reason I placed so great a burden on my shoulders was not because I was unaware of my weakness, but because I knew that this kind of battle—that is, literary ones—is unique in that in them, there is profit in being defeated. Thus it happens that even the weakest man can and should, by right, not only not refuse these contests but seek them out. For he who yields receives a benefit from the victor, not an injury; since through him, he returns home wealthier—that is, more learned—and better equipped for future battles. 

Animated by this hope, I, a weak soldier, have not feared at all to engage in such a heavy battle with the strongest and most strenuous of all. Whether this was done rashly or not, someone could judge more rightly from the outcome of the battle than from my age.

It remains for me to answer those who are offended by the numerous multitude of proposed topics, as if this burden sat upon their shoulders, and not rather that this labor, however great it is, had to be drained by me alone. It is certainly unseemly and overly peevish to wish to set a limit on another's industry, and, as Cicero <margin>Cicero</margin> says, to desire moderation in a matter which is the better the greater it is. In such grand undertakings, it was entirely necessary for me either to succumb or to satisfy. If I were to satisfy, I do not see why what is laudable to perform in ten questions should be considered blameworthy to have performed in nine hundred. If I were to succumb, those who hate me would have reason to accuse me; those who love me would have reason to excuse me. For in so grave and great a matter, that a young man with slender genius and small learning should fail was more worthy of pardon than of accusation; since, according to the poet: "if strength fails, the daring will certainly be praised, and in great things, to have willed is enough" <note>Propertius, *Elegies* 2.10.6.</note>. 

And if in our age many, imitating Gorgias of Leontini <margin>Gorgias of Leontini</margin> <note>A Greek Sophist famous for claiming he could speak on any subject given to him.</note>, have been accustomed—not without praise—to propose a disputation not only on nine hundred, but on all questions of all arts, why should I not be allowed, at least without blame, to dispute about many things, which are nevertheless certain and determined? 

But they say this is superfluous and ambitious. I, however, contend that this was done by me not only in a way that is not superfluous, but is necessary—which they themselves, if they consider my method of philosophizing, must plainly and even unwillingly confess. For those who have devoted themselves to any one of the families of philosophers—namely, favoring Thomas <margin>Thomas</margin> or Scotus <margin>Scotus</margin> <note>Thomas Aquinas and Duns Scotus, the leaders of the two dominant and often competing schools of medieval scholastic thought.</note>, who are now most often in people's hands—they can indeed make a trial of their learning even in the discussion of a few questions. But I have so established myself that...

# DEFENSE

Sworn to the words of no single master <note>original: "in nullius uerba iuratus." A famous quote from the Roman poet Horace, signaling Pico’s intellectual independence and refusal to follow a single philosophical sect.</note>, I have poured myself out through all the masters of philosophy, examined every scrap of writing, and recognized all the "families" <note>Referring to the various schools of thought, such as the Peripatetics, Stoics, or Platonists.</note> of thought. Therefore, since I had to speak about all of them—lest, by defending only a private dogma and neglecting the rest, I should seem biased—it was necessary that even if I proposed only a few things from each school, there would be many items when taken all together. Nor should anyone condemn me for the fact that "wherever the storm carries me, I am brought as a guest" <note>original: "quocunq; ferar tēpeſtas deferar hoſpes." Another allusion to Horace (*Epistles* 1.1.15), describing a mind that is not anchored to one sect but wanders where truth leads.</note>.

For it was always observed by all the ancients that, in unrolling every kind of writing, they would pass over no commentaries they could find unread. This was especially true of Aristotle, who for that reason was called the *anagnostes* <note>original: "αναγνωστης." A Greek term meaning "The Reader."</note>—that is, "The Reader"—by Plato. And truly, it is a mark of a narrow mind to have confined oneself within a single Portico <note>The "Stoa" or "Porch" where the Stoic philosophers taught.</note> or Academy <note>The school founded by Plato.</note>. Nor can one rightly choose a path for oneself from all of them, if one has not first become intimately familiar with them all...

<summary>Pico defends his syncretic approach to philosophy, arguing that a true scholar should not be restricted to one school but must study all traditions, citing Aristotle's reputation as a tireless reader as a precedent.</summary>

# GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

Just as a husband hates sterility in his wife, surely the divine mind, joined and associated with the soul, will hate an unfruitful soul all the more, insofar as a far nobler offspring is desired from that union. Therefore, I was not content to have added—beyond the common doctrines—many things from the ancient theology <note>original: "priſca theologia." This refers to the Renaissance belief in a single, true theology that threads through all ancient religions and was given by God to humanity in the distant past.</note> of Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "Mercurii trimegiſti." A legendary Hellenistic figure believed to be an ancient Egyptian prophet and author of the *Hermetica*, which Pico and his contemporaries valued as a source of divine wisdom.</note>; many things from the teachings of the Chaldeans <note>original: "Chaldæoꝝ." Referring to the *Chaldean Oracles*, a set of mystical texts Pico believed contained the wisdom of ancient Babylonian magi.</note> and of Pythagoras; and many things from the more secret mysteries of the Hebrews <note>original: "hebræoꝝ." This refers to the Kabbalah, the Jewish mystical tradition which Pico was among the first Christian scholars to study and integrate into Western philosophy.</note>. I have also proposed many things discovered and meditated upon by us regarding natural and divine matters to be debated.

<margin>The harmony of Plato</margin> We have proposed, first, a harmony between Plato and Aristotle, <margin>and Aristotle</margin> believed in by many before this time, but sufficiently proven by no one. <margin>conciliated.</margin> Boethius <note>Boethius (c. 477–524 AD) was a Roman philosopher who famously attempted to translate and reconcile the works of Plato and Aristotle to show their underlying agreement, but he was executed before he could complete the project.</note> among the Latins promised that he would do this, but he is never found to have accomplished what he always wished to do. # JOHN PICO OF MIRANDOLA

There are many who, just as dogs always bark at strangers, so they themselves often condemn and hate those things they do not understand. I come now to those things which I have brought forth, unearthed from the ancient mysteries of the Hebrews, to confirm the holy and Catholic faith. Lest these things perhaps be thought—by those to whom they are unknown—to be invented trifles or the fables of charlatans, I want everyone to understand what they are and of what sort, from where they are sought, by which and how famous the authors who confirm them, and how recondite, how divine, and how necessary they are for our people to defend religion against the persistent slanders of the Hebrews.

<margin>Esdras</margin> Not only the famous doctors of the Hebrews, but also from among our own, Esdras <note>Ezra the Scribe, a key figure in the return from the Babylonian exile and the reorganization of Jewish life and law.</note>, Hilary <note>Saint Hilary of Poitiers (c. 310–367), a leading Latin theologian.</note>, and Origen <note>Origen of Alexandria (c. 184–253), a prolific early Christian scholar and theologian.</note> write that Moses, on the mountain, received from God not only the Law, which he left for posterity inscribed in five books, but also a more secret and true explanation of that Law. 

<margin>Hilarius</margin> 

<margin>Origenes</margin> Moreover, it was commanded him by God that he should indeed make the Law public for the people, but that he should neither commit the interpretation of the Law to writing nor broadcast it. Instead, he himself should reveal it only to Joshua, the son of Nun <note>original: "Iesu naue." In the Latin Vulgate, Joshua is often called Jesus, and "Nave" is the Greek-derived form of Nun.</note>, and then Joshua to the others succeeding him as leaders of the priests, under a religious obligation of great silence. And rightly so. For it was enough for the common people to recognize through the simple history now the power of God, now His wrath against the wicked, His mercy toward the good, and His justice toward all; and through divine and salvific precepts, to be instructed in living well and blessedly and in the worship of true religion.

But to make public to the common people the more secret mysteries and the hidden secrets of the highest divinity, lurking under the rough shell of the Law and the pretext of words—what else would that be than "to give that which is holy to dogs and to scatter pearls among swine"? <note>A reference to the Gospel of Matthew 7:6.</note> Therefore, it was not by human counsel but by divine command that these things were kept hidden from the common folk to be shared with the perfect—among whom alone, Paul says, he speaks wisdom. <note>Referencing 1 Corinthians 2:6.</note>

The ancient philosophers also observed this custom most sacredly. 

<margin>Pythagoras</margin> 

<margin>Dama</margin> Pythagoras wrote nothing except a few small things which, when dying, he entrusted to his daughter Dama. <note>Dama was a Pythagorean philosopher; tradition says her father entrusted his secret writings to her with orders never to share them with those outside the circle.</note> 

<margin>Plato</margin> The Sphinxes carved on the temples of the Egyptians warned of this: that mystic dogmas should be kept inviolate from the profane multitude by means of the knots of enigmas. Plato, writing to Dion concerning the highest substances, said: "It must be spoken in enigmas, lest by chance, if the letter should come into the hands of others, what we write to you might be understood by them." 

<margin>Aristotle</margin> Aristotle used to say that his books on "First Philosophy," <note>original: "libros primæ philosophiæ." This refers to Aristotle's *Metaphysics*.</note> in which he treats divine matters, were both published and not published. What more? 

<margin>Jesus Christ</margin> 

<margin>Origen</margin> Origen asserts that Jesus Christ, the Master of Life, revealed many things to his disciples which they were unwilling to write down, lest they should become common to the crowd. 

<margin>Dionysius</margin> This is most strongly confirmed by Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A first-century judge converted by St. Paul, though the writings attributed to him (the *Corpus Areopagiticum*) are now known to date from the late 5th century. He was a central authority for Renaissance Neoplatonists.</note>, who says that the more secret mysteries were poured from soul to soul—that is, from mind to mind <note>original: "idest ex animo in animū." Pico adds this gloss to clarify Dionysius.</note>—without letters, through the medium of the spoken word.

In this very same way, when that true interpretation of the Law, divinely handed to Moses, was revealed by God’s command, it was called **Cabala** <note>original: "Cabala." Now usually spelled Kabbalah, from the Hebrew *Qabbalah*, meaning "reception."</note>, which is the same among the Hebrews as "reception" among us. 

<margin>Cabala</margin> This is because that doctrine was received by one from another as if by a hereditary right, not through literary monuments, but through regular successions of revelations.

<margin>Cyrus</margin> 

<margin>Zerubbabel</margin> However, after the Hebrews were restored from the Babylonian captivity by Cyrus, and after the Temple was restored under Zerubbabel, they applied their minds to the restoration of the Law. 

<margin>Esdras</margin> Esdras, then the leader of the Church, after the book of Moses had been corrected, clearly recognized that because of the exiles, slaughters, flights, and captivity of the Israelite people, the custom established by their ancestors of handing down the doctrine by hand could not be preserved. He saw that the secrets of celestial doctrine, divinely granted to him, would perish; for without the intervention of commentaries, their memory could not long endure. He decided that, having called together those wise men who then survived, each one should bring into the open what he held in his memory concerning the mysteries of the Law. With scribes employed, they compiled seventy volumes—for there were roughly that many wise men in the Sanhedrin <note>original: "sinedrio." The supreme council or court of the ancient Israelites.</note>...

<summary>Pico argues that Moses received a secret oral tradition (Kabbalah) alongside the written Law, intended only for the wise. He traces this practice of concealing sacred truth through Pythagoras, Plato, and early Christianity, concluding that Esdras eventually recorded these secrets to prevent their loss during the Jewish exile.</summary>

...a certain and determined manner of Christ’s descent. Whence there was not lacking a certain doctor <note>Pico often refers to "doctors" of the Church, meaning established theological authorities like Thomas Aquinas or Duns Scotus.</note>—whose condemnation on this article I have never read—to whom it seemed probable and defensible alongside the truth of the article that the soul of Christ was not presentially <note>original: "præsentialiter." This refers to being physically or substantially present in a location rather than just acting upon it from afar.</note> in hell. <margin>Franciscus</margin> All the authorities which both Franciscus <note>Franciscus de Mayronis (c. 1280–1328), a prominent Franciscan theologian and student of Duns Scotus.</note> brings forward in the fourth book [of the *Sentences*] and other theologians in the third, might seem to someone to be explainable as a descent through effect rather than through real presence—even by following the manner of explaining scripture used by those very doctors who hold the opposite view. For it is read in the twenty-fourth chapter of Ecclesiasticus: *I will penetrate all the lower parts of the earth.* <margin>Thomas</margin> Thomas [Aquinas], in the third part of the *Summa*, says this must be understood through effect; <note>original: "per effectum." This means Christ's power was felt in the lower parts of the earth, even if he was not personally there.</note> therefore, by a similar reasoning, someone might perhaps be able to explain the authorities who say that He "penetrated" into limbo <term>Limbo: In Catholic theology, the place where the souls of the righteous who died before Christ's resurrection waited.</term> or into the bosom of Abraham. <note>original: "sinum Abraæ." A biblical term for the place of rest for the sanctified dead before the opening of Heaven.</note> For to "penetrate" is the same as to enter deeply and within, which is even more than merely to "descend." Wherefore, if it is said that He not only entered but even entered deeply and within the lower parts of the earth—not because He was really present there, but only because He was there through effect—then it could also be said that He was in the bosom of Abraham, and entered the bosom of Abraham, through effect only and not through real presence.

However, I do not say these things because I have ever believed that Christ, while existing presentially elsewhere, is said to have been in hell only because He performed some work there—just as a king residing in his palace is said to be in another place in his province where he effectively performs something by the authority of his power and his command. For that was never my opinion, as will soon be clear in the declaration of my view. Rather, I firmly hold and have held, and have always said both publicly and privately, that if the soul of Christ was anywhere during those three days [between his death and resurrection], it was in hell, and that it was truly present there. But I wished to say these things for a fuller examination of this matter, <margin>Augustine, Epiphanius, Philastrius</margin> so that we might see verified that saying of Augustine in his book *On Heresies*: that nothing is more difficult than to define what is heretical or not heretical. Whence he says it happened that when two very famous writers, Epiphanius and Philastrius, wrote about heresies, they disagreed greatly in numbering them, for no other reason than because what seemed heretical to one did not seem so to the other.

But now I come to manifest my opinion on the manner of Christ’s descent and to perfectly declare my conclusion: first, setting forth its meaning in summary; second, explaining and proving it more broadly. <margin>Summary sense of the conclusion</margin> The summary sense of my conclusion is this: Because Christ descended to the underworld according to His soul alone, and it seems that being localized or moved locally does not belong to a soul—as it does not belong to any separate substance <term>Separate substance: An entity that exists without a physical body, such as an angel or a human soul after death.</term>—except by reason of its operation; therefore I say that to have "descended to hell," or to have been in hell locally, seems not to have belonged to Christ except by reason of His operation. Thus, although the soul of Christ was truly presentially in hell, its substance was not the reason for its presence, but only its operation. <margin>A twofold opinion of those who posit that separate substances exist in a place through a transitive operation. First: Gregory of Nyssa.</margin> So that these words may be more fully understood, it should be noted that there is a twofold opinion among those who posit that separate substances are not in a place except through a "transitive operation" <note>An action that passes from the actor to an external object.</note>. For some say that incorporeal substances are in no way owed a place by reason of their substance, just as a soul is truly never white or black. And so, according to them, it can not irrationally be said of a soul that it is not in a place and is nowhere—just as it is also truly said that it is neither hot nor cold.

But the authorities of scripture which seem to give a place to angels when they say they are "in heaven" or are "sent to this place" or to that, are to be understood thus: not that they are here or there (since they are not properly in a place), but that they operate here or there, or begin to operate where they previously did not operate. And these scholars lean heavily on the words of Gregory of Nyssa, who says that when we ought to say the spirit "operates here," we improperly <note>original: "abusiue." In scholastic logic, this means using a term in a non-literal or figurative sense.</note> say that it "is here." And so this opinion holds that the substance of an angel or a separate soul can never be said to be present to this place or that, except by being present negatively—that is...

<summary>Pico begins his defense regarding Christ's descent into hell, arguing that while Christ was truly present in the underworld, the nature of a "separate soul's" presence is defined by its actions (operation) rather than physical occupation of space.</summary>

# **JOHN PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA**

undistanced. But if it is ever said to be or to have been somewhere, it is the same as saying it acts or has acted somewhere. They add that this way of speaking is a metaphor taken from physical things; because we see that we cannot act unless we are present—at least according to common opinion—therefore, believing the same about incorporeal things, we conclude that wherever they act, and where their operation is found to be, there also their substance is locally present. They conclude finally that it is a crudeness of intellect and a lack of imagination to be unable to understand that something can be a being and yet not be in a place; and they argue that the argument of those who say that "to be" <note>In this context, *to be* refers to existence itself, while *to act* refers to exercising power or influence.</note> presupposes "to act" is frivolous, because that proposition is only true in the sense that a non-being cannot act. For an agent must be in actuality—according to the principle that some moving species will always be perceived—but it is not true in the sense that acting in a place presupposes being in that place, since an acting agent may be of such a nature that local presence or distance is no more relevant to it than being white or black would be. <note>Pico is arguing that since souls do not have physical properties like color, they also do not have to have physical properties like "location" in the way we understand it.</note> Therefore, those who hold this opinion would say that Christ’s soul, separated from the body according to its substance, was neither in hell nor outside of hell, but truly was nowhere. It is said, however, to have been in hell because it acted in hell; and it is said to have been most primarily in that part of hell where it most primarily acted. 

Although many doctors <note>Theologians and scholars of the Church.</note> hold this opinion regarding the mode of being presentially in a place, I do not hold it, nor did I follow it in my conclusion; rather, I held the one which I will immediately subjoin. There is, therefore, another opinion which says <margin>The second opinion, which the author held</margin> that a separated substance <note>original: "substantia separata." This refers to a soul that has been separated from its body by death, or an angel which never had a body.</note>, such as an angel or a soul not united to a body, is indeed truly in a place. And thus it is truly and definitively present locally, just as a physical thing is commensurately <note>original: "commensurative." This means a physical object occupies a space that exactly matches its dimensions; an incorporeal being like a soul is "definitively" in a place, meaning it is there, but not by filling physical volume.</note> present locally. And in this, this path agrees with the common view, which is the path of Scotus and all the Scotists. <note>Followers of John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a major Medieval philosopher.</note> But they differ in this: the Scotists say that the definition and limitation of the essence—and ultimately the intrinsic determination of its substance—is the reason for a separated substance being in a place. 

However, the opinion which I followed in my conclusion says that just as a physical substance is commensurately in a place, yet the reason for its being so in that place is not its substantiality but its quantity (which is extrinsic and foreign to the nature of its substance); so also, although an incorporeal substance is truly and definitively in a place and locally present, yet the reason <margin>Clarification of the opinion</margin> for its being in that place is not its substance, but its operation passing from it to the outside. I judge this opinion should be understood in this way, and so understood, I judge it not only to be non-heretical, but even more probable than its opposite. And it is this: even if the finiteness or limitation of a separated nature is the reason why it is not everywhere—or the reason why, if it is in one place, it is not simultaneously in another as a whole—nevertheless, it is not the reason for its being simply in that specific place. Instead, its effect or operation is the reason—taking "operation" to mean every relationship to a body or place, whether acting or being acted upon. This is distinct from the condition of local presence, and this is understood as a matter of fact, not denying another possible mode of descent or location of the separated soul (as I say in the following conclusion), though that mode is unknown to us. Following this opinion in my conclusion, I say that Christ was in hell only through His effect.

<summary>Pico examines two philosophical opinions on how souls and angels exist in a physical location, ultimately arguing that Christ’s soul was present in hell through its power and effects rather than through physical occupation of space.</summary>

After resolving the arguments commonly brought against the foundations of the position I followed in my conclusion regarding the manner of Christ’s descent <note>Pico refers to his controversial thesis about Christ descending into hell 'virtually' or 'legally' rather than locally.</note>, I wish also to bring forward the words of our Albert <margin>The Great</margin>, who is no less great in learning than in his surname "the Great" <margin>Albertus</margin>. "There are also many moderns who concede the consequence of this reasoning, although they know the logic is invalid. For from Logic we know that an argument is invalid if it proceeds from the destruction of the antecedent to the destruction of the consequent <note>A formal fallacy where one argues: 'If P then Q; P is false; therefore Q is false.' And therefore, although it is true that 'that which is not is nowhere,' it does not follow from this that 'that which is, is somewhere.' And although this does not follow from what was said, there are nevertheless many who say that 'everything that exists is in some place,' using such reasoning: because everything that exists is a particular thing; a particular is 'here and now'; and what is 'here and now' is somewhere; therefore everything that exists is somewhere. Furthermore: everything that exists has a definite essence, because it is constrained within its own limits; and that which has a definite essence is 'defined' in a place; and what is defined in a place is in some place."

<margin>John Damascene</margin> But these men make a distinction based on John Damascene <note>John of Damascus (c. 675–749), an Eastern Church Father often quoted by Scholastics for his definitions of spiritual presence.</note>, saying that for something to be in a place is said in two ways. <margin>Being in a place in two ways</margin> For something is there **circumscriptively**, to which a beginning, middle, and end are assigned in a place; and in this way they say bodies are in a place. Also, something is in a place **definitively**, whose essence is so finitely enclosed in one place that nothing of it is found outside that place; and in this way they say indivisible things are in a place, and similarly intelligences <term>angels</term> and souls, etc.

But we do not believe these things: for even the "highest heaven" <note>The Empyrean, the boundary of the physical universe.</note> is neither defined nor circumscribed by a place, because everything that is in a place is enclosed and contained by the place in which it is; and an intelligence, by its nature, is not in a place nor in any spatial distinction. These are Albert’s words to the letter. He does not approve of that common distinction of being in a place "definitively" and "not circumscriptively"—a distinction which certain masters nevertheless thought it an absolute sacrilege to deny in any way. # APOLOGIA

[...to be] understood the words of my conclusion; and that I may declare also by the force of the wording that the conclusion itself is Catholic <note>original: "catholicam." From these points, it is clear that the aforesaid conclusion is a single negative copulative proposition <term>a statement that denies two things joined together</term>, or one concerning a joined extreme where the negation is placed before the copulative conjunction. The sense of which is: It is not the case that Christ truly and according to a real presence, in the manner that Thomas posits, descended into hell, etc. And that copulative statement is equivalent to a single affirmative disjunctive <term>a logical "either/or" statement</term> of...

<meta>Continuity: Pico continues his defense of his eleventh thesis regarding Christ's descent into hell. Having previously established that his statement should be read as a "negative copulative" (a specific type of logical denial), he now moves into a grammatical analysis of the word "as" to prove his statement is not heretical.</meta>

# GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

...is granted among all theologians: it is necessary also that they grant that in our proposition in which it is said, "Christ did not descend **as** Thomas says," the word <term>Pico uses the Scholastic marker "ly" to highlight the specific word being analyzed</term> "**as**" <note>original: "ut"</note>, just as it can be taken relatively <term>serving as a simple link between the subject and the authority cited</term> so that the meaning is "Christ did not descend, even though Thomas says He did," so it can also be held—just as well and just as properly—in a specific sense, being equivalent to this: "Although Christ descended by presence, yet it was not in that manner of presence which the **common way** <term>the standard consensus of Scholastic theologians</term> describes." And this is the sense that I intend. But perhaps someone might say <margin>Objection</margin> that you still have not escaped <note>Pico implies the "escape" from the trap of a heresy charge.</note> because you then add: "but only as far as the effect." Therefore, you do not only exclude real presence in the way the **common way** posits it, but you simply exclude **all** real presence, since you say "only as far as the effect." Thus, these critics will say the proposition is not a negative copulative <term>a logical statement denying a specific combination of ideas</term> as you claim, by denying, namely, the p[art]...

<summary>Pico employs Scholastic logic and grammar to argue that his denial of Christ's descent into hell was not a denial of the event itself, but rather a rejection of the specific physical "presence" described by Thomas Aquinas. He addresses an anticipated objection that his focus on the "effect" of the descent might still be interpreted as a total denial of Christ's physical presence in hell.</summary>
