# APOLOGY

<margin>Defense regarding the followers of Thomas</margin>
But whatever the case may be regarding the opinion of Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the Dominican theologian whose work was the gold standard for Catholic orthodoxy at the time.</note>, it is irrelevant to the matter at hand: because to err regarding the opinion of Thomas is not to err in the faith. Furthermore, there is often a variety of opinions among the Thomists <term>followers of Thomas Aquinas</term> regarding his actual views. It is sufficient that this is clearly apparent: that when I proposed my conclusion, I believed this to be the opinion of Thomas. And I am not now twisting the proposition to a sense <margin>Note.</margin> foreign to the one I held then. That I believed this from the beginning, and that this was my judgment regarding Thomas’s opinion when I set forth my conclusions, is most clearly evident from this: I proposed the conclusion that Thomas and Scotus <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a rival Scholastic philosopher to Aquinas known for different views on metaphysics.</note> do not differ regarding the way angels exist in a place. It is well known, however, that Scotus expressly says that even if all operation <term>active influence or power</term> is excluded, a location is still owed to an incorporeal substance <note>Incorporeal substances include angels and human souls.</note>. Therefore, it was necessary for me to believe that Thomas held this same view. 

And thus, although I firmly hold that Christ was truly and personally in the underworld—and in this I agree with Thomas and with all Catholics—nevertheless, because I thought Thomas believed his very substance was the reason for his locatability rather than his operation, I said in my conclusion: "not in the way Thomas and the **common way** <term>the standard school of thought among theologians</term> posits." <margin>That Saint Thomas sometimes felt different things.</margin> Nor should it seem strange to anyone that Thomas follows one opinion in one place and another elsewhere. For in his first book on the *Sentences* <note>The *Sentences* of Peter Lombard was the standard theology textbook; every scholar had to write a commentary on it.</note>, he follows the opinion of the **Commentator** <note>Averroes (1126–1198), the Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were essential to medieval scholars.</note> regarding things generated from decay <term>spontaneous generation, where life was thought to arise from rotting matter</term>, which he then rejects in the seventh book of his *Metaphysics* and elsewhere. Likewise, in his second book on the *Sentences*, he follows the Commentator’s opinion regarding the matter of the heavens, which he later rejects in his work *On the Heavens* and in the *Summa* <note>The *Summa Theologiae*, Aquinas's most mature and influential work.</note>. Likewise, in his fourth book and in his questions on Boethius's *On the Trinity*, he holds the Commentator's view on indeterminate dimensions, and then in his own booklet (as is believed) and in many other places, he does not hold it. 

Likewise, in the first book of the *Sentences*, he says that the same action understands the intelligible thing itself and the act of understanding itself. In the first part of the *Summa* and in the third book of the *Sentences*, however, he holds that a reflexive action differs from a direct one. Likewise, in his writings <note>Referring to his earlier commentary on the *Sentences*.</note>, he holds that the soul of Christ, insofar as it was joinable to a body, was like the soul of a **wayfarer** <term>a living person on the journey through life</term>; but insofar as it was joinable to the Word <note>The Logos, or the second person of the Trinity.</note>, it was like the soul of a **comprehensor** <term>one who has reached the end of the journey and sees God in heaven</term>. In the *Summa*, however, he holds that the soul of Christ was totally and in all respects like the soul of a comprehensor, and that the fact it did not pour the gift of clarity and impassibility <term>the quality of being unable to suffer or be harmed</term> into the body was by divine dispensation. He also feels one way about the knowledge of Christ in his writings and another way in the *Summa*, and so it is with many other things; it is possible to see in which matters he followed different opinions in different places.

But if these men contend absolutely that the opinion regarding the "mode of being in a place through operation" belongs to Thomas as well, they will have nothing more against me except that my opinion regarding the manner of Christ’s descent is all the more probable—and should be judged less heretical—insofar as it is true even according to the opinion of Saint Thomas. <margin>Note.</margin> For this reason, I marvel all the more that these masters condemned my conclusion; for before they judged this conclusion heretical, I had not only declared my intention to them in these words but had even dictated them to be written down and noted, saying: "Let no one understand me to say by this conclusion that the soul of Christ did not descend to the underworld, or that the soul of Christ was not in the underworld during the three days <note>The three days between the Crucifixion and the Resurrection.</note>; indeed, I confess both. But I say that neither local motion nor being located in a place is suitable for any separated substance <term>a soul existing apart from its body</term> (such as the soul of Christ then was) except by reason of its operation." Precisely these words and no others I pronounced to be noted by them, word for word, as a brief declaration of this conclusion. How they could still judge it heretical afterward—when they could now hold it as Catholic—I do not see. 

<margin>He argues against his opponents.</margin>
And to show briefly, by way of a summarizing argument, that those who believe my proposition cannot be defended from heresy are themselves erring in faith, I argue thus: one who posits a conclusion that is heretical in itself can be accused of heresy insofar as heresy exists in the intellect. But one who posits my aforementioned conclusion cannot, by its very position, be accused of heresy...

<summary>Pico defends himself against charges of heresy by demonstrating that even Thomas Aquinas changed his mind on various philosophical points, arguing that disagreeing with a specific "Thomist" view is not a violation of faith. He clarifies that he fully accepts Christ's descent into hell but questions the metaphysical mechanism by which a bodiless soul occupies space.</summary>

# GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

If, therefore, the aforementioned conclusion is not in itself heretical—and my opponents take the major premise <note>In a formal logic argument (a syllogism), the 'major premise' is the broad general statement. Here, Pico assumes his opponents agree that if the core idea isn't heretical, then the conclusion shouldn't be either.</note> as granted—I shall prove the minor premise <note>The 'minor premise' is the specific case being applied to the general rule.</note> as follows. 

Whenever someone posits everything that necessarily follows from a proposition "A," they cannot be accused of heresy, and the person positing proposition "A" itself cannot be accused either. But one who posits everything that follows from the position of my conclusion, in the way it was posited by me, cannot be accused of heresy; therefore, the person positing the proposition itself as I have posited it cannot be accused. 

I prove the minor premise in this way: the contradictory of this statement—that the reason for being in a place (that is, "here" or "there") in the manner declared above for separate substances <term>incorporeal beings like angels or human souls separated from the body</term> is their operation <term>their active power or influence</term> and not the limitation of their nature—is not a matter of faith <note>original: "non est de fide." This is a crucial legal distinction; if a point of philosophy is "not of the faith," disagreeing with it cannot be heresy.</note>. 

And the contradictory of this statement—that it is not permitted to argue from a whole conjunction <term>a "copulative" statement joining two parts with "and"</term> to one of its parts—is not a matter of faith. 

And the contradictory of this statement: "If anyone, having set forth some negative or affirmative assertion, adds the authority of some doctor <note>A "Doctor of the Church," such as Thomas Aquinas.</note> with the word 'as' <note>original: "ly ut." Pico is performing a grammatical analysis of the Latin word "ut" (as/so that).</note>, the word 'as' can be taken just as well determinatively as relatively." This is because it can just as well be equivalent to the phrase "in the manner in which," as to the word "which"; similarly...

<summary>Pico employs formal Scholastic logic to argue that his thesis is not heretical. He asserts that the technical reasons for how souls exist in a location are philosophical opinions rather than established dogmas of faith.</summary>

# APOLOGY

It defends the conclusion without any abuse of terms or oratory, and without any forced interpretation. And finally, although this suffices for the defense of my conclusion, yet for a fuller discussion of this matter, I say that even interpreting the conclusion in the way they <note>Pico's critics or the papal commission.</note> themselves interpreted it—namely, that Christ was in hell "effectively" only and not "essentially" <term>"Effectively" means Christ’s power or influence reached Hell; "essentially" or "presentially" means his actual soul was located there.</term>—it might still perhaps seem presumptuous of them to have determined that the conclusion was simply heretical. 

<margin>The conclusion is supported by the authority of Durandus out of an abundance of caution.</margin>

For it is a fact that Durandus, a very great theologian of the Order of Preachers <term>the Dominicans</term>, who perhaps exceeds these current masters in learning no less than I am exceeded by them, held that opinion to be probable and well-defensible alongside the truth of the article of faith. For thus he writes in the third book of the *Sentences* <note>original: "in tertio sniar̃" (in tertio Sententiarum). This refers to the *Sentences* of Peter Lombard, the standard theological textbook of the Middle Ages which every doctoral candidate had to comment upon.</note>:

<margin>Durandus. The words of Durandus.</margin>

--- Page 97 ---
<meta>Continuity: Following the previous page, Pico continues to quote or paraphrase the Dominican theologian Durandus of Saint-Pourçain to support his argument that Christ’s "descent into Hell" should be understood as an "effective" presence—exerting power or influence—rather than a literal, physical movement of his soul to a subterranean location.</meta>

# GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

Likewise, by way of appropriation, just as Christ was blessed according to his soul, so it is attributed to him that he was the cause of blessedness in others. For it is fitting that a **being in potentiality** <term>A philosophical concept where something has the possibility to become something else; here, the souls in Limbo have the potential for salvation but need an external force to realize it.</term> should be brought to **actuality** by that which is already in act. According to some, there was another effect toward which the soul of Christ acted directly as an agent: namely, to illuminate the souls of the Fathers who were in **Limbo** <note>In medieval theology, the "Limbo of the Patriarchs" was the temporary state of the righteous who died before Christ’s redemption.</note> and regarding the mysteries that fall under revelation. 

For according to Dionysius in the seventh chapter of *The Celestial Hierarchy* <margin>Dionysius 9</margin> <note>original: "Dionysium septimo caelestis gerarchiae." Pico likely refers to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a highly influential mystical theologian.</note>: Christ, according to his soul, has the task of teaching the angels; and by reason of this twofold effect, the soul of Christ can be said to have descended into Hell. 

This is confirmed by a threefold reason. The first is because to be moved or to descend belongs to a **separated soul** <term>A soul that has been released from the body after death.</term> <margin>The first reason</margin> not by the manner of the movement of bodies, but in the manner that movement belongs to a spiritual substance. However, for other spiritual substances—namely, God and the angels—to be moved from place to place does not belong to them by a movement that exists within them as subjects, but rather through the **effect** they have in other things. Therefore, in a similar way, it belongs to a separated soul, and it belonged to the soul of Christ. 

The second reason is as follows: Christ is said to have descended into Hell <margin>The second [reason]</margin> so that he might illuminate the souls of the Holy Fathers to see God. At the very instant in which Christ died, the Holy Fathers saw God. But in that same instant, the soul of Christ could not have been in Hell through physical movement. Therefore, he did not descend there through a movement that was in the soul itself, but through the effect which he had upon others. 

Likewise, just as in that three-day period <margin>The third [reason]</margin> the soul of Christ is said to have been in Hell with the souls of the Holy Fathers, so in that same period or part of it, he is said to have been in **Paradise** with the soul of the thief, to whom it was said in Luke 23: *Today you will be with me in Paradise.* But this cannot be understood in terms of a location acquired through physical movement. For according to those who posit that a spirit is in a place **definitively** <term>A Scholastic term meaning the spirit is "contained" by the limits of a place without occupying physical volume.</term>, when it moves from place to place, that same spirit cannot be in multiple places at once, nor be moved simultaneously by several movements tending toward different places. 

Wherefore it must be understood according to the effect. For if anyone should say that "Paradise" is spoken of in two ways <margin>Paradise</margin>: in one way as a corporeal place—namely, the **Empyrean Heaven** <note>The highest, most outer heaven in medieval cosmology, believed to be the dwelling place of God.</note>—and in this sense, the soul of Christ was not in Paradise until after the Ascension. In another way, Paradise is called the **vision of the Divine Essence** <margin>in two ways / in three ways</margin> <note>The "Beatific Vision," or the direct experience of seeing God.</note>; and in this way, the soul of Christ was in Paradise from the instant of his conception, and the soul of the thief was in it on the day of the Passion. In this manner, it is not contradictory for the soul of Christ to have been simultaneously in Paradise—that is, that he saw God—and to have been locally in Hell. 

If this is said, it is not valid, because just as "Paradise" is spoken of in two ways, so is "Hell." <margin>Hell</margin> For in one way, Hell is called a place corresponding to the interior of the earth. <margin>in two ways / in three ways</margin> In another way, it is called the **privation of the divine vision**. Therefore, just as the soul of the thief is not said to have been with the soul of Christ in Paradise except because, by the merit of Christ’s Passion, the soul of the thief saw God; so the soul of Christ is not said to have been with the souls of the chosen Fathers in Hell except because their souls, which lacked the divine vision (and thus were said to be in Hell), were purged of this lack by the merit of this Passion. Therefore, both should be understood equally in terms of effect, not in terms of place or local motion existing within the soul itself. 

However, although this may be said probably and seems to sufficiently preserve the **article of faith** <note>The formal Church teaching on Christ's descent into Hell.</note> and the words of Scripture, yet because divine power is not fully grasped by human reason, it must not be obstinately asserted that the soul of Christ could not have descended into Hell by some other way unknown to us. 

To the first argument, it must be said that the same finite thing cannot be in several places at once definitively or **circumscriptively** <term>Being in a place such that every part of the object corresponds to a part of the space; usually reserved for physical bodies.</term>; nor is it posited in this way that the soul of Christ was simultaneously in Paradise and in Hell. But according to effect, nothing prohibits the same finite thing from being said to be in several places when the effects are compatible and are simultaneously subject to the power of the same agent. And thus, the soul of Christ is said to have been in Paradise and in Hell at the same time, because by his merit, the soul of the thief saw God (which is to be in Paradise), and the souls of the Fathers, who lacked the divine vision and for this reason were said to be in Hell...

<summary>Pico uses the theological arguments of Durandus to argue that Christ's "descent into Hell" was an "effective" presence—bringing the vision of God to the souls in Limbo—rather than a physical travel of his soul through space.</summary>
<keywords>Descent into Hell, Durandus of Saint-Pourçain, Limbo, Divine Essence, Paradise, spiritual substance, Scholasticism, Beatific Vision</keywords>

<meta>Continuity: Following the previous page, Pico continues to quote the Dominican theologian Durandus of Saint-Pourçain, who argues that Christ’s "descent into Hell" was an "effective" presence—exerting his power to save the Patriarchs—rather than a physical travel of his soul.</meta>

->APOLOGIA<-

...they were liberated from this lack <note>Referring to the "lack of the divine vision" or the state of being separated from God's presence before Christ's sacrifice.</note> and consequently from hell. Indeed, according to one and the same effect—namely, according to the liberation of the Fathers—the soul of Christ could be said to be simultaneously in paradise and in hell, considering the point from which they were moved and the point to which they were led by reason of that effect. For by reason of the lack of the divine vision from which they were liberated through the passion of Christ, the soul of Christ could be said to have been in hell; but by reason of the divine vision to which they were admitted, it could be said to be in paradise. Regarding the second point, it must be said that by the very fact that we are liberated from guilt and punishment through the passion of Christ, Christ is said to have descended into hell, because by the merit of his passion some have been snatched from the punishments of hell. That descent is not considered according to **local motion** <term>In medieval physics and theology, "local motion" refers to the physical movement of an object or soul from one geographic place to another.</term> existing in the soul, but according to the effect he had in those to be saved. These are the words of Durandus, verbatim. Since I have never found that he retracted such an opinion, if this opinion is simply heretical and consequently against what has already been determined by the Church, it follows that Durandus died a heretic.

<margin>Exclamation / Order of Preachers / Thomas</margin> O illustrious **Order of Preachers** <note>The Dominicans, the religious order to which both Thomas Aquinas and Durandus belonged.</note> and greatest splendor of our religion, can you suffer this? Your teacher—perhaps the first after **Thomas** <note>Saint Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the most influential Dominican theologian.</note> or without doubt among the first—whose books are held, read, and honored daily in your schools, your cloisters, and your libraries, is now pronounced a heretic. You must plead the case of your teacher; I have pleaded mine. Or rather, O Church, you must plead your own case, you who permitted Durandus to be read publicly for so many years and still permit it. Either you never recognized his foul heresy (according to these masters) out of ignorance, or you recognized it and did not condemn it out of negligence and contempt for divine matters.

If they say there was no need for a new condemnation because this opinion is among those already condemned: First, from this follows what I said above, namely, that Durandus died a heretic. 

<margin>Durandus / Capreolus / Durandellus</margin> Second, it follows that **Capreolus** <note>Jean Capreolus (c. 1380–1444), known as the "Prince of Thomists," who defended the views of Thomas Aquinas.</note> and **Durandellus** <note>Nicolaus de Saint-Pourçain (often called Durandellus), an early critic and commentator on Durandus.</note> and many other doctors who recite the opinion of Durandus and yet do not charge it with heresy, were ignorant and unrefined in the faith, not knowing how to discern a heretic from a non-heretic. Third, let those fathers tell me where they themselves read the condemnation of this opinion. As for me, I confess I do not remember ever reading it. They can certainly bring forth no determination of the Councils against Durandus. For not only was this opinion never condemned in Councils, but no mention was even made of it in any of them. 

<margin>Scotus</margin> Likewise, I do not know how they can cite the words of Sacred Scripture against him, unless **Scotus** <note>Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a major Franciscan philosopher and rival to the Thomist school.</note> lies, who says on the testimony of Francis that even regarding the reality of Christ’s descent—let alone the *mode* of the descent—no express mention is made in the Gospel doctrine, as is clear from what we set forth at the beginning. This is evident in the way Durandus would perhaps use to explain the authorities of Scripture that might seem to be against him. Regarding the authorities of the **Saints** <note>The "Saints" here refers to the Church Fathers, such as Augustine or Jerome.</note>, they could perhaps bring forward many who say that the soul of Christ was in hell during those three days just as his body was in the tomb, and similar things. And whatever may be of Durandus’s "fantasy"—namely, the way he would explain the aforementioned authorities, perhaps by saying this is said of the soul and not of the whole composite person because he worked principally through the soul—whatever he might say (and I neither hold his opinion nor have I ever held it), I say this and firmly assert it: this logic is not valid: "This opinion is against the sayings of **Augustine** or **Jerome** or **Gregory** <note>The foundational Latin Doctors of the Church: St. Augustine of Hippo, St. Jerome, and Pope St. Gregory the Great.</note> and so on for the other doctors of the Church; therefore it is heretical." 

<margin>Note / On the authority of the doctors, i.e., Augustine Jerome Gregory & others</margin> The truth of this statement is believed by all good and subtle theologians, and it will also be evidently proven by me. For although the writings of the holy doctors placed outside the **biblical canon** <term>The list of books officially recognized as Holy Scripture; writings outside this (like those of the Church Fathers) are considered "tradition" but not divinely inspired in the same way.</term> are to be passed down and read and received with due reverence, their sayings are not of such firm authority and immutability that it is not permitted to contradict them or to doubt them, unless they are either proven otherwise evidently and expressly by Sacred Scripture, or it has been firmly determined by the Church itself—authorizing them—that they contain firm and indubitable truth. Therefore, an opinion cannot be clearly convicted as heretical precisely through the sayings of the saints outside the biblical canon. For where there is no infallible truth, there is no faith.

<summary>Pico defends himself against charges of heresy by arguing that the theologian Durandus held similar views on Christ’s descent into hell without being condemned. He challenges the idea that contradicting a Church Father is equivalent to heresy, asserting that only the Bible and Church Councils carry infallible authority.</summary>
<keywords>Durandus of Saint-Pourçain, heresy, descent into hell, authority of the Church Fathers, Thomas Aquinas, Duns Scotus, biblical canon, Dominican Order, scholasticism</keywords>

<meta>Continuity: Pico continues his argument from the previous page regarding the "Apologia," shifting from the specific case of Durandus to a broader argument about the authority of Church Doctors versus the Holy Scripture.</meta>

# GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

...certain and indubitable. Since certain faith rests upon infallible truth—indeed, regarding such matters, there is no infallible Reason for assent nor firm adherence <note>Pico is arguing that while faith is certain, human reasoning about theology is often subject to doubt.</note>. From this, it follows that where there is no certain truth and indubitable faith, one does not always assent to it without doubt and the fear of falsehood. For as Augustine says in his letter to Jerome, in the eleventh book of *Against Faustus* (chapter 8), and in the sixteenth book of the same work, if Scripture did not contain infallible truth and were found to be false in any part, there would remain in it no certain faith by which it could be firmly believed; because of a falsehood found in one part, the whole would be held suspect, and thus faith would waver. For as Augustine says in *On Christian Doctrine* (chapter 7), "faith wavers if the authority of the Holy Scriptures vacillates." 

<margin>The first proof: that the sayings of the saints outside the Bible are not of infallible truth.</margin> However, regarding the fact that there is no infallible truth in the sayings of the saints outside the biblical canon, three proofs occur to me for the present purpose. The **first proof** is because the Doctors <term>The "Doctors of the Church" are influential Christian theologians and saints whose writings are considered authoritative but not divinely inspired in the same way as the Bible.</term> themselves doubt whether they have erred in their sayings or not. Hence, Augustine in the first book of *The Trinity* (chapter 1) says: "Let it not trouble me to seek where I hesitate, nor will it shame me to correct myself where I err." And in chapter 2: "Therefore, let whoever reads this proceed with me where he is equally certain; let him seek with me where he equally hesitates; let him return to me where he recognizes his error, and let him recall me where he recognizes mine." 

From this comes Augustine's *Book of Retractions*, in which he condemns and retracts many things from his earlier sayings. Hence, in the second book of *The Trinity*, he says: "I would rather be rebuked by anyone than praised by one who is either in error or a flatterer. For the one who praises and is in error confirms the error, while the flatterer lures one into error. But the righteous man will correct me in mercy and rebuke me; let the oil of the sinner not anoint my head." <note>Pico is quoting Augustine's use of Psalm 141:5 to express a preference for harsh correction over false praise.</note> 

<margin>Guido the Carmelite</margin> And as **Guido the Carmelite** <note>Guido Terreni (c. 1270–1342), a Carmelite theologian known for his work on heresy and papal authority.</note> says in his *Book on Heresies*: although Augustine speaks humbly in these sayings, he nonetheless speaks truly. Hence, Augustine himself says to Vincent: "I cannot nor should I deny that, just as in the works of my predecessors, so in my many little works, there are many things which can be rebuked by a just judgment and without any rashness." And in the book *On True Religion*, he says: "Whatever error is found in my books, this alone is to be attributed to me; but whatever is true or well-explained, let that be attributed to God, the one rewarder and giver of all things." Therefore, the sayings of Augustine, that distinguished and divine doctor, do not always contain indubitable truth in all things, since he himself doubted whether he had erred or not. And what has been said of Augustine should be understood similarly of other Doctors.

<margin>The second proof: from the discord between Augustine and Jerome.</margin> The **second proof** is taken from the discord that exists among the authors themselves. For discord among writers is a testimony to falsehood, since it is necessary that at least one of those disagreeing says what is false, because one side of a contradiction is necessarily false. Therefore, Augustine, in the sixteenth book of *The City of God*, proves the truth of Holy Scripture from the mutual harmony of its writers, in which all agree and no one disagrees with another; this testifies to the indubitable and infallible truth of Holy Scripture. For to the truth and to the "true," as the Philosopher <note>Pico refers to Aristotle as "The Philosopher," specifically his *Nicomachean Ethics*.</note> says in the first book of the *Ethics*, all things are in harmony, which does not happen in other writings. 

How great the discord is in the sayings of the saints outside the canonical scriptures, no one is ignorant unless they have not read their books. Augustine disagrees with the other holy Doctors regarding the understanding of the **Six Days of Creation**. <note>The *Hexameron*, or the work of the six days described in Genesis.</note> For others posit that God made those works of the six days according to a succession of time; Augustine disagrees with them, positing that all things were made at once <term>In Latin, *simul*. Augustine argued for "simultaneous creation" rather than a chronological week.</term>, according to the verse: "He who lives forever created all things together." 

<margin>Regarding the works of the six days.</margin> Hence, moved by this, Augustine numbers those six days not according to a succession of time, but according to the distinction of the angelic knowledge of things in their own kind and in the Word. And yet, neither these nor those are called heretics, though it is certain that one of the opinions is false and, consequently, their sayings do not rest upon infallible truth. 

<margin>Regarding the authorship of the Psalms.</margin> Similarly, **Jerome and Augustine** disagree, because Augustine makes David the author of all the Psalms, which Jerome denies. They similarly disagree regarding the rebuke of Peter by Paul, whether it concerned a mortal or venial sin on Peter's part...

<summary>Pico argues that while the Bible is the only source of infallible truth, the writings of Church Doctors (like Augustine) are subject to error and disagreement. He provides evidence through Augustine's own admissions of fallibility and the contradictions between various saints on theological issues like the timeline of Creation.</summary>

For the declaration of the conclusion, five things must be noted. First, it should be noted that in sin, two things can be considered: <margin>First thing to note regarding sin: Conversion and Aversion</margin> "Turning toward" a created good and "turning away" from the unchangeable and uncreated good. <note>original: "Conversio ad bonum creatum & auersio a bono incommutabili & increato." This is a standard theological distinction. Sin is seen as both a positive act toward a worldly thing and a negative rejection of God.</note> In the first way, sin is a finite evil, even according to all the Doctors. In the second way, sin is a finite evil according to the common path. And because the "turning toward" a created good (which the sinner misuses by sinning) is of the intrinsic nature of the sin itself, it is therefore said that sin is *intrinsically* a finite evil. <margin>Second thing to note</margin> However, the "turning away" from the uncreated good causes it to be *extrinsically* infinite, because it is only called an "infinite evil" insofar as it is a turning away from an infinite good. Therefore, it only remains that it be an extrinsically and objectively infinite evil.

Secondly, note that by "time," we can understand only the "time of the way" <note>original: "tempus viae." In medieval theology, the "way" (via) refers to our earthly life where we are "wayfarers" or travelers toward eternity.</note>; and in this way, it is certain that neither sin nor anything else pertaining to man can be infinite according to the "time of the way," since the life of any traveler is not only finite in duration, but even brief. In another way, we can understand by "time" both the "time of the way" and the "time of the end" <note>original: "tempus viae & termini." The "end" refers to the state after death, either in heaven or hell.</note>; and it is in this way that it is taken in the conclusion. Thus, something in a man can last for an infinite time, as is evident.

Thirdly, note that mortal sin can be understood in two ways. <margin>Third: Mortal sin taken for the act or for the guilt</margin> In one way, for the prohibited act or the omission of an act commanded by God. In another way, for the "guilt" <term>guilt (reatus): A technical term in Scholasticism meaning the liability to punishment that remains as a "stain" or legal debt even after the physical act of sinning has ended.</term> left behind from the aforementioned prohibited act or omission of an act; which guilt, indeed, is called "sin" in many places of Holy Scripture. By such a sin, someone is named a "sinner" even when the act of the sin (in the first sense) has ceased or passed away. From this third note, it is clear that it is reasonably said that although in the person who is damned for mortal sin, the sin itself for which he is damned sometimes "ends" as far as the intrinsic entity of the act is concerned (which is called sin in the first way), it does not "end," however, as far as the guilt is concerned. Indeed, if it were to end in that way, eternal punishment would not be owed to him. And thus, the sin to which infinite punishment is owed is infinite according to time as far as the guilt is concerned.

<meta>Continuity: This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s defense within his "Apologia." Having previously discussed the "de-acceptance" of the sinner by God, he now addresses the specific logical responses to the nature of sin and its eternal punishment.</meta>

-># APOLOGY<-

<margin>Responses which the author had given</margin>
...leading to an enduring state of guilt. <margin>First</margin> It must be understood that the nature of the offense is tied to the persistence of the will. <margin>Second</margin> While the act itself is transitory, the turning away from the Divine remains. <margin>Third</margin> Therefore, the punishment is not for a past action that has ceased, but for a state of being that the soul refuses to abandon.

<margin>Question</margin>
If the act of sinning is finished in a moment, how can the punishment endure? 

<margin>Response</margin>
The response lies in the distinction between the act and the debt. Through sin <note>original: "peccato"</note>, the soul enters a state of debt that it cannot repay on its own. Unless the sinner repents, they remain in that sin <note>original: "peccato"</note> eternally. Thus, the infinity of the punishment corresponds to the infinity of the duration of the sin <note>original: "peccato"</note> itself within the soul of the damned. 

<margin>Note</margin>
It is important to note <note>original: "Nota"</note> that the gravity of the sin <note>original: "peccati"</note> is also considered infinite in a relative sense, because it is an offense against God, who is the Infinite Good.

<margin>Recapitulation</margin>
To summarize the argument: the sinner is not punished eternally for a finite moment of pleasure, but for an eternal persistence in that sin <note>original: "peccato"</note>. The duration of the penalty matches the duration of the guilt.

He argues that the "infinity" of Hell is a response to the sinner's eternal persistence in their state of sin rather than the brief duration of the sinful act itself.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: This page transitions from the general discussion of eternal punishment into the specific theological controversy regarding the "Adoration of the Cross." ->APOLOGIA<-

<margin>Against the foundation of the opinion.</margin> it cannot be said of a created thing. But even the divine persons themselves, by reason of their relative properties, are not the formal object <term>formal object: the specific aspect or reason why something is targeted by an action, in this case, the reason for worship.</term> of adoration. However, the foundation of Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> seems equally effective to some as it does to others. But the Philosopher <note>Aristotle, usually referred to simply as "the Philosopher" in medieval texts.</note> only intends this: that the recollective movement by which the soul understands an image, insofar as it is an image, is the same as its movement toward the exemplar <note>original: "exemplari" — the original subject the image represents.</note>; and thus, whatever is owed to one is also owed to the other. But the Philosopher only means that the recollective movement by which the soul is moved toward an image—insofar as it is an image—is also terminated at the thing imagined. It also has another true sense: if I have a definitive concept of one relative term, I also understand the other. But that every movement of the soul—and especially of the will—is the same toward the image and the thing imagined is something the Philosopher in no way intends. This is clear by a similar example in the way of speaking used by Thomas himself. For he often says that the movement of the will is the same when the will is carried toward the end <note>The final goal or purpose.</note> and toward those things which lead to the end <note>The means to achieve that goal.</note> when it desires them for the sake of the end. And yet it is certain, even according to him, that this movement, as it reaches the end, is "enjoyment" <term>enjoyment: translated from "fruitio," the delight in a thing for its own sake.</term>, but as it reaches those things leading to the end, it is "use" <term>use: translated from "usus," using something as a means to another goal.</term> and not enjoyment.

<margin>The opinion of other doctors.</margin> It seems, therefore, to other doctors that it should in no way be said that we adore the image of Christ, even as an image, with the adoration of *latria* <term>latria: the supreme worship due to God alone.</term>, because as such it is a created thing not united to the divinity; and what is more, as such it is a relative entity. <margin>The opinion of Durandus.</margin> For this reason, Durandus <note>Durandus of Saint-Pourçain, a 14th-century philosopher known for his independent thinking.</note> says that the proposition "the cross of Christ is adored with latria" is false in its proper sense, though it has a true sense when used improperly. And it is this: Christ, as remembered through the cross, or as present in the cross (just as the thing imagined is present in its image), is adored with the same adoration as if he were present in himself. And according to this sense, I also concede this proposition: the Cross is adored with the adoration of *latria*. This is therefore what Durandus says: that it is adored "recollectively." <margin>The opinion of Robert Holcot, Henry, John of Guarra, and Peter of Aquila.</margin> Robert Holcot intends the same meaning when he says that the more proper way of speaking is to say "we adore *before* the cross" rather than "we adore the cross." Finally, Henry <note>Henry of Ghent.</note> and John of Guarra intend the same meaning when they say it is adored *per accidens* <term>per accidens: incidentally or indirectly.</term>; and Peter of Aquila says the same.

<margin>What Henry and John of Guarra add.</margin> Truly, what Henry and John of Guarra add—who speak more completely on this matter—is this: they say that the honor which is owed *per se* <note>in itself</note> to the thing imagined and remembered is owed to the image *per accidens* or through recollection. It is certain, however, that nothing is owed *latria* in itself except the Triune God and Christ, because of the unity of his person <term>person: translated from "suppositi," the underlying subject or substance.</term> with God; but an image cannot be God. It remains that if there is any image to which *latria* is owed incidentally and through recollection, it is the image of Christ. Truly, because such an image principally represents to us the humanity of Christ, and secondarily his divinity, it seems that primarily and incidentally it is owed the same honor that is owed in itself to the humanity of Christ. <margin>The opinion of Francis of Mayronnes and the Scotists.</margin> The humanity of Christ, however, taken in itself, is only adored with *hyperdulia* <term>hyperdulia: a level of veneration higher than that given to saints (dulia) but lower than that given to God (latria).</term>; therefore, such an image will primarily and incidentally only be owed the adoration of *hyperdulia*. Secondarily, however, and incidentally, it will also be owed the adoration of *latria* in the manner described: because the image itself also secondarily represents and reminds us of the divinity of Christ himself. In this, Francis of Mayronnes and all the Scotists <note>Followers of John Duns Scotus.</note> agree, saying that *latria* is not owed to the humanity of Christ.

<margin>The opinion of Thomas is somewhat dangerous in this matter.</margin> Thomas, however, because he seems to hold the opposite view regarding the adoration of Christ's humanity, would perhaps also dissent from Henry in this case. And truly, the opinion of Thomas, as Francis says in the third book <note>Referring to the commentaries on the *Sentences*.</note>, is somewhat dangerous; and in this matter of adoration, his path does not seem to me to be very safe. For he proceeded so far as to say, even in the third book of the *Sentences*, that some adoration was owed even to the physical cross on which Christ hung as an inanimate thing. <margin>John Capreolus.</margin> And yet we know, according to all theology, that that which cannot be a subject capable of holiness or virtue cannot be the object of any adoration. Even John Capreolus, the defender of Thomas, himself admits that this statement of Thomas cannot be defended, nor does he have any other way of saving Thomas's argument except...

<summary>Pico critiques Thomas Aquinas’s view that religious images (specifically the Cross) should be adored with latria, siding instead with theologians who argue such worship is only incidental or indirect. He warns that Aquinas’s position—that even the physical, inanimate wood of the Cross deserves adoration—is theologically "dangerous."</summary>

### JOANNES PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

Pico says that Thomas himself seems to have later felt differently in his *Summa* <note>Referring to the *Summa Theologiae*, the massive compendium of theology by Thomas Aquinas.</note>. From these points, therefore, it can be clearly seen that my conclusion is Catholic and more reasonable than its opposite, and more in harmony with the common way of the theologians. Briefly recapitulating its meaning, I say that this proposition, "The cross of Christ <margin>Recapitulation of the sense of the conclusion</margin> is adored," can have two senses. One is the proper sense: namely, that the cross of Christ—whether as a physical object, or as an image, or as a partial or total object—is adored as the final point <term>terminus: the intended end-point or goal of an action.</term> of the adoration. And this is the sense which Thomas intends and which I deny. The other is the improper sense of the said proposition, and it is this: "The cross of Christ is adored," meaning Christ is adored *in* it as in a reminder of Him, as if He were present in Himself. And this sense I grant, and with the Church I pray, saying: "O Cross, hail, our only hope," <note>original: "O crux ave spes unica" — a line from the hymn *Vexilla Regis*.</note> and "We adore Your cross, O Lord." From what has been said, many things can now be made clear. First, it is clear <margin>Many things are deduced</margin> what I meant when I said elsewhere that, following the opinion of Henry <note>Henry of Ghent, a 13th-century philosopher and theologian.</note> and John of Guarra, the image of the <margin>First point</margin> Crucified is owed *hyperdulia* <term>hyperdulia: a level of veneration higher than that given to saints (dulia) but lower than that given to God (latria).</term>. This was to be understood by reason of that which is primarily brought to our memory, which is the humanity of Christ. I said this curtly because I was referring back to those authors whom I considered to have been read and re-read ten times already by these masters, as if they were veterans of the subject.

Second, it is clear that they falsely claimed I deny every mode of the adoration of *latria* <term>latria: the supreme worship and sacrificial devotion due to God alone.</term>. For I <margin>Second point</margin> expressly say in my conclusion that I deny the mode of Thomas. Even if I had not said this, but the proposition stood simply as "neither the cross nor any image is to be adored with *latria*," still, by the force of the language, that proposition would not deny every mode of the adoration of *latria*. For it is clear according to sound logic that the negation or distribution of an equivocal term <note>A word that has multiple, distinct meanings.</note> does not negate or distribute it for every possible meaning. Otherwise, this proposition, "Every dog is a star," would have to be simply granted or simply denied. Therefore, just as one does not say collectively that every celestial dog <note>The "Dog Star," Sirius.</note> and every sea-dog <note>A shark or seal.</note> and every barking dog is a star (although one might say it of each individually), so in this negative statement "The cross is not adored with the adoration of *latria*"—where the word "adored" is equivocal between adoration as a final point and adoration as a reminder—it does not negate every mode of adoration collectively, though it does so individually. Third, it is <margin>Third point</margin> clear that this proposition could be stated thus absolutely and without distinction: "The Cross is not to be adored with the adoration of *latria*," because in the proper sense it is true, or at least more probable than its opposite. The proper sense of a word is more to be attended to by the rigor of speech than the improper sense, in which it is false. For just as an analogical term placed by itself stands for its most famous meaning, so a word having both a proper and an improper sense, if spoken without specification, is to be taken more according to its proper sense than its improper one. And therefore, as I said, I could have put it forward without distinction, intending to declare the sense in which I understood it during the debate. From this I infer that although in <margin>Note</margin> a multi-faceted proposition it might perhaps be better to do as I did—that is, to determine the sense in which it is put forward rather than putting it forward indistinctly—there is nonetheless a greater defect in condemning a proposition as false simply and without distinction when it is true in its proper sense, just because it is false in an improper sense. I wanted to note this here not only for this conclusion, in which I determinately deny the mode of Thomas, but also on account of many other conclusions which, although they have a Catholic sense (which I always promised to declare, as I am declaring now), were nevertheless condemned simply and without distinction. Truly, however it may be regarding my conclusion, they cannot excuse their condemnation of it from being an error. I clearly declare it thus: this was formally their determination, because they denied every mode of the adoration of *latria* toward the cross, according to the way of the Catholic doctors and the prayer which the universal Church makes to the cross. Therefore, we say the aforementioned conclusion is scandalous, offensive to pious ears, and against the custom of the universal Church. This was precisely their judgment. First, let them say...

# ->APOLOGY<-

It seems that God could **substantify** and **supposit** <term>supposit: A technical term in Scholastic theology meaning to provide the personal subject or "hypostasis" that sustains a particular nature.</term> any nature whatsoever. The second reason is that during the **three days** <note>original: "triduo." The period between Christ's death and resurrection.</note>, God supposited the body that was in the tomb, which nonetheless was not rational at that time. And just as He supposited it for those three days, He could have supposited it for as long a time as He wished. These are the two principal foundations of the opposing opinion. And these very points, as seen in the recitation of his opinion, **Henry** <note>Henry of Ghent (c. 1217–1293), a major Scholastic philosopher whose views Pico is examining.</note> brings against himself. 

<margin>Solution to the first reason</margin> To the first reason, as we have seen, he responds that it is true that the fullness of all "being" is in God, and every reason for **substantifying** and **suppositing** is found most fully in Him. However, this is not the total cause of the **assumability** of any nature, but rather a co-cause. For unless there were an "Assumer" [God], He could not assume. But beyond this, something is required in the thing being assumed by which it is "assumable"; and this is the **reason of the image** <note>The "imago Dei" or reflection of God's nature.</note> and, ultimately, a supernatural aptitude for elevation to **beatific operation** <term>beatific operation: The activity of the soul in heaven where it directly perceives and enjoys God.</term>. Since this is found only in an intellectual nature, it seems fitting that only such a nature is "assumable." For it seems reasonable that a nature which cannot be elevated to the **second act** <note>In Aristotelian terms, the "first act" is existence or capacity; the "second act" is the actual functioning or operation of that capacity (here, knowing God).</note> cannot even be elevated to the first. From this response, it seems Henry wishes to maintain that nothing is taken away from **divine omnipotence**. Indeed, everything that those [opponents] claim to be in God, concluding that He can thus supposit anything, Henry also attributes to God. Nor does he deny that, by reason of what is required on the part of the Assumer, God most fully possesses the power to assume any nature. Rather, he says this limit exists because an irrational nature is itself not "assumable"—not because of a defect in divine omnipotence, but rather because of the **excellence of the divine nature** and the **unfitting deficiency of the irrational nature**. 

<margin>A multi-part second solution: Part One</margin> To the second reason, it seems many things can be said. First is the response of Henry, who says that He assumed the nature of that body insofar as it was ordered toward an intellectual soul; by reason of this ordering, even the body itself can be called "intellectual" in a **ministerial** and **dispositional** sense. And to respond more completely, it must be said that when it is stated that nothing can be assumed by God except an intellectual nature, it is understood that nothing *besides* that can be assumed in such a way that it is the **primary assumed thing** and the whole, adequate object of the assumption. The body in the tomb, however, was not assumed in that way, as is evident, but only as a part of the **rational nature** which was the total and primary thing assumed. 

Furthermore, perhaps someone might say <margin>Second part</margin> that the body was not properly said to be "supposited" during those three days, because it is not a nature that can be supposited by its own individual subject. Hence, it could consequently be said, not improbably, that to terminate the dependence of the nature of that body is not the same as to "supposit" it. Otherwise, everything that terminates the dependence or leaning of a part would "supposit" it, which is not said to be the case. Thus, although the **Word** <note>The Logos, the second person of the Trinity.</note> during the three days terminated this dependence of the body—which the entire humanity would have terminated—and by virtue of this, the body in the three days communicated to Christ its **idiom** <term>idiom: From "communicatio idiomatum," a theological rule where properties of the human nature (like "lying in a tomb") are attributed to the Person of the Word.</term> of "lying in the tomb," nevertheless, He did not properly "supposit" the body as He would supposit a human nature. The most evident sign of this is that the nature of that body did not communicate to Christ the idiom "body" during the three days in the same way the human nature had communicated to Him (and still communicates) the idiom **"man"** in a **concrete** sense. 

And so the response is clear to the aforementioned objections against the opinion of Henry, who seems to say this concerning other irrational natures: that the Word could not assume them through **interpenetration** <note>original: "circumincessionem."</note> or "supposit" them with a "supposition" that has a final cause. For he himself says that no purpose could exist for the assumption of any nature other than an intellectual one, because assumption exists only for the **promotion** of the assumed nature—a promotion which only an intellectual nature is capable of receiving. 

<margin>Augustine</margin> Hence **Augustine** says in his commentary on John: "the Word wished to be born of man, so that you might safely be born of God" <note>original: "uerbum uoluit naſci ex homine: ut tu ſecurus naſcereris ex deo."</note>. From this, it seems that God would have been born in vain from any other nature that is not born of God through grace. From these points, it can be clear that not irrationally...

<summary>Pico addresses arguments that God's omnipotence should allow Him to assume any creature, explaining that only intellectual natures are "assumable" because they alone can be elevated to know God. He clarifies the status of Christ's body in the tomb, arguing it was assumed only as part of a rational whole, not as an independent irrational nature.</summary>

# ->GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA<-

I can hardly have an explicit act of contradicting this opinion in particular. And because these masters [my accusers] were especially insistent that such conclusions should not even be disputed because of the **scandal** <note>In a theological context, "scandal" refers to an obstacle to faith or something that shocks the religious sensibilities of the common people.</note> they might cause, I wish to say this regarding that conclusion: even if the opposite view were truer and more in line with the common path, nevertheless, if it were publicly disputed, it would be far more scandalous among the common people and offensive to **pious ears** <note>original: "piarum aurium offensiva." A standard legal phrase used by the Church to describe ideas that, while not necessarily heretical, are distressing to the faithful.</note>. For what unrefined or simple person would not be offended if they heard someone saying it is possible that these propositions are true: **"God is a donkey"** or **"God is wood"**? What if they heard those things which many who follow the aforementioned opinion [of my accusers] concede: **"God can be damned to hell"**; **"God could be tortured by the devil in hell"**; or **"The devil can be God"**? 

While these things may cause no scandal among many learned men when speaking of **absolute power** <term>absolute power: (Latin: "potentia absoluta") The theological concept of what God could do through His omnipotence, regardless of the laws of nature or His current decrees.</term>, the common and simple folk would certainly be much more offended than if they heard that **a donkey cannot be united to the divine nature in the unity of a "supposit"** <term>supposit: The personal subject that "owns" or sustains a nature. Here, Pico argues a donkey's nature cannot be "owned" by God as a person.</term> as is stated in the manner already declared in my conclusion. These fathers [my accusers] have said that, by the **force of the words** <note>original: "ex vi sermonis." This refers to the literal, grammatical meaning of the text without considering the author's intent.</note>, my statement derogates from divine omnipotence and therefore **savors of heresy** <note>original: "sapere haeresim." A technical legal grade of suspicion where a statement sounds like heresy but hasn't been formally proven as such.</note>. I do not know what logic, or rather what theology, they are leaning on. 

For let them tell me, I pray: does he who says he does not assent to a proposition say—by the rigor of the words—the opposite of that conclusion to which he does not assent? Let them say whether this sequence of logic holds: "I do not assent to" or "I do not have an act of assent for this conclusion: 'The Pope is sitting'"; therefore, "I believe this: 'The Pope is not sitting.'" Would not the first part be true of a man who is **sleeping**? Such a man would have no act of assent at all, yet the second part [the conclusion that he believes the opposite] would be false. Furthermore, if the present conclusion were to derogate from divine omnipotence according to true theology, it would not merely "savor of heresy," but should be judged **heretical**. Indeed, even a sleeping Catholic or a small child who does not yet have the use of reason—and who thus has no act of assent to the proposition "God can supposit any created nature"—would be a heretic, or at least would err in the faith; yet no one would say such a thing. From this it is clear that their condemnation is not right.

For this was formally their determination, considering the response of the proponent himself [Pico] and the opinion, motives, and reasons of **Henry**, upon whose opinion the one posing the conclusion relies: "It has seemed to us that the aforementioned conclusion, by the force of the words, derogates from divine omnipotence, and through this, it savors of heresy." 

First, they were deceived because when I said I was following **Henry** in this, they did not understand that by the pronoun "this" I was denoting the conclusion itself about which they were asking for an explanation. Therefore, "in this"—that is, in the conclusion itself—that is, in **not assenting** to this: "God can [supposit] any nature, etc.", I said I followed Henry. I did not mean by "this" the opinion that says "God *cannot* supposit every nature." 

But perhaps they believed there was no difference between one statement and the other. Yet, if they are learned theologians, they ought to know the difference between **not explicitly believing** that something is possible by the power of God, and **explicitly disbelieving** it. Second, they ought to remember that from their words it follows that the famous Henry—who because of the excellence of his teaching is called the **Solemn Doctor** <margin>Henry, the Solemn Doctor</margin>—must have died a heretic. For as was seen above, in his old age he inclined toward this opinion and remained in it: namely, that not every nature can be "supposited" by God. Third, just as in the condemnation of the previous conclusion, so also in this one: however it may be regarding the conclusion itself, they are entirely in error. For if it were true, as they say, that the conclusion is against the omnipotence of God, then the conclusion is **simply heretical**, and not merely "savoring of heresy" as they claim. Fourth and finally, they erred because even if Henry's opinion were entirely heretical, my conclusion—by the force of the words—would not be heretical, because it does not logically imply that opinion, as has been most extensively declared. And yet, they specifically condemned it "by the force of the words."

## ->FIFTH QUESTION CONCERNING NATURAL MAGIC AND THE HEBREW KABBALAH<-

**T**he fourth conclusion condemned by those men was this: **"There is no science that provides us with more certainty of the divinity of Christ than magic and Kabbalah."** <note>original: "Nulla est sciētia quæ nos magis certificet de diuinitate Christi q̃ magia & cabala." In explaining this conclusion, I stated that among the sciences—specifically those sciences that do not rely on revelation <term>revelation: Knowledge given directly by God, such as scripture, as opposed to knowledge discovered through human reason or observation.</term> in their method of proceeding, their principles, or their conclusions—there is none that provides us with more certainty (in the way that sciences discovered by human effort can provide certainty) than that **magic** about which I have posited conclusions, which is a branch of **natural science**, and that branch of **Kabbalah** which is a science and is not "revealed theology." 

Those masters <note>Pico's accusers, the papal commission appointed by Pope Innocent VIII.</note> argued that my explanation did not align with the intent of the words in the aforementioned conclusion. They claimed that the conclusion, according to the **literal force of the words** <note>original: "de uirtute sermonis." A legalistic way of saying "as it is written," ignoring any nuance or authorial intent.</note>, was false, erroneous, and heretical. Regarding this condemnation of theirs, 

<margin>First</margin>

I ask that we examine individually how many things are being condemned. First, let them tell me how it can be...

**->GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA<-**

...standing <note>The text begins mid-word, likely concluding a phrase about human understanding or intellect.</note> through which it is known that those works which Christ performed could not be done through natural powers. Therefore, I placed this proposition among my magical conclusions: **"The miracles of Christ could not be performed through magic,"** <note>This refers to one of Pico's 900 Theses where he argues that by knowing the full extent of natural magic, one can prove Christ's miracles were truly supernatural.</note> specifically that conclusion whose truth can be obtained from this science. 

And thus it is clear that the judgment of those masters <note>The papal commission of theologians appointed to examine Pico's work.</note> was not truly "masterly," especially since they condemn the statement based on the **literal force of the words** <term>literal force of the words: original: "de uirtute sermonis," a scholastic legal term meaning the strict, technical meaning of a sentence as written, regardless of the author’s intended meaning.</term>. This statement is such that even if the meaning we described were not orthodox, the statement itself would still not be condemned in its own right. This is because, according to the literal force of the words, it does not imply that [heretical] sense; for it is a negative proposition that must be explained disjunctively through three categorical propositions, as was stated above. <note>Pico is using a technical point of scholastic logic to argue that his accusers are misreading his grammar to find heresy where there is none.</note>

# APOLOGY

<margin>The Great Persian Magi</margin> Our doctors <note>theologians and authorities of the Church</note> say that all magic is prohibited. If, therefore, all magic is prohibited, it follows that none is permitted. But you say that some magic is not prohibited; therefore, you stand in contradiction to the doctors of the Church.

<margin>Pythagoras</margin> Truly, the ignorance of those speaking this way is marvelous. First, indeed, the assigning of names is not something done by us today; rather, we use names and their meanings according to the custom of the ancients. If, therefore, those ancients wished to call this part of natural science "magic," why do you wish me to innovate new names? And why should that which they named "magic" be called "geometry" or "arithmetic" by me?

<margin>Druids</margin> I am neither the first nor the latest to call this science "magic." Many before me, both holy and learned men, have done so. Let *them* be brought to court; let *them* be condemned, if it is a damnable thing for this science to be called by this name. Nevertheless, I shall show that this naming was correctly established:

# GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

...approving this natural magic <note>Pico is distinguishing between "natural magic," which uses the hidden powers of nature, and "diabolical magic," which involves demons.</note> as something distinct from superstitious and diabolical practices is not only free from scandal, but can even be edifying to the simple-minded. From this, I have seen many people who, upon hearing that the Magi came to adore Christ, believe that the name "magi" means nothing other than "necromancers" <note>Those who communicate with the dead or demons.</note>. <margin>Note</margin> From this, they mistakenly argue that magic is not prohibited and is not against the Christian faith, since practitioners of magic were the first to adore Christ himself. It is useful, therefore, to have taught the faithful that when they hear the word "magus," they should not always understand it to mean a worshipper of demons. And when they hear that among the Persians, the Magi were held in the highest honor and reverence because of their learning and wisdom, let them know that those men were philosophers, not necromancers—whom all nations have always chased away and treated poorly as destructive, harmful, and indeed pestilential to the people.

Similarly, when they read that Albert <note>Albert the Great (c. 1200–1280), a renowned medieval theologian and scientist.</note> <margin>Albert</margin> spent much time on "experiments of magic," let them understand this as natural magic and not the prohibited kind. This ensures that they do not devote themselves to what is forbidden by presuming they may do what was permitted to such a great man. Therefore, my magical conclusions remove scandals from the minds of the faithful rather than creating them. Furthermore, if they ever read in the works of the Doctors <note>Authoritative theologians of the Church.</note> that "all magic is prohibited," they will immediately understand from the reasons for that prohibition that those authors are speaking only of that magic which has commerce with demons, and that they intend nothing concerning natural magic. For, as Hilary says, <margin>Hilary</margin> <note>Saint Hilary of Poitiers (c. 310–367), an early Church Father.</note> "the understanding of words must be taken from the reasons for speaking them." <note>original: "intelligentia dictoꝝ ex cauſis aſſumenda dicendi." This is a legal and theological principle: to understand a law, you must understand the problem it was meant to solve.</note>

But if they wish to return to the strict force of the words, they can know from logic that the negation or distribution of a "multiple term" <note>A word with more than one meaning, or an equivocal term.</note> does not negate or distribute that term for every possible meaning simultaneously. Therefore, since this term "magic" is equivocal—referring to both the superstitious and the natural—a general distribution added to it does not apply to every possible meaning joined together. Rather, from the statement that "all magic is prohibited," it will be understood only that all species of *superstitious* magic are prohibited, as those are all grouped under one name and one definition. For many types are indeed prohibited, and all these things are clear and lucid even to the moderately learned.

In no way, therefore, should my magical conclusions have been suspect to these masters. For, as I said in my first conclusion, I reject all magic prohibited by the Church, damning and detesting it, and protesting that I speak only of natural magic. I declared more expressly through a special conclusion that through this magic, we perform nothing except by activating or uniting natural virtues. For thus says the eleventh of the magical conclusions: "The wonders of the magical art exist only through the union and actuation of those things which are contained seminally and separately in nature." And it is the same thing I said in the thirteenth conclusion: that to practice magic is nothing other than **to marry the world.** <note>original: "maritare mundū." A famous phrase of Pico's, suggesting that the magus acts as a priest or matchmaker, bringing together celestial influences and earthly materials to produce wonders.</note>

Furthermore, I intend for the aforementioned specification and restriction of my intention toward natural magic to be applied to every particular conclusion. And so, when I speak of the "activity of characters and figures" <note>symbols and geometric shapes used in Renaissance magic.</note> in a magical work, I am speaking of their true and natural activity. For it is clear that they possess such activity according to all philosophers, both in how they act and in how they are acted upon. And although, according to the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle, who focused on physical, material causes.</note>, they possess far less activity and power than material qualities, the Pythagoreans <margin>Pythagoreans</margin> would say otherwise. In conclusion 24, I call their philosophy a "more secret philosophy" because it is less known and less in use. They argue that just as mathematical things are more "formal" <note>Existing in the mind or as pure structure.</note> than physical things, they are also more "actual" <note>Having a more direct and powerful reality.</note>. And just as they depend less on matter for their existence, so too they depend less on matter for their operation. And so, what I said about their greater power—even if the disagreement between Pythagoreans and Peripatetics is indifferent to the faith—I did not state as something absolute in itself, but as a consequence of the "secret philosophy" of the Pythagoreans, to be understood in the manner described. Among all mathematical things, it is their opinion that numbers are more formal and thus more actual; and among the odd numbers, the number three <note>the "ternary."</note> is foremost. Because it is the first odd number, and the first in any genus is the most perfect in that genus...

# DEFENSE

...and it goes through even numbers to ten <note>original: "denarium"</note>, which is the sum of all numbers, as is evident. For beyond ten, we do not count except by repetition. Furthermore, Catholic doctors <note>Theologians and authorities recognized by the Church.</note> attribute effectiveness and power to numbers, both for good and for evil. <margin>Hilary</margin> Hence Hilary, in his commentary on the Psalms, addresses the reason why the order of the Psalms is not according to history—often a Psalm that was composed earlier is placed later in the sequence. He says: "It must not be ignored that among the Hebrews, the numbering of the Psalms is indistinct and they were recorded without any notation of order. For they do not mark them as first, second, third, fiftieth, or hundredth; rather, they are mixed together into one without any prescription of order. <margin>Ezra</margin> For Ezra <note>original: "Hesdras"; the biblical scribe and priest credited with reconstituting the Jewish scriptures after the Babylonian exile.</note>, as ancient traditions relate, collected and brought them back into one volume after they had been disorganized and scattered due to the diversity of authors and times. But the seventy elders <note>The Septuagint: the 72 Jewish scholars who, according to tradition, translated the Hebrew Bible into Greek.</note>, remaining in the synagogue to guard the law and the doctrine according to the tradition of Moses—after the care of translating the entire law from the Hebrew to the Greek language was mandated to them by King Antiochus <note>Pico likely refers to Ptolemy II Philadelphus; historical accounts of the Septuagint's origin vary.</note>—understanding the powers of the Psalms through spiritual and celestial knowledge, reduced them to a number and order. They assigned each number according to its own efficiency and perfection, arranging the order of the Psalms as complete and effective works." This is <margin>Jerome</margin> Hilary's text word for word. From this, it is most clearly evident that number bestows power and effectiveness. Jerome, too, against Jovinian, says that the number twenty is unlucky, being the number in which Jacob served, and Joseph was sold, and which Esau loved when receiving certain gifts. In the same place, he praises the number ten, saying he has often spoken of its glories. And in the same book, chapter eight, he says that for this reason, on the second day of creation, it was not said: *and God saw that it was good* <note>original: "et vidit deus quoniam bonum"; Genesis 1:6-8 omits the usual blessing, which Jerome interprets as a slight against the number two.</note>, because the number two <note>original: "binarius"</note> is evil <note>In this tradition, "two" represents division and discord, moving away from the "one" (unity).</note>. Furthermore, from the number two, he draws an argument against those who marry twice <note>original: "bigamos"</note>; and for this reason, he says all the unclean animals entered into Noah's ark in pairs, but the clean ones in groups of seven. <margin>Basil</margin> You will find a hundred similar things in Basil, <margin>Gregory of Nazianzus</margin> Gregory of Nazianzus, Ambrose, <margin>Ambrose</margin> Origen, Augustine, and others. Again, it is not without mystery, but because of the hidden property of the number itself, that they wish it to be that Moses fasted for forty days, Elijah for forty, and Christ for forty; and that Christ ascended forty days after the resurrection; and was in the underworld for forty hours; and that after forty days Nineveh—which is a type or figure of this world—would be subverted; and the Lord rained upon the earth for the same number of days and nights. They also say it contains a great sacrament that in the number fifty, in which the remission of sins occurs <note>A reference to the Year of Jubilee in Leviticus.</note>, the Holy Spirit also descended. And in that same number is placed the Psalm *Have mercy on me, O God* <note>original: "Miserere mei deus"; Psalm 50 in the Vulgate (Psalm 51 in modern Bibles).</note>, which <margin>Hilary</margin> Hilary and Origen especially note. And in all things, the mysteries of the Cabalists <note>Practitioners of Kabbalah, Jewish mysticism.</note> greatly agree with these, for they <margin>Origen</margin> attribute the number fifty to the Holy Spirit, which among them is also signified by fire—in which form and in which number of days it descended upon the apostles. <margin>Note</margin> And among them, the Holy Spirit is the third person or property in divine matters, proceeding from the first and from the second; which second is called Wisdom and proceeds from the first; and it differs from both only by the reason of procession—just as, for instance, that which proceeds differs from those from whom it proceeds, although it is nevertheless the same with them in substance and essence. The Cabalists say these things expressly; yet their words, which were brought forward by me against the Jews, were being loathed by these masters as suspect regarding the faith. <margin>What the sin against the Holy Spirit properly is.</margin> Moreover, they also call that same third property "Repentance," which agrees with what was just said: that the same number is attributed to the Holy Spirit as to the sacrament of Penance. From this we can also gather that the sin against the Holy Spirit is properly the sin of impenitence <note>The refusal to repent or accept God's mercy.</note>, which is not forgiven in this world nor in the future. Finally, Moses received a twofold Law on Mount Sinai: a literal and a spiritual one. <margin>Rabbi Ishmael</margin> He wrote down the former and, by God's command, communicated it to the people. He likewise commanded them not to write it down, but to reveal it to their successors by living voice <note>original: "uiua uoce"; the tradition of oral teaching.</note>, then they to others, and so on in a perpetual order. <margin>Rabbi Nachman</margin> From which manner of tradition, this science—received through the successive reception of one from another—was itself called the science of Kabbalah, which is the same as the "science of reception," <margin>The origin of "Kabbalah"</margin> because "Kabbalah" signifies the same thing among the Hebrews as [reception] does among us.

->APOLOGIA<-

Among our people, the **Art of Lull** <note>original: "Ars Rai"; referring to the system of logic and mysticism developed by Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1316).</note> is called the **Art of Raymond**; although perhaps they proceed in a different manner.
