# JOHN PICO OF MIRANDOLA

...that his determination can hardly be defended from error, because if it were the case that the conclusion intended to preserve the truth of the sacrament according to the institution of Christ which the Church holds (as they say), then it is not only erroneous but simply heretical. If, however, the meaning of the conclusion is the one explained by me, it is not only not erroneous in faith, but rather it is erroneous to say the opposite. For there are many things which are heretical regarding "how things are" <note>original: "de sic esse"</note>, whose opposite regarding "what is possible" <note>original: "de possibili"</note> would be heretical. For example, to say that the Father was incarnated is heretical regarding "how things are," but to say that the Father *could* be incarnated is not only not heretical, but its opposite is heretical <note>Pico is using a classic scholastic argument: God has the power to do many things He chose not to do. Denying God's power to do them is a greater error than misidentifying what He actually did.</note>. Let these things suffice for the declaration of the conclusion and its defense.

But let us, for the sake of scholastic exercise, leaving aside my conclusion, see: <margin>Question</margin> Whether it is true that the body of Christ could be on the altar in another way than through the conversion of the bread into it—namely, through the **sustenance of the bread-nature** <note>original: "paneitatis"</note> in the divine person <note>term: "supposito" (person/subsistence); in theology, this refers to the underlying identity (the Word) that "holds up" a nature.</note> together with the assumed humanity, so that there would be one person in three natures: namely, divinity, humanity, and bread-nature. By reason of the person, there would be a predication of each nature in concrete relation to the person taken from the other; there would be a **communication of properties** <note>term: "communicatio idiomatum" (communication of properties); the theological rule where attributes of one nature (like "eating") are attributed to the person who possesses both natures (God).</note>, such that "God is bread" and "man," and vice versa; and "Christ the man is on the altar" just as "Christ the bread is on the altar," and similar things. And this would be sacramentally or by the power of the sacrament, if a power for this were divinely given to the sacred word. Nor shall we concern ourselves with whether the phrase "This is my body" would suffice for this with the aforementioned power, or if something else would be required.

And first, we argue for the affirmative side <margin>First argument for the affirmative side.</margin> that this should be held, because **John Damascene** <note>original: "Damā."; John of Damascus (c. 675–749), an influential Syrian monk and Church Father.</note> seems to hold this as a fact—namely, that the sacrament exists through **assumption**. For thus he says when asked how the bread is the body of Christ and the wine and water are the blood of Christ: "I say to you also, the Holy Spirit comes upon it and does that which is above reason and intellect. The bread and wine are assumed," and further in the same place: "and just as in baptism, because it is the custom for men to be washed with water and anointed with oil, <margin>Damascene.</margin> God joined water and the grace of the Holy Spirit, and made it the bath of regeneration; so, because it is the custom for men to eat bread and drink wine, God joined his divinity to them and makes them his body and blood." And further in the same chapter, speaking of this sacrament of the altar: "Isaiah saw a burning coal; but a coal is not simple wood, but wood united to fire. So also the bread of communion is not simple bread, but united to the divinity." <margin>Dionysius</margin> **Dionysius** <note>original: "Dionysius"; referring to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century theologian whose works were highly authoritative in the Middle Ages.</note>, however, in the third chapter of *The Ecclesiastical Hierarchy*, calls this sacrament "assumption." Therefore, what these doctors seem to say regarding "how it is" can much more easily be held regarding "what is possible."

Secondly, it is argued <margin>Second argument.</margin> because, according to **Augustine** <note>original: "Aug. ad Volusianū"; St. Augustine's Letter 137 to Volusianus.</note> in his letter to Volusianus, in miraculous things "the whole reason for the deed is the power of the Doer." Thus, to restrict this wonderful sacrament to a specific mode of defense that is not explicitly found in the canon of Scripture or the Church's determination is to restrict divine power to the capacity of our intellect—which is dangerous, and against Augustine, who says in that same place: "If a reason is sought, it will not be wonderful; if an example is provided, it will not be unique. Let us grant that God can do something that we confess we cannot investigate."

Thirdly, it is argued: <margin>Third argument.</margin> that whose opposite is not clearly held from the sayings of the saints as a matter of fact, can much more be held as a matter of possibility. But the opposite of this—namely, that as a fact the **bread-nature** <note>original: "paneitas"</note> remains on the altar substantiated by the divine person—is not clearly found in the sayings of the saints; therefore, etc. This is proved because that saying of <margin>Gregory</margin> **Gregory** <note>original: "Gregorius"; Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604).</note> in his Easter homily: "the appearance <note>original: "species"</note> and likeness are names of things that were before," namely bread and wine; those holding this opinion explain "what they were before" to mean they were *only* that; but now they are not *only* that because the body of Christ is hidden there. Likewise, that saying of <margin>Ambrose</margin> **Ambrose** <note>original: "Ambro."; St. Ambrose of Milan (c. 340–397).</note> that "the power of God which creates creatures from nothing, here changes the creatures"; and other sayings which state that bread and wine do not remain after consecration but are converted. These will be explained such that the bread which *was* bread does not remain, even though the "bread-nature" is the same; and this because...

<margin>Fourth argument</margin> Fourthly, it is argued thus. This opinion is approved regarding "how things are" in the confession of Berengar, which was approved by Pope Nicholas in Rome before 114 bishops: therefore, it can be held much more as a possibility. <margin>Berengar</margin> The premise is deduced thus: because Berengar confesses that after the consecration, not only the sacrament but also the true body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ are on the altar; and that they are handled sensibly, not only sacramentally but in truth, by the hands of priests, broken, and ground by the teeth of the faithful. These words seem impossible to be taken in a clear and plain sense—such as the words of a confession so solemnly approved ought to be—unless by the "sustenance" <note>original: "substentiationem"</note> of breadness in the person of God with the body of Christ in the aforementioned way. 

This would mean that it is the same body of Christ: of man and of bread. Thus, it would be whole insofar as it is the body of a man, and ground insofar as it is bread; just as Christ on the cross died and lived, but the former as man and the latter insofar as God. <margin>Master of the Sentences</margin> That some have taken the words of the aforementioned confession in this way is clear from the **Master of the Sentences** <note>The "Master of the Sentences" is Peter Lombard, whose textbook was the standard for all medieval theology students.</note> in Book 4, Distinction 7. His words are these: "Others hand down that the body of Christ is essentially broken and divided, and yet remains whole and incorruptible; they assert they gather this from the confession of Berengar, who confessed before Pope Nicholas and many bishops that the bread and wine placed on the altar after consecration are not only a sacrament but also the true body and blood of Christ; and are sensibly, not only in the sacrament but also in truth, handled and broken by the hands of priests, and ground by the teeth of the faithful." 

Behold, the confession of Berengar, as heard and examined by the Church, contains the idea that the body of Christ is ground by the teeth of the faithful not in sacrament only, but in truth. This, if taken plainly, would have truth through the communication of idioms: for it is ground by the teeth according to the "breadness," and remains whole according to the humanity. 

Now, if anyone wishes to explain the said confession by saying that the phrase "in truth and not in sacrament only" refers only to the immediate word—namely, being "handled by the hands of priests"—and that the following words refer to the "species" <note>term: "species" (appearances); the Catholic view that only the appearance of bread (taste, color) remains, not its substance.</note> or to the outward sacrament, under which the broken and ground body of Christ is received whole: it seems that the words of the confession are then not being accepted plainly as they lie and as they sound on the surface. Yet the words of a confession so examined ought to be accepted without violent exposition and extortion, according to the sense they openly present. 

<margin>First [argument] to the opposite</margin> But it is argued to the contrary: because this opinion regarding the remaining of the substance of bread on the altar has been condemned by the Church, it must therefore be avoided as heretical. <margin>First response</margin> It is answered by those who hold this opinion: first, that it was condemned as "how things are," not as "what is possible." <margin>Second response</margin> Second, that the condemned opinion differs from this one, which posits that the breadness remains hypostatized by the Word-man. 

<margin>Difference between this opinion and the condemned opinion</margin> For that condemned opinion posits multiple persons <note>original: "supposita"</note> of the man Christ and of the bread after consecration; this one posits one Person in three natures—just as in the Divine there is one nature in three Persons. That opinion posits that the bread and wine remain; this one does not, but rather "another bread," even though it is the same breadness. From that condemned opinion, it follows that the body of Christ cannot truly be on the altar under the sacrament, since the bread is in no way changed. But from this opinion, it does not follow, since it posits that the bread is changed and is breadness only as to its being. From that opinion, it is not verified that "the bread is the body of Christ," since there are two persons. From this one, however, it is verified because of the unity of the Person, which is one in two natures. From that condemned opinion, it follows that whatever is in this sacrament is not to be adored with **latria** <note>term: "latria" (supreme worship); in Catholic theology, this is the worship due to God alone. Here, Pico distinguishes between Christ *being* a body (genus) and the body being merely a *part* of him.</note> and not merely as a part; thus, it concerns the body which is Christ himself, derived from the "corporeity" which is a nature and can be predicated **directly** <note>term: "in recto"; a logical term meaning the subject is identified directly with the predicate (e.g., "This man is Christ").</note>. And when it is argued that Christ’s body should not be spoken of as a "body" in the sense of a genus, the response is: quite the contrary. Just as we speak of a "creature of salt" (meaning that which *is* salt) and the "Word of God" (meaning the Word which *is* God), and just as it is said, "By the Word of the Lord" (meaning the Word which is God) "the heavens were established." We also say that the substance of matter remains throughout every natural transformation—that is, the substance which *is* matter. In the same way, it is said by my opponents that the substance of the bread is converted into the body of Christ—meaning the substance which *is* bread, <margin>Damascene</margin> not just a part of the bread. Thus also John of Damascus, in Book III, Chapter 17, accepts the "flesh of Christ" (that is, the flesh which is Christ) as a genus, saying that the "flesh of the Lord is said to be deified and consubstantial with God." Perhaps a sacramental power would be divinely given to any words whatsoever; indeed, God could grant to these words—"This is my body"—any power he chooses, even if they were not naturally significant of the act, because the power of God is not <margin>Response to the third point in opposition.</margin> bound to the human meaning of words. Furthermore, when it is argued that even if the bread were the body (and vice versa), it does not follow that where there is bread, there is the body on the altar, the response is that it most certainly does follow. For whatever is said of the predicate is also said of the subject. For instance, because God is man and God is everywhere, it follows that the man Christ is everywhere as God is; and just as God is enclosed in the cradle, is the son of a Virgin, and sucks at the breast as the man Christ, so too it follows that if the man Christ is bread (and vice versa), then if the bread is on the altar, Christ the man is also there—and not only by reason of his being everywhere as God, but because the bread is on the altar. For the properties of the assumed natures are shared on the part of the subject, especially because the subject stands for the **person** <note>original: "supposito"; the individual identity of Christ.</note>. This is said on the part of the subject because, on the part of the predicate, the properties are perhaps not necessarily shared, because there the term stands for the nature itself. Hence, it is perhaps not necessary that Christ be man everywhere just because he is God everywhere, even though on the part of the subject, the man Christ is everywhere. Nor is the argument about the soul and body during the **three days** <note>term: "the three days"; the period between Christ's death and resurrection when his soul and body were separated but both remained united to his divinity.</note> valid, because they were not then united in the person in such a way that they were predicated of the person or of each other, since they were united as parts of a single nature. Therefore, it is not necessary for them to share properties among themselves like those natures which are predicated of one another. However, it is certain that even if it does not follow <margin>First response to the fourth point.</margin> by necessity, it follows at least as a possibility. As for the claim that if there is a "sustaining" of the bread’s essence, it must end in the same thing we say the "conversion" ends in (namely, the body), the response is that <margin>Second response.</margin> there is no necessity for this. # GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

...is a man who is visibly on the altar; and that he is the food of the faithful by reason of the **bread-ness** <note>term: "bread-ness" (paneitas); a scholastic term referring to the essential nature or "what-ness" of bread.</note> he has assumed, just as Christ as God began to be in the lap or womb of his mother in a new way by reason of the humanity he assumed. Regarding what is said about the assumption of a pre-existing bread-ness into his own **person** <note>term: "person" (suppositum); the underlying individual identity. Pico argues that just as the Word "holds" human nature, it could "hold" the nature of bread.</note>: <margin>Response to the sixth [objection].</margin> The response is that God can assume any "assumable nature" that pre-exists in its own personhood, and in the act of assuming it, deprive it of its own independent existence and draw it into His own being. For it is well-established that the **Word** <note>term: "the Word" (Verbum); the Second Person of the Trinity, Jesus Christ in his divine nature.</note> could set aside his human nature, which would then immediately have its own independent subsistence and the character of a person—even though it does not have this while united to the Word—and it would be the same humanity in essence that was previously united. Therefore, in a similar way, He could assume a nature (the bread) that previously existed in its own personhood. It would then be the same nature, now assumed, which was previously not assumed.

But when it is argued that power cannot be conferred upon the Word for this purpose: perhaps it can, and perhaps it cannot. <margin>Response to the seventh [objection].</margin> If an **inherent power** <note>term: "inherent power"; a capacity that lives "inside" a created thing.</note> cannot be given—because such a power would be a created thing—perhaps an **assisting power** <note>term: "assisting power"; a divine power that works alongside a thing rather than being part of its own nature.</note> can be given, for such a power would be uncreated. And in this way, there would be an "assumption of bread-ness" sacramentally by the power of the Word; this is the same way that great men <note>Pico refers to established theologians like Thomas Aquinas or Duns Scotus.</note> propose that power is conferred upon the sacraments of the New Law. And perhaps if an inherent power can be conferred upon the sacramental word to convert the whole [of the bread] into the whole [of Christ], and especially into something already pre-existing without increasing its size, it can also be conferred for the aforementioned effect; for perhaps to some it will seem that the latter is just as difficult as the former.

Regarding what is said about the **breaking of the fast** <note>The "Eucharistic fast" required priests to have an empty stomach before Mass. Critics argued that if the bread remained, the priest would be "eating" and thus breaking his fast.</note>: <margin>First response to the eighth [objection].</margin> one might respond that the rule about not breaking the natural fast follows the commonly held view—namely, that the substance of the bread does not remain. If we propose that the substance *does* remain, we will say something else. <margin>Second [response].</margin> Or perhaps it will be said that a priest is not said to be "fasting" after taking the sacrament because the substance of the bread is gone; for no matter how much the substance is gone, if a Jew or a Christian were to consume the **sacramental appearances** <note>term: "sacramental appearances" (species); the visible qualities of bread (taste, smell, color) that remain even after the "substance" is gone.</note> as physical food and with the intention of being nourished, he would break his fast. But because the priest does not consume it as physical food, but as a sacrament, the fast is not broken. And it would be similar if the substance of the bread remained: he would still not break his natural fast, provided it was not consumed as physical food.

As for the claim that "Christ does not set aside what he once assumed": <margin>First response to the ninth [objection].</margin> this is said by presupposing that he is only held to have assumed human nature, just as in fact he only assumed that. However, he could assume another nature and set it aside. <margin>Second [response].</margin> It can also be said that if "bread-ness" were assumed by the Word, it would never be set aside by the Word of its own accord or on its part. But it would be set aside **incidentally** <note>term: "incidentally" (per accidens); happening as a side effect rather than by essence. Here, as the bread is digested or "corrupted," the union ends naturally.</note> due to the condition of the assumed nature and its natural defects; He would set it aside because of the corruption of the assumed nature, just as he "set aside" his humanity during the three days [in the tomb]. <margin>Another question.</margin>

But again, let us inquire through discussion whether it can be maintained that the Body—which is a part—is truly on the altar without the conversion of the bread into it. <margin>Argument for the affirmative side.</margin> It seems so: for just as **color** is sustained in a substance as in its subject by means of another **accident** <note>term: "accident"; a quality (like color or shape) that exists only *in* something else. Pico is using the logic of physics to explain how Christ's body can "hold" the bread's qualities.</note>—for example, a surface—not because the surface is the "subject" of the color (since one accident is not the subject of another, as the Philosopher <note>The "Philosopher" always refers to Aristotle.</note> says that a "quality has no quality"), but because color does not exist in a subject except in relation to the surface. In the same way, "bread-ness" can be sustained in the Word by means of the Body. This does not mean the Body is the immediate sustainer of the assumed bread-ness (with the Word being primary), but rather that the bread-ness is not sustained in the person of the Word except in relation to the Body of Christ as a part. For God can establish this order between "assumable natures," even if they do not have that order in their own nature; just as He can take away from some things the natural order they have between themselves—as he did with **heat and the act of burning** in the furnace of the Chaldeans and in many other cases. <note>Pico refers to the biblical story of the three youths in the fiery furnace (Daniel 3), where the fire was hot but lost its "natural" power to burn the skin of the faithful.</note> Therefore, just as color—because it exists in a substance in relation to a surface—is spoken of in connection to the surface as an accidental quality...

<margin>Fourthly</margin> **Fourthly**, [this view is preferred] because it can be explained without a multiplication of miracles. **Fourthly**, because Paul says in the first letter to the Corinthians, chapter 10: <note>original: "Panis quẽ frãgimus nõne participatio corporis dñi est"</note> "The bread which we break, is it not the participation in the body of the Lord?" 

<margin>Fifthly</margin> **Fifthly**, because Christ is sacramentally present where he is directly by the power of the sacrament. However, Christ becomes present on the altar more directly through **assumption** <note>term: "assumption" (assumptio); the act of taking something into oneself. Pico argues that just as the Word "assumed" a human nature to become Jesus, the Word "assumes" the nature of bread in the Eucharist.</note> than through **conversion** <note>term: "conversion" (conversio); the theological term for Transubstantiation, where the substance of bread turns into the substance of Christ's body.</note>. This is because the form of this sacrament, which achieves its effect by what it signifies, more directly achieves that which it more properly signifies. This is the union through assumption, by which the **properties are shared** <note>original: "communicantur idiomata"; a technical term in Christology where the attributes of both the divine and human (or bread) natures are attributed to the one Person of Christ.</note> so that this thing is truly what the formal words <note>The "words of institution" spoken by a priest: "This is my body."</note> <note>original: "hoc est corpus meũ"</note> "this is my body" sound like. It is not, however, a union of conversion, because through conversion the bread is not Christ, nor vice versa; rather, the bread "becomes" Christ or is "converted" into Christ. 

<margin>Sixthly</margin> **Sixthly**, because that method of conversion is intricate and holds many difficulties, whereas this method [of assumption] is clear and accessible. For we already believe in **assumption** through another Article of Faith <note>The Incarnation, where God became man.</note>. Furthermore, whatever things are limited within the same **subject** <note>term: "supposito"; the underlying individual person or subject that "owns" the natures or properties.</note>, wherever one is, the other must be. It is just as wherever there is "loud music," there is also the "whiteness" of the musician <note>A classic Aristotelian logic example: if the musician is white, the music and the whiteness exist in the same person/subject.</note>. I say "limited," however, because if one were limited and the other unlimited, where the limited one was, the unlimited would be, but not necessarily vice versa. But if the bread were assumed, the human body of Christ and the body of the bread would be one in their **subject**, and both would be limited. Therefore, since the assumed bread would be on the altar, the body of Christ would consequently be there as well. Furthermore, the "middle" is closer than the "extreme." If Christ were to assume the bread or "bread-ness," he would do so by means of his **corporeality** <note>The state of having a physical body.</note>; for a less worthy thing to be assumed is done through the mediation of a more worthy thing, according to the fitness of the assumption. Therefore, since the Subject of Christ—the one who assumes—would be on the altar with the assumed bread, much more so would the body of Christ be there, as it would be the medium of the assumption.

<margin>Finally</margin> **Finally**, it seems that the authorities of the Saints regarding "conversion" can nonetheless be upheld while holding to "assumption." Since **being** <note>original: "esse"</note> differs from **essence**, one can be assumed while the other is not. Thus, the Word is not "incarnate" (made flesh) in the same way it is "impanate" (made bread). In the Incarnation, the essence was assumed before it had its own being; thus it never had a being other than the divine being communicated to it, which is why that was an assumption without any conversion of the assumed into the assuming or vice versa. This is why the Church says "not by the conversion of the divinity into flesh"—nor, one should add, vice versa—"but by the assumption of humanity into God." But the pre-existing bread already has both **being** and **essence**. The assumption into the humanity of the Subject consumes the bread's own independent existence—not through **annihilation**, but through the assumption of its substantial essence—and thus perfects this mystery. In this way, all authorities speaking of "transubstantiation" and "conversion" can be understood to refer to the **being** and not to the **essence**. And those authorities saying that after the consecration the bread "does not remain" but "was," are true regarding its **being** <note>Pico is using a highly technical distinction: the "bread-ness" (essence) remains, but its independent "existence" (being) is swallowed up by Christ's existence.</note>, because it remains only according to its essence. From these points, it appears that the body of Christ can truly be sacramentally on the altar through the assumption of "bread-ness" without conversion, just as is currently commonly held through conversion.

<margin>Assumption</margin> Indeed, a good distinction between these three terms—**assumption**, **conversion**, and **annihilation**—cannot be understood except by presupposing the logic of this opinion. We say that something is **assumed** when something that previously possessed a subject-like being of its own is taken up into the new being of a [different] subject. 

<margin>Annihilation</margin> That which simply ceases to be is **annihilated**, such that its reproduction would be a [new] creation. Whether something succeeds it or nothing succeeds it is entirely irrelevant to this definition, because that is entirely external to the thing which ceases to be. 

<margin>Conversion</margin> However, that thing is **converted** which, remaining according to its essence, passes into the being of another subject after losing its own subject-being, and truly becomes that subject. 

<margin>The definition of conversion</margin> This is the true definition of conversion, in which two things are understood: first, that it remains through its essence (which distinguishes it from **annihilation**); and second, that it becomes something else by reason of its subject (which distinguishes it from a thing that is not converted). While it becomes something else by reason of its own subject, it lets go [of its own being], which distinguishes it from **assumption**. However, if one holds the common view of conversion [Transubstantiation], the bread is not "converted" but "annihilated"—and those who wish to...

Those which are discordant, I judge should be cast aside and rejected.

### SEVENTH QUESTION: ON THE SALVATION OF ORIGEN.

<note>A large, ornate initial letter "R" contains a miniature illustration of a man, likely a scholar or saint, set against a natural landscape, marking the start of a new major section.</note> **It is more reasonable to believe that Origen is saved than to believe he is damned.**

These masters <note>The ecclesiastical committee investigating Pico's theses.</note> have said that this conclusion is rash, blameworthy, "smelling of heresy," and contrary to the determination of the universal Church. I, however, to speak of them more modestly, wish to show that their judgment is not correct: that this conclusion is not against the determination of the 
<margin>Seven articles: how the declaration of the conclusion should proceed.</margin>
Church, and furthermore, even if everything they bring against me were true, it still cannot be said that this conclusion is heretical or "smells of heresy." For a fuller declaration of this matter, there will be seven articles. In the first, it will be seen whether **Origen** <note>A 3rd-century scholar and one of the most influential Greek Church Fathers, whose later "Origenist" followers were condemned for views on the pre-existence of souls and universal salvation.</note> ever wrote or believed any heretical opinion concerning matters of faith. In the second, assuming he did write such things, whether he transcribed them dogmatically <note>meaning: as established doctrine.</note>, or as a personal adherent, or merely as an inquiry. In the third, assuming he wrote as an adherent, whether he did so in such a way that by writing them he sinned mortally and could be called a heretic. In the fourth, assuming he wrote in such a way that he erred, whether he ever repented for such things. In the 
<margin>For the first article.</margin>
fifth, assuming that neither his repentance nor his lack of repentance is certain, whether it is more reasonable to believe him damned or saved. In the sixth, what should be judged from the text of the decrees regarding what the Church has determined about Origen. In the seventh, how much the determination 
<margin>Rufinus</margin>
of the Church binds our belief in this matter. Regarding the subject of the first article, there was a bitter 
<margin>Jerome</margin>
contention between **Rufinus** and **Jerome**. To them (as **Augustine** says, who deplored the dissension arising between them), 
<margin>Augustine</margin>
God had granted that, as the closest and most intimate friends, they might together lick the honey of the Holy Scriptures. Rufinus is of the opinion that the heretical dogmas found in Origen's books 
<margin>On the controversy of Jerome and Rufinus regarding the first article.</margin>
were falsely inserted by heretics who corrupted his books, and that they are not from Origen’s own mind. Jerome thinks the opposite. But let us see what probability each opinion holds, and it will perhaps appear that—saving the faith and fully satisfying all those things which we are bound to believe by the necessity of salvation—it can still be freely and probably believed that those principal heresies for which Origen is convicted of sin and consequently damned were not from Origen’s mind, but were falsely attributed to him by faithless heretics corrupting his books. First, on this side, there is the

...of the one to whom he ascribes it, then he says: "But let us suppose that this little book is not by a martyr, but by any single person from the Church. Did he not use his own words, whoever that writer is, so that it might be seen that the author’s merit should yield to the volumes of Origen themselves?" He sets forth examples from Origen's own volumes and shows what he feels about individual points, not through his own defensive words, but by the words of the very man who is accused. And therefore, a question about the author is superfluous where such a defense is of the kind that needs no advocate <note>original: "assertore non egeat"; a legal metaphor meaning the evidence is so clear it doesn't need a lawyer to argue it.</note>. Thus says Rufinus.

To those things which Jerome says, someone might perhaps respond on behalf of Rufinus as follows. First, when Jerome says that **Eusebius** <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), the "Father of Church History," who was often accused of leaning toward the Arian heresy.</note> wrote six books in which he proves Origen to be an **Arian** <note>term: "Arian" (Arianum); a follower of Arius, who taught that Jesus was a created being and not co-eternal with God the Father. This was the era's most significant theological conflict.</note>, and that the first of these was translated by Rufinus under the name of **Pamphilus**—how can this stand, that the book of Pamphilus is the first book of Eusebius, when entirely diverse and clashing intentions are found in those books? For Eusebius, through you, O Jerome, tries in his books to prove Origen to be an Arian. In the book of Pamphilus, however, nothing else is done except to prove that Origen was *not* an Arian. Rather, it argues that whatever things confirming the Arian heresy are found in Origen's books were inserted by the Arians themselves—of which kind both Eusebius and many others were. Therefore, this book must be entirely different from the one by Eusebius, as it pleads a completely different, indeed a contrary, case.

Nor is it enough if someone says that those things pertaining to the Arian heresy were simply changed or edited out of the book of Eusebius. For regarding what pertains to other heresies, Jerome cannot say that Eusebius showed Origen’s books were corrupted in those matters. Because Jerome himself, in his second book against Rufinus, says that except for what pertains to the Son and the Holy Spirit, in other dogmas Eusebius and **Didymus** <note>Didymus the Blind, a scholar who, like Origen, held some controversial views on the pre-existence of souls.</note> most aptly concede to the sect of Origen. Therefore, it cannot be well understood how the same things read in the book of Pamphilus could have been read in the first book of Eusebius, unless perhaps some common things about Origen, not pertaining to the specific point of this conclusion, were discussed. Nor does it seem as marvelous as Jerome wonders, if Pamphilus and Eusebius wrote some similar things; for as Jerome himself says, they were **roommates** <note>original: "contubernales"; close companions who shared a library and living quarters.</note>. Eusebius could have either recounted things he read in Pamphilus’s works in his own books, or, as happens daily, discovered and thought them out for himself by a similar movement of the mind. And so much for the first book of Eusebius.

As for Jerome saying that Eusebius writes in the *Life of Pamphilus* that, out of humility, Pamphilus wrote nothing of his own work except for letters; and adding that Eusebius, a defender of Origen and a praiser of Pamphilus, says this—perhaps Rufinus would respond that this does not work much against him. 

**First**, <margin>First</margin> because that little treatise of Pamphilus leans more toward the brevity of a letter than to the magnitude of a full book. 

**Second**, <margin>Second</margin> because that brief apology for Origen cannot perhaps be rightly called an "original work," since Pamphilus does not **dogmatize** <note>term: "dogmatize" (dogmatizet); to establish new religious doctrines or laws.</note> anything there; indeed, no general question is treated there, but it deals briefly only with a particular man, namely Origen. To write whether a man's books were corrupted or not is not the same as "composing an original work." Nor is it a case of a writer avoiding the title of "author" out of humility. 

**Third**, <margin>Third</margin> it is possible that this book did not even come to the notice of Eusebius, both because of the smallness of the book and because of the author’s own humility, as he wrote nothing grand and preferred to hide those thin and tiny things he did write rather than show them off. 

**Fourth**, <margin>Fourth</margin> Rufinus will say it is also possible that Eusebius, as a defender of the Arian perfidy, did not only want to hide the book of the martyr which deprived his sect of Origen's testimony, but also acted through this indirect testimony of his so that it would not be believed by posterity to be Pamphilus's work. Therefore, what Jerome says as if to strengthen his reasoning—that Eusebius, the defender of Origen, says Pamphilus wrote nothing—is rather against Jerome than for him. For since Eusebius defended Origen not as a Catholic but as an Arian, he could rightly be suspect in this matter, as I have said. But why is it necessary to labor in these things? Or how can Jerome prove anything at all from the testimony of Eusebius...

**APOLOGY**

...you might suspect. Furthermore, just as it could have happened, according to you, that those authors either simply erred, or wrote with a different meaning, or spoke innocently and with too little caution, why could it not similarly have happened that **Origen** either simply erred, or wrote with a different meaning—as <margin>**Didymus**</margin> **Didymus** <note>Didymus the Blind (c. 313–398 AD), a prolific Alexandrian theologian who defended Origen’s orthodoxy.</note> contends—or spoke innocently and less cautiously of certain things that cannot escape the slander of perverse men? No reason for such a difference appears.

<margin>**Hilary**; the **Synod of Ariminum**.</margin> **Rufinus** <note>Tyrannius Rufinus (c. 345–411 AD), the monk and translator whose defense of Origen sparked a bitter conflict with Jerome.</note> also reports that the book of **Hilary the Confessor** <note>St. Hilary of Poitiers (c. 310–367 AD), a staunch defender of the Trinity against Arianism.</note> was falsified by heretics after the **Synod of Ariminum** <note>The Council of Ariminum (359 AD), where many Western bishops were deceived into signing a creed that leaned toward Arianism.</note>. He says that for this reason, when a question was raised against him in a council of bishops, Hilary ordered his book to be brought from his home—a book that, without his knowledge, a heretic was keeping in his chest. He says that when it had been produced and judged heretical by everyone, the author of the book, **Hilary**, left the council excommunicated. **Jerome** <note>St. Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), the primary translator of the Latin Vulgate and Pico's chief intellectual opponent in this section.</note> says this is false and a fiction made to slander Hilary, though he brings forward no other evidence. But whether it was true or not cannot be well known, nor does it pertain much to the defense of Origen. This much is true: that **Rufinus**, about to recount this regarding Hilary, prefaced it with these words: "And lest anything be lacking to your ready belief, I shall reveal things that are still within our memory, so that the truth of the testimony may be hidden from no one." Therefore, it was either true, or **Rufinus** was of great impudence to weave a blatant lie and a new fable concerning a matter of such recent memory. But whether it be true or false, it does not seem to have been invented or recounted to slander Hilary; rather, it slanders those who had corrupted Hilary's book more than Hilary himself, whom he testifies was innocent of heresy and unjustly excommunicated because he was craftily deceived.

After this, <margin>**Tertullian**; **Cyprian**.</margin> **Rufinus** reports that **Tertullian's** <note>An early Christian author (c. 155–220 AD) from Carthage.</note> book titled *On the Trinity* was being read in Constantinople under the name of **Cyprian the Martyr** <note>Bishop of Carthage and martyr (c. 210–258 AD).</note> by heretics of the **Macedonian faction** <note>A 4th-century sect that denied the full divinity of the Holy Spirit.</note>. **Jerome** says it is neither **Tertullian’s** book, nor does he say it is **Cyprian’s**, but **Novatian’s** <note>Novatian (c. 200–258 AD), a Roman priest whose rigorist views led to a schism.</note>. But for this one <note>referring to Satan</note> who is said to have fallen from heaven, there will be <margin>of Origen</margin> no conversion even at the end of the age. These are Origen's words. 

Furthermore, that heresy which is imposed upon him—that the Spirit does not understand the Son and the Son does not understand the Father—is clearly falsely attributed to him. This is evident from what he himself says regarding that passage of Paul: *O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God* <note>original: "O altitudo divitiarum sapientiae et scientiae dei," from Romans 11:33.</note>. For he says that while this depth of God is inscrutable to every creature, he could not say such things regarding the Son and the Holy Spirit; for the Son says to the Father in the Gospel: *Father, all mine are yours, and yours are mine* <note>original: "Pater omnia mea tua sunt et tua mea," from John 17:10.</note>. And concerning the Holy Spirit, Paul himself pronounces, saying: *No one among men knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man which is in him; so also no one has known the things that are in God except the Spirit of God* <note>original: "Nemo scit hominum quae sunt hominis nisi spiritus hominis qui in ipso est: ita et quae in deo sunt nemo cognovit nisi spiritus dei," from 1 Corinthians 2:11.</note>. Therefore, when Paul says, *Who has known the mind of the Lord?*, he is speaking of creatures, but he excepts the nature of the Trinity. These are Origen's words.

One heresy attributed to Origen seems to remain: namely, his opinions regarding the soul—that they were <margin>For the heresy</margin> created from eternity and fell from heaven into bodies. Regarding the soul, Origen <margin>regarding souls</margin> himself writes in his commentaries on Paul’s letter to Titus that he can determine nothing <margin>creation</margin> from ecclesiastical dogma except that all souls are of the same species, that they possess <margin>objects</margin> free will, that they are rational, that they are immortal, that they were created by God, and <margin>defense.</margin> that they will have punishments for their evils and rewards for their good deeds. However, he says he affirms these things about the soul because there are evident testimonies for them in the Scriptures. But in other questions concerning the soul, he says he proceeds according to what seems more probable to him, and he speaks by way of inquiry rather than by way of determination, because nothing has been determined regarding those matters in ecclesiastical dogma. 

But as for that which Origen thought was more likely—that souls were created in the heavens and living there before they entered bodies—all agree harmoniously. And <margin>Rufinus</margin> Rufinus, in his apology to Anastasius, Bishop of the city of Rome, after recounting three opinions regarding the soul, concludes thus: 

"But I, having read each of these, call God to witness that until the present I hold nothing certain or defined regarding this question; rather, I leave it to God to know what is true. And if he deigns to reveal it to anyone, I do not deny that I have read these individual opinions, and I confess I am still ignorant—except for that which the Church clearly hands down: that God is the creator of both souls and bodies." 

In the book of Pamphilus <note>Saint Pamphilus of Caesarea (died 309 AD) was a scholar and martyr who wrote a famous defense of Origen while in prison.</note> as well, it is not denied that Origen adhered to that opinion, but it is written <margin>Book of Pamphilus</margin> thus in his defense: 

"Now indeed, since there is diversity among churchmen and some think one thing and others another regarding the soul, and all think differently, why should this man be accused more than the others?" 

Then, after these words, the opinions about the soul that existed at that time are recited—including the one now held by Catholics. And when it is shown that manifest proofs for these cannot be produced from the Holy Scriptures, and that great difficulties occur for the authors of those views, it is concluded thus: 

"What we wish to show from all of this is that, just as those who believe any one of these opinions we have set forth above to be true are not rightly called heretics—since nothing certain or manifest seems to have been said about them in the Divine Scriptures, nor is it thought to be contained in the ecclesiastical preaching—so also it is not just to blame this man for discussing what seemed more likely to him." 

I, however, infer two propositions from all the things said above. The first is that <margin>First proposition</margin> if Origen thought in a Catholic manner regarding both the Trinity and the salvation of demons—as seems more fully proven by the testimonies—we cannot convict him based on his erroneous opinion regarding the soul.

# DEFENSE

...condemnation. Because Origen was not bound to believe all those things explicitly about the soul in his own time that we are now required to believe; for these things were neither manifest in Scripture, nor had they been determined by the Church at that time as they were later. Indeed, this was true not only in Origen's time but even in the time of Augustine—<margin>Augustine lived about 200 years after [Origen].</margin> who lived about two hundred years after Origen. It was still a matter of debate among Catholics (that is, the universal Church) regarding his letter to Jerome: whether, for instance, individual souls are created for individual bodies <note>This refers to "Creationism," the theological view that God creates a new soul for every human being at conception, which is the standard Catholic position.</note>, as orthodox tradition now holds. From that opinion, it seemed to Augustine that it might follow that God was unjust; <margin>And also a doubtful opinion regarding the creation of the soul.</margin> or [he questioned] whether from that one soul which was made by God in Adam, others were subsequently propagated, soul from soul, just as body is from body <note>This refers to "Traducianism," the view that souls are generated by parents. Augustine wrestled with this because it seemed to explain the transmission of Original Sin more easily than Creationism did.</note>. And you should not believe that Augustine doubted this matter only in his youth.

JOHN PICO OF MIRANDOLA

and with clear speech, preserving the faith of the fathers, I would say that he did not write these things at all, but they were maliciously forged and written by heretics in order to cloud his illustrious name, and then titled with his name <note>Pico is likely quoting a defense of Origen written by the historian Rufinus, who argued that Origen's works were tampered with by bad actors.</note>. These are his words exactly. These things were said concerning the first article being examined and investigated, whether those two opinions of Origen were heretical or not; in which matter, as in all others, I always place the judgment of the Church before the judgment and reasoning of all others.

Regarding the second article, <margin>For the second article</margin> it seems more reasonable that Origen should be excused for this reason: if he wrote anything that is not accepted by Catholics, he did not proceed in those writings either dogmatically or assertively, but always in a manner of doubt and inquiry. Therefore, just as in Augustine’s books on Genesis there are many things which are not accepted, yet they are excused by us for the reason that, as he himself says in the book of *Retractations* <note>Augustine’s *Retractations* was a late work where he reviewed his earlier writings and corrected his own errors, a model of intellectual humility Pico admires.</note>, there are more things sought after than found in that book; so too there can be many things in the books of Origen that are to be rejected and condemned, but because he spoke them not by making a final determination but by inquiring, he should not for that reason be called a heretic. <margin>Heresy properly defined</margin> For heresy is properly called an asserted dogma against the expressed truth of either Scripture or the determination of the Church. That Origen always spoke in this [inquisitive] way is clear from many places. For even after a discussion on the soul, <margin>Note the words of Origen</margin> he says: "Let these things, according to our opinion, not be dogmas, but only things sought after and put forward, lest they seem entirely unexamined." <note>original: "haec iuxta nostrā sniam nō sint dogmata sed quaesita tantum atq, proiecta ne penitus intractata uiderent"</note> And elsewhere, speaking of the resurrection, he says: "If these things are not contrary to the faith," and so on. And further down: "A threefold suspicion therefore suggests itself to us regarding the end, from which the reader may judge which is true and better." He then adds three opinions about the resurrection. And in the preface to his books on Genesis, he says: "If something deep occurs, it should indeed be spoken of, but not affirmatively." And further: "Concerning great matters which are above us, we are not ignorant of our own ignorance." And on the second book of the Epistle to the Romans: "Let these things be said by us on the condition that if any say something better and more reasonable, they should hold those things rather than these of ours." And in the fourth book: "These things, as far as we were able, have been set forth in places so arduous and difficult; if someone perhaps considers the labor of our mind, he will be able to embrace it. If, however, he wishes to note the weakness of our perception, we ask for pardon, and we gladly yield to him who is able to discuss or explain these things better." And elsewhere: "Let the reader prove which of these is more agreeable to the apostolic sense and hold to that." And in the fifth book: "In the meantime, these things were able to occur to us in this present place. If anyone, however, perceives something better, let him not be loath to look to those things, leaving these aside." And as he reads further in the book *Peri Archon* <note>The Greek title of Origen's major work, *On First Principles*.</note>, <margin>The book *Peri Archon* for the third article</margin> we will see him proceed in this order: that first he places those things which seemed to him to be expressly determined in the Scriptures; and in those things, he wanders in no way from the Church. Other things he says are doubtful to him and he wishes to inquire about them, asserting regarding all of them that only that truth is to be received which in no way opposes apostolic and ecclesiastical dogmas.

Regarding the third article, which is as if a confirmation of the second, I state this proposition: <margin>Note this proposition.</margin> if there is anyone holding an erroneous opinion concerning matters of faith not yet determined by the Church, provided that in his will there is no stain, but rather a firm purpose to always believe in consonance with Scripture and the Church, he neither sins mortally nor is properly called a heretic. From which proposition it follows as a corollary <margin>Corollary.</margin> that it is possible for the holding of a certain opinion to be a mortal sin at one time, which would not be so at another time. And this is because one can believe something without pertinacity <note><term>Pertinacity</term> refers to the stubborn, willful adherence to an error even after being corrected by the Church. In Catholic law, it is the "stubbornness" that makes a mistake into a heresy.</note> at one time, which at another time he could not believe without pertinacity—namely, after the determination of the Church or the clarification of Holy Scripture. Regarding the opposite of what is believed, the opinion of all the Doctors bears witness, saying that it is not precisely an error of the intellect that makes a man a heretic, but it is necessary that there be malice and perversity in the will. Therefore Augustine said: "I am able to err, but I cannot be a heretic." <margin>Augustine.</margin> This is confirmed by the determination of the universal Church, <margin>Confirmation.</margin> which has canonized many who nevertheless persisted until death in erroneous opinions...

->GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA<-

...that one who brings forward an opposing view, not dogmatically but because it seemed more probable to them, can be called a heretic; and I prove this clearly from a certain saying of Jerome himself, cited above. For where Jerome says that even if in the books of Clement <note>original: "Clementis"; likely referring to Clement of Alexandria, a 2nd-century theologian whose works were influential but occasionally controversial.</note>, the disciple of the apostles, and others like him, some faulty things are found, he would not immediately judge them to be heretics. He adds a fourfold reason: First, that the books could be corrupt. Second, that they might have written with a different meaning. Third, that they might have simply erred. Fourth, that they spoke with less caution. In these words, we must notice that even granted that the book of Clement—in which he says the Son of God is a creature—is not corrupted, and granted that the author did not intend another meaning, still Clement is not immediately to be judged a heretic, because he could have simply erred. What is "to have simply erred" <note>original: "simpliciter erraffe"</note> if not to have erred from a defect of the intellect and an erroneous judgment of reason, and not from malice or perversity of the will? 

For if in that heresy—that the Son is a creature, which is the greatest charge brought against Origen—someone can "err simply" because there was not yet a determination of the Church on the matter, or a more certain verification through a greater clarification of the Scriptures, then such an error cannot be held against them. And if at that time Clement was not bound under penalty of mortal sin to believe with explicit faith that which we can say Origen was obliged to believe explicitly, regarding those matters in which he is said to have erred. <margin>Note</margin> It must be noted, however, that because heresy can exist both in words spoken badly and inordinately (as Augustine says) and in the underlying meaning, <margin>Augustine</margin> therefore the Master Jerome gives a way of excusing the one who has erred in both, <margin>Jerome</margin> together or separately, from a defect of the intellect alone and not the will. He says either they spoke "less cautiously" (and this applies if the heresy appears in the words) or they "simply erred" (and this applies if the sense is heretical, but produced by a simple and upright will though from a weak and wandering intellect). Those words of Jerome are well worth noting and weighing, because in them a useful and healthy teaching <note>original: "dogma"; here meaning a settled principle or doctrine.</note> concerning heretical obstinacy is rightly founded.

<margin>Regarding the fourth article.</margin> Regarding the fourth article, certain people who say that Origen repented cite the *Lament of Origen* <note>A famous but widely considered forged document in which Origen supposedly bewails his lapses during the Decian persecution.</note>; but that book is considered apocryphal, as found in the decrees, distinction fifteen. <margin>Apocryphal book</margin> I, however, cite the testimony of Jerome himself, which cannot be held as apocryphal, who expressly witnesses that Origen repented of his errors. I do not bring this forward because it is reasonably necessary for believing in Origen's salvation (as will be clear in the following article), but because these masters never cease shouting: "I show you that Origen erred; you show me that he repented! You will never show this, you will never find it written that Origen repented of those things which he wrote." 

Let these reverend fathers, therefore, hear Jerome himself, by whose authority they strike down Origen, in his *Apology to Pammachius and Oceanus*, in which he shows himself to have followed Origen's learning but not his dogma. After reciting Origen’s errors, he adds these words: "Origen himself, in the letter which he writes to Fabian, Bishop of the city of Rome <margin>Pope Fabian</margin>, performs penance for why he wrote such things, and refers the causes of his rashness <note>original: "temeritatis"</note> to Ambrose <margin>Ambrose</margin> <note>This is not St. Ambrose of Milan, but Origen's wealthy patron and friend, who reportedly published Origen's private notes without his permission.</note>, because he brought into public what had been produced in secret." These are Jerome's words, verbatim. What could be clearer? What more express? How then, or with what face, can they say it is nowhere found that Origen repented? 

I will also mention what happened to me these days with two of those who were condemning this conclusion in a similar discussion. <margin>Note the wit</margin> For when I—in order to defend Origen from the charge of obstinacy—said that Origen was condemned for "obstinacy in the soul" by a determination of the Church, I stated that I had it from Greek histories that Origen's teachings were condemned many years after his death. I referred him (if he did not have the books at home) to the Bishop of Trogir <margin>Bishop of Trogir</margin> <note>Bishop Christopher de Teramo (reigned 1487–1504), a noted scholar and friend of Pico.</note>, a man no less outstanding in learning and character than in his dignity, at whose house I had seen a Greek book in which many things concerning the councils were collected. That "good father" said: "Why do you refer me to the Greeks, when you know I do [not know] Greek?"

<margin>Note another.</margin> The following day, another man compelled me even more sharply, carrying a quite large book in his hand. “By what way,” he said, “or by what path at all do you dare to defend Origen from the punishment of eternal fire? Behold, I will show you a testimony you cannot contradict, which says Origen cannot be defended.” “Produce your witnesses, venerable man,” I said, “if you have them.” Then he said, “Here is a certain great witness,” and he added the name. I, however, wish to keep the name silent. “These are his sermons and preachings.” Then I said, “What sermons do you bring me? What trifles!” “Trifles!” he replied, now totally inflamed. “Trifles, I say,” I replied, “in which—if he discusses this matter (for heaven forbid I should ever read such things)—nothing but the most manifest error will be found. Now I wish to crush the head of Origen on Ixion’s wheel <note>original: "Ixionis rota"; a mythological punishment where Ixion was bound to a perpetually turning wheel of fire. Pico is mocking the opponent’s desire for extreme punishment.</note> with you.” 

Impatient and now boiling over with bile, he opened the book and began to read, raging with a very loud voice: “Wednesday, Sermon 11: On the Origenists.” Then, following the things that were written, he exclaimed at every single word: “Is this not an error?” And behold, while he was shouting thus to the envy of Stentor, <note>A Greek herald in the Iliad known for having a voice as loud as fifty men.</note> he read these words written in the book: “Finally, Jerome confesses that he himself read six thousand of Origen’s books.” And immediately striking the blow, he shouted again: “Is this not an error?” “This is indeed an error,” I said, “and a great one. Here is an open lie, here is an expressed falsehood.” 

And to restrain the man immediately, I ordered the letters of Jerome to be brought. Running straight to the second book of his *Invective Against Rufinus*, I showed him where Jerome, speaking to Rufinus, mentions that <margin>Pope Epiphanius <note>Pico points out that the opponent’s book mistakenly calls Epiphanius "Pope." He was actually the Bishop of Salamis.</note></margin> Epiphanius boasted of having read six thousand of Origen’s books, and Jerome responds with these words: “Regarding the six thousand books which you pretend were read by him: who will believe either that you are telling the truth or that he could have lied? For if Origen had written six thousand books, it might be possible that a learned man, instructed in sacred letters from infancy, might have read another’s work out of curiosity and knowledge. But since he did not write that many, how could he have read them? Count the index of his books, which are contained in the third volume of Eusebius (in which he wrote the *Life of Pamphilus*), and you will not find—I do not say six thousand—but even a third part of that number.” 

These are Jerome's words, verbatim. The man blushed, and my case was saved. 

<margin>Epilogue</margin> But let us now return to the proposition by concluding: either with Rufinus and the others we cited above in the first article, we must concede that Origen never sinned; or, if we contend with Jerome that he did sin, let us know that we must also concede with Jerome that Origen repented of his sin in a personal book <note>original: "libello"; a small book or formal written statement.</note> given to the Bishop of Rome. For my part, after I diligently weighed and examined those things said of Origen specifically by Eusebius, Rufinus, and Jerome, I conjecture that Origen, laboring long in the scrutiny of the Scriptures, was ambiguous concerning many arduous and principal questions of theology since they were not yet certainly and indubitably [defined]...

JOHN PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

[Main Text]
...he himself saw that he could assert nothing regarding those matters based on the testimony of the scriptures. For this reason, regarding many mysteries of the faith, he perhaps said many things by way of inquiry and dispute in the earlier years of his life which the Catholic faith would not accept. Therefore, Origen—who, as he himself says, was not ignorant of his own ignorance <note>original: "suā ignorantiā nō ignorabat"; a Socratic sentiment Origen often expressed, acknowledging the limits of human understanding regarding divine mysteries.</note> and clearly recognized that he had not yet attained the truth of those questions—never wished for the things he preached in the churches to be taken down by shorthand writers <note>original: "notariis"; ancient stenographers who recorded sermons and lectures in real-time.</note> before his sixtieth year, as Eusebius reports. Let us observe, therefore, what Eusebius writes in the thirty-sixth <margin>Eusebius</margin> chapter <note>original: "xxvi. capite"; Pico likely means chapter 36 of Book 6, where this is discussed.</note> of the sixth book of his *Ecclesiastical History*: that in the third year of the reign of Emperor Philip, and under Pope Fabian, when Origen was already passing his sixtieth year, he began to commit his sayings and letters to the public. And let us observe what he says above in the seventeenth chapter: that under Pope Urban, whom Pontianus succeeded, already before the time of Fabian, Origen began the task of writing commentaries on the Holy Scriptures, with Ambrose <note>Not the famous Saint Ambrose of Milan, but Origen’s wealthy friend and patron, Ambrose of Alexandria, who provided him with shorthand writers and parchment.</note> compelling him and forcing him by the great power of prayers and entreaties. Eusebius says this man was seen as most worthy for this duty to be bestowed upon him, and to whom whatever was secret and hidden, covered in the sacred letters, should be opened. From these two passages of Eusebius, in which an apparent contradiction appears, it is evidently gathered: that at the urging of Ambrose, he dictated certain things in his earlier years before he had yet discovered anything certain, though these were to be communicated privately to Ambrose himself and not published to the public—since he did not yet know them to be safe and in harmony with apostolic truth. However, Ambrose brought those things, which had been produced in secret, out into the public. Later, when the Catholic truth was discovered by Origen (now a sixty-year-old), he then began to write boldly and in a Catholic manner for the public. He was vehemently pained that those things which he had written for the private use of Ambrose had already been published by him. For his own purging <note>That is, the clearing of his reputation or "apology."</note>—as I gather from the words of Jerome and Eusebius—writing to Fabian, the Bishop of Rome, regarding the sequence of the whole matter, he offered testimony concerning his Catholic faith, recounting that those things found written by him earlier were not written by him to be published, as he himself was doubtful whether they were Catholic or not. But Ambrose had published them. For this is what Jerome says: Origen himself, in the letter which he wrote to <margin>Jerome</margin> Fabian, the Bishop of the city of Rome, performs penance for why he wrote such things, and refers the cause of the rashness to Ambrose, who brought into the public things produced in secret. Moreover, Eusebius, recounting what he wrote after his sixtieth year—after he enumerated the book *Against Celsus*, and twenty-five books of commentaries on Matthew, and twenty on the Prophets—adds: "He also wrote to Fabian, Bishop of the city of Rome, and to very many other leaders of the churches concerning his Catholic faith." Thus he says. Let it be true, then, that before his sixtieth year Origen was doubtful concerning many mysteries of the faith. And let it be true that he communicated many things in writing to Ambrose in secret, which he then held not by adhering firmly but by inquiring doubtfully, and which are now not to be received by Catholics. And so, let Jerome speak the truth: that those things found in many of Origen's books which are not Catholic belong to Origen, because they were truly dictated by him—though not as things believed, but as things sought after rather than found. Consequently, they are not to be culpably ascribed to Origen, to whom the Catholic truth was afterwards discovered, and in which many things were also devised by heretics, according to Rufinus <note>Rufinus of Aquileia argued that Origen's works had been corrupted and altered by later heretics to support their own views.</note>. We can also accept this as true especially because Origen himself complained of this very thing while he was alive. Let it be true, then, according to Eusebius in the *Ecclesiastical History* (approved as true by Jerome), that Origen should not be held responsible for works as his own—that is, in which he says anything definitively and with adherence—except those which he wrote after his sixtieth year. And let it also be true, according to Jerome, that he repented of the things previously written and rashly published by Ambrose, and consequently died a Catholic. Thus, not only according to Rufinus, Pamphilus, and Eusebius, but even according to Jerome, it is more reasonable to believe that <margin>Regarding the fifth</margin> he is saved than to believe that he is damned. <margin>article.</margin> Regarding the fifth article, I say this proposition: <margin>First proposition</margin> however much someone might sin gravely and mortally in life, and it is established that he sinned mortally...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s defense of the early Christian scholar Origen. Building on the previous page's discussion of Origen’s caution in publishing his works, Pico now moves into a formal theological argument regarding the nature of divine judgment and the impossibility of certain knowledge regarding a person's salvation or damnation without direct revelation.</meta>

-># **APOLOGIA**<-

<margin>Corollaries to the first proposition</margin>
...unless his final impenitence is established, it is rash to truly assert that he is damned. The truth of this proposition is evident from the common opinion of all doctors who agree on said proposition. From this proposition, I infer two corollary propositions. The first is this: Just because someone has sinned mortally during their life, and it is not certain to us whether they repented, we must not firmly judge that person to be in hell. This is clear because, although a mortal sin <note>In Catholic theology, a "mortal sin" is a grave offense that destroys charity in the heart; however, it only leads to damnation if the person dies without repenting.</note> may have occurred, the full condition for eternal damnation has not yet been met. Rather, beyond the sin itself, one must establish and be certain of **final impenitence** <note>The state of dying without regret or confession for grave sins.</note>. And I, who deny that we must firmly believe him to be in hell, do not have to prove his repentance to you. But you, who assert that he is damned, must

<margin>Henry of Hesse</margin>
certify his impenitence. Much support for this is found in the saying of Henry of Hesse <note>original: "Henrici de assia"; a 14th-century German theologian and scientist known for his work at the University of Vienna.</note> who, in his exposition on the third chapter of the book of Genesis, says these formal words: "If, therefore, the argument of some were effective—by which they persuade us that someone is damned, as they do concerning Solomon <note>King Solomon’s salvation was a major point of debate in the Middle Ages because the Bible records his later idolatry but not his repentance.</note>, because Scripture commemorates his sin and makes no mention of his righteousness or repentance—then the first man [Adam] would be proven damned by his sin just as the first angel was." Thus says Henry. For nowhere is 

<margin>Origen Adamantius</margin>
mention made of the repentance of Adam, but only of his sin. Similarly, in the eighth chapter of Judges, we read of the sin of Gideon and not of his repentance; and yet it is well believed by the doctors that he was saved. You might also say that by this same argument some were so deceived that they erroneously said Moses was damned, because his sin at the waters of contradiction <note>original: "aquis cōtradictionis"; a reference to Meribah, where Moses struck the rock in anger.</note> was read, yet nothing was explicitly held regarding his repentance. And yet God said to Joshua: "Moses my servant is dead."

<margin>Second corollary proposition</margin>
The second corollary proposition is this: no one can be certain that someone is damned to hell unless they have this from a special revelation from God, or from those to whom it is believed God has revealed it. The truth of this is clear from the preceding propositions, because no one can be certain of final repentance or impenitence except He who knows the secrets of the heart and to whom He has wished to reveal them. Since no one is as certain of another’s state as he is of his own—because no one knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man which is in him, as is said in the second letter to the Corinthians—and since a man cannot even be certain of himself whether he is worthy of hatred or love, as it says in Ecclesiastes chapter nine, how much more will he be unable to be certain about another unless he has a special revelation regarding it?

From this main proposition, with its corollaries, I infer for my conclusion: that even granted that Origen sinned mortally by erring in those errors, nevertheless, since we are uncertain of his final impenitence or repentance, to assert that he is damned is an altogether rash judgment and to be rejected. Since, therefore, we cannot be certain either of his salvation or his damnation, it is nonetheless pious and very reasonable to believe, as I have said, that God

<margin>Words of Jerome</margin>
saved a man of such and so great knowledge. Of him, Jerome says in the preface to the Song of Songs: "While in other things he surpassed everyone else, in this he surpassed himself," and of him this is verified: "The king has brought me into his chamber." And elsewhere, wishing to imitate Origen in part, Jerome says: "No one but the unskilled denies that he [Origen] was the master of the churches after the apostles." And elsewhere:

<margin>Origen Adamantius</margin>
"Origen sweated with such labor over the scriptures that he justly received the name **Adamantius** <note>meaning "the Indomitable" or "Man of Steel," referring to Origen's legendary stamina and prolific writing.</note>." And after certain other things, he adds: "Who could ever read as much as he wrote? And for this sweat, what reward did he receive? He is condemned by Bishop Demetrius, with the exception of the priests of Palestine, Arabia, Phoenicia, and Achaia. The city of Rome itself consents against him; it gathers a senate <note>original: "senatū"; here meaning a local church council or synod.</note> against him, not because of the novelty of his doctrines, nor because of heresy (as rabid dogs now falsely pretend against him), but because they could not bear the glory of his eloquence and knowledge." Why I have written this, and dictated it to a poor man's lamp with a quick but not cautious speech, you can understand if you consider the Epicureans and Aristippans <note>Followers of Aristippus, who advocated for pleasure; Pico is likely using these as types of worldly or envious critics.</note>. These are the words of Jerome, word for word. I ask, O ingenious reader, that you [weigh] each word...

<summary>Pico argues that since no human can know the final state of another's soul without divine revelation, it is rash to claim Origen is damned. He cites Henry of Hesse and Saint Jerome to show that many biblical figures like Moses and Adam are considered saved despite their recorded sins, and that Origen's original condemnation was born of professional envy rather than heresy.</summary>
