<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s defense of the Church Father Origen. Having previously argued that we cannot certain of Origen's damnation, Pico now gathers testimonies from other saints—specifically Jerome, Augustine, and Bernard—to illustrate Origen's immense virtue and his "martyrdom of the will," which Pico argues would have cleansed any intellectual errors he might have made.</meta>

# JOHN PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

Reader, attend diligently: and through these points, understand for yourself those things which I do not explicitly state. In his Hebrew preface to the questions concerning this same Origen, Jerome speaks thus: "This one thing I say: I would wish to have his knowledge of the Scriptures, even with the envy directed at his name." Jerome counts as worthless the "images and shadows of ghosts" <note>original: "imagines umbrasque laruarum"; a metaphor for superficial or superstitious fears that terrify the immature.</note> whose nature is said to terrify little children and chatter in dark corners. I pass over what Jerome proclaims about the same man: that he trampled upon avarice; that he castrated himself out of zeal for God <note>According to tradition, Origen took the verse in Matthew 19:12 literally and castrated himself to avoid temptation while teaching women; this was later cited as a reason he could not be ordained a priest.</note> (though not according to knowledge <note>original: "non secundum scientiam"; a common theological critique that Origen’s zeal was misguided in its physical application.</note>); and that he sweated over the explanation of Scripture days and nights. For those who clarify the Scriptures shall have eternal life, as the Wise Man says. And as Jerome writes to Vigilantius, Origen explained the obscurities of the prophets and revealed the greatest mysteries of both the New and Old Testaments. I also pass over the fact that <margin>Note.</margin> he was not only the son of a martyr, but he himself was barely removed from the merit of martyrdom.

For Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), the first great historian of the Christian Church.</note> says that even as a small boy, Origen burned with such a great passion for seizing martyrdom that he would willfully throw himself into dangers. Later, during the time of the <margin>Decian persecution</margin> Decian persecution <note>The persecution of Christians under Emperor Decius (c. 250 AD), known for its intensity and systematic nature.</note>, he endured new crosses, new kinds of punishments, and torments unheard of in all ages. Thus, as Eusebius says, he was harassed by "a thousand deaths" so that the one death he truly desired would not happen to him; for his persecutor acted with the highest effort to ensure that neither a final end was granted nor the pain ceased. See how little he lacked the praise of martyrdom, which so many of his disciples achieved under his leadership and encouragement. I say again, he was indeed barely removed from the praise of martyrdom; rather, he earned a merit almost equal to it.

For Augustine also says in his book *On the Good of Marriage*: "The merit of martyrdom is not unequal in <margin>Augustine</margin> John [the Evangelist], who did not suffer death, and in Peter, who did suffer." Note these words of Augustine well. Thus, just as John—though he did not pass by the sword—was nevertheless ready to endure martyrdom when he was cast into the cauldron of boiling oil, so too was Origen. Although he did not undergo death by martyrdom, he was nevertheless ready—indeed, most eager—to undergo it. He suffered so many torments, as Eusebius says, that he underwent a thousand deaths in place of one. And this is what Bernard says in <margin>Bernard</margin> his sermon on the holy martyrs: that there is a <margin>Triple martyrdom</margin> triple martyrdom: a martyrdom of will only; a martyrdom of deed only; and a martyrdom of both deed and will. John the Evangelist suffered a martyrdom of will only, of whom it was said (along with his brother): "You shall drink my cup" <note>Matthew 20:23.</note>. Regarding this, <margin>Cyprian</margin> Cyprian says: "In the servants of God, among whom martyrdom is contemplated and the mind is conceived as devoted to the good, they are crowned by God as judge. For it is one thing for martyrdom to be lacking from the soul, and another for the soul to be lacking from the martyrdom."

If, therefore, the soul was never lacking from the martyrdom of Origen, and he underwent a thousand deaths for the sake of one, how can we not believe him to be crowned by God the judge, unless the martyr Cyprian is a liar? And if he was damned, who, I ask, damned him to the death of Gehenna <note>Hell.</note>? Was it Christ Jesus, for whom he himself wished to die so many times? Rather, just as Augustine says of the same Cyprian: "The blood of martyrdom washed away every stain of heresy in him." So too regarding Origen: we may piously believe that the blood of martyrdom—poured out by him not so much outwardly upon the earth as inwardly upon his celestial soul, burning with zeal for God and charity—washed away every stain of heresy. 

<margin>Augustine</margin> Let us say with David <note>A paraphrase of Psalm 1:1 applied to Origen.</note>: "Blessed is Origen, who, even if he sometimes went into the counsel of those who err, nevertheless did not stand in the way of sinners through impenitence, and never sat in the seat of pestilence through pertinacity <note>Pertinacity is the "stubborn persistence" in an error; in canon law, an error only becomes "heresy" if the person remains pertinacious after being corrected.</note>. But his will was in the law of the Lord, and in His law he meditated day and night. Blessed is Origen, whose iniquities are forgiven through baptism and whose sins are covered through penance, and to whom the Lord did not impute sin because of his martyrdom." Finally, let us believe that such a great man—even if he sometimes erred in the mysteries of the faith out of a defect of intellect and not out of any malice of will—was not abandoned by the Lord in his final moments. Rather, by the visitation of His most merciful mercy, he was illuminated regarding the secrets of the faith (if he erred in any) and called back from an erroneous path to the way of salvation. And this is what I meant in my brief response when I said elsewhere: "Since he is not found to have been pertinacious, it is likely to believe that God saved him"—that is, by visiting him with the visitation of which I have spoken.

<summary>Pico argues that Origen's extreme suffering and willingness to die for Christ during the Decian persecution constitutes a "martyrdom of the will," which, according to Church Fathers like Augustine and Cyprian, would cleanse any intellectual errors or stains of heresy.</summary>

# APOLOGY

...most mercifully placed him in a state worthy of salvation; and by illuminating him regarding the secrets of the faith in which he had erred, God called him to a salvific repentance for those mistakes. Whether this actually happened or not, no one can know with certainty unless it has been revealed to them from above. However, to believe that it was so, rather than not, seems more consistent and thus more reasonable when considering the acts and life of Origen. For in doubtful matters, one should always reasonably adhere to the more favorable side. These things are said so that they may carry weight even if Origen's repentance were not established—though we have most aptly shown above, through the testimony of the most blessed Jerome, that it was indeed established.

<margin>For the sixth article.</margin> Concerning the sixth article, I say it does not seem believable that the Church ever determined that Origen’s soul was damned to hell. I prove the truth of this proposition with two reasons.

<margin>First reason.</margin> The first reason is this: regarding a matter where one side or the other cannot be determined with certainty except by rashness, it should not be believed that a determination has been made by the Church. But regarding this question of whether Origen is saved or damned, neither side can be determined without rashness, at least not without a special revelation from God. Therefore, since no such revelation is established, it should not be believed that a determination on this matter was made by the Church. The major premise is well-known, and to believe the opposite would be injurious to the Church—namely, to believe that anything could be judged by her inadvisedly or rashly.

<margin>Confirmation.</margin> The minor premise is clear from the articles discussed above. It is confirmed because the Church could not be certain of Origen’s damnation except through a special revelation made concerning him; but of such a revelation having been made, no mention is found anywhere; therefore, etc.

<margin>Second reason.</margin> The second reason is this: if there is anything that persuades people that the Church determined Origen’s damnation, it is certain texts of the decretals <note>The Decretals were collections of papal decrees that formed the basis of medieval Canon Law.</note> which seem to sound that way to those who interpret them in a crude manner. Yet, when these texts are rightly examined, they work against such people rather than for them. These are the texts they usually bring forward: First, from Distinction 15, the chapter "The Holy Roman Church," <note>original: "di. xv. c. sancta Ro. ecclesia"; a reference to the Gelasian Decree, a famous 5th or 6th-century list of approved and prohibited books.</note> as written by Pope Gelasius. It says: "Likewise, we accept to be read some small works of Origen which the blessed Jerome does not reject. All the rest, however, we say are to be refused along with their author." Also, from Book 24, question 3, the chapter "Certainly." Likewise, if anyone recurs to the times of Theophilus of holy memory <note>Theophilus of Alexandria was a leading opponent of Origen in the late 4th century.</note> or earlier, they will find Origen anathematized <note>Anathematized: formally cursed or excommunicated by the Church.</note> after his death; which your Holiness also does, as did Julius, the most religious bishop of Rome. And the gloss there says: "Since he was damned, are not his writings also excluded?" And in the chapter "Of Fraternity" regarding heretics, it is written: "Since Celestius and Pelagius were damned in the <margin>Synod of Ephesus.</margin> Synod of Ephesus, how can their chapters be received, whose authors are damned?"

From these authorities, some believe that the damnation of Origen’s soul to hell is proven. I, however, say that nothing more is contained in the aforementioned texts except that the Church condemns the opinions and dogmas attributed to Origen as heretical, and condemns and detests him as a "dogmatizer" <note>A "dogmatizer" is one who formally teaches or originates a doctrine; Pico distinguishes between condemning the teacher's role and the teacher's eternal soul.</note>, intending nothing at all regarding the damnation or salvation of his soul. That this is true is clear for many reasons.

<margin>First.</margin> First, because it does not pertain to the Church to damn or save the souls of men; that belongs solely to Him who is the judge of the living and the dead. Therefore, it is ridiculous if one reads in the decrees, "We damn Origen," to interpret it as "We damn his soul to the punishment of hell."

<margin>Gelasius</margin> This is also clearly evident from the manner of speaking used by Gelasius himself, who says that "the rest of the works..."

<summary>Pico argues that Church condemnations of Origen are directed at his erroneous doctrines and his status as a teacher of error, rather than a definitive judicial ruling on the fate of his eternal soul. He asserts that only God, not the Church, can judge the salvation or damnation of an individual after death.</summary>
<keywords>Origen, salvation, damnation, Church authority, Pope Gelasius, Canon Law, dogmatizer, judgment of God</keywords>

--- Page 157 ---
<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s argument that the Church's condemnation of Origen applies only to his erroneous doctrines, not to the eternal state of his soul.</meta>

->JOHN PICO OF MIRANDOLA<-

<margin>Secondly</margin> Secondly, I argue against those based on the gloss <note>original: "glosa"; a standard medieval or Renaissance commentary on legal or theological texts</note> which they themselves cite, which says: "If the man himself is not damned, neither are his writings." <margin>He argues against them.</margin> I ask these people: if this logic holds—"Origen himself is damned, therefore his writings are also damned"—how is the term "damned" being used in the first part of the statement? If it means "not approved in his doctrine" and "not accepted as a teacher," then my point is proven. However, if it is understood as "damned in his soul to the punishment of hell," then the logic is worthless. For it is possible for many scholars <note>original: "doctores"</note> whose writings are orthodox <note>original: "catholica"</note> and are read daily as such to be in hell; this is because a person might err in nothing regarding the faith and hold correct views on all articles of belief, yet still be in a state of mortal sin and die in that state. The damnation of a soul is entirely irrelevant to the condemnation of a doctrine. The former depends on the malice of the will, while the latter depends on a defect of the intellect. Therefore, the reverse is also not valid: "This man is in paradise, therefore his sayings are orthodox." For <margin>Papias.</margin> Papias is in paradise, as are <margin>Irenaeus.</margin> Irenaeus, <margin>Victorinus.</margin> Victorinus, <margin>Cyprian,</margin> and many others whose writings are nevertheless rejected as heretical in many points which they are never recorded to have retracted. <margin>Confirmation.</margin> I confirm this from the very saying to which the gloss refers concerning heretics in the *Decretals*, chapter *Fraternitatis* <note>A reference to Canon Law, specifically the Decretals of Gregory IX</note>, where it is asked: if Caelestius <note>The text says "Celestinus," but refers to the follower of Pelagius condemned at Ephesus</note> and Pelagius were damned in the Synod of Ephesus, how could those chapters be received whose authors are damned? It is certain, however, that in 그 synod, Caelestius and Pelagius were not damned in themselves—that is, in their souls—but in their doctrine. This is both because the Church neither usually nor potentially damns men in that way (as stated above), and because we must understand a judgment to apply to the matter that was originally questioned and disputed. But in that synod, as is clear from the acts of the council, the question was not whether the souls of Caelestius and Pelagius were in paradise or in hell, but whether their sayings and teachings were orthodox or not. Therefore, we must understand the judgment as pertaining to the truth of their teachings and the approval or rejection of the author specifically in the capacity of one teaching those things.

<margin>Thirdly.</margin> Thirdly, it is foolish to say that the Church determined Origen’s soul to be damned. The Church does not usually damn people in the same way it canonizes them—that is, by decreeing through a formal sentence that they are in hell. The reason it usually does the one and not the other is this: to decree that someone is saved, we must be certain that they died in a state of grace. We can have indications of this—though not absolute certainty—from what they did in life; however, these are not sufficient, because as long as someone is "on the way" <note>original: "in via"; a theological term for being alive and capable of change</note> there is always room for merit or demerit, and for changing from one intention to another. But we have signs after death, such as miracles or something similar. On the other hand, it is not easy to find any sign by which we might be convinced of someone's damnation after their death. Indeed, without a doubt, no other sign can be had unless there is a special revelation concerning it. If such a revelation happened or had happened, the Church would surely make mention of it when damning someone, just as it testifies to miracles and other reasons when it canonizes someone, so that it would not appear to have decreed such a thing rashly or without consultation. Yet the Church nowhere tells such a story regarding Origen. We must therefore understand Origen to be "condemned" by the Church in the way that follows from what the Church narrates and testifies about him. Nothing else is narrated about him except that he erred regarding the mysteries of faith. Absolute damnation of Origen in himself does not follow from this error, but only the condemnation of his writings and doctrine, as is clear from what was said before. And thus we should judge him "damned" by the Church and not otherwise. Furthermore, we know he was not <term>obstinate</term> <note>In canon law, heresy requires "pertinacia" (obstinacy)—willfully clinging to error after being corrected by the Church</note> against the determination of the Church in those opinions, because the councils in which those opinions were condemned took place long after Origen's death, as is clear from both Greek and Latin histories. And we can in no way know if he remained unrepentant of them; indeed, we have proven above from Jerome that he either did not write those things, or if he did write them, he repented.

<summary>Pico argues that the Church condemns doctrines (errors of intellect) rather than the eternal fate of souls (matters of will), noting that the Church lacks the divine revelation required to declare Origen—or anyone—definitively in Hell. He concludes that since the councils condemning Origen's ideas met long after his death, he could not be a "pertinacious" heretic.</summary>

that it is precisely thus: because he wishes to hold such an opinion. This is Aristotle's view in the second book of *On the Soul* <note>original: "de anima"</note>, in the commentary on text 254, where Aristotle posits a difference between imagination and opinion. And this judgment <term>sententia: a formal philosophical or theological opinion</term> of Aristotle has not only not been rejected, but indeed has been unanimously approved by all our theologians. 

The second part of the conclusion, however—which is that no one believes something to be precisely true simply because he *wants* to believe it is true—is the view of Augustine. He states this in many places, saying quite often that no one can believe by free will—that is, by the mere impulse of the will—without the persuasion or motive of reason. 

My entire conclusion summarily maintains this opinion: when a doubtful proposition is proposed, the mere apprehension of the terms and the mere command of the will are not sufficient to make someone believe or disbelieve it. <meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's defense of his thesis regarding the relationship between the will and the intellect, specifically arguing that belief is not a voluntary choice but a response to intellectual perception. He continues to cite historical theological authorities and logical proofs.</meta>

->**GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA**<-

<margin>Henry of Oyta, Henry of Hesse. The University of Paris.</margin> Henry of Oyta <note>original: "Henricus oeta"; a 14th-century philosopher and theologian</note> and Henry of Hesse <note>original: "Henricus de assia"; a scholar known for his works on physics and theology</note>. And when I was in Paris, almost the entire University of Paris held this view; indeed, many Catholic doctors consider it so true that they regard the opposite view as impossible. Furthermore, I have not yet read any doctor who contradicts this opinion.

<margin>Declaration of the corollary proposition.</margin> However, the corollary proposition <term>correlaria propositio: a statement that follows naturally from a previously proven point</term> is not to be understood or accepted otherwise than with the restriction or qualification placed in the antecedent <note>the first part of a logical argument</note>: namely, that it is not within the free power of the will to believe an article of faith to be true whenever it pleases, and to believe it to be false when it pleases. So it is that the intellect does not believe precisely because it pleases the will for the intellect to believe. Nor is such an understanding of one proposition through another linked to it unusual; indeed, in Holy Scripture, the meaning of the letter is often derived from what precedes or follows it, which ought especially to be done in our case. 

Therefore, because this statement—"it is not in our power," etc.—is not something I propose as a statement on its own or as a separate conclusion, but I propose it as a corollary from the preceding one. But if it does not please them to take the meaning of the present corollary from its principal premise to which it is attached and linked, let them consider that something is said to be "in the liberty" or "in the free power" of the will in two ways.

<margin>Two ways something is said to be in the liberty or free power of the will.</margin> **First:** because, once an apprehension <note>the act of the mind grasping a concept</note> is placed in the intellect, with no other act of the intellect required, it is within the commanding power of the will to produce that act. <margin>First. Second.</margin> And in this way, it is denied in this conclusion that the act of believing is in the free power of man. Nor is it necessary for every act of commandment, whether meritorious or demeritorious, to be in the power of man in such a way. For to believe, the mere apprehension of terms is not enough. 

<margin>Augustine. It is argued first.</margin> This act is affirmed by Augustine in many places, as I have said, and also by most effective reasons. And **first**, it is argued thus: It is not in the free power of man to form an opinion that something is this way or that way whenever he wishes. Therefore, it is not in the free power of man to believe it is this way or that way whenever he wishes. The consequence is clear. Because if that which seems more likely to be present is not present, then [the less likely is also not present]. <note>This is an *a fortiori* argument: if we cannot even control our uncertain opinions, we certainly cannot control our firm beliefs.</note>

But it is less of a struggle to adhere to something with a fear of the opposite <note>referring to a "doubtful opinion"</note> than without such fear <note>referring to "certain belief"</note>. <margin>Aristotle.</margin> Therefore, the antecedent is expressed by Aristotle in the second book of *On the Soul* <note>original: "ii. de anima"</note>, in the commentary on text 153. And it is evident by experience. For anyone experiences within themselves that when a doubtful proposition is offered, if it is purely doubtful to them, they are not inclined by assent to hold either opinion, until a new appearance occurs, either through syllogistic reasoning, or through intuitive knowledge, or through the testimony of many, or through the authority of a speaker, or something similar.

<margin>Second.</margin> **Second**, it is argued thus: It is not in the free power of man to make something appear true to his intellect and to make it appear not true. Therefore, it is not in the power of man to believe thus or so—that it is or is not true. The consequence holds because it is a contradiction for someone to believe something and assent to it, and yet for that thing not to appear true to him. 

<margin>It is confirmed.</margin> The premise is proved because for this or that to appear in such a way to the intellect is for this or that to be represented in such a way to the intellect. And this cannot depend on the command of the will, because this representation precedes the act of the will. This is **confirmed** because something appearing in such a way to the intellect is due to the object that is represented being such, and the evidence (or whatever else makes it credible or not credible) being such, and the intellect itself being such. But to make the object be such, or the intellect be such, is not within the choice of the will.

<summary>Pico argues that belief is not a voluntary choice, but a result of how the intellect perceives truth and evidence, citing Aristotle, Augustine, and the University of Paris to support his view.</summary>

**APOLOGIA**

...of the will. Therefore, for a thing to appear in one way or another to the intellect is not within the command of the will.

**Third.** The third argument is as follows: Whenever there is any power that is purely neutral and indifferent toward two opposing <term>secondary acts</term> <note>In the logic of the time, a 'secondary act' (actus secundus) is the actual exercise of a faculty, like the act of thinking, whereas the 'primary act' is the underlying capacity or state of being.</note>, it cannot manifest in either of them unless it is first determined by something that serves as a <term>primary act</term>, or occupies the place of a primary act in relation to one of those secondary acts. 

But it is the case that the intellect is a power that is purely neutral and indifferent toward the <term>specification</term> <note>The process by which a general mental faculty is directed toward a specific thought or object.</note> of any of its secondary acts. Therefore, it cannot be determined toward any such specification unless something else intervenes which is either a primary act or stands in the place of a primary act regarding that determination. 

Then, under this line of reasoning, I assume this logical consequence: a mere act of the will cannot serve as the primary act regarding the specification of the acts of the intellect. Therefore, by the command <note>original: "imperium"; the authoritative direction of one faculty over another.</note> of the will alone, the intellect cannot be determined toward such a specification. This consequence is well-known from the reasoning already established, and the premise is clear from the common opinion <note>original: "communi sententia"; the general consensus among the scholastic doctors of the Church.</note>.

<summary>Pico presents a formal logical argument stating that because the intellect is a neutral faculty, it cannot be directed to believe something specific by the will alone, but requires a prior cause or evidence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s defense (Apologia) of his disputed theses. He is concluding his argument that the act of faith is not a voluntary choice of the will but a necessary result of evidence presented to the intellect, citing the respected medieval theologian Robert Holcot to show that his own views are within the bounds of orthodox scholarly debate.</meta>

**OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA**

Let these points suffice for the defense of my conclusion. However, I wish to say this: there was also a certain doctor—and I must confess I have never read of his condemnation on this article of faith—who held simply that the act of believing was not free. This was held assertively by <margin>Robert Holcot, a most subtle doctor.</margin> Robert Holcot, a most subtle doctor <note>original: "subtilissimus doctor"; a title of high respect in scholastic circles</note> of the Dominican Order <note>original: "ordinis predicatorum"</note> in his first book on the *Sentences*. And when it is argued that it would follow that the act of believing or not believing would not be meritorious or demeritorious, he says this objection is void and frivolous. For an act is not meritorious because it is free, but because it is in conformity with some law promising a reward for that act to the person performing it or to another.

Consequently, he says the act of believing is not meritorious because it is free, but because it is in conformity with the divine law which promises such a reward—namely, eternal life—to anyone who believes. He adds that God could change this law and decree that whoever should happen to fall upon a cornerstone tomorrow by chance should be saved; then that fall would be meritorious of eternal life. This is because our acts are not meritorious because they are free, but because they are accepted by God for eternal life. God can accept natural acts just as easily as voluntary acts. Thus, He seems to have accepted the death of the Innocents <note>The "Holy Innocents," the infants killed by King Herod in the Gospel of Matthew.</note> for eternal life, <margin>In the Innocents, there was no use of free will according to Augustine.</margin> in whom there was no use of free will. Nor does God act irrationally in doing so, because His will is a sufficient reason for all things which He decrees or ordains.

Hence Holcot concludes that if we take "believing" to mean adhering with firm assent to things whose truth is not evident to us except by the testimony of others—in the way Augustine defines it in his homily on John, saying "what is faith but believing what you do not see?"—then such an act of believing is not within the free power of man. But if "believing" is taken to mean assenting to whatever is revealed by God and witnessed by miracles, <margin>Believing according to the third chapter of Augustine.</margin> and willing to live and act according to them, then because this "believing" includes both an act of the intellect and the will, he concedes that it is free. It is in this way that Augustine, defining it in his homily on John, says: "To believe in God is to love by believing, to go to Him by believing, to cling to Him by believing, and to be incorporated into His members." It was of this kind of belief it was said: "Abraham believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness." But regarding the first kind, it is said: "The demons believe and tremble." The first type <note>Holcot's "first type" here refers to the faith formed by love, which is meritorious.</note> is meritorious; the second <note>The simple intellectual assent.</note> is not. 

And when it is said that "faith exists only in those who are willing," <margin>Holcot</margin> Holcot says this must be understood as <term>formed faith</term> <note>Faith animated by Christian love (charity), which was considered "complete" faith in medieval theology.</note> according to this second mode, which is faith working through love, and not concerning faith accepted in the first mode. For he maintains that through witnessed miracles, a faithful person can be necessitated to believe. I do not believe this opinion is true, and after his initial inquiry, the same doctor, re-examining several of his opinions, says that although the will is necessitated to believe when evidence is present in the reason that something should be believed, nevertheless, because it was the cause of such necessity for itself, it is therefore imputed to it as a sin. He says the cause was that the person neglected to consider, search out diligently, and discuss those things which produced the false evidence; had they done so, it would not have appeared that way to the intellect, but otherwise. And so he concludes that when someone believes or disbelieves wrongly, their first sin is negligence. This is the opinion of Robert Holcot on the freedom of believing, which never appeared good or probable to me. Let these Fathers <note>The papal commission investigating Pico's 900 theses.</note> consider whether they should anathematize this doctor as a heretic along with Durandus, Henry, and the others.

**QUESTION NINE CONCERNING ACCIDENTS IN THE SACRAMENT.**

Whoever says that an accident cannot exist unless it exists in <unclear>the subject</unclear> of the Eucharist would be able to hold the sacrament even while holding that the substance of the bread does not remain. <note>This refers to the doctrine of Transubstantiation, where the "accidents" (the taste, smell, and appearance of bread) remain even after the "substance" has turned into the Body of Christ.</note>

Indeed, these masters did not say this conclusion was heretical or that it savored of heresy, but only that it was erroneous. If they had brought forward any reasons for this opinion of theirs, I might be able to either believe them or answer them. But they, neither in the condemnation of this nor of other conclusions, <margin>Note</margin> offered any...

To these accidents, the body of Christ could have a real presence, just as it currently has in relation to the accidents that are not supported by any subject. Whatever may be the reality of the Eucharist as it was instituted by Christ and believed by the Church, in which we harmoniously agree...

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s philosophical defense regarding the Eucharist. He is specifically addressing the technical metaphysical question of what happens to the "existence" (esse) of the bread during Transubstantiation, moving then into his tenth disputed conclusion regarding the logical function of the words of consecration spoken by a priest.</meta>

**GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA**

...according to common opinion. The essence of the bread, however, agrees with the essence of the body of Christ in matter and genus; whence one can be converted into the other even by nature, if the body were mortal. But the *existence* <note>original: "esse"; in scholastic philosophy, "existence" is the actual being of a thing, whereas "essence" is what the thing is.</note> of the bread does not share in matter nor in genus with the substantial *existence* of the body of Christ, since that [Christ's existence] is uncreated and divine, belonging to the divine person, as in Christ there is only one *existence* of actual substantial existence. Therefore, it is impossible for the *existence* of the bread to be converted, and it is necessary for it to remain. 

I am of the opinion that it is not necessary for it to remain: <margin>The author's opinion</margin> both because if it cannot be converted, it can nevertheless be annihilated, or it can be corrupted by yielding into the potentiality of matter. Thus, just as humanity could be assumed <note>Referring to the Incarnation, where the Son of God took on human nature.</note> without the *existence* being assumed, but remaining in the potentiality of matter, so the essence can be converted without the *existence* being converted, but rather reduced into the potentiality of the essence—though, to tell the truth, these reductions are more easily said than understood. 

Likewise, although the *existence* of the bread cannot be converted into uncreated *existence*, it can nevertheless be converted into a created essence, because things which share in matter are mutually transmutable, even granted they do not share in "proximate" matter but only in "remote" matter <note>"Proximate matter" is matter already shaped by a form (like flour for bread), while "remote matter" or "prime matter" is the most basic, formless substrate of all physical things.</note>, just as an element can be converted into a living soul and vice versa. Moreover, the *existence* of the bread and the essence of the body of Christ agree in prime matter, which is the remote potentiality of both, even if they do not agree in proximate matter; for matter is pure potentiality, while essence is potentiality with act. 

Indeed, if that reasoning were valid, it would conclude that of all the food which Christ consumed before his Passion, only the essence would have been converted into him and not the *existence*, but the *existence* either remained or was corrupted by some way other than conversion; for the substantial *existence* of Christ was uncreated before the Resurrection just as it was after. 

Likewise, some say that just as water, which by ordained power <note>term: "ordained power" (potentia ordinata); the regular way God acts through the laws of nature and the Church, as opposed to his "absolute power" (potentia absoluta) by which he can do anything that is not a logical contradiction.</note> cannot be converted into the blood of Christ, is first converted into wine and afterwards the whole is converted into blood, so if *existence* cannot be converted into something of Christ by absolute power, it is first converted by nature into its own essence, passing into it like a form that yields into the potentiality of matter; and after that, the whole essence is converted into the [divine] essence, and thus it is not necessary for the *existence* to remain. However, just as it seems erroneous to me to say that the *existence* must necessarily remain, it is no less erroneous to say that it *cannot* remain.

### THE TENTH QUESTION ON THE WORDS OF CONSECRATION.

<note>A large decorative initial "I" contains intricate floral and vine designs, marking the start of a new section of the argument.</note> Those words, "This is my body," which are spoken in the consecration, are held materially and not significatively.

These masters <note>The members of the commission investigating Pico's work.</note> have said that this conclusion is scandalous and contrary to the common opinion of the holy doctors, and that the opinion of the Glossator <note>Likely referring to the standard legal or biblical commentary (the *Glossa Ordinaria*).</note> is not to be held in this matter. 

But I say that their determination is scandalous and contrary to the common opinion of many doctors, and that the opinion of the Glossator is to be held in this matter rather than theirs. And that this is so will be clearly evident once the meaning of the conclusion is understood. It must first be noted, therefore, <margin>Note</margin> that I do not intend for these words to have been taken materially when they were uttered by Christ, but only when they are uttered by a priest of the Gospel performing the consecration; and therefore I said in the conclusion: "the words which are spoken in the consecration," that is, those which are now uttered by the ones consecrating. 

It is certain, however, that the priest in consecrating recites the aforementioned words of Christ, so that the prayer uttered by such a priest stands for the prayer uttered by Christ, which was used significatively <note>term: "significatively" (significative); using words to point to their actual meaning (e.g., when Christ said it, he meant the bread *was* his body), as opposed to "materially," where the words are treated as a quoted formula or objects in themselves.</note>. And such an opinion is not only not erroneous or scandalous, but rather the opinion opposite to the aforementioned sense seems to be contrary to the form of consecration, in which the priest speaks those words by way of recitation. For the priest, in consecrating, recites that Christ said to the apostles: "Take and eat, etc." But the priest consecrating neither speaks to the apostles nor says to them "Take, etc." except by way of recitation. For he alone receives the sacrament, nor does he speak to those standing by, saying "Take and eat, etc." Similarly, when he says, "This is my body," that which is recited by the priest is that prayer "This is my body" taken materially for a similar prayer...

# DEFENSE

...and composed of similar words uttered significatively by Christ, which is evident through those words said before or after the consecration of the blood: namely, "which will be poured out for you and for many, etc." <note>original: "qui pro uobis & pro multis effundet &c."</note> For these words would be false if they were taken significatively, because the blood of Christ will not be shed from now on; therefore, those words are taken only recitatively. <note>In scholastic logic, "significative" use of a word means it is intended to perform its meaning in the present, whereas "recitative" means the speaker is merely quoting another's words.</note> What, however, is being recited except a word uttered by another, for which the word of the reciter himself stands? And for that reason, this voice, reciting another’s voice, is to be taken materially. <note>original: "materialiter sumẽda"; meaning the words are treated as the "matter" or object of a quote rather than an active assertion by the priest.</note> Likewise, even if these words were taken not recitatively but significatively, they would denote that the blood of Christ is shed for others and not for the one consecrating, since it says "which will be poured out for you and for many." It ought rather to be said, "which for us, etc." I do not say these things because I believe the opposite opinion cannot be defended, but so that it may be clear that my conclusion is not only Catholic, but also more probable than its opposite. From which it is clear that the present conclusion is not scandalous but probable, and the opinion of the solemn glossator <note>Referring to the standard legal commentary on the "Decretum Gratiani," a collection of canon law.</note> in the section *De Consecratione*, distinction 2, chapter "Timore," is not to be rejected in this matter but approved, just as it has never been rejected by the Church up to these times.

### QUESTION ELEVEN CONCERNING THE MIRACLES OF CHRIST.

The miracles of Christ are the most certain argument of his divinity, not by reason of the thing done, but by reason of his mode of doing. <note>original: "Miracula christi non ratione rei factae sed ratione modi faciendi suae diuinitatis argumentum sunt certissimum."</note>

In declaring this conclusion, I have said that because it is a firm teaching of the theologians that those miracles which Christ performed could be performed by a mere human through the power of God. For Christ says in John 14: "Amen, I say to you, he who believes in me, the works that I do, he will do also, and greater than these will he do." Therefore, it is also unanimously concluded by those same theologians that the thing from which we can conclude Christ was God is not the deed itself, but the *mode of doing* it. For he acted in the same way as those who act by their own power <note>original: "uirtute ppria"</note> and not by power received from elsewhere—which is the unique property of God, to act independently and not by another’s power. This mode of acting cannot be communicated to a creature. Because Christ performed many things in such a way—not by praying or by asking, but by commanding and ordering as one having authority—it is clear that he worked as one who exists as God, and not as a man existing in the power of God.

Having seen this declaration of mine, they [the critics] said the conclusion could be drawn toward an evil sense, because it implies magic, even granted that my declaration is true. Regarding this judgment of theirs, I wonder so much that I cannot wonder more. First, let them tell me whether my words, to anyone interpreting them rightly and according to the correct and accustomed mode of speaking, could have any other sense than the one I stated. For what could be clearer or more express than these words: "The miracles of Christ are the most certain argument of his divinity, not by reason of the thing done, but by reason of his mode of doing"?

Secondly, let them tell me whether this is the judgment of a righteous judge: "This conclusion, although it is true and Catholic, is nevertheless to be condemned because it can be drawn toward an evil sense." If so, then the statement "Christ cast out demons" must be condemned because the Jews drew it toward an evil sense, saying that "by Beelzebub, the prince of demons, he casts out those demons." And this statement must be condemned: "The Father is greater than I," because Arius <note>Arius (c. 250–336 AD) taught that Jesus was a created being, subordinate to God the Father, a view condemned as the Arian heresy.</note> used it to argue for the inequality of the Son to the Father. And this must be condemned: "He knew her not until she brought forth her firstborn son," because Helvidius <note>Helvidius (4th century) argued against the perpetual virginity of Mary, using this verse from Matthew 1:25 to suggest she had other children.</note> derived a heresy from it against the perpetual virginity of Mary. And this must be condemned: "Of that day, not even the Son knows," because from it some wish to know more than the Father, or more than the Son knows. Indeed, almost all Evangelical propositions would have to be condemned, because they could be drawn toward an evil sense by heretics. Since my proposition is placed in these same terms in which it is placed by many Catholic doctors, why should we condemn it, even if it is true, just because some might draw it toward an evil sense? Surely, if any interpret it poorly, their sense is the one that is evil...

<margin>Augustine</margin> I marvel at the learning of those fathers and their extensive reading of sacred matters, who say that it should never be said of an angel—neither properly nor improperly—that he is "rational." <note>Pico is responding to critics who attacked his terminology. <meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s "Apologia." Following his defense of specific theological terms, Pico here addresses the circumstances of this book's composition—noting it was written in haste to answer his critics—and begins to clarify several of his most controversial propositions regarding Christ's descent into hell, eternal punishment, and the salvation of the Church Father Origen.</meta>

# GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

Although these things have been dictated by me now with a hurried pen, I intend to write at another time with greater leisure and care, producing more and perhaps better work. This work itself, such as it is, was composed by lamplight in twenty nights; in its publication, speed was more desirable to me than diligence. For it was necessary that my friends have something to throw to my barking enemies—like a morsel to Cerberus <note>In Greek mythology, Cerberus is the three-headed hound guarding the gates of the Underworld; Pico compares his critics to this beast, needing to be silenced with a "morsel" of explanation.</note>—and thus that I might immediately confront the disease of unjust infamy that was coming upon me. 

Whatever we have written <margin>Note.</margin> and shall write in the future is always said with this preface: that it holds only that to be valid and sacred which the Supreme Pontiff <note>The Pope.</note> and all those whose judgment he approves shall decree as valid and sacred. And would that he had already decreed something concerning these opinions of ours that have been called into doubt, according to his wisdom and authority. I would not have undertaken this task, since it would be rash to defend what he condemned and superfluous to defend what he approved. 

Therefore, while we cannot yet make use of the sentence of so great a judge, we have written these things so that my "left-handed" <note>original: "sinistri"; meaning malicious or biased.</note> detractors might not have grounds to speak ill of the questions I proposed for debate, nor the unlearned and simple suspect wrongdoing. For it can happen that when someone less learned comes upon them, reading this proposition—"Christ did not descend to hell truly and in terms of his real presence as the common way posits"—they are immediately offended by that phrase "not truly." Such a person might believe the meaning of the proposition is that the article of faith regarding Christ's descent into hell is not true. <note>Pico is distinguishing between the *fact* of the descent, which he accepts, and the *philosophical mode* of how Christ was "present" there, which was a subject of intense scholastic debate.</note> 

Likewise, when they read that "infinite punishment is not owed to a mortal sin of finite time," <note>Pico had argued that because a human sin is committed in a finite moment, the logic of its punishment being literally infinite in duration was philosophically problematic, though he does not deny the existence of Hell.</note> they may suspect me of holding the heresy that the punishment of Gehenna <note>Hell.</note> is not eternal. And when they understand that I hold a favorable opinion concerning the salvation of Origen, <note>Origen (c. 185–253 AD) was a massively influential early Christian theologian whose later condemnation by the Church remained a point of debate for Renaissance humanists like Pico.</note> they might suspect that it is not Origen’s life, character, doctrine, and penitence that I love, but rather Origen's condemned dogmas. 

It is similar with many other propositions which perhaps here, at first glance, might offend "holy rusticity"—that is, ears that are as pious as they are unlearned. Therefore, just as we have written these things so that they may be read so that no one thinks ill of us or of the orthodox dogma of our holy religion, I would not wish these propositions themselves—raw and unexplained, as it were—to be read by our people unless they have first reached these explanations, since many things could be inferred from them that are as alien to the Catholic faith as they are to my own mind...

<summary>Pico explains that he wrote this defense in only twenty days to counter his critics and reaffirms his total submission to Papal authority. He clarifies that his controversial statements on Christ's descent into hell, eternal punishment, and Origen were intended as technical philosophical inquiries, not denials of Church dogma.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from Pico della Mirandola’s general defense of his intentions to a formal list of the "Conclusions" (theses) he is defending. He begins with his controversial stance on Christ’s descent into hell, moving into the logic of theological language, and concluding with the nature of mortal sin and eternal punishment.</meta>

->THE CONCLUSIONS WHICH I DEFEND IN THIS WORK AS CATHOLIC ARE WRITTEN BELOW.<-

### First conclusion.
The soul of Christ descended to the underworld by a true and real descent; and thus, during the three days <note>The "triduum," the three days between the Crucifixion and the Resurrection.</note>, Christ was in hell according to the true and real presence of his soul.
**Corollary.** I do not approve of the opinion of *Durandus* <note>Durandus of Saint-Pourçain (c. 1275–1334), a philosopher who argued Christ’s descent was not a physical movement of the soul but merely an "effect." Pico is distancing himself from this view here to appear more orthodox.</note> regarding Christ’s descent into hell.

### Second conclusion.
Although this is the case, the reason for the true and real descent and the true and real location of Christ's soul in hell was not its essence or substance—as the common way of the *Scotists* <note>Followers of John Duns Scotus.</note> and *Nominalists* <note>A school of thought that denied the existence of universal concepts outside the mind.</note> holds, which is commonly held at Paris, and which Saint *Thomas* <note>Thomas Aquinas.</note> seems to adhere to in the third part of the *Summa*—but only its effect or operation.

### Third conclusion.
The meaning explained through the conclusions written above is the meaning I intended by this proposition: "Christ did not truly and regarding his real presence, as *Thomas* and the common way posit, descend into the underworld, but only regarding his effect."

### Fourth conclusion.
The question of whether the aforementioned proposition, according to the rigor of logic and the force of the words, permits that meaning is not a question of faith.

### Fifth conclusion.
One who believes that this proposition, by the virtue of the speech, permits that meaning does not err in faith.

### Sixth conclusion.
He who believes something is a matter of faith which is not a matter of faith does not judge rightly concerning the faith.

### Seventh conclusion.
One who puts forward a proposition having a double meaning, if he asserted and continues to assert it in a Catholic sense, is not bound to revoke the proposition, but to clarify it.

### Eighth conclusion.
In the aforementioned case, and given the multiplicity of meanings, we ought to judge the proposition according to the sense intended by the proposer rather than according to the sense which the words more strongly suggest.

### Ninth conclusion.
Mortal sin is demeritoriously worthy of eternal punishment.

### Tenth conclusion.
Anyone departing this life in mortal sin, even if he departs in only one, shall be punished forever.

### Eleventh conclusion.
Unless the <term>guilt of mortal sin</term> <note>original: "reatus peccati mortalis"; "reatus" refers to the state of being liable for a crime or the "stain" of the sin that remains after the act is done.</note> endured eternally in the soul of the sinner, the punishment of the sinner would not endure forever.

### Twelfth conclusion.
Just as this term "mortal sin" is sometimes taken for the act of sinning—whether of omission or commission—so also, and frequently and properly among Catholic doctors, it is taken for the guilt.

### xiii. conclusion.
When we say that a punishment or a reward is owed in some place, we can understand it in two ways: either that one is demeritoriously or meritoriously worthy of such punishment or reward, or that such punishment or reward is actually paid to him.

### xiiii. conclusion.

<summary>Pico outlines fourteen theological conclusions, primarily defending his interpretation of Christ’s descent into hell as an "effect" rather than a "substance" and defining the nature of mortal sin and eternal punishment.</summary>

The distinction of this word "ought," placed in the preceding conclusion, is not erroneous in faith. <note>This refers to a technical linguistic point in the previous page's argument about the necessity of belief.</note>

### xv. conclusion.
The Cross of Christ and images are to be adored in the same way that the Church adores them.

### xvi. conclusion.
The manner of adoring images and the Cross put forward by *Petrus de Aquila*, *Henry of Ghent*, *Johannes Guarra*, *Durandus*, *Robert Holcot*, and commonly by all the *Scotists* <note>Followers of the philosopher John Duns Scotus.</note> is more probable than the manner put forward by *Thomas* <note>Thomas Aquinas. Pico is siding with a more moderate view of image worship over the stricter Thomist view that images of Christ deserve the same worship as Christ himself.</note>.

### xvii. conclusion.
It does not follow that because someone denies that images are to be adored in the manner that *Thomas* posits, they consequently deny they are to be adored in the manner the Church posits.

### xviii. conclusion.
Since in God there is the fullness of all being, God can—insofar as it depends on Him—make any nature into a <term>hypostasis</term> <note>original: "hipostatizare"; in theology, this refers to the act of giving a nature an individual existence or personal reality, as in the Incarnation of Christ.</note>.

### xix. conclusion.
Regarding this question—whether an irrational nature (due to the defect of its own nature) is incompatible with being assumed into the divine nature in a unity of <term>person</term> <note>original: "suppositi"; the underlying substance or individual personhood.</note>, as *Henry* believed, or whether it is not incompatible, as the common way holds—a Catholic may be so uncertain that he does not have a positive act of contradicting *Henry's* opinion.

### xx. conclusion.
A position that denies assent to a particular statement does not, by the power of the words themselves, imply a positive assent to the opposite statement.

### xxi. conclusion.
All magic which is commonly called <term>necromancy</term>, and absolutely any art or science—if such things should even be called arts or sciences—which involves a pact or communion with demons in any way, whether explicit or implicit, whether as a primary part or an accessory, whether coming before, during, or after, or in any way at all, is a forbidden and superstitious thing and is justly condemned by the Church.

### xxii. conclusion.
That science which is justly said to be the practical part of natural philosophy, and which is called <term>natural magic</term> <note>In the Renaissance, this was not "sorcery" but the study of hidden natural properties, such as magnetism or the medicinal power of herbs.</note> by *William of Auvergne* <note>original: "Guilielmo Parisiensi"</note>, *Roger Bacon*, and all Greek authors, contains nothing in itself that is repugnant to the Catholic and orthodox faith.

### xxiii. conclusion.
There is no science—extending the name "science" to both revealed and non-revealed knowledge—that can make us certain of the divinity of Christ, other than the Gospel doctrine and the science of Christian theology.

### xxiiii. conclusion.
Among the non-revealed sciences (those discovered and acquired by human effort), there is none that helps us more in knowing the divinity of Christ than that which allows us to know what can be done by the power of natural agents, both sublunary <note>Earthly or below the moon.</note> and celestial. From this, we may then understand from the works of Christ that he was the true Lord and author of nature, who performed by his own power things that exceed the limits of all natural power, both celestial and earthly.

### xxv. conclusion.
A believer is not obligated to always use the term "science" in all their speech as a common category for both revealed and non-revealed sciences.

### xxvi. conclusion.
Among the many parts of the <term>Kabbalistic science</term> <note>original: "scientiæ cabalisticæ"; a Jewish mystical and interpretive tradition that Pico was the first to attempt to synthesize into a Christian framework.</note>, there is one that concerns the powers of the celestial bodies.

### xxvii. conclusion.

<meta>This page continues the theological section of Pico della Mirandola’s 900 theses. The heresies attributed to Origen are impious and detestable and were rightfully condemned by the Church.
**28th conclusion.**

Since it is the case that either Origen never believed those opinions—but they were falsely attributed to him by heretics, as *Rufinus*, *Pamphilus*, *Methodius*, *Didymus*, and *Haymo* <note>These are early Christian authors and defenders of Origen (c. 184–253 AD), a brilliant but controversial theologian whose views on the soul and universal salvation sparked centuries of debate.</note> maintain—or, if he did believe them at some time, he repented of them in the end—as *Jerome* <note>original: "Hieronymus"; St. Jerome was a contemporary of some of these debates and famously vacillated in his opinion of Origen.</note> suggests—it is reasonable to believe well regarding the salvation of his soul, and we are not bound to believe the opposite as a necessity for salvation.
**29th conclusion.**

The act of believing is a free act.
**30th conclusion.**

The act of believing is not within a person's power in such a way that, when a purely doubtful proposition is presented, the intellect can adhere to one side rather than the other through the sheer and sole command of the will. <note>Pico is arguing that belief requires intellectual conviction; one cannot simply "force" oneself to believe something that seems factually doubtful just by wanting to.</note>
**31st conclusion.**

One who believes this proposition—that it is not within the free power of the will to believe an article of faith is true when one pleases, and to believe it is false when one pleases—does not err in faith, provided the explicit sense of the preceding conclusion is allowed.
**32nd conclusion.**

<term>Accidents</term> <note>original: "Accidentia"; in medieval philosophy, these are the properties of a thing (like color, texture, or taste) that are not part of its essential substance.</note> in the sacrament of the altar exist in no subject. <note>This refers to the miracle of Transubstantiation, where the properties of bread remain but the "substance" of the bread is gone.</note>
**33rd conclusion.**

It is possible, by the absolute power of God, for the *existence* of the bread to remain without its *essence*, and for the <term>accidents</term> of the bread to be grounded in that existence; and this assumes a real distinction between essence and existence.
**34th conclusion.**

One who believes this proposition—that one who says an <term>accident</term> cannot exist unless it exists within the Eucharist could uphold the sacrament while also holding that the substance of the bread cannot remain (verifiable by what was said in the preceding conclusion)—does not err in faith.
**35th conclusion.**

"Bread-ness" does not remain in the sacrament of the Eucharist supported by Christ, God-man; but through conversion, it passes into the essence of the body of Christ.
**36th conclusion.**

If one follows the common path—that God can provide a <term>hypostasis</term> <note>original: "suppositare"; the act of giving a nature an individual, personal existence.</note> to any nature—it is possible that Christ assumes "bread-ness" into the unity of the divine <term>person</term> <note>original: "suppositi"; the underlying individual reality of a person.</note>: and it is possible that through such a process Christ is present on the altar where the bread is. Thus, without the conversion or the annihilation of the "bread-ness," Christ could be on the altar according to a possible truth of the sacrament of the Eucharist—not indeed the one instituted by Christ, but one that *could* have been instituted. <note>Pico is exploring a "thought experiment" in theology: could God have made Christ present in the bread in a different way than the Church currently teaches? He argues that exploring these possibilities is not heresy.</note>
**37th conclusion.**

One who believes this proposition—namely, if the common path regarding the possibility of God providing a <term>hypostasis</term> to any creature is held, I say that without the conversion of the substance of the bread into the body of Christ or the annihilation of the bread-ness, it can happen that the body of Christ is on the altar according to the truth of the sacrament (speaking of what is possible, not what currently is)—does not err in faith, allowing for the explicit sense in the preceding conclusion.
**38th conclusion.**

These words, "This is my body," etc., when they were uttered by Christ, were held *significantly* <note>original: "significative"; meaning the words themselves had the power to transform the reality they described at the moment Christ spoke them.</note> and not materially.
**39th conclusion.**

These same words, when they are uttered by a gospel priest during consecration, are held *materially*—that is, *recitatively* <note>original: "recitative"; meaning the priest is quoting or re-enacting Christ's original words, acting as a vessel for Christ's power rather than originating the miracle themselves.</note>—and not significantly.
**40th conclusion.**

The miracles of Christ, in terms of the actual deed performed, are an argument that they were done through divine power.
**41st conclusion.**

The miracles of Christ, in terms of the manner of their performance, are an argument that Christ himself, in exercising divine power, possessed it from himself and not from another source. <note>Pico distinguishes between prophets, who performed miracles as agents of God, and Christ, whom he argues performed them by his own inherent authority as the Son of God.</note>
**42nd conclusion.**

God knows both himself and all things other than himself in the most perfect mode of knowledge.
**43rd conclusion.**

Therefore, He is <term>simply all perfection</term>. <note>original: "perfection simpliciter"; in scholastic philosophy, a "simple perfection" is a quality—like wisdom or existence—that is better to have than not to have, and which God possesses to an infinite degree without any limiting "parts."</note>
**44th conclusion.**

If we use the name <term>intellectual</term> according to the manner of *Dionysius* <note>original: "Dionysii"; referring to Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century theologian. He argued that God is beyond all human names and concepts.</note>—as describing a knowledge proper to the angelic nature, just as "rational" describes a knowledge proper to the human nature—then we say improperly that God is "intellectual" or that He "understands." <note>Pico is explaining a hierarchy of thought: humans use "reason" (logical steps), angels use "intellect" (immediate intuition), but God’s nature is so far above both that even these high-sounding words are technically inaccurate descriptions of His being.</note>
**45th conclusion.**

Through that hidden act of understanding which is direct and permanent, without the aid of the senses or the <term>phantasy</term> <note>original: "fantaſiæ"; in the psychology of this era, the "phantasy" or imagination was the faculty that created mental images from sensory data. Pico argues that the soul’s self-awareness is purely spiritual and does not require these mental "pictures."</note>, the soul understands itself alone, actually and distinctly.
**46th conclusion.**

The soul, through its multiple and various other acts, understands things other than itself that are various and multiple.

<meta>This page transitions from the legal defense of Pico’s 900 Theses to one of his most important philosophical works, *De Ente et Uno* (On Being and the One), written around 1491. This treatise marks Pico’s attempt to reconcile the two giants of Western philosophy, Plato and Aristotle, who were often seen as contradictory in their views on the nature of reality.</meta>

# ON BEING AND THE ONE
## GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA ON BEING AND THE ONE TO ANGELO POLIZIANO. PREFACE.

**N**ou were telling me a few days ago <note>original: "Narrabas mihi ſupiorib⁹ dieb⁹"; Pico is addressing his close friend, the renowned humanist poet and scholar Angelo Poliziano.</note> what **Lorenzo de' Medici** <note>The ruler of Florence and patron of the arts; Pico describes him here as a man of "multifaceted genius" who remained devoted to philosophy despite his heavy state duties.</note> had discussed with you regarding **being and the one**. He was disputing against **Aristotle**—whose *Ethics* you are publicly lecturing on this year—relying on the arguments of the **Platonists**. He is a man of such effective and versatile talent that he seems made for all things; in him, I especially admire that, although he is always most occupied with the affairs of the Republic, he is always either speaking or meditating on something literary. Because those who believe Aristotle disagrees with Plato also disagree with me, since I make the philosophy of both concordant, you asked how Aristotle might be defended in this matter and how he might agree with his master, Plato. I said what then came to my mind, confirming what you had replied to Lorenzo during the dispute rather than bringing forward anything new. But this was not enough for you; for you demand that, although I intend to write more extensively on these matters in the *Concord of Plato and Aristotle* <note>original: "Platonis Ariſtoteliſq con/cordia"; this was Pico's projected but unfinished masterpiece intended to harmonize the two philosophical traditions.</note> which I am still laboring to produce, I should nevertheless briefly outline for you in a short commentary those things I spoke to you about in person regarding this question. This was especially since **Domenico Benivieni** <note>A Florentine theologian and close associate of Pico and Savonarola.</note> happened to be present, who is very dear to both of us for his learning and integrity. Truly, what can I deny you in a literary matter, you who are almost my inseparable companion? Permit me, however, as a champion of refined language, to use certain words that have perhaps not yet been granted "citizenship" in the Latin language <note>original: "latii iure donatis"; a metaphor for using technical philosophical terms that may sound clunky or "barbarous" to a classical stylist like Poliziano.</note>. The novelty of the subject and a certain necessity have forced them out. Do not look for the allure of an elegant style here; for as **Manilius** <note>original: "Mallius"; referring to the Roman poet Marcus Manilius, author of the *Astronomica*.</note> says: *The subject itself refuses to be adorned, content to be taught.* These, then, if I remember correctly, were the points we were discussing.

### Chapter one, in which he recounts the arguments of the Platonists: By which they wish to prove that the "One" is superior [to Being].

**A**ristotle in many places says that these things correspond to each other and are of equal scope: namely, the **One** <note>term: "Unum" (The One); in Neoplatonism, the ultimate, simple source of all reality, often placed above existence itself.</note> and **Being** <note>term: "Ens" (Being/Existence); the state of being real or having an essence.</note>; also Truth and the Good, but of these more later. 

<margin>

thinks

What the
Platonists
think
</margin>

The Academy <note>Referring to the Neoplatonists, the followers of Plato's later tradition.</note> resists this, holding that the "One" is prior to "Being." When they say "prior," they want it to be understood as both simpler and more universal. Therefore, they say that God (who is of the highest simplicity) is the "One," but is not "Being." Likewise, they claim that the first raw matter of all things—which is crude and formless—is included within the boundaries of the "One," yet lies outside the limits of "Being" as they see it. Then they assert that the opposite of the "One" is not the same as the opposite of "Being": for nothing is opposed to Being, but "multitude" is opposed to the One. By the same law, they judge that those two—Being and the One—are distinct, so that they are not considered interchangeable or to correspond to one another.

### Chapter two, in which it is asked where Plato spoke of being and the one; and it is shown that his words favor the opinion saying the One and Being are equal, rather than those who want the One to be above Being.

**T**hey rely on these arguments; before we dissolve them, it would not be irrelevant to bring into the open what I find expressed by Plato on this question. I find Plato disputing about Being and the One in two places: namely, in the *Parmenides* and the *Sophist*. The Academics contend that in both places the "One" is placed above "Being" by Plato. I, however, will first say this regarding the *Parmenides*: that in that entire dialogue, nothing is affirmed; and even if it were affirmed to the highest degree, nothing can be found clearly enough for us to ascribe a dogma of that kind to Plato. Certainly, the book is not to be counted among the dogmatic ones, since it is entirely nothing other than a certain dialectical exercise. The very words of the dialogue are so far from contradicting our opinion that no interpretations are more arbitrary and forced than those brought forward by those who seek another sense...

reasoning on
the Good

What should
be thought
concerning
Plato
</margin>

...all interpreters. Let us omit what it begins, what it aims at, what it promises, and what it executes. "Exercise yourself more diligently while you are young," he says, "in that faculty which seems useless to many, and is called by them 'trifling' or 'garrulity' <note>original: "nugacitas siue garrulitas"; Pico is quoting a famous passage from Plato’s *Parmenides* (135d) where the elder philosopher advises a young Socrates to practice the rigors of logic—even if it sounds like empty chatter to the uninitiated—before attempting to define the nature of truth.</note>; otherwise, truth will flee you."

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's systematic defense of the harmony between Plato and Aristotle. Having established the logical nature of the Parmenides, he now begins to define the metaphysical terms "Being" (Ens) and "The One" (Unum) to show they are co-extensive.</meta>

->OF MIRANDOLA<-

### Chapter three, in which it is explained how "being" is understood by Aristotle when he makes it equal to "the one" and encompassing all things.

[Large initial D] This word, **"being,"** <note>original: "ens"; the most fundamental concept in metaphysics, referring to anything that exists in any way.</note> about which there is debate as to whether it is equal to **"the one,"** <margin>Being can be understood in two ways.</margin> can be understood in two ways. The first way is that when we say **"being,"** we understand everything that is outside of nothingness. This is the way Aristotle used it when he made "being" equal to "the one." Nor did he use the word thus without reason; for as it is truly said, we should think like the few, but speak as we ought <note>original: "sentire ut pauci, loqui ut debemus"; a common philosophical maxim advising scholars to hold refined private views but use language that the general public can understand.</note>. We think and hold opinions for ourselves, but we speak to others—that is, to the multitude—and therefore we speak to be understood. Now, the common people and everyone else understand "being" in such a way that everything is called a "being" which does not lack "to be," and which cannot truly be called "nothing." 

But even those held to be the wisest among the very people who disagree with us are found to have used this word in this way. For **Parmenides the Pythagorean** <note>An ancient Greek philosopher who argued that reality is a single, unchanging "One."</note>, when he said that the "one" is that which is, understood it as **God**. This is true if we believe **Simplicius** <note>A 6th-century Neoplatonist commentator who worked to reconcile the various schools of Greek philosophy.</note> and many others who wish to defend Parmenides against those who slander him as if he had said all things are simply one thing. <margin>The first testimony.</margin> For with one voice they respond that it was never believed by Parmenides that there is no division, multitude, or plurality in things—which he himself openly admits elsewhere in his poems. Rather, when he said "the one is that which is," he judged that the name of **"being"** truly fits that which truly is only one, and that this "one" is God. 

Therefore, if we believe Parmenides and his defenders and the Platonists, the "one" cannot be above "being" unless it is above God; and Parmenides is so far from denying that God is "being" that he grants the true name of "being" to God alone. <margin>According to Simplicius.</margin> And so, the solution to the first argument of the Platonists occurs to us in passing. But also **Dionysius the Areopagite** <margin>The solution to the first Platonic argument.</margin> <note>A late-antique theologian whose writings on the "Names of God" were highly influential in the Renaissance.</note>, whom those disputing against us claim as a supporter of their opinion, will not deny that it is truly said of God to Moses: **"I am who I am,"** which we read in Greek as *ego eimi ho on*, that is, "I am being" <note>Exodus 3:14. Pico is arguing that even mystical theologians like Dionysius accept that God calls Himself "Being."</note>. <margin>Dionysius.</margin> 

Indeed, since they themselves say that "nothing" or "non-being" is opposed to "being" just as "multitude" is opposed to the "one," they must necessarily concede that what is not "being" is nothing or non-being. Just as what is not "one" is many or a multitude. Therefore, if they preserve the same law of speech, they must admit either that God is nothing—which the ears themselves dread to hear—or that He is "being." In this way, when "being" is understood, we establish that first axiom and universal principle: of anything, it must necessarily be said either that it *is* or that it *is not*, and of nothing can both be said or thought at once. <margin>The fourth [point].</margin> Since, therefore, there is nothing outside of all things except nothingness itself, if "being" understood in this way excludes only nothingness from itself, it undoubtedly encompasses all things. Therefore, the "one" cannot encompass more than "being" unless it encompasses nothingness—which Plato denies in the *Sophist* <note>One of Plato's dialogues exploring the nature of truth, falsehood, and "non-being."</note> when he says that non-being or "nothing" cannot be called "one." <margin>The fifth [point].</margin> If it does not encompass fewer things, as they themselves wish, then "being" and "the one" are equal.

### Chapter four, in which he explains how something can be said to be superior to "being."

[Large initial E] We have explained one of those ways in which we said "being" can be understood; those who use it thus correctly affirm that nothing is more common than "being." <margin>Concrete names from abstract [names].</margin> It remains for us to explain the other way, according to which it will be manifest that it can nonetheless be truly said that there is something placed above the excellence of "being." 

Of names, some are **concrete**, others **abstract**. <margin>Diversity.</margin> Concrete names are: *hot, shining, white, man*. Abstract names are: *heat, light, whiteness, humanity*. Now, the power and diversity of these is such that what is called "abstract" denotes that which is such by itself, not from another. A "concrete" name, on the other hand, signifies that which is such not by itself, but by the benefit of another. Thus, a shining thing shines by light; a white thing is white by whiteness; and a man is a man by humanity. Since truly nothing participates in itself <note>A philosophical rule stating that a thing cannot "share" in its own essence, because it *is* that essence.</note>, nor can the same condition exist in the same thing both by itself and by the participation of another, it follows that what is called abstract cannot be named from the concrete. Therefore, it is not fittingly said that "whiteness is white" or "blackness is black." Indeed, one who would say such things would be ridiculous—not because whiteness is black or heat is cold, but because whiteness is as far from blackness and heat from cold as anything can be.

O ii

<summary>Pico defines "Being" in two ways: first as everything that exists (making it equal to "the One"), and second as a concrete term distinct from its abstract essence. He argues that even mystical authorities like Dionysius identify God with Being.</summary>
