### Chapter three (continued), in which it is explained how "being" is understood by Aristotle when he makes it equal to "the one" and encompassing all things.

<margin>It can be denied in two ways that something is attributed to someone.</margin> 
Indeed, it should be known that a thing can be denied in two ways <note>original: "bifariam"; meaning something can be understood or categorized in two distinct manners.</note> to any given subject. This happens either because that thing is altogether lacking in the subject, or because it exists in that subject in a way that is much more excellent than the word itself can signify. 

For instance, if we say that God is not a "being," <note>original: "ens"</note> we do not mean that He does not exist, but rather that He is something more than a "being"—namely, "to be" itself <note>original: "ipsum esse"; a distinction where God is not just an individual thing that exists, but the very act of existence from which all things flow.</note>. If we follow this path of reasoning, we must determine that it is true that **God is the Good**; yet if we speak like the more refined philosophers, we would say he is "beyond the good." 

Furthermore, if there is one ruler of all, as the saying goes:

->**Let there be one lord, one king.**<-
<note>original: "εἷς κοίρανος ἔστω, εἷς βασιλεύς" (eis koiranos esto, eis basileus); a famous line from Homer’s *Iliad* (2.204). Pico uses this Greek citation to illustrate that just as there is one ruler of the universe, there must be one primary principle in philosophy—the One.</note>

It follows that if "being" and "the one" are converted <note>In logic, "conversion" means that the terms are interchangeable; if everything that is a "being" is "one," and everything "one" is a "being," they are equal in scope.</note>, then whatever is not "one" is also not a "being." This is why Aristotle, who sought to describe the nature of things as they are found in the world, rightly taught that "being" and "the one" are equal. For nothing can exist unless it is unified within itself. If you take away the unity of a thing, you take away its existence. 

<margin>Being is not denied to God.</margin> 
But even if we say that "the one" is higher than "being," we do not therefore deny "being" to God. We simply elevate Him above the common definition of things that exist. Thus, we may say that God is "one" in a way that exceeds our understanding of "being," but he is nonetheless the source of all that is. 

<summary>Pico explains that "being" and "the one" are interchangeable terms in Aristotle's philosophy. He argues that even when theologians place God "above being," they are not saying He does not exist, but that His existence is of a higher, more unified order.</summary>

An example of the first type is sensory knowledge <note>original: "cognitio sensualis"; information gathered through the physical senses rather than pure reason.</note>, which is imperfect not only because it is merely knowledge and not desire, but because it is also an imperfect form of knowledge. This is because it requires a dull and physical organ, and because it only reaches the outermost surfaces of things...

<meta>This page continues Pico’s defense of the unity of "Being" and "the One," moving from a discussion of divine transcendence to the practical ways these concepts relate to created things. He is now beginning to reconcile the views of Aristotle, Averroes, and Plato on how "Being," "One," "True," and "Good" are essentially the same thing looked at from different angles.</meta>

# MIRANDOLA

In many places, he interpolated the philosophy of Aristotle <note>original: "phiãm Aristo."</note>; from which great wars were fought with Averroes <note>Averroes (Ibn Rushd) was a 12th-century Islamic philosopher known as "The Commentator" on Aristotle. Pico refers to the intense intellectual battles between different schools of Aristotelian thought in the Renaissance.</note>. But as far as this matter is concerned, there is little discord in reality. For these thinkers divide what Plato understands under "the One" into "the One" and "Something"—a distinction that is not inconsistent with Plato, who in his dialogue the *Sophist* enumerates "Something" among these most common terms. They also partition what is contained under "Being" into "Being" and "Thing." But regarding these matters elsewhere—let us pursue these four <note>Being, One, True, and Good</note> as we began. They exist in God in one way, and in those things which come after God in another; for God has these from Himself, while others have them from Him.

Let us first see how they are in created things: all things after God have an efficient, exemplary, and final cause. For "from Him, through Him, and to Him are all things." <note>A reference to Romans 11:36, emphasizing God as the source, the model, and the goal of all existence.</note> If, therefore, we consider things as they are constituted by God as the efficient cause, they are called **beings**, because they participate in being through His action. If we consider them as they relate to their exemplar—which we call the "Idea" according to which God established them—they are called **true**. For an image of Hercules is called a "true" image when it is truly conformed to Hercules. If they are considered as they tend toward Him as to their ultimate end, they are called **good**. If, however, each thing is taken absolutely in itself, it is named **one**.

<margin>Order in</margin>
<margin>these four</margin>
There is, however, an order here: first, each thing must be conceived under the notion of being. This is because an agent acts upon a thing before that thing is anything in itself; otherwise, it would not be from the agent according to its whole being. Thus it happens that there is nothing after God that we can conceive without understanding it as being from another—a finite being, a participated being. 

**One** follows being. The third is **Truth**, because after a thing exists in itself, it must be seen whether it is such as the exemplar according to which it was formed. If it is found to be similar, it remains for it to turn toward that exemplar—as if toward something related and kin—through **Goodness**.

Who does not see that these four encompass the same scope? Grant that something exists, and it is certainly also one. For he who does not say "one" says nothing, as Plato says in the *Sophist*. 
<margin>Plato.</margin>
For whatever a thing is, it is undivided from itself and divided from all other things that are not itself. When we say this, we understand the "One," or to use Plato’s words: it is "the same as itself" and "different from others." In that same dialogue, he confirms that this applies to every single thing.

<margin>True is</margin>
<margin>convertible with</margin>
<margin>being.</margin>
It is also true by necessity. For if it is a man, it is certainly a "true" man. It is the same thing to say "this is not true gold" and "this is not gold." 
<margin>Augustine.</margin>
For when you say it is "not true gold," you mean this: it looks like gold and is something similar to gold, but it is not gold. Therefore, Aurelius Augustine, defining truth in his *Soliloquies*, says: "The true is that which is." <note>original: "verum est id quod est."</note> This should not be taken to mean that "being" and "truth" are identical in every way. For although they are the same in reality, they are different in reason and definition; therefore, one should not be defined by the other. Rather, Augustine wanted to express that a thing is called "true" when it is exactly what it is said to be: gold is "true" when it is gold and nothing other than gold. This is what he meant by "the true is that which is." Some, not noticing this distinction, slander his definition.

<margin>Good is</margin>
<margin>convertible with</margin>
<margin>being.</margin>
Similarly, a thing is also "good," because whatever exists is good insofar as it exists. In my opinion, Olympiodorus <note>A 6th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who argued that the Good and Being were distinct.</note> is far mistaken in believing he can prove that the "Good" and "Being" are different on the grounds that we desire the "Good" simply. 
<margin>He disputes</margin>
<margin>against</margin>
<margin>Olympiodorus.</margin>
He argues that we do not desire "being" simply, but "well-being," and thus it could happen that if things go badly for us, we might desire "not-being." For—even if we set aside the question of whether those who are miserable can seek "not to be" with a right and natural desire—he fails to notice that just as "being" is manifold, so "goodness" is manifold.

First, there is the **natural being** of things: for a man to be a man, a lion to be a lion, or a stone to be a stone. A natural goodness follows this being indivisibly. There are other forms of being which can be called **adventitious** <note>In philosophy, "adventitious" or "accidental" refers to qualities that are added to a thing but are not part of its core essence, like being wise or being healthy.</note>, such as for a man to be wise, beautiful, or healthy. Just as wisdom and beauty are different "beings" from humanity, so they are different "goods." For humanity is one good, by which a man is a man; wisdom is another good, by which he is not just a man, but becomes a wise man. Just as one is one type of being and the other is another, they are so called. Therefore, just as all things seek the good, so all things seek being. First, they seek that goodness which follows natural being, since this is the foundation...

<summary>Pico explains that Being, One, True, and Good are "convertible" terms that refer to the same reality from different perspectives (efficient, formal, and final causes). He defends the unity of these concepts against critics like Olympiodorus by distinguishing between "natural being" and "adventitious" qualities like wisdom.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the argument that Being and the One are identical in their essence. Having established that God is the source of these qualities, Pico now examines how they manifest in created things and why their opposites—such as evil and nothingness—are fundamentally the same lack of existence.</meta>

->**ON BEING AND THE ONE.**<-

...foundation of the following goods, all of which come to a thing in such a way that they cannot exist without it. For how can someone be happy if they do not exist at all? <note>original: "Quomodo.n.erit fœlix qui oino nō erit"</note> Indeed, that goodness which things first acquire when they come into being is not enough for them; rather, they desire to attain the remaining goods that might complete and adorn that first one. Just as we say truly that they seek other goods beyond that primary goodness, so we can say truly that they desire other ways of being beyond their primary existence. This is because it is one thing to be a human being, and another to be happy. <note>Pico is distinguishing between "essential being" (existing as a human) and "accidental being" (possessing qualities like happiness).</note>

And if anyone grants that it is possible for someone to wish not to exist if they are not happy, it does not follow—as Olympiodorus <note>Olympiodorus the Younger was a 6th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote commentaries on Plato and Aristotle.</note> thinks—that the Good is one thing and Being is another. Rather, it means being a human is one thing and being happy is another. Likewise, the goodness of a human is one thing, and the goodness of happiness is another. Therefore, a person does not want the first (existence) unless they also have the second (happiness). I leave aside for now whether something is called "good" in a simple sense for the same reason it is called "being" in a simple sense. This is not the place to dispute all these matters. 

I was right, therefore, to say that everything that exists is good to the extent that it exists. For **"God saw all the things he had made, and they were very good."** <note>original: "uidit.n.deus cūcta quæ fecerat & erāt ualde bona"; a reference to Genesis 1:31.</note> And why not? They are from a good craftsman, who impresses his own likeness upon all things that come from him. In their **existence** <term>entitate</term> <note>The state of being or existing.</note>, we can admire the power of God as the Maker; in their **truth**, we can venerate the wisdom of the Artist; in their **goodness**, we can proclaim the generosity of the Lover; and in their **unity**, we can receive the unique simplicity of the Creator. This unity has joined everything to itself and all things to one another, calling everything back to the love of oneself, then to the love of others, and finally to the love of God. 

Let us also examine whether their opposites are equal in scope: the **False** and **Nothingness**.

<margin>Evil and nothingness are interchangeable. Against the error of the Manichaeans. Nothingness and the divided are interchangeable. Aristotle.</margin>

The things we said above show that these are the same. If we say that **Evil** and **Nothingness** differ, both philosophers and theologians will protest. Therefore, to "do evil" is to "do nothing." It is often said that evil does not have an "efficient" cause (a cause that produces something), but a "deficient" cause (a failure to act correctly). <note>This is the classic Augustinian view that evil is not a "thing" created by God, but a lack or privation of good.</note> This refutes the insanity of those who postured two principles—one of good and one of evil—as if there were some productive principle of evil. <note>The Manichaeans believed the universe was a struggle between two equal powers of Light/Good and Dark/Evil. Pico argues evil has no substance of its own.</note>

Furthermore, to divide a thing is the same as to destroy it. We cannot take away the natural unity of a thing without it ceasing to exist in its integrity. For a "whole" is not merely its parts, but that **one** thing which results from the parts, as Aristotle teaches in the eighth book of his *First Philosophy* <note>original: "primæ phĩæ"; referring to Aristotle's *Metaphysics*.</note>. Therefore, if you divide a whole into parts, the parts remain, but the whole that was divided does not remain; it ceases to exist in "act" (reality). It remains only in "potency" (potential), just as the parts—which were previously potential—now begin to exist in act. For while they were in the whole, they did not have their own separate unity in reality; they only obtain it when they are separated from the whole and stand by themselves.

### Chapter IX. In which it is declared how those four are in God.

**E**Xaminemus rurſus <note>Let us examine again...</note> how these four exist in God, in whom they do not exist by reference to a cause, for he has none. He is the cause of all and is from no one. These can be considered in God in two ways: either insofar as he is the cause of others—a distinction that does not apply to created things in this context, because God can exist without being a cause, whereas other things cannot exist without being from him—or as he is in himself. 

Therefore, we first conceive of God as the "universality of all act," the "fullness of being itself." From this understanding, it follows that he is **One**, so that no opposite can even be conceived. See how far they wander from the truth who imagine many primary principles or many gods! Immediately, it is also most true: for that which possesses what appears to be being, but is not "Being Itself," must certainly follow after Truth itself. 

<margin>The three conditions of the Good according to Plato.</margin>

But God will also be **Goodness** itself. For there are three conditions of the "Good," as Plato writes in the *Philebus*: it must be **perfect**, **sufficient**, and **desirable**. <note>original: "perfectū ſufficiēs expetendū"</note> That which we conceive as God will be **perfect**, because nothing will be lacking to him who is all things; it will be **sufficient**, because those who possess it will lack nothing, finding all things within it; and it will be **desirable**, because all things that can be desired for any reason are from him and in him. 

God, therefore, is the fullest **Being**, the indivisible **Unity**, the most solid **Truth**, and the most blessed **Goodness**. 

<margin>Pythagoras.</margin>

This, if I am not mistaken, is that **Tetraktys** <note>original: "τετρακτυσ"; a mystical Pythagorean symbol consisting of ten points arranged in a triangle, representing the organization of the universe.</note>—that is, the "Fourness"—by which Pythagoras used to swear, and which he called the "principle of ever-flowing nature." For these four qualities are the principle...

<summary>Pico argues that existence and goodness are inseparable, refuting the idea that evil is a creative force. He concludes by defining God as the ultimate manifestation of Being, Unity, Truth, and Goodness, linking these to the Pythagorean Tetraktys.</summary>

->MIRANDOLA.<-

...we have demonstrated that they are God, who is all things; <note>original: "ſunt deus oium eſſe demoſtrauimus"</note> but we also swear by those things which are holy, firm, and divine; what could be firmer, holier, or more divine than these? But if we assign these four names to God insofar as He is the cause of things, the entire order is inverted. For first, He will be the One, because He is understood in Himself before He is understood as a cause. Second, He will be the Good; third, the True; and fourth, Being. For since the cause which is called the "end" <note>The final cause, or the purpose for which something exists.</note> is prior to that which is "exemplary," <note>The formal cause, or the pattern/idea in the mind of the creator.</note> and the exemplary is prior to the "efficient," <note>The agent cause, or the force that actually brings the thing into existence.</note> we first desire that by which we may be protected from the harm of storms <note>The final cause: the purpose of shelter.</note>; then we conceive the idea of a house in the mind <note>The exemplary cause: the blueprint or mental plan.</note>; and finally, we form it in matter by external making <note>The efficient cause: the actual construction.</note>. 

Therefore, if—just as we defined in the previous chapter—the Good relates to the final cause, the True to the exemplary, and Being to the efficient, then God, as He is the cause, will first have the nature of the Good, then the True, and finally Being. We touch upon all these matters briefly here; otherwise, they are a thicket of many and great questions. <note>Pico is acknowledging that these brief points summarize a vast and complex tradition of Scholastic and Platonic metaphysics regarding the "Divine Names."</note>

<meta>This page begins the "Objections" section of the treatise. It records the critical response of Antonio Faventino (Antonio Cittadini) to Pico della Mirandola's work "On Being and the One." Faventino challenges Pico's attempt to harmonize Plato and Aristotle on the nature of God and existence.</meta>

# ON BEING AND THE ONE.
## THE FIRST OBJECTIONS OF ANTONIO FAVENTINO AGAINST THE LITTLE BOOK ON THE ONE AND BEING.

<margin>First objection.</margin>
**S**hould any little book deserve to be titled "On Being and the One," it is necessary that it explain the nature and properties of each—both "being" and "the one." However, in this little work that recently came into my hands, and which is titled *On Being and the One*, several things are treated that are almost foreign to the title and inscription. For the author's principal purpose is to dispute whether, according to Plato, "being" <note>original: "ens"</note> and "the one" <note>original: "unum"</note> follow each other mutually <note>This refers to the concept of "convertibility"—whether everything that exists is one, and everything that is one exists.</note>; or whether, as the Academics <note>The followers of the later Platonic tradition.</note> think, "the one" is more common than "being." But this is not to treat of being and the one, but rather the mutual conversion of being and the one; nor is it even done absolutely, but only according to Plato. For if a philosopher were to discuss only the question of whether the soul is immortal, he would not properly be disputing "On the Soul," but would only be treating of the soul's immortality.

<margin>Second</margin>
Furthermore, the author of the work says that the Academics believe, according to Plato, that God is not truly and properly "being." I wonder greatly at this. For if he means all Academics or Platonists—as his phrasing seems to signify—it is sometimes not stated absolutely. 

<margin>Themistius</margin>
To say that the Academics feel this way is perhaps not without falsehood. For Themistius, a not ignoble author among the Platonists, testifies that according to Plato's opinion, the "Idea"—which is the principle of things—is truly and properly "being" and "the one." Indeed, the Platonists, either all or most of them, do not think that the Idea is one thing and 

<margin>Third.</margin>
God, the maker of things, is another. Furthermore, he <note>Pico</note> says in sequence: If it can be defended in any way according to Plato that "the one" is more common than "being," it must be judged thus: he says that words which in Latin are called "concrete"—such as *white*, *shining*, or *being* <note>original: "ens"</note>—signify something "alien" <note>In Scholastic logic, "concrete" terms like "white thing" imply a subject plus a quality, whereas "abstract" terms like "whiteness" imply the quality alone. Pico argued "Being" implies a subject that *has* existence, whereas God *is* existence.</note>, especially that by which the thing obtains the name of the word. For whiteness is one thing, a white thing another; man is one thing, humanity another. "Being," therefore, will be called that in which *to be* <note>original: "esse"</note> is one thing, and that which subsists is another. Therefore God, who is *to be* <note>original: "ipsum esse"</note> itself, cannot be considered a "being" <note>original: "ens"</note>, but rather "the One," because he contains and encloses all things. But does not this kind of defense hold together poorly? For by the same reason that *white*, *man*, and *being* signify something alien, it is necessary that *the One*, *the Blessed*, *God*, and many similar terms also signify something alien. Therefore God—who is Unity, Blessedness, and Deity all at once—could neither be called "the One," nor "the Blessed," nor even "God." How then is he 

<margin>Confirmation</margin>
not "being" but "the one"? Furthermore, a "being" <note>original: "ens"</note> is so called because it "is" <note>original: "est"</note>. Just as it cannot happen that one who sits is not a "sitter," so it cannot happen that he who truly and properly "is" is not a "being." For He says: "I am who I am." <note>A reference to Exodus 3:14, where God defines His own name as existence itself.</note>

<margin>Fourth.</margin>
But it may seem even more admirable that he tries to defend that God is not "being," not only according to Plato, but also tries to pull Aristotle himself into the same opinion. For he says that in the fifth book of the *Metaphysics*, "being" is divided into *being per se* <note>Through itself</note> and *being per accidens* <note>Through accident or chance</note>. Furthermore, *being per se* is divided into the ten categories. But, he says, God cannot be placed in any category, just as he thinks Blessed Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> has demonstrated. Therefore, if God is not *being per se* nor *being per accidens*, then according to Aristotle, He will not be "being." Furthermore, "being" is separated into substance and accident according to the most common division; but God is neither accident nor substance (for He is [above] those). God exceeds the limits of any genus. But I truly do not see by what reason the author of this work ascribes a Platonic opinion to our Aristotle (if indeed it is Plato's opinion). For the division of "being" into *per se* and *per accidens* 

<margin>St. Thomas</margin>
is a division of "complex being," <note>Being as expressed in a complete proposition or statement.</note> just as Blessed Thomas—to whom he gives much authority—writes subtly in that place. 

<margin>Aristotle</margin>
The same is manifest from examples: for *being per accidens* according to Aristotle is threefold: either an accident is predicated of a subject, or a subject of an accident, or an accident of an accident—all of which pertain to "complexion" <note>The way words are joined together in a sentence.</note>. In the same way, things are called *per se* beings in which something is predicated that pertains either to substance...

Faventino contends that if God "is," He must be "Being," citing the biblical "I am who I am" as proof.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the specific logical objections raised by Antonio Faventino against Pico's "On Being and the One," focusing on the classification of God and the definitions of truth, falsehood, and evil. It then transitions into the beginning of Pico’s personal response to Faventino.</meta>

**GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA**

...pertains either to quantity or to another genus, provided that what is predicated of a subject belongs to it through itself <note>original: "per se." In logic, this means a property that is essential to the subject's nature.</note>, as "white" belongs to Socrates—though not to "man" in general—or as "animal" belongs to a horse. Furthermore, the division of "being" <note>original: "ens"</note> into substance and accident also encompasses God. For a division is made through affirmation and negation: substance is that which relies on nothing else but exists through itself, while an accident is that which exists in another, as if in a subject. Between these two, there is no middle ground, as Blessed Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the influential Dominican theologian.</note> thinks; indeed, no middle state can be imagined between "having a subject" and "not having a subject." Therefore, substance—which is the opposite of accident—will not be a "genus" <note>A broad category or classification in Aristotelian logic.</note> if God is contained within no genus. 

<margin>Confirmation</margin>
Moreover, Aristotle’s opinion—that God is not contained by any genus through Himself—is not beyond doubt. There are some followers of Aristotle who believe that God is placed within a category <note>original: "praedicamento"</note> through Himself. I personally believe that the distinguished philosopher Boethius <note>An early 6th-century philosopher who bridged classical Greek thought and medieval Latin theology.</note> held this view; I could show, if necessary, that this can be aptly gathered from the words of Boethius as well as Augustine. 

<margin>Boethius</margin>
<margin>Augustine</margin>
<margin>Fifth objection</margin>
Again, he [Faventino] says that the negation of the "one" is division. He proves this by the fact that a thing is destroyed when it is pulled apart and divided. But how can "divided" and "negation of unity" be opposed? For there is a contradiction between affirmation and negation; yet a chimera <note>A mythological creature used in logic to represent something that cannot exist in reality.</note> is neither "one" nor "divided." Nor is the statement "the diameter is commensurable" <note>A classic example of a mathematical impossibility.</note> either "one" or "divided." 

<margin>Sixth objection</margin>
<margin>Blessed Thomas</margin>
He also considers "falsehood" to be the negation of "truth." While this might be defended in some way, falsehood is actually a "contrary" rather than a "negation," as Blessed Thomas shows. For a chimera is neither true nor false, unless we utterly abuse the words. The "true" is that which is; this is, as Thomas himself explains, that which is what it appears to be and what is said of it. Falsehood, therefore, will be that which is not what it appears to be and what is said of it, such as a "false coin." Thus, nothing happens to be false unless it appears to be something that it is not. Between "that which appears to be what it is" and "that which is not what it appears to be," there is no formal contradiction. Therefore, falsehood and truth are not opposed by the simple opposition of affirmation and negation. 

<margin>Seventh objection</margin>
<margin>Aristotle</margin>
He also thinks "evil" is the negation of "good." Aristotle, however, affirms in his *Categories* <note>original: "praedicamentis"</note> that good and evil are "genera of contraries." That which is a negation cannot be a genus. 

<margin>Confirmation</margin>
Furthermore, the good is to be sought precisely because it is good; the evil, however, is to be fled. Seeking and fleeing are contraries to one another, just as gathering and scattering are. Therefore, good and evil will be contraries. Boethius also asserts this in his commentary on the *Categories*, regardless of what others may have said on the matter.

**Response to the first objections.**
**GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA SENDS GREETINGS TO ANTONIO FAVENTINO.**

**Q**uestions of yours against that little book which I recently published *On Being and the One* I have read with as much pleasure as they were written by you with both affection and freedom of spirit. I owe you much for this service. If we were to bestow such honesty upon our friends more freely, or demand it from them more willingly, we would certainly be far better and more learned than we are. But a deadly persuasion has seized the minds of men: that we should think we do not please those whom our errors do not please. We interpret the free judgment of friends as hatred or gloominess, while interpreting flattery as love and natural goodness. Thus it happens that while we prefer to be praised—even when undeserving—rather than be corrected when we deserve it, we are always mocked and never truly deserve praise. See how greatly we err! For almost all praise is always useless and often harmful. For if it is true, what utility does it bring? If it is false, it surely makes us who are praised insane, and those who praise us ridiculous. Reprehension is certainly always useful: if it is just, it rouses us to knowledge; if it is less than just, it excites us to the defense of truth. Finally, what else is it to be corrected than to become better through another's labor? Or what else is it for a friend's book to be polished by a file, than for you to benefit from his sleepless nights while you yourself were sleeping? I cannot, therefore—as I was saying—help but owe you much, for you have freely signaled to me what you found less pleasing in my book. In your writings, I recognized not only your benevolence but also that quality which is already well known to me...

In Scholastic philosophy, a point is "one" because it cannot be divided, but God is "One" because He is absolutely simple, meaning He has no parts or internal distinctions.</note>

For <note>original: "pene"</note> almost all the terms we apply to God are intended to show His eminence rather than to define His limits. <margin>On the Truth of God</margin>

But <note>original: "uerum"</note> indeed, it is necessary to examine the following point. It <note>original: "dicetur"</note> will be said by some that if God is not contained within the category of Being, He must be "nothing." This is the error of those who <note>original: "tenentur"</note> are held or bound by a literal interpretation of the categories. It <note>original: "existimatur"</note> is thought by many—following the Platonists—that the "One" is a higher and more ancient principle than "Being." However, I maintain that they are equal. As Aristotle <note>original: "aꝑ"; aperte</note> openly demonstrates in his *Metaphysics*, "Being" and "One" are convertible terms; they refer to the same reality but from different perspectives. 

When we discuss <note>original: "deuʒ"; Deum</note> God, we are discussing the very source of this unity. This perspective finally resolves the <note>original: "q̄ſtionez"; quaestionem</note> question that has caused so much strife: whether the One is "above" Being. In God, who is the height of simplicity, there is no such division.

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s defense of his work "On Being and the One" (De Ente et Uno). **OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA**

...stating what He is and how He is all things, and that from Him, in whatever way, all things exist. For "one," says Dionysius, God is called because He is uniquely all things; again, He is called "one" <margin>Dionysius</margin> because He is the principle of all things that exist, just as unity is the principle of all numbers. These things I wrote there word for word. If, therefore, when we call God "one," we wish to declare what He is, I admit with you that He cannot be called "one" by the same reasoning that He cannot be called "being": because both, clearly, are concrete names. Indeed, I myself previously and openly asserted this in that same book through these words: "these names—'being,' 'true,' 'one,' and 'good'—denote something concrete and, as it were, participated." <note>Pico is distinguishing between "Being" (a noun for a thing that exists) and "Existence itself." In Scholastic logic, "concrete" terms imply a subject participating in a quality, whereas God is the quality itself.</note> For which reason we say again that God is above being, above truth, above unity, and above goodness: because He is existence itself, truth itself, unity itself, and goodness itself. Thus it was written there.

It did not, therefore, escape me when I was writing that "being" and "one" are equally concrete, and by reason of their concreteness, either neither or both are equally to be removed from God. But, as I had advised above: when we call God "one" but not "being," we do not signify what God is, but how He is that which He is: namely, because He is most primarily and simply all things. This manner can in no way be indicated or represented through the name of "being," but it can be through the pattern and designation of "unity." For beings are related to one another like numbers, as Aristotle writes: and the unity of numbers is both the most <margin>Aristotle.</margin> primary and the most simple. You add that you wonder that I wish to defend—not only according to Plato but also according to Aristotle—that God is not "being." <margin>Solution to the fourth objection.</margin> Indeed, if you have run through the book more attentively, in this whole work I primarily strive to show that God both is and is properly called "being," not only according to the dogma of Aristotle but also following Plato, <margin>Aristotle / Plato</margin> consequently holding that "one" is not superior to "being." But, lest those who said God is not "being" but "above being" should seem to be entirely insane— <margin>Aristotle / Plato</margin> among whom, if neither Plato nor Aristotle be included, certainly Dionysius the <margin>Dionysius</margin> Areopagite is, who is greater than both—I have attempted to prove that there is some reason for this way of speaking which, if we follow it, will not be discordant with the truth: that God is greater than the designation of "being." This mode of speaking is even occasionally used by the Peripatetics <note>The Peripatetics were the followers of Aristotle, known for their rigorous logical classifications.</note>, though you may shrink from it. You cannot, however, deny it unless you deny the authority of those to whom, even in your opinion, the first place in that family is owed. 

For who does not know that the division of "being" into "substance" and "accident" is frequent among the Aristotelians? When "being" is so divided, it is the opinion of your Thomas <margin>Thomas Aquinas</margin> <note>original: "Tho."</note> that God is not "being" but "above being." Concerning him, you used to say: "Take away Thomas, and Aristotle will become mute." Thomas’s words are nearly these: "God is neither an accident nor can He properly be called a substance; both because substance is so called because it 'stands under' <note>original: "substat." This is a pun on the etymology of 'substance'—that which stands under or supports qualities.</note>, and because substance indicates a 'quiddity' <note>original: "quidditatez"; Quiddity refers to the "what-ness" or essence of a thing.</note> which is different from His existence." Therefore, that division of "being" into substance and accident is a division of created being. Thus says he. Furthermore, when Aristotle says that the first philosopher treats of being insofar as it is being, and the causes and principles of being, there are many among the Peripatetics who wish that God not be placed there by Aristotle among beings, but among the causes of being. That He can, on the other hand, be properly called "being" by another manner of speaking, I not only did not deny but asserted and confirmed by many <margin>Solution of the confirmation</margin> reasons in the third chapter of the same work. I do not know, however, why you, always an imitator <margin>Boethius.</margin> of illustrious authors, now defect from those most famous Peripatetics. <margin>Solution to the fourth objection</margin> Those who place God under a "genus" <note>A logical category or class.</note>—among whom I have no doubt Boethius would by no means wish to be numbered. Finally, you contend that the division of "one" is not the negation of many, nor that "false" is the negation of "true," nor "bad" of "good." Indeed, I know the controversy regarding these oppositions is not easy among great authors, on account of which I was treating them in passing in the book...

And just as that thing does not exist whose parts—from which it would be constituted if it did exist—are divided; so too, that thing not only does not exist, but cannot possibly exist, whose parts are neither united nor can be united by the power of nature. For this reason, we not only say that a chimera does not exist, but we believe it is impossible for it to exist, for no other reason than that it is not credible that the beasts from which we imagine it could ever come together into a single animal composition. <meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's complex metaphysical argument regarding the relationship between "Being" (existence) and "the One." He is responding to an opponent—likely his friend Antonio Cittadini—who argued that God is superior to Being and should only be called "The One," following a Neoplatonic tradition. Pico, however, seeks to harmonize Plato and Aristotle, arguing that God is both truly Being and truly One.</meta>

# ON BEING AND THE ONE

...a question arises regarding the velocity of movements: whether it follows an arithmetic or geometric proportion. Since at the beginning of this work the author promised he would take much from geometry, this little book could have been titled "On Geometry," as it deals so much with motion. But let us omit these matters as frivolous. In another small book, I wrote on this opinion: I said that no one should say the Platonists feel differently unless all or most of them feel that way. If, however, Themistius <note>A 4th-century philosopher and statesman who wrote influential paraphrases of Aristotle; Pico treats him as a bridge between Platonic and Aristotelian thought.</note>—who is no obscure figure among the Platonists—affirms according to Plato’s opinion that the "Idea," which is the principle of things, is truly and properly <term>Being</term> <note>Latin: *ens*. In this context, it refers to the very act of existing or the essence of existence.</note>, it should not have been absolutely pronounced that Platonists, following Plato, do not consider God to be truly and properly Being; for the "Idea" is God. 

But you respond that the "Idea" is one thing and God is another. Even if it were granted that the "Idea" is God, you say it does not follow that God is properly and truly Being; for God and the "Idea," if not in reality, nonetheless differ in reason. But I would not wish to dispute in this place whether the Platonists think God is one thing and the "Idea" another, since that question is far removed from our purpose—even though many authors, both Greek and Latin, place Plato’s "Ideas" in God, imitating Plato himself. I seem to have done enough for my purpose by showing that a certain Platonist (and by no means an obscure one) asserts, according to Plato, that the "Idea"—and therefore God—is truly and properly Being. Nor does that "distinction of reason" <note>A technical term in scholastic logic meaning a distinction made by the mind rather than a physical separation in the object itself.</note> to which you retreat do anything to help your case. 

For the "Idea" is relative <note>In the sense that an Idea is always an "idea of" something else.</note>, while God is an absolute thing. If, therefore, God is truly and properly Being in that part by which He is referred to outward things, how much more must He be considered Being by that reason which is God and consists in His own nature? For why is the "Idea," insofar as it is an "Idea," truly and properly Being? No reason, I say, can be assigned unless it is said to be truly and properly Being because it truly and properly *is*. Therefore, God, by the very reason that He is God, will much more be truly and properly Being. For He said: "I am who I am" <note>original Latin: *ego sum qui sum*. This is the famous self-identification of God in Exodus 3:14, which Pico uses as the ultimate proof that God is "Being" itself.</note>.

Furthermore, this objection was raised: if the Platonists can be rightly defended when they say God is not truly and properly Being, but "the One"—because the name "Being" is a concrete term <note>In logic, a "concrete" term (like 'human') implies a subject and a quality, whereas an "abstract" term (like 'humanity') refers to the essence. The opponent argues "Being" implies a composition that shouldn't exist in God.</note> which signifies something foreign to that which is—then by the same logic it can be concluded that God is not "the One." For "One" is also a concrete name. Indeed, He would be neither "Blessed" nor "God," for both of those words are concrete. 

But you respond that God is not called "the One" as if the substance of God were shown by the name of "one," but rather to explain how He is that which He is. But I ask: to what end is this? The objection is not yet solved. You say God is not Being, but the One, because the name "Being" is concrete. If, therefore, "One" is also concrete, must it not be concluded by the same reason that God is not "the One," nor even "God"—which is a name that pertains to substance, just as "Being" does? <margin>Confirmation</margin> Furthermore, if He is "One" because He is uniquely that which He is, why should He not also be called "Being"? For by being "One," He is all that He is: namely, wisdom, goodness, and power. He is not called "One" simply because He is the only one who is one. Therefore, by the same reason, He can be called "Being," even if He were not the only Being; for He is Being in the highest degree.

Furthermore, that argument was not yet resolved which stated: God is truly and properly Being, for He said, "I am who I am." Again, I wondered how you could defend the idea that, even according to Aristotle, God is sometimes not considered by the name of "Being," because He would not be Being through itself <note>original Latin: *per se*</note>, nor by accident <note>original Latin: *per accidens*</note>, nor substance, nor accident. For I have shown that God is neither Being through itself nor by accident in the way created things are, nor can anything intermediate be imagined between substance and accident. 

You, however, answer nothing to the first objection. ## 10. MIRANDOLA

<margin>Platonists</margin> I do not know why you indeed so obstinately contend that Themistius <note>Themistius (c. 317–388 AD) was a statesman and philosopher famous for his paraphrases of Aristotle’s works.</note> should be numbered among these: <margin>Themistius</margin> for if you ask the ancients, they will all respond that Themistius is a Peripatetic <note>original: *peripateticum*; a follower of Aristotle.</note>, <margin>not a Platonist</margin> not a Platonist. If you ask the man himself, I think he would call himself a paraphraser and follower of Aristotle, and not of Plato. <margin>to be [a follower] but peripatetic</margin> But perhaps (allow me to joke) you drag him into the Academy <note>The Academy was the school founded by Plato; Pico is suggesting his opponent is forcing a non-Platonist into that camp.</note> against his will, lest you appear entirely ignorant of Platonic and Greek matters—you who have at least read Themistius thanks to the benefit of our <margin>Hermolaus</margin> Hermolaus <note>Hermolao Barbaro (1454–1493), a prominent Italian scholar and friend of Pico who translated Themistius into Latin.</note>, who made him Latin. But let Themistius be a Platonist. Let him even be truly so; we have already declared abundantly enough, both in this and in the previous letter, that nothing he says contradicts our opinion. For the Platonists will speak of God in one way as He is God, and in another way as He is an Idea. 

<margin>Solution to another argument</margin> Let us come to this: in what way "the One" <note>original: *unum*</note> is predicated of God, even though "Being" <note>original: *ens*</note> is not predicated of Him. Recall to memory what we wrote to you in our first letters. When the Platonists call God "the One," they do not announce **what** <note>original: *quid*</note> He is, but rather **how** <note>original: *quomodo*</note> He is that which He is. But you do not understand this sufficiently either. I will speak more aptly. If you ask a man of the Academy what God is, he will respond that not only can he not answer you what He is, but you also have no right to ask this; indeed, it is an unworthy question concerning Him. For He who is above all essence and above all that can be understood, can only have this much asserted about Him: that He is most similar to unity. For just as unity is the principle of numbers, so He is the principle of all things that are. Just as unity embraces all numbers, both even and odd—itself being neither even nor odd—within its individual simplicity, so He closes and contains all things within His indivisible infinity. Do you see what was said? That through the name of "the One," it is not indicated what God is, but how He is that which He is? Finally, if we say: "God is similar to unity," what we wish to signify when we give Him the name of "the One" will certainly be true. If we say to our listeners: "God is similar to being," we will surely cause laughter. But why say more to you who are apt? For he says these things are enough, though I know not what words could be enough. 

<margin>Why God is under no genus.</margin> He also gathers from this why God is under no genus <note>In Aristotelian logic, a genus is a broad category. Pico argues God is too transcendent to be categorized.</note>. For the genera of things belong to essence; however, God is neither an essence nor possesses an essence. Therefore, since "being" is sometimes understood by the Peripatetics in such a way that it encompasses only the ten genera <note>The ten Categories of Aristotle (Substance, Quantity, Quality, etc.).</note>, it is manifest that God is not contained under the name of "being," which even the followers of Aristotle sometimes use. But you insist that Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas.</note> and others from the same family <note>The Dominican order of theologians.</note> often use both "substance" and "being" in such a way that God is called both substance and being. As if I were ignorant of this—which no one knows not—or as if it were not enough for me if they sometimes do otherwise; for I said that they were accustomed to using that manner of speaking not always, but occasionally. 

<margin>Solution to another objection, namely of the main ground.</margin> Pass on to those things you object regarding the opposition of "the One" and "the divided"; indeed, I think you are testing me with childish quibbles as if in play. For if you say the "divided" is false, then certainly the "false" is not false. For the false is not divided from itself, because the false is the false. Likewise, you say that the dead by no means fight with themselves; for they are dead who are already dead. Furthermore, Antony, when I said that things which are false fight with themselves—if this fight happens with a fist, or even with a weapon—I confess the dead do not fight among themselves, nor are they false. But just as the false is simple, so to be false is not false, but true; therefore it is not divided but one. 

<margin>Another clearer solution.</margin> You add that it is falsely said by me that what is false encloses a contradiction. This is because many things are false which, by the power of nature or of man, could be true. But consider this: everything that is false, as long as it is false, encloses a contradiction. But just as some things are so false that they can become true, others are so false that they can never be true. Thus there are some things so contradictory to themselves and fighting with themselves that they can never return to friendship and harmony. Some hate each other in such a way that they can nonetheless return to favor. 

<margin>Example</margin> This will be manifest by an example: "A man is a lion" is always false, because it always encloses a contradiction; and just as it can never be reduced to unity, so it can never be reduced to truth. But "that I am sitting" is neither [always] true nor false. But if you add that I am sitting while I am standing, it immediately [becomes] falsehood. So...

**ON BEING AND THE ONE**

You even bring up a contradiction. For "me sitting while I stand" includes a contradiction; and as soon as it ceases to be false—for instance, when I begin to sit—it immediately returns from division to unity. 

<margin>Solution to the second argument</margin> 
Moreover, the objections you raise concerning the opposition of both kinds of falsehood were already resolved in the previous letter. For you say: "if it is true: that which is seen, is; while it is false: that which is seen, is not." Since there is no contradiction between "being seen to be" and "being seen not to be," falsehood would not be the negation of truth. I, however, do not accept the definition of falsehood as merely "appearing to be something that is not." Rather, I maintain its essence lies in this: that it *is not* that which it is said to be. For example, "false gold" <note>original: *Aurum enim falsum*; a common alchemical and philosophical example of something that has the outward appearance of a substance without its essential nature.</note> is false precisely because it is *not* gold; and as far as the definition of falsehood is concerned, it happens to either appear as gold or be something else besides gold. 

As for your claim that I have not resolved your argument by which you prove that "Good" and "Evil" are contraries, I will speak frankly. 

<margin>Solution to the second argument</margin> 
I did not think a solution was needed where there was no knot <note>In scholastic logic, a "knot" (*nodus*) is a difficult or perplexing point in an argument that requires untying.</note>. 

<margin>Note</margin> 
Your argument is as follows: "Good is to be sought; Evil is to be fled. Seeking and fleeing are contrary motions. Therefore, Good and Evil are contraries." To me, however, your reasoning seems so effective and of such great strength that it would prove not only Good and Evil—about which someone might perhaps doubt—but even "Being" and "Non-being" (which everyone knows are contradictories <note>In logic, "contradictories" (like Being and Non-being) cannot both be true or both be false, while "contraries" (like black and white) are opposites that can both be false but not both true.</note>) to be contraries. For we would conclude thus: "Being is to be sought; Non-being is to be fled. Seeking and fleeing are contrary motions. Therefore, Being and Non-being are contraries." So, either grant me that Being and Non-being are contraries, or I will not grant you that Good and Evil are contraries. 

But you will say another reason must be resolved: "Non-being" is not a genus; how then is "Evil" nothing, when Aristotle says in the 

<margin>Solution to the second argument</margin> 
*Categories* <note>original: *praedicamentis*; Aristotle's work on the classification of things into ten basic categories.</note> that Good and Evil are the "genera of contraries"? All the interpreters of 

<margin>Aristotle</margin> 
Aristotle are full of solutions to this question, to whom I had referred you in my previous letter, so as not to involve us both in unnecessary work. To pass over the fact that it does not displease 

<margin>Simplicius</margin> 
Simplicius <note>Simplicius of Cilicia (c. 490–560 AD), an influential Neoplatonist who wrote extensive commentaries on Aristotle.</note> that Aristotle spoke there according to the custom of the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras, known for organizing reality into a table of ten opposites, such as light/dark or good/evil.</note>—who establish two orders of things, one contained under Good and the other under Evil—certainly Aristotle often uses examples in his logical commentaries from the opinions of others rather than his own. I respond with what you could also have read in Simplicius: Good and Evil are called "genera of contraries" because one of the contraries always has the quality of evil and deficiency; for example, black compared to white, or bitter compared to sweet. In this way, all contraries are reduced to Good and Evil insofar as every defect has the nature of evil. This is why in the first book of the *Physics* <note>original: *physicæ auscultationis*; literally "Physical Listening," a standard title for Aristotle's work on the nature of change.</note> it is said that contraries are always compared to one another according to the logic of "the better" and "the worse."

<margin>Porphyry</margin>

<margin>Thomas</margin> 
Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the preeminent scholastic theologian who integrated Aristotelian philosophy with Christian doctrine.</note> also descends to this opinion: that Good and Evil oppose each other as contraries. For what else does he primarily do in that disputation but prove that "evil is nothing"? If evil is nothing, it cannot be the contrary to good, since the nature of each contrary is to be "something." And this is exactly what Thomas confirms there by the authority of Simplicius. See how far you wander, believing an opinion is confirmed by the testimony of Simplicius which he himself refutes using Simplicius's testimony. You might not have fallen into this error if you had at some point read the book of Simplicius himself, in which no mention is ever made of a "contrary opposition" of Good and Evil. 

If you object to me regarding ophthalmia <note>An inflammation of the eye; used here as an example of a physical evil/defect.</note> and sickness, in which Thomas seems to acknowledge contrariety, I will bid you to look more carefully at his words. For he does not say these are truly contraries, but that since they are privations <note>A "privation" is the absence of a quality that should naturally be present, like blindness being the privation of sight.</note>, they are nevertheless sometimes *called* contraries. 

<margin>Note</margin> 
If you pay attention, you will see why he wishes this to be so: because evil itself [lacks] all properties of a contrary...

<meta>This page continues Pico’s rigorous defense against his critic, focusing on the interpretation of Thomas Aquinas regarding the definition of "Being." Pico is clarifying the distinction between "being" as a statement of existence and "being" as a definition of essence, specifically addressing how terms like "evil" or "blindness" can be said to "be" without having a positive substance.</meta>

# **OF GIOVANNI MIRANDOLA**

**Being** <note>original: *ens*</note> is said to be that which can answer the question "does it exist?" <note>original: *an est*. This is a standard scholastic distinction: asking if a thing exists versus asking what its nature is.</note>—whether it is a true and positive being or not. From this, he adds an example, saying: and thus evil "is," just as blindness "is." That is to say: evil is a "being" just as blindness is a "being." For in the works of **Thomas** <note>St. Thomas Aquinas</note> there is no difference in words whether one says "it is" or "it is a being." But as for what he adds next—that "to be something" does not only signify this—he does not intend to suggest that if someone asks "what is the moon?" or "what is thunder?", it is a reasonable answer to say "it is a being" or "it is something," as you seem to have thought. For such a solution is **ridiculous**. Rather, this "to be something" signifies—especially according to the first mode—that which can reasonably answer the question "what is it?" For instance, it signifies being a substance, or an accident, or an animal, or a color, or something of this sort which can rightly be answered to one asking "what is it?" However, blindness and evil are none of these things.

That **Blessed Thomas** does not wish the first part of this division to be interpreted with your mindset, he himself explains in the *First Part* <note>of the *Summa Theologiae*</note>, Question 48, Article 2, where it is asked whether evil is in things. For responding to the second argument, he speaks thus: "As it is said in the sixth book of the *Metaphysics*, **Being** is said in two ways. In one way, according to what signifies the 'entity' of a thing, as it is divided through the **ten predicaments** <term>ten predicaments: Aristotle’s ten categories (substance, quantity, quality, relation, etc.) used to classify everything that exists.</term>; and in this way, 'being' is interchangeable with 'thing.' In this sense, no **privation** <term>privation: the absence of a quality that should normally be present, like sight in an eye.</term> is a being, and therefore neither is evil. In another way, 'being' is said of that which signifies the truth of a proposition, which consists in composition, the indicator of which is this word 'is'; and this is the 'being' that answers the question 'does it exist?' In this way, we say that blindness 'is' in the eye, or any other privation; and in this way, even evil is called a 'being.'" These are the words of Thomas.

Do you not see, then, how he declares that the first part of the division is interchangeable with "thing"? Truly, he does not deny that God is a "thing," nor anything that is good; for by that argument and by the first question on evil, he confesses that every good is a "thing." If these points are true, the reason I stated against the **Platonists** has not yet been refuted: "being" is so called because it "is," just as "a seater" is so called because he "sits." God, however, not only "is," but he "is" properly and truly; therefore, He is truly and properly **Being**. For you wished to resolve the argument not from the Platonists, but from Thomas, ascribing things to Thomas that anyone who has read him knows are entirely foreign to the man’s thought.

Hence, that other reason I gave is not resolved: if God is "being" in that respect by which He is an **Idea**, He is much more so in that respect by which He is God. For the latter is something absolute, while the former is relative. For what you just responded is not true—namely, that God is "essence" <note>original: *essentiam*</note> in the respect that He is an Idea, but not in the respect that He is God; for it has already been shown that He is both "being" and "essence." Furthermore, if God is "being" and "essence" in the respect that He is an Idea, it is necessary that there be **composition** <term>composition: the state of being made of parts. In medieval theology, God was defined as "Simple," meaning He has no parts or internal divisions.</term> in God, which is easily proven in this way: for you previously said that, according to the Platonists, God is not "being" because God's "to be" <note>original: *esse*</note> is not different from God Himself. If, therefore, the Idea is "being," it must be because the "to be" of the Idea is different from the Idea; but the "to be" of the Idea cannot be placed or imagined outside of God. If God is the Idea (as has been granted), then it is necessary that there be composition in God.

You say, moreover, that God is called "the One" by the Platonists because He is similar to **Unity**, which, although it contains all numbers in its power (namely even and odd), is itself neither even nor odd. By Hercules, what a "subtle" reason for naming Him! Beyond the fact that God cannot be similar to things (as **Cicero** says, and **Thomas**), for the model of the world is not similar to the world, nor is a man similar to a painting, no other cause for this can stand.

**[Marginal Notes:]**

<margin>**Ridiculous:** Since you do not ask ridiculously, you do not solve it; although many things are asked ridiculously which are solved ridiculously when they are solved, lest they seem unsolved because they cannot be solved. Therefore, to one asking if the moon is a "being," it will rightly be answered that it is a being. But to one asking further what kind of being it is, it is certainly ridiculous to answer simply that "it is a being."</margin>

<margin>**To be something:** You say nothing. For who does not know that a thing is "not something" simply because it is neither a substance nor an accident?</margin>

<margin>**He says thus:** These same words follow in the previous question on evil, and they favor me, just as those do.</margin>

<margin>**A thing truly:** In the same way "thing" is said of God, it is both affirmed and denied, just as "being" is.</margin>

<margin>**If these:** But we have shown that they are not true, therefore the reasoning is refuted.</margin>

<margin>**But from Thomas:** But you yourself, in explaining the words of Thomas above, fell into our opinion when you said God is called "being" insofar as it answers the question "does it exist?", but not insofar as it signifies the essence of the thing.</margin>

<margin>**Those things of Thomas:** I do not ascribe falsehoods to Thomas, for I do not imitate you. Compare what you say from the opinion of Thomas: that good and evil are properly and truly contraries, and that this is even confirmed by the authority of **Simplicius** <note>A 6th-century Neoplatonist commentator on Aristotle.</note>. Regarding this matter, when I showed that there is not a single word of this in Simplicius, you respond that you "gathered" that Simplicius says this. But the book is in our hands, fellow-father! Simplicius does not say it; therefore, you gathered it poorly.</margin>

<margin>**Already shown:** It has also been demonstrated that you have not demonstrated well.</margin>

<margin>**Previously:** For God and Idea are the same. Nor is the "to be" of the Idea anything other than the "to be" of God; but because the reasons are diverse, one thing is pronounced of God as He is God, and another as He is Idea.</margin>

<margin>**Composition:** This composition is according to reason, not according to the reality of the thing.</margin>

<margin>**Subtle:** So subtle that, although it has been repeated a hundred times now, you still cannot understand it, as will soon be evident from the trouble you are giving us.</margin>

<margin>It is not possible: It is not permitted for you to speak unless within pre-defined limits. <margin>Furthermore if: The "One" that the Platonists predicate <note>term: predicate (to state or assert something about a subject)</note> of God is not a descriptive label, but a substantive noun. This you do not know because you are entirely ignorant of Platonic thought and cannot understand the Greek language. See, therefore, how subtle this method of naming is.</margin>

<margin>Furthermore: It is clear from this how "matter" is called "one" in one way, and God is called "One" in another.
Of the Platonists: Why do you say I follow the reasoning of the Platonists rather than Dionysius? <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century Christian theologian whose works were heavily influenced by Neoplatonism.</note> As you boast with a loud voice, you have never actually read either the Platonists or Dionysius. You should know that among the Platonists, the "Unity" is the model of God, and for Dionysius, God is "One-ly" <note>original: *unice*</note> all things.</margin>

<margin>The root you lean on: See how firm that root is—one which you could neither overcome with any strength nor tear up with hard iron.
I therefore: All these things were satisfied in the previous letters.
This is true: You love gold too much, my fellow-godfather <note>original: *compater*. This is a personal jab at his opponent's materialistic interests.</note>, that you grant it so much as to believe it could exist even if God did not.
They think there are worlds: Those who say these things—that gold exists—speak contradictions and do not understand their own words.
If God were not: And if gold existed, gold would be gold, and gold would not be gold; for the impossible gives birth to the impossible.</margin>

Whatever borrows a name from another thing due to a likeness or analogy is usually called by the proper name of that thing itself. For example, we call a statue that imitates a human a "man," not "human-ish." Likewise, we call the "Place" which is the difference between propositions <note>term: Place (original: *locus*). In ancient logic, a "topos" or "place" was a category or source-point for finding arguments.</note>—or a "maximal proposition" derived from the analogy of a natural physical place—simply a "place," and not a "local thing." Therefore, if God obtained His name from unity because of a likeness, He should not be called "One," but rather "Unity." 

Furthermore, if every concrete name signifies one thing and another <note>In scholastic logic, a concrete term like "white" signifies both the quality (whiteness) and the subject (the thing that is white).</note>, why do the Platonists call God "Likeness" rather than "Like"? Furthermore, if matter, according to the Platonists, is "one" as you write, and the unity of matter is not one thing and the matter itself another—which I do not think you would deny—by what reasoning can it be defended as "one"? For it is not similar to unity; otherwise, it would also be similar to God. 

Furthermore, you previously said that God is "one" because He is "one-ly" <note>original: *unice*</note> all things. Now, however, you seem to approve of the reasoning of the Platonists rather than that of Dionysius, perhaps having cast aside the former. If you still hold to it, it remains for you to respond to the arguments that have been written. For the "root" you lean on to solve my objections is not true: namely, your claim that God is not "being" nor "essence," as I have already fully declared.

But let us now come to the definition of "Truth" put forward by you. You said in your earlier booklet that Truth is defined by **Augustine** in this way: "Truth is that which is." <note>Pico is quoting St. Augustine's *Soliloquies*.</note> And, lest the definition of "Truth" and "Being" seem to be the same, you say one must add: "Truth is that which is that which it is said to be." 

I, therefore, opposed your definition in this way: "to be that which it is said to be" seems to signify nothing other than "to be that which it is called." But for a thing to be called by this name or that name is for it to "appear" as this or that. Therefore, it seemed to follow that "to be what it is said to be" is nothing else but "to be what it appears to be." Since, therefore, there is no contradiction in appearing to be what is, and appearing to be what is not, I was proving that "falsehood" would not be the negation of "truth" if your definition held firm.

Since you have now explained your definition more clearly, there will be many more points that seem to disprove your formal definition. For you say, "Truth is that which is said." This means "Truth is that which is what it itself is"—for example, gold is "true gold" because it is gold. But against this is the fact that if God did not exist and gold still existed, gold would be what it itself is, and it would be "true," yet it would not "be" <note>Pico is using a logical *reductio ad absurdum*. He argues that if things don't depend on God for their "truth," then the definition of truth becomes meaningless.</note>, because it would match no "Idea." 

Later, you say that true things are those which match and respond to "Ideas." If the true definition of a human is a "rational animal," it is a contradiction to think that if God did not exist and a human were a rational animal, that the human would not be a human. Nor can the answer be given—which has been said elsewhere—that it is a contradiction for God not to exist while gold exists. For there is no contradiction there, as theologians, philosophers, and logicians themselves openly confess. For one can imagine that gold exists, yet God does not exist—neither the First Cause nor the First Being. For those who think there are infinite worlds, or that the heavens are infinitely multiple, or other such things, do not for that reason deny that the gold which is seen with the eyes and handled with the hands exists. 

Furthermore, whether it is a contradiction or not, the argument is not yet resolved. For I say this: If God did not exist and gold did exist, gold would be gold, but it would not be "true." Therefore...

<meta>This page continues Pico’s philosophical refutation. Having previously critiqued his opponent's view of "The One," Pico now turns to the "formal definition of truth." He argues against the simplistic definition that truth is merely "that which is," as this would lead to logical absurdities regarding evil and non-existence.</meta>

**OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA**

...the formal definition of the true is to be that which it is. Just as it would not be a formal definition of a human if I said: "If God did not exist and a human were a rational animal, he would not for that reason be a human." For nothing can be stripped of its own definition, nor can a definition apply to anything to which the name being defined cannot also be fitted. Furthermore, you cannot deny that gold is gold by its nature before it conforms to the Idea of God; for the absolute <note>term: absolute (something considered in itself, without reference to other things)</note> is prior to the relative. Gold, therefore, even if it be gold, nevertheless cannot be [true gold] unless a certain likeness comes to it beyond the nature of gold, through which it corresponds to its own exemplar <note>term: exemplar (the divine "blueprint" or Idea in the mind of God that a physical thing mimics)</note>—whether that likeness is something different from the gold or not, which is a separate question of its own.

Furthermore, you seem to set the definition of "being" <note>original: *entis*</note> in this way: "being is that which is." Otherwise, you would not say that the definition of Augustine <note>St. Augustine (354–430 AD), whose definition of truth as "that which is" Pico is analyzing here.</note> must be completed in this way: "The true is that which it is." We say this so that, if we merely said "that which is," the definition of the true and of being might seem to be the same. If, therefore, the definition of being is "that which is," then by the same reasoning that being is "that which is," it is also itself and being. Therefore, by the same reasoning that something is a being, it must necessarily be true; but this is entirely false.

Furthermore, if the true is "that which it is," then blindness will be true, and death, and falsehood, and even non-being. For blindness is blindness, and death is death, and falsehood is falsehood. Non-being also is non-being; any of these would be "true" even if no intellect were thinking of them at all. But if any of these is true, it must also be "one."

But I know you will soon say: "Did I not concede that any of these 'is,' and is therefore 'true' in those words I wrote to you? Just as falsehood is falsehood, so 'falsehood being falsehood' is not false, but true; and therefore it is not divided, but one." 

But against this is the fact that every "one" is a "good," and in the same way, "true." Blindness, however, is not only evil, but according to what you write, it is entirely evil and tastes of nothing good. Similarly with death. For you seem to call the nature of blindness and death an absolute nature of evil, unmixed with good. Therefore, none of these is true, nor are they "one," especially when the soul is not thinking about them. 

Furthermore, the "true" is that which conforms to an Idea; but blindness and death have no Idea <note>In Platonic thought, only positive realities have divine "Ideas"; evils or "privations" like blindness are merely the absence of a good and thus have no celestial archetype.</note>. 

Furthermore, if God did not exist, nor anything else capable of intelligence, nonetheless non-being would be non-being, and nothing would be nothing; for it is either something or nothing. It is certainly not "something," as is evident; therefore it is "nothing" and "non-being." It would therefore be that which it is now, and would be then. If, therefore, the true is "that which it is," then non-being and nothing would be true—which is impossible, for they would conform to no Idea. Therefore, the formal definition of the true is not "to be that which it is."

Furthermore, you attempt to defend what you previously said: that any falsehood contains a contradiction. You say that every falsehood contains a contradiction as long as it is false. You also add these words: "But 'me sitting' is neither true nor false. If, however, you add 'me sitting' while I am standing, immediately, just as you bring in falsehood, you also bring in contradiction; for 'me sitting while I am standing' contains a contradiction. And as soon as it ceases to be false—such as when I begin to sit—it immediately returns from division to unity." But I ask you to see whether...

<margin>Absolute. For this is not an accidental relation <note>term: accidental relation (a property that is not essential to the thing's nature, such as a gold coin being "in a pocket")</note> distinct from the gold, but a substantial one; concerning which, see Henry of Ghent <note>Henry of Ghent (c. 1217–1293), a major scholastic philosopher known for his theories on being and essence.</note>, unless you disdain him.</margin>

<margin>We said the same. Everything that is, is this: the very thing that it is. Wherefore every being is true, and every true thing is a being. But the rationale for each is different.</margin>

<margin>Blindness, however: It is one thing for "blindness to be true," and another for it to be "true that blindness is blindness." Therefore, you labor with many words in vain to show that blindness is not true.</margin>

**ON BEING AND THE ONE .10.**

<margin>Truly indeed: "that I am sitting" is always either true or false, because I am always either sitting or not sitting. And as for what is said—that "me sitting" is neither true nor false—this means that this proposition does not, by its own nature, determine its own truth or its own falsehood, as necessary propositions <note>term: necessary propositions (statements that must be true by their very nature, like "2+2=4," as opposed to "contingent" statements like "I am sitting" which depend on circumstances)</note> do. But since it is possible for it to be true (namely, when I am sitting) and false (when I am not sitting), it is in itself indeterminate toward either. But no doubt, my fellow-godfather, you abound in both paper and leisure to descend to these matters which are known even to children.</margin>

<margin>But it is true: Good and evil are in things; falsehood and truth are in the mind. Therefore, a true proposition can signify an evil thing, because the proposition itself, insofar as it is true, is good; yet the thing itself, insofar as it is evil, may be considered "false" <note>In this context, "false" refers to a lack of being or a deviation from a thing's proper nature, rather than a spoken lie.</note> in that same respect. It is one thing to say, "That Judas sins is true," and quite another to say, "The sin of Judas is a true [thing]."</margin>

<margin>Furthermore: Every "falsehood" is divided, as we said in the previous book. But "not to be false" is not equally false <note>original: *ex æquo falsum*</note>; for which reason, "not to be false" is divided unequally, as we said in the letters to you. For those things which are necessarily false and always false are not false in the same way as those things which are not necessarily false nor always false. Therefore, the former and the latter do not possess the same logic of division. See if there is anything among these points that I should have feared to say, or that you might be able to refute.</margin>

...you agree. For you think the true and the false are opposed, not indeed as contraries, but as affirmation and negation. How then can a middle ground be found, unless there is a middle between affirmation and negation? <note>Pico is invoking the "Law of Excluded Middle," a fundamental principle of logic stating that for any proposition, either it is true or its negation is true—there is no third option.</note> Furthermore, every statement is either true or false, unless you deny that first principle: that in any contradiction, one part is true and the other part is false. How then is "that you are sitting" neither true nor false? Indeed, I do not see by what reason you could defend that, unless you do away with all philosophy and every concept of contraries.

Furthermore, if every falsehood implies a contradiction <note>original: *contradictionem claudit*</note> as long as it is false that "God does not exist"—which is false and implies a contradiction so long as God exists in the nature of things—consider this: if God did not exist, it would neither be false that "God does not exist," nor would it be a contradiction. If, therefore, the false is the negation of the true as you posit, it would be "true" that God does not exist if God were not to exist. But every truth is a "good," as you grant; therefore, if God did not exist, it would be a "good" thing that God does not exist—which seems absurd. For neither...
