...therefore, it is established: But whatever is, is in some way being and good; therefore, it is not "not-good." Furthermore, you deny the truth of what Aristotle says in the *Categories* <note>original: *prædicamentis*, the title of Aristotle's work on the basic classifications of things</note>, namely that good and evil are the classes <note>original: *genera*</note> of contraries; yet this is something that neither Boethius nor the Latin commentators dare to deny. You, however, having set aside the Latin interpreters, take refuge only in Simplicius <note>A 6th-century Greek philosopher and influential commentator on Aristotle</note>, who says that good and evil are the classes of contraries for this reason: that between contraries, one is always "good"—that is, it is better—and the other is "evil"—that is, it is worse. Blessed Thomas [Aquinas] also relates this from Simplicius. But if one may oppose Simplicius, the counter-argument is this: Aristotle says in the same place that not only is good the contrary of evil, but sometimes evil is even the contrary of another evil. If indeed Aristotle calls that which is "better" "good," and that which is "worse" "evil," then good would always be the contrary to evil. Furthermore, if the "good" and "evil" which Aristotle says are the classes of contraries are merely "better" and "worse," then good and evil would be placed in the category of *relatives* <note>Terms that only make sense in relation to something else, like "double" or "half"</note>, among which are "better" and "worse," which are relative terms. Yet Aristotle says that good and evil are not *in* a class, but are themselves classes.

Finally, you wonder that I affirm evil and good to be contraries according to Thomas's opinion; and what is more, you say I have strayed because you claim I falsely cite Simplicius. You also say I have falsely stated that Blessed Thomas proves, by Simplicius's testimony, that evil and good are contraries of each other. But take care lest *you* are the one who errs, you who have weighed my small mind or my words. Indeed, the words written to you in the second letter read in this sequence: "I say, therefore, once again: I approve that good and evil are contraries to one another; not indeed in the same way as white and black, or hot and cold—which are all truly qualities—but in the same way as healthy and sick, perhaps, or strong and weak, rare and dense, beautiful and ugly, and many similar things." Nor does Blessed Thomas deny this; rather, that most eminent man, in the first question *On Evil* <note>Thomas Aquinas's treatise *De Malo*</note>, regarding the solution to the second argument, demonstrates how good and evil, even if they are opposed as privation and possession <note>original: *priuatiōis & habitus*. In logic, a privation is the absence of a quality that should naturally be present, like blindness in an eye.</note>, are nevertheless usually counted among the contraries; and he confirms this by the authority of Simplicius. Remember, therefore, that Aristotle in the *Categories* assigns four types of opposition. Also, remember that Aristotle separates these types of classes from one another. Again, note...

...so that health and sickness are counted among the contraries by him; for this reason, therefore, by which Aristotle distinguishes contraries from the other types of opposition. I have affirmed that good and evil are contraries; and again I admit it. This is also what Blessed Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274), the most influential medieval theologian</note> said in the first question *On Evil* <note>original: *De Malo*, a major work by Aquinas discussing the nature and origin of sin and suffering</note>: Good and evil are contraries, just as health and sickness are; but not in the same way as sight and blindness <note>In logic, "contraries" are opposites that can both be absent (like black and white), whereas "privation" is the absence of a quality that should naturally be there (like blindness being the absence of sight in an eye)</note>.

But you say: "I will show you how evil is entirely ignorant of the property of a contrary. For although a certain evil might seem to be the contrary of a certain good—as sickness is to health—because it leaves behind some portion of the good, I will nevertheless present an evil which can in no way be opposed to the good by this reasoning: namely, death and blindness."

But indeed, I do not know if you are pretending. For if you have read the words of Thomas more carefully, it can be clearly understood how neither blindness nor death nor any other evil can take away the good entirely. Blindness, certainly, takes away sight—and takes it all—but it does not take away life or the body. Death, indeed, takes away life completely, but it takes away neither the body nor prime matter <term>prime matter: in Aristotelian philosophy, the most basic, formless substance that remains when all specific qualities are stripped away</term>. Therefore, what has deceived...

<summary>Pico della Mirandola argues that Good and Evil are "contraries" rather than total "privations," citing Thomas Aquinas to show that even "absolute" evils like death and blindness do not destroy the fundamental existence (prime matter) of a subject.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s rigorous defense of his philosophical position against an unnamed critic. Having previously established the distinction between "contraries" (like black and white) and "privations" (the absence of a quality, like blindness), he now uses the example of a "Chimera"—a mythological beast—to explore whether something can be "entirely evil" or "entirely non-existent."</meta>

# **ON BEING AND THE ONE**

<margin>Whether true: Why then do you not frankly admit that you have erred? For it is no wonder, as you are only human.</margin>
<margin>Or a chimera: In that chimera of yours, you fashion many chimeras <note>Pico is playing on words here; a "chimera" can mean both the mythological monster and a foolish, groundless fancy or logical fallacy.</note>.</margin>
<margin>To be created: If a chimera can be created by God, this power is not in the chimera, but in God.</margin>
<margin>Furthermore, the Chimera: The notion I form for myself concerning the chimera, insofar as it is something, is good; but the chimera itself, insofar as it is nothing, is likewise not good.</margin>
<margin>Aristotle, *Metaphysics*, Book IV: Good and evil according to you are contraries, and each of the contraries is something positive; therefore, that which is good is something positive, and that which is evil is something positive. And according to you, non-being is good; therefore, according to you, non-being is something positive. And "something" and "being" are interchangeable; therefore, according to you, non-being is positive being: see where your chimera has led us.</margin>
<margin>Furthermore, evil is: But according to you it is a contrary, not a privation <note>term: "privation" (Latin: *privatio*). In medieval logic, this refers to the absence of a quality that should naturally be present, like blindness in an eye, rather than a separate "thing" called darkness.</note>.</margin>
<margin>Augustine says: He did not say evil is good, but that it exists within the good.</margin>
<margin>Furthermore, if evil: It is a privation to the extent that a privation is formally a negation.</margin>
<margin>Show it, then: Reread the previous letters, and you will see this shown to you in them, perhaps even more than you desire.</margin>

Therefore, Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note>, who says that Simplicius <note>A 6th-century commentator on Aristotle</note> claims those things are properly called contraries of which each is something distinct—since he explains the reason why health and sickness are numbered among contraries—it is necessary that he concludes "blind and seeing" are not so, according to Simplicius. He interprets Aristotle on this point; whether that interpretation be true or false is a matter of no importance for us to dwell upon. 

But since in your last letter you seemed to call "evil" that which you think is a negation of "good"—an evil that would be entirely evil—and in the same way you define "falsehood" as the division of the "one true thing," I wish to ask you: Do you think a chimera is entirely a "non-being"? 

If you deny it, you must contradict yourself, for you said before that a chimera is entirely non-being and false. But if you grant that it is entirely non-being, I shall proceed in this way: "non-being" and "entirely evil" are equivalent; a chimera is entirely non-being; therefore, it is also entirely evil. But this cannot be. For a chimera does not contain a logical contradiction; it can, therefore, be created by God. That which can exist, however, is good. Therefore, that which can be created can be good. Since the potential for goodness is itself good, the chimera is therefore not entirely evil. 

Furthermore, a chimera can be understood both by God and by us; it can therefore exist within our mind and soul. Therefore, in whatever way it can exist, it participates in goodness in that same way. Thus, the chimera is not entirely evil. Furthermore, nothing can be "evil" unless it is something to be avoided; yet nothing can be avoided or shunned unless it is known, either by the one who flees or by God, who implanted the natural instinct for flight. It is necessary, therefore, that every evil can be known in some way. But "knowledge" is a certain kind of good; therefore, "to be able to be known" is also a good, for the potential for a good is itself a certain kind of good. 

Furthermore, Aristotle in the fourth book of the *Metaphysics* says that negations and privations are, in a certain way, "beings"; indeed, he even says that "non-being" itself is in a certain way "being." The sign of this, he says, is that we say "non-being is non-being." But whatever is in some way a "being" is in some way "good." Therefore, the chimera—to which the name of "non-being" is truly applied—is in some way a "being" and "good." 

Furthermore, evil is the privation of good; but every privation is the negation of a form in a subject suited by nature to have that form and habit. Therefore, nothing can be "evil" that is not capable of and suited for "good." But the capacity and aptitude for good is itself good. Evil, therefore, cannot be entirely evil; hence Augustine says that "evil is always within the good." 

Furthermore, if evil is the privation of good, as you say, how can it be the negation of good? For the opposition between a "privation" and a "habit" is one thing, but the opposition between an "affirmation" and a "negation" is another. 

Furthermore, it is your part to show that the argument you made previously was valid—the one by which you tried to prove from Aristotle and Thomas that God is "not being" <note>original: *deum ens non esse*</note>. For I have weakened both of your points. It is not enough to say: "I know that sometimes God is called 'being' by the Peripatetics <note>term: "Peripatetics." The followers of Aristotle, so named because Aristotle allegedly taught while walking (Greek: *peripatos*).</note>, but I also know that among the same people, God is sometimes not included under the name of 'being'." Show me, I ask you, in what place either Aristotle or the Aristotelians do not consider God under the name of "being"?

Otherwise, if you have time, explain how you defend that God is "existent" and "One," yet God is not "God." For if the name is understood, it is necessary that some description be formed by the mind; which, once given, it follows immediately that "God is God." Nor indeed...

<summary>Pico challenges his opponent's definition of evil as a total "non-being," arguing that even a hypothetical Chimera has some goodness because it can be thought of by God. He concludes by demanding proof for the claim that Aristotle did not consider God to be "Being."</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s rigorous defense of his philosophical position against an unnamed critic (likely Antonio Civitella). Having previously established the distinction between "contraries" and "privations," Pico now addresses the fourth set of objections regarding the definition of God and the relationship between essence and existence.</meta>

# **10. MIRANDOLA**

<column-break/>

The poet Simonides <note>Simonides of Ceos (c. 556–468 BC), a Greek lyric poet. According to Cicero, when the tyrant Hiero of Syracuse asked him "What is God?", Simonides continually asked for more time to deliberate, eventually concluding that the more he thought, the more obscure the matter became.</note>, when asked by a tyrant what God is, would have requested time to respond unless he had already conceived in his mind both the interpretation of the name and its designation; for in every question, the first priority is the meaning of the word. Furthermore, if God is "one," then another "one" is God—which can be nothing other than God. Likewise, if God exists and yet is not "God" <note>This refers to the logical distinction between the being of God and the linguistic category of the word "God."</note>, He is something other than God. It is therefore necessary that He be other than Himself. Furthermore, if God is not "God" because the name of God is a concrete term signifying something else, then it should not be conceded that God exists or that God is one; for there is nothing in the nature of things that is "God" by participating in divinity <note>term: "participation" (Latin: *participatio*). In Platonic and Scholastic thought, this is the idea that created things have qualities (like goodness or beauty) only by "participating" in the ultimate source of those qualities, whereas God possesses them by essence.</note>. Finally, you shall show how you either prove or defend against the contradiction of concluding that "God does not exist" and "gold exists." Such a disputation will be pleasing to me, and it ought not to be troublesome to you; for **disputation is the sieve of truth**, the sweetest food of the soul, having nothing unpleasant about it. Farewell.

<margin>A</margin> **The Fourth Objections.**
It was not said that "God is not being" because "to be" is in God through His essence, but because "to be" is not distinct from His essence—which is a vastly different thing. Otherwise, the very "being" of a stone, which is in it by its essence, would be neither being nor good; for the "being" of a stone is not its essence, but is for itself both its own "to be" and its own essence. If one cannot ask what things *are* in the case of negations and privations—since these are not sufficient to form the question "what is it?" to know the thing—then one must know more: both its "to be" and its "being something." Therefore, it is ridiculous and irrational to respond "being" or "something," whether "being" is taken in the first or the second way <note>term: "first or second way" (*prioro modo... secundo*). Likely referring to the Aristotelian distinction between being as substance and being as an accident or truth-value.</note>. If one asks what "sin" is, the question concerns the word rather than the thing. If something is "being," then according to your position it is "being" because its "to be" is distinct in reality from its essence; you say humanity is one thing, a man another; whiteness (or the quality of white) is one thing, and a white thing another. Therefore, if an "Idea" <note>Referring to the Platonic Ideas or Forms.</note> is "being," it will be being precisely because the "to be" of the Idea is distinct from the Idea itself. But the Idea is God; therefore, the "to be" of the Idea is distinct from God. Thus, in God there would be a composition according to reality, and not only according to reason. According to the definition of denominatives, "one" is named from "unity"; but God, according to your position, is called "one" from a likeness to unity. Therefore, that predication does not belong to the substance of God, which the Platonists say: "God is one." Furthermore, when we say "God is one," you think that not *what* He is, but *how* He is, is signified; but "how" (mode) belongs to the category of accidents. Therefore, the word "one" in God is not substantive, nor does it pertain to the thing itself. This is why those who have either not learned the Platonic sect or are ignorant of the Greek language are not sufficient to defend the Academic discipline. If God did not exist and gold existed, you say gold would exist, and gold would not be gold; therefore, it would be gold. Thus, if the definition of truth stands, there will be a truth that corresponds to no Idea. If "Socrates sits," it is neither true nor false because it is not necessary <note>A reference to the problem of future contingents or non-necessary propositions in logic.</note>; indeed, I shall defend that not every affirmation or negation is true, for in some cases neither one nor the other possesses necessary truth. If "good" and "evil" are in things, but "true" and "false" are in the soul, where is your opposition of affirmation and negation? For negation posits nothing. How, then, is a "chimera" both in things and in the soul if it is entirely non-being and false, since you think "non-being" and "evil" are interchangeable? If "blindness is blindness" is true, who does not see that blindness is "true"? For they are the same thing; once blindness alone is posited, it posits this fact: that blindness is blindness; and once removed, it is taken away. By the same reasoning, "Socrates" and "Socrates being Socrates" are the same, and both are generated by the same generation and through themselves; God also and "God being God" are the same; for both are eternal and the First Truth.

<column-break/>

Furthermore, pay attention; I will soon explain that when, through this word "God," you conceive only what is signified by the name, this word does not function as a **predicate** but as a **subject**. For it is that about which one asks what can or ought to be enunciated concerning it, not that which is enunciated about another. Therefore, this was not unknown either to Simonides or to the tyrant who consulted him. Likewise, when you ask whether "if God cannot be called God, is He something other than God?", I ask of you what you conceive through this word "God" which you enunciate concerning God? If you conceive nothing, you do not err, because you say nothing. If you conceive something, I say that God is something other than what you conceive and what you explain through this word "God." For He is above everything that can be conceived by us.

**On God not being:** Let us come, then, to your "gold," which you do not wish to lose at all, even if God is lost. It is impossible for anything to be if **Being itself** <note>original: "ipsum esse" – This is the technical term for God in Thomistic and Scholastic philosophy: God is not a "being" among others, but the act of Being itself.</note> is not; it is therefore impossible for gold to be if God is not. Furthermore, if God is not, then there is the "infinite." If there is the infinite, there is nothing; for if it is infinite, it is not finite. But if the infinite is, then the infinite is not; because the infinite destroys itself, just like other things that contain a contradiction. If there is nothing, then there is no gold. I believe these things are sufficient for you, a man as ingenious as you wish to be. Farewell.

<summary>Pico responds to objections regarding the nature of God's existence, arguing that God is "Being itself" (ipsum esse) and therefore the necessary foundation for the existence of anything else, including gold. He utilizes the anecdote of Simonides to highlight the difficulty of defining God and explores the logical consequences of essence versus existence.</summary>

# **ON BEING AND THE ONE**

->**ON BEING AND THE ONE**<-

If everything false is simply divided <note>In scholastic logic, "divided" often refers to the separation of a predicate from a subject in a false proposition.</note>, as you do not deny has been proven, it should not have been said that something false is divided only under this condition—that is, as long as it is false. For if every human is simply and absolutely capable of laughter <note>term: "risible" (Latin: *risibilis*). A classic example in logic of a "proper" attribute: something that is not part of the essence of being human but is found in all humans and only humans.</note>, it is not necessary to add a condition by which you restrict it, saying: "every human is capable of laughter as long as he is a human." Nor should a restriction be added because not all false things are equally divided or false; for not all beings are equally good, yet all things are absolutely good. How it is concluded that good and evil are contraries will be easily established if "pursuing" and "fleeing" are contraries—provided the logic of contrary movements has been sufficiently understood by you. Why do you wonder if I say that the Latins <note>Western Christian scholars</note> do not deny Aristotle, whom Simplicius <note>Simplicius of Cilicia (c. 490–560 AD), a Neoplatonist commentator on Aristotle.</note> denies, but Boethius does not? Is it because of this that I either do not imitate Boethius or I extol the barbarians <note>original: "barbaros". Pico often used this term to refer to the medieval Scholastic philosophers like Thomas Aquinas or Duns Scotus, who were criticized by Humanists for their "unpolished" Latin but admired by Pico for their rigour.</note>? Do you call this a strange thing? I would call *you* marvelous, for thinking that while I imitate Boethius and set Simplicius aside, I actually despise Boethius and follow the barbarians. 

If good and evil are contraries, you wish to prove that a chimera <note>A mythological beast, used here as a standard logical example of a "non-being" or something that cannot exist.</note> is something that exists in the nature of things. But if it were understood in what sense I called good and evil "contraries"—which you either do not yet wish to or cannot understand—you would prove nothing from the chimera. <margin>Pri-</margin> <note>Likely an abbreviation for *Privationes* (Privations).</note> You wonder greatly that certain privations are called "partial" <note>original: "semiplenas". Literally "half-full."</note> by me, and you prove they are non-existent in this way: "Evil is nothing; therefore, it is not a partial privation." But I, following your argument, shall say this: sickness is bad; therefore, it is nothing; therefore, it is not a partial privation. Yet sickness is a certain privation; therefore, it is not a partial privation of health or of any good, but rather a full and perfect one—which is impossible. Therefore, privations are partial, such as sickness, rarity, or ugliness. Blindness is a "perfect" <note>In this context, "perfect" means "complete" or "absolute."</note> privation of sight, but an "imperfect" privation of good; for it does not take away the whole good that exists in the one who sees <note>meaning the being itself still exists and is therefore "good" in the sense of having existence.</note>.

If it is true, as you write, that all evil leaves some good behind, then the chimera—which is entirely non-being and evil—must retain some good. If it preserves some good, it is not entirely evil, nor entirely non-being. Although the power by which it can be created and exist is in God, and the concept by which it can be understood is in the mind, it is not denied that the chimera is potentially good and a being; for there is the power of God and the power of the chimera in different senses. Nor do we deny that the Antichrist is potentially good, whose power to exist is partly in matter, partly in the heavens, and in man.

Furthermore, how can the Chimera—if all thought and the power of God are excluded—be entirely non-being and evil? For in order to be non-being, it certainly cannot be evil; for evil is a privation that exists in a subject, and that subject must necessarily participate in goodness. Otherwise, it could not be a subject; for that which is entirely non-existent cannot be a subject.

You have not yet disproved what I said; and you confirm it by the authority of Simplicius, except you say Simplicius does not say it. But you should not boast on that account, for I did not say that Aristotle feels every being exists either through itself or by accident, nor did I falsely attribute anything to Blessed Thomas <note>St. Thomas Aquinas.</note>.

Although every privation is a certain negation, it is not yet established that there is not one opposition of affirmation and negation, and another of privation and habit <note>term: "habit" (Latin: *habitus*). In scholastic logic, the "habit" is the presence of a quality (like sight), while "privation" is its absence (like blindness).</note>; nor is it necessary that if evil is the privation of good, "evil" and "non-good" are interchangeable.

Your defense, by which you wish to protect the claim that God is not God, I [consider] neither for the truth nor for the Blessed...

### **GIOVANNI PICO OF MIRANDOLA**

I think these points are consistent with Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-century Christian theologian and philosopher whose works were highly influential in medieval mysticism.</note>, nor did the blessed Dionysius ever deny that God is God. But as the Blessed Thomas <note>Thomas Aquinas</note> interprets it, no name of God can fully explain His nature in its entirety. Nor does he think for any other reason that the affirmations concerning God are "uncompacted" <note>original: "incompactas". This refers to the idea that human language cannot perfectly bind or "compact" a definition that fits the infinite nature of God.</note>. But you say that if the name of God contains a description, it has the character of a subject, but not also of a predicate. Even if this is granted, the argument remains: let **a.** be the definition of the name, and let it be said in this way: "God is **a.**" For the definition of anything is predicated of that which it defines. Therefore, by a simple conversion, "**a.** is God." Thus, "God is God." 

Likewise, you say that when one asks whether God is something other than God or not, one must know what is conceived by the name "God." Whatever else may be given, you say I will call it "God." For He is above everything that can be conceived. but does not such a solution contradict itself? For if you confess a proposition of this kind—which is "God is above that which can be conceived"—do you not clearly affirm something about God? Let there be, therefore, a definition of the name: that speech which is "above that which can be conceived," and the argument will still hold. Furthermore, it follows that if "God is above everything that can be conceived," then God cannot be conceived; otherwise, the same thing would be above itself. Therefore, He could neither be loved nor worshipped <note>Pico is pointing out a logical trap: if God is entirely beyond thought, humans would have no way to relate to Him, which contradicts religious practice.</note>. 

Finally, you might think the power of gold is so great that, whether we wish it or not, it necessarily pulls God along with it, either in reality or in the mind, in this way: "Gold is. Therefore, existence itself is. Therefore, God is." <note>Pico appears to be mocking a circular or overly materialistic logical proof of existence.</note> Likewise: "God is. Therefore, He is infinite. He is infinite; therefore, He is nothing." If you say an infinite being is not finite, you are arguing as if to say: "The finite is not; therefore, it is nothing." Then you say: "The infinite is; therefore, the infinite is not," for you say the infinite destroys itself. 

Indeed, I think if anyone had written such arguments to Nicoletto <note>Nicoletto Vernia (c. 1420–1499), a prominent Aristotelian professor at Padua and a contemporary rival of Pico.</note>, he would have given no answer. Nor shall I oppose anything further, lest I seem to doubt a matter that appears clearer to me than light. Yet if you prove your "refinement" with these same arguments, I truly fear you may "lose your gold" <note>original: "aurum perdas". A metaphorical way of saying "waste your efforts" or "lose your investment."</note>. If you wish, respond something to these objections, my dearest friend, so that we may finally bring an end to this disputation; for we have played enough. Moreover, I would not want you to think I have turned to these things out of hatred or ill will. I know you remember that before I wrote anything to you, I asked if you were willing. Indeed, I call God to witness that I love and venerate my Mirandolan companion. If you ever care to put me to the test, you will find I have told no lie.

# **GIANFRANCESCO PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA TO THE DISTINGUISHED PHILOSOPHER ANTONIO FAVENTINO, GREETINGS.**

**Q**<note>The text begins with a large decorative red initial Q.</note> lthough all the vigor of my studies and all the hope that had been placed almost entirely in him have faded with the death of my uncle Giovanni Pico—for while he was alive, I hoped that the study of philosophy would be restored to its ancient purity, yet enriched with great resources, and that the Christian faith would be fortified with the strongest towers against its enemies, once errors were entirely eliminated and heresies driven out—I am not, however, so dismayed in spirit that I have not labored with all my might. I have done this so that all his night-watches and his unfinished works <note>original: "lucubrationes". Literally "work done by lamplight," referring to Pico's legendary late-night scholarly sessions.</note>, which flowed from that man who was admired everywhere in literature, should not utterly perish. 

Therefore, looking out for myself and for our people, I hurried to Florence by the fastest possible routes. I took every care I could so that whatever had been noted down by him—though unpolished and unrefined—should be placed into our power. My efforts were not entirely in vain; for even if the accounts were not yet open nor a known heir appointed, the chests were such that we could inspect and turn over all his commentaries. We saw in those scattered paper volumes the man's incredible diligence: every kind of reading, and concepts admirable beyond the grasp of the human mind. Truly, in organizing his writings, there was a lack of care that is not to be praised; everything was cast about and scattered here and there. But more on these things at another time. While I was diligently...

<meta>This text transitions from the specific logical arguments regarding the definition of God into the preface for Giovanni Pico della Mirandola's treatise "On Being and the One" (De Ente et Uno). It is written by his nephew, Gianfrancesco Pico, addressed to Antonio Faventino.</meta>

# **ON BEING AND THE ONE**

While I was carefully examining his little work *On Being and the One* <note>original: "De Ente et Uno," a famous treatise by Giovanni Pico that attempted to reconcile the philosophies of Plato and Aristotle on the nature of existence and unity.</note>, published nearly four years before his death, there fell into my hands three letters written by you against it, along with the responses to them. Because of the novelty of the matter, I did not merely read them through, but drank them in—or rather, as they say, devoured them. (For I had known by rumor that this had occurred, but I did not have a sufficiently clear understanding of what weight of argument had been brought forward.) 

I began to think and debate with myself whether I ought to give that work to the printers for public release alongside the other works which I had collected and judged worthy of publication, making no mention of your objections; or whether it would be more advisable if it went out to the public fortified—attacked on one side by "offenses" <note>original: "offensaculis," referring here to the critical objections or stumbling blocks raised by the correspondent.</note> and defended on the other by "bulwarks" <note>original: "propugnaculis," referring to the defensive responses or counter-arguments.</note>. After a long discussion of the matter, a final decision at last settled in my mind. Truly, the work might seem to carry marks of infamy when met by learned men if it appeared not only to fear its accusers, but also lacked the courage to summon them rightly to judgment, as if it had little faith in its own conscience. Therefore, it also seemed appropriate that the work should go forth accompanied by the responses, just as witnesses are called to defend the cause of innocence.

# **GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA**

...province <note>The text begins mid-word with "cia," likely completing "provincia" (field or province of study) from the preceding page.</note>, which I began to measure with my uncle Giovanni Pico and our friend Giovanni Mainardi <note>Giovanni Mainardi (1462–1536) was a celebrated physician and a close intellectual collaborator of the Pico family.</note> as my guides. This was at a time when I realized that the knowledge of nature should be directed not toward exhausting ourselves in literary contests <note>original: "litterarios desudandos agones," referring to the highly competitive and often vanity-driven academic debates of the Renaissance.</note>, but toward recognizing the Creator of nature Himself.

# DEFENSE

...can be called created things and beings. For this reason, it is declared by his followers, especially **Capreolus** <note>Johannes Capreolus (c. 1380–1444) was a French Dominican theologian known as the "Prince of Thomists" for his defense of the teachings of Thomas Aquinas.</note> when there is a question concerning the distinction between being and essence, that the "being" of created things is neither received into the number of true beings nor into the number of creatures. For if it does not receive the name of "being," it undoubtedly does not receive the name of "good" either, since "being" and "good" follow one another and are reciprocal in their scope <note>This refers to the medieval doctrine of the "transcendentals," where Being, Goodness, and Truth are considered different names for the same reality.</note>.

<margin>Solution to the second objection.</margin>
In the second place, you argue in this manner: if, in cases of negations and privations <note>A "privation" is the absence of a quality that should naturally be present, such as blindness being the privation of sight.</note>, it cannot be asked *what* they are; since they exist, it is not enough to form the question "what is it" simply to know that the thing being asked about exists. Rather, the questioner must know both *that* it is and *that it is something*. Therefore, it is ridiculous and irrational to answer "being" or "something," whether "being" is taken in the first sense or the second. But if one asks what "sin" is, the question concerns the word rather than the thing itself. To this objection, we reply: he never said that in privations and negations one could not ask what they were. Rather, he said that it could not be answered *what* they were in their essence. 

<margin>Thomas, Giles</margin>
This point was brought forward for the sake of **Thomas** <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274).</note>, whom he cited in previous letters when you were doubting this—whether it was true or false—with these words: "you must admit it is true unless you abandon your Thomas." We also find this same point asserted by **Giles of Rome** <note>Giles of Rome (c. 1243–1316) was a philosopher and theologian, a pupil of Thomas Aquinas.</note> in the second book of his commentaries on the theological sentences. For it is sufficient to form the question "what is it" simply to know that the thing under inquiry exists. It is not necessary for someone who is going to investigate what a thing is to know that the thing exists as a "being" in the first sense <note>Being in the "first sense" usually refers to a thing having its own substantial essence or quiddity.</note>, but only in the second sense—that is, that it "is." But if you contend that you understood the question to be formed only when it can be answered affirmatively and correctly: first, if you think that the question cannot be correctly formed unless the thing being asked about is of such a nature that an answer can be given through it, I do not agree with you. 

<margin>Aristotle</margin>
For it is the opinion of **Aristotle** that one can inquire whether a centaur exists or not; yet a centaur is not the kind of thing that can provide an answer to the question "is it," since it is a mere fable and a total fiction. Similarly, I disagree if you believe that the questioner must already know this same thing; for (as we have shown) he who correctly inquires "what a thing is" does not need to know more than *that it is*. Therefore, to someone who knows a thing exists, the answer "it is something" is not ridiculous when given to someone who does not know and is inquiring about it. But because we are not accustomed to teaching those who ask "what a thing is" simply that it is "being" or "something"—to answer more fully—it happens that those who already have explored that it is *something* might still search for what *kind* of being it is. Therefore, we satisfy not only their expressed petition but also their desire for investigation when we dissolve their questions—both conceived and unexpressed—by anticipating them with our responses. 

However, those words—that if it is asked "what is sin," the question is of the word rather than the thing—which were made as an objection against you, do not seem to have carried much weight. For when you previously argued from the opinion of Thomas: namely, that "being" is called according to the first sense that which answers the question "what is it," and to one asking what it is that preserves and moves the world, "God" is reasonably answered; from which you concluded that God is "being" and "something" in the first sense. He replied: "See how greatly you are deceived; evil, according to Thomas, is not such that we can answer anything to one asking what it is, or call it 'being.' And yet, to one asking what 'sin' is, we can answer that it is 'evil'." Therefore, this answer of yours—that if it is asked "what is sin," the question is of the word rather than the thing—does not help you at all. For the question "what is it that governs the world?" is no more a question of a name than "what is sin?", since He who governs the world (that is, God) does not have a <term>quiddity</term> <note>original: "quidditatem"; the "what-ness" or essential definition of a thing.</note>, as the more recent thinkers say. All confirm this most clearly, except those who place Him in a "category" <note>Aristotelian categories are used to classify created things; many theologians argued God is "beyond category."</note>. 

<margin>Dionysius</margin>
And as the most holy **Dionysius** <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-6th century Christian philosopher whose works were highly influential in mystical theology.</note>, the leader of our theology after the Apostles, says: He has neither a name nor a definition; furthermore, not even in those things you said before...

### GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

This response is consistent when you first say that evil itself is not nothing but something positive; but now you confess that the question is formed only regarding the name itself.

<margin>Third objection.</margin>
You object thirdly with these words: if something is a being, then according to your position it is a being because *to be* is, in terms of reality, different from essence. You ask whether humanity is one thing and a human another, or whiteness one thing and a white thing another. Therefore, if an "Idea" <note>In Platonic and Scholastic thought, an "Idea" refers to the divine archetype or form in the mind of God.</note> is a being, it will be a being because the *to be* of the Idea is different from the Idea itself. But the Idea is God; therefore, the *to be* of the Idea is different from God. Consequently, there is a composition in God according to reality, not just according to reason <note>Scholastic philosophers distinguished between "real composition" (parts that actually exist separately, like body and soul) and "rational distinction" (distinctions made by the mind about a single simple reality).</note>.

<margin>Solution.</margin>
To these things, we say that a response has already been given. For when you argued with almost the same means you now use in your third letter, he <note>Referring to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola.</note> replied that the composition of being and essence in divine matters is according to reason, not according to reality. Therefore, we deny that the first proposition of this hypothetical syllogism <note>A logical argument structured as "if P, then Q."</note> you bring forward is true. For even if in created things essence differs from existence in reality, it does not follow from this that it is necessary for whatever can in any way be called a being to be composed of essence and *to be* (or existence) as if from parts. Therefore, essence and existence, which are distinct in reality, do not meet in the Idea, which is the exemplar of creatures. 

But this composition is made by us in it when we weigh it as the exemplary cause of essence and being (or *to be* and existence) which are found in created things. We apply this composition and distinction equally to even the simplest things, and we call it "according to reason" when our intellect has fashioned it. The Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note> use this very frequently—a common view which, as he says, was repeated by **Antipater** <note>Antipater of Tarsus, a Stoic philosopher.</note>, 

<margin>Antipater.</margin>
<margin>Peripatetics.</margin>
mentioned by **Posidonius** <note>Posidonius (c. 135–51 BCE), a Greek Stoic philosopher and polymath.</note> in the letters of **Seneca** <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca, Roman Stoic philosopher and advisor to Nero.</note>. For that reason, we can say that the Idea is composed of essence and existence in this way according to reason, and call it a being—namely, 

<margin>Antipater.</margin>
considering it as the exemplar of creatures composed of essence and existence which differ in reality. We do not place this composition in God when we contemplate Him not as the exemplar of others, but as enjoying Himself in the innermost retreat of His divinity.

<margin>Posidonius.</margin>
<margin>Seneca.</margin>
<margin>Fourth objection.</margin>
Fourthly, you say that according to the definition of denominatives <note>A "denominative" is a term derived from another, like "brave" from "bravery."</note>, "one" is a denominative from "unity"; or, according to your position, God is called "one" from the similarity to unity. Therefore, the predication by which the Platonists say "God is one" does not pertain to the substance of God. Furthermore, when we say "God is one," you think it signifies not *what* He is, but *how* He is. But "mode" <note>A "mode" refers to the way a thing exists, often considered an accidental rather than essential quality.</note> belongs to the category of accidents; therefore, the word "one" in God is not substantive. You say this because either I have not learned the Platonic sect or I am ignorant of the Greek language—for that is not enough to defend the Academic discipline <note>The "Academic discipline" refers to the school of philosophy descending from Plato's Academy.</note>. 

<margin>Solution.</margin>
But the response is easy. Since it has been said by the Platonists that the "one" which is predicated of God is substantive and not merely denominative, it has been correctly asserted. And again, since it has been asserted that He is called "one" because He is similar to unity, it is not incongruous. Nor can it be said for that reason that it is not substantive; for even if a name is adapted to something from a property or similarity of some thing, it does not necessarily follow that the name is not substantive when it is taken as a substantive name, which signifies not by way of an adjective but as standing by itself. It is clear that the "one" predicated of God is understood not as something inherent but as standing by itself, so that it needs no proof. 

You have, therefore, the property from which the name is taken, which does not take away from the thing to which it is applied the fact of being substantive. For your **Thomas** <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274).</note>—or rather ours—both in other places and in the first part, reports that the thing to signify which a name is imposed differs from the source from which it is imposed. 

<margin>Thomas.</margin>
For example, he explains that this name "stone" <note>original: "lapis"</note> is imposed to signify that substance so named from a related property, namely, that which "hurts the foot" <note>original: "lædit pedem"; this is a traditional medieval etymology of *lapis* as *laedens pedem*.</note>. Hence, in another place, he teaches it was used by grammarians to write that a name denotes substance with quality, which **John Scotus** <note>Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a major High Scholastic theologian.</note> also affirms in the first book of his commentaries on the *Sentences*.

<margin>Jo. Scotus.</margin>

# **APOLOGIA**

Therefore, my dear Anthony, when we speak of God as "one," we speak truly and use it as a substantive name, <note>original: "substantivū nomē"</note> because we both conceive and declare it in the manner of something that stands by itself. Furthermore, when we say that "truth" is applied to God based on the likeness of His unity and its properties, we approach the divine as closely as is lawful for us. We do this because we are using an appropriate word to signify that divinity which remains ineffable <note>Beyond the power of words to describe.</note> and far above all created things, since God is the principle <note>The fundamental source or beginning.</note> of all things that exist, just as unity is the principle of all numbers. From these words, you will also gather the solution to your other argument concerning the category <note>original: "de modo quod de genere"</note> of accidents. You claim that in the declaration "God is one," only the *way* in which God is one is signified; nevertheless, you should consider that the word "one" is substantive in relation to God. If you consider from what source the name is derived and what it is assigned to denote, you can also recognize a very brief solution to your doubt from the words of my uncle.

<margin>A brief solution from the words of my uncle.</margin> He says: "How can you say that I follow the reasoning of the Platonists <note>Followers of Plato who emphasized the 'One' as the highest principle.</note> or rather of Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a highly influential mystical theologian who blended Christian and Neoplatonic thought.</note>, when you have never even read Dionysius or the Platonists, though you boast of it with such a loud voice?" You should know that among the Platonists, "Unity" is the Type <note>The archetype or essential form.</note> of God, and according to Dionysius, God is "uniquely all things." No one could rightly desire a clearer solution: for when it is said that Unity is the Type of God, it refers to likeness and manner; but when it is said that God is "uniquely all things," it refers to His substance. Yet, it is asserted that these two are entirely the same. Furthermore, in the Greek language—which my uncle knew well—both the abstract and the concrete can sometimes be signified by the same word.

<margin>Solution to the fifth objection.</margin> To provide the solution to your fifth doubt, many words are not needed. My uncle stated: "If God did not exist and gold existed, then gold would exist and gold would not exist." You add these words: "Therefore gold would be truth, yet a truth corresponding to no Idea." <note>This refers to the Scholastic belief that things are "true" only because they match an "Idea" or archetype in the mind of God.</note> Please add also these few words which he said followed from his own statement, and you will recognize how truth would "correspond to no Idea." What, I ask, is impossible? An impossibility gives birth to an impossibility; therefore it is no wonder if, from your impossible premise, you make whatever you wish follow. For if God did not exist and gold did exist, it would be a truth corresponding to no Idea, since the impossible is born from the impossible. Not only logicians <note>original: "dialectici"</note> but also theologians agree with this.

<margin>John Baconthorpe.</margin> For if you were to ask John Baconthorpe <note>A 14th-century English Carmelite monk known as the "Prince of Averroists."</note>, the Carmelite, whether it could happen that gold exists and God does not exist, he would answer you in his first book on the *Sentences* <note>A reference to Peter Lombard's "Sentences," the standard theological textbook of the Middle Ages.</note> that no thing whatsoever can be understood unless God is understood first. Since God is involved in the understanding of all things, you may gather for yourself whether it can be pronounced—beyond all controversy even among novice logicians—that it is impossible for gold to exist and God not to exist. But we shall speak of this again at the end of the work, if you later consult the Cardinal of Cambrai <note>Pierre d'Ailly (1351–1420), a famous French theologian and philosopher.</note>. 

<margin>The Cardinal of Cambrai.</margin> You will hear that man, who was well-practiced in all philosophy, saying in his first commentary on the *Sentences* that a contradiction follows from any impossible premise.

<margin>Solution to the sixth objection.</margin> In the sixth place, you said that if it were neither true nor false that "Socrates is sitting" (as my uncle had asserted because it was not a necessary truth), you could defend the idea that a negation or affirmation is not true in every case, since in some cases neither one nor the other has a necessary truth. Solving this objection, we reply that this statement—namely, "Socrates is sitting"—does not necessarily determine its own truth or falsehood by itself. However, it does not follow from this that an affirmation or negation is not true of everything. Nevertheless, if you understand it in the way he teaches, you could even deny that an affirmation or negation is "true" of everything in such a way that one part must *necessarily* be true. For he says: "That I am sitting is always either true or false, because I am always either sitting or not sitting." And what is said—that "me sitting" is neither true nor false—means that this proposition, by itself, has neither truth nor...

## **GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA**

...to determine with falsehood, which is what necessary propositions <note>Statements that must be true or false by their very nature, such as "a triangle has three sides."</note> do. But since it is possible for a statement to be true when, for instance, "I sit," and false when "I do not sit," the statement is in itself undetermined in either direction.

Furthermore, you insist on certain of his words regarding good and evil, and truth and falsehood, which he had proposed occur in things <margin>Seventh objection</margin> and in the soul, arguing in this manner: "If good and evil are in things, but truth and falsehood <margin>and the solution</margin> are in the soul, where is your opposition of affirmation and negation? For a negation establishes nothing, just as a chimera <note>A mythical creature; in logic, it represents a "non-being" or something that cannot exist in reality.</note> exists in things and the soul. If it is entirely a non-being <note>original: "non ens"</note> and false, then you must think that non-being and evil are interchangeable." 

But I pray you, pay attention and notice that evil and good are declared to be in things for this reason: they are considered in relation to things, just as truth and falsehood are considered in relation to the soul—this is not so. For truth and falsehood are not in things themselves, as Aristotle writes in the sixth book of his *First Philosophy* <margin>Aristotle</margin> <note>Referring to Aristotle’s *Metaphysics*, where he discusses the nature of truth residing in the mind's judgment rather than in the objects themselves.</note>, but in the mind. Nor does it necessarily follow from this that a thing which is entirely evil is a "true thing." Indeed, even those "true" and "false" things of which Aristotle makes mention in that place are complex terms <note>Propositions or sentences, rather than single words.</note>. Likewise, it does not follow that if good and evil are in things, they cannot be opposed contradictorily for that reason. For when evil is declared to be in things, it is not said to be in them so that it might be understood as being a specific "thing" <margin>Note on the nature of evil</margin> itself, but because it is observed and considered regarding the things themselves—that is, insofar as a thing is deprived of its perfections and is made "not good." A chimera, however, is not in things at all, because it is entirely a non-being and entirely evil. Nevertheless, if it were possible for such a thing to be produced by nature, it would be both a thing and good. It is "false" only insofar as it exists as nothing at all and corresponds to no idea. Nor do we even affirm that the chimera itself is in the soul, but rather the *notion* of the chimera; and this notion, as it is a certain "thing" in the mind, is both good and true, though it is "false" insofar as it represents a chimera, since the chimera itself is both nothing and evil.

After this, you believed you could prove that "blindness" is true, which he <note>Giovanni Pico</note> had denied. <margin>Eighth objection</margin> If he had been asked whether "blindness is blindness" is true, he would neither have denied it nor granted it. <margin>with the solution.</margin> Instead, he would have said these are far different things. You argued in this way: "If 'blindness is blindness' is true, and who does not see that blindness is true? For they are the same thing. For if blindness alone is posited <note>Assumed to exist.</note>, it establishes this fact: that blindness is blindness; and if it is taken away, it removes it. Hence, by the same reasoning, 'Socrates' and 'Socrates is Socrates' are the same thing. And by the same generation, both are generated; and through itself, God and 'God is God' are the same, for both are eternal and the First Truth." 

But I, my dear Anthony, contend the opposite and deny that these are the same as you affirm. For if one of those things you bring forward is posited, the other is not necessarily posited. For if blindness alone is posited without any intellect considering it, blindness will indeed exist, but this proposition "blindness is blindness" will not exist <note>Because a proposition requires a mind to formulate the sentence.</note>. For this reason, the argument concerning God and the generation of Socrates is also resolved. For Socrates is generated through himself, but the proposition "Socrates is Socrates" is not, since complex propositions are not "generated" in that way. Even if I were to grant you that they are the same, we say it still does not follow what you were concluding, because of the different way of signifying—namely, "complexly" and "incomplexly" <note>Scholastic terms: an "incomplex" term is a single word like 'blindness'; a "complex" term is a full statement like 'blindness is blindness'.</note>. Indeed, this argument would be of no value: "blindness and 'blindness is blindness' are the same, but this statement is true, therefore that object is true." By that same logic, it would follow that "this is a complex statement, therefore that object is a complex statement," which is absurd, since "blindness" is a simple name, not a complex one or any kind of Enunciation <note>A formal statement of a proposition.</note>. Therefore, "blindness is true" is one thing, and "'blindness is blindness' is true" is another.

And although these points should suffice for the defense of my uncle, nonetheless, do not believe that we lack further ways of defending and attacking. So that a more absolute response may reach you, I would have you know <margin>Gregory of Rimini</margin> that I could have spoken according to the opinion of Gregory of Rimini <note>A 14th-century Augustinian philosopher known for his work on the logic of propositions.</note>. <margin>The Cardinal of Cambrai</margin> Even if, when blindness alone was posited, the statement "blindness is blindness" were posited, it does not necessarily follow that they are the same. For he denies this consequence and many of this kind: "setting aside everything else other than God, God is; therefore God is 'God exists'." The Cardinal of Cambrai <note>Pierre d'Ailly (1351–1420), a famous theologian and philosopher.</note> also denies all speeches in which something is enunciated about an infinitive speech accepted significatively...

<meta>This page continues the "Apologia" (Defense) by Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola, defending his uncle Giovanni Pico della Mirandola against critics of his logical and metaphysical theses. The discussion continues to address specific objections regarding the nature of truth, falsehood, and the categorization of good and evil.</meta>

# DEFENSE

<margin>Ninth objection and the solution to the objection.</margin>

He asserts that those [propositions] are both false and inconsistent, as can be seen in his first book of *Sentences* <note>original: "sententiarum libro"; referring to a commentary on Peter Lombard’s *Sentences*, the standard medieval textbook for theology and logic.</note>. You then complain that a false statement ought not to have been pronounced with this condition—namely, "as long as it is false." You explain this in these words: if everything false is simply divided <note>In scholastic logic, "divided" often refers to the separation of a predicate from a subject in a proposition.</note> (which you do not deny has been proven), it should not have been said that a certain falsehood is divided only with this condition, "as long as it is false." For if every human is simply and absolutely capable of laughter <note>original: "risibilis"; a classic logical example of a "proper" attribute—something that belongs to all humans and only humans, but is not part of their essential definition.</note>, one does not need to add a condition to restrict it by saying, "every human is capable of laughter as long as he is a human." Nor should a restriction have been added because not all false things are equally divided or false. For not all beings are equally good, yet all things are absolutely good. 

But consider his words carefully, through which you will be able to cast aside every scrap of doubt. He says that every falsehood is divided, but not every falsehood is equally false; because those things which are not necessarily and always false are not equally divided from the truth as those which are always and necessarily false. Therefore, Anthony, that phrase "as long as" was rightly added for those things that are not always and necessarily false—things which, although false, can become true and united either by the work of nature or by an artist. This is something you also said in your second set of objections. Nevertheless, as long as they are divided, they are false; but those things that can never return to friendship <note>A poetic way of describing logical "reconciliation" or the joining of terms in a true statement.</note> are always false, as is abundantly seen in the response to the second objection. 

Nor does the comparison regarding beings and the capacity for laughter support your case at all. For beings are always and absolutely good. Although they are not equally good, and some participate in the nature of goodness more than others, they are nonetheless always and necessarily good. For insofar as they are beings, to that extent they are good; they cannot become non-beings and non-good unless they are reduced to nothingness. But a falsehood and a division that consists in a complex statement <note>term: "complexione" (complexion) — in logic, this refers to a proposition made of multiple terms combined together.</note> can conveniently be made non-divided and true. Therefore, the comparison does not fit. For although not all false things are equally divided, they are nonetheless false insofar as they are not united and not true. Furthermore, this objection should have troubled us very little. For who would doubt that a human (who is absolutely and always capable of laughter) can be pronounced as being capable of laughter with the condition "as long as he is a human"? Would learned men find fault with the expression "a human is capable of laughter as long as he is a human"?

<margin>Solution to the tenth objection.</margin>

The tenth head of your objections brings nothing else against him except that what you said could have been easily established if the principle of contrary motions had been sufficiently understood by him. But he, unless he is mistaken, complained that you did not prove what you so often said would follow: namely, that from the contrariety of pursuing and fleeing, the contrariety of good and evil is inferred. For he asks: by what reasoning is the good to be sought and the evil to be fled? And since fleeing and seeking are contraries, how do you prove from this that good and evil are contraries? This is what you must prove, yet you have never said a single word to prove it, nor do you do so now. He denies this—namely, the form of your argument—perhaps for this reason: because seeking and fleeing are not properly contrary "motions" from which one can conclude that the terms themselves are contraries. 

<margin>Aristotle</margin>

Furthermore, even by Aristotle himself, a certain contrariety of changes is assigned in the sixth book of his *Physics* <note>original: "physicae auscultationis libro"; Aristotle's *Physics* was often referred to as "Lectures on Nature."</note>, where the terms are not contraries but contradictories: namely, "being" and "non-being," when generation proceeds from non-being to being, and corruption falls from being into non-being. You, however, have treated this contrariety of good and evil again without bringing forward any other proof. Do not doubt that he has carefully examined the principle of contrary motions, even from his "fingernails" <note>An idiom meaning "from the very beginning" or "thoroughly."</note> as they say. On the contrary, he has quite often not only repelled your arguments against him regarding this contrariety, but also acted against you when, in his second letter, he deduced that your proof implies not only that evil and good are contraries, but that contradictories are contraries. Secondly, when he turned your own weapons back against you...

<summary>Gianfrancesco Pico defends the logical precision of using conditional statements (like "as long as") when discussing truth and falsehood. He also refutes the critic's attempt to define good and evil as contraries based solely on the human impulses of pursuit and avoidance, citing Aristotle's Physics to clarify the distinction between contraries and contradictories.</summary>

# GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

...in this way: good and evil, in themselves, are contraries; and since each of two contraries is something positive, and in itself "non-being" is good, it follows that "non-being" in itself is something positive. Furthermore, "something" and "being" are convertible <note>In scholastic logic, "convertible" terms are those that refer to the same thing even if their definitions differ; for example, "being" and "good" were traditionally held to be convertible.</note>; therefore, non-being in itself is something positive.

When you said in the third letter that he [Giovanni Pico] fled to Simplicius <note>Simplicius of Cilicia was a 6th-century Greek philosopher and one of the last great Neoplatonists who wrote extensive commentaries on Aristotle.</note>, abandoning the Latin interpreters <margin>Eleventh objection</margin> as far as the opposition of good and evil was concerned, he replied as if in amazement: why would you—who used to be a follower of Boethius <margin>Solution</margin> and a "derider of barbarians" <note>The "barbarians" here refers to medieval scholastic thinkers whose Latin was considered crude or "barbaric" by Renaissance humanists like Boethius was perceived to be.</note>—then mock those who followed the Greek interpreters after putting aside the Latins? Or perhaps you were finding, most conveniently, that you felt wrongly if you thought Greek philosophers should not be held in high esteem, whom Boethius—whom you hold in the highest price and highest honor—had always honored, and had used as both teachers and guides. <margin>Boethius</margin> To which you reply that the matter is not worthy of wonder, since you would say that the Latins do not deny Aristotle, whom Simplicius also does not deny, and so on.

But it does not seem to me that Simplicius denies Aristotle when he interprets him correctly, nor does it appear that the Latin interpreters vary from Simplicius’s opinion, since they embrace it with their whole mind and carry it out in their works. If he was amazed that you denied that the Latin expositors follow Simplicius, he would perhaps have fallen into a greater stupor if he understood you to have claimed that the Latins do not deny Aristotle, while Simplicius does deny him. Furthermore, Simplicius and those who followed him clearly elucidate Aristotle's mind when he said that good and evil are contraries by this reasoning: because one of the contraries always has the nature of evil and deficiency. On which account, in the first book of the *Physics*, he taught that contraries are always compared according to the ratio of a better and a worse thing respectively, also imitating the Pythagoreans, <margin>Pythagoras</margin> who established two orders of things: one contained under good, the other under evil. 

And he [Aristotle] used this frequently in his logical books with external examples. This exposition, as your Thomas <margin>Thomas</margin> says—who is not only a Latin but the chief among the Latins—not only relates but also proves; to whom we also add Aegidius <note>Aegidius Romanus (Giles of Rome), a prominent 13th-century theologian.</note> in his second book of *Sentences* <margin>Aegidius</margin>, and many others, namely Burley <margin>Burley</margin> and d'Ascoli <margin>d'Ascoli</margin> <note>Walter Burley and Cecco d'Ascoli, two major figures in medieval logic and science.</note>, who feel the same. Even John Duns Scotus <margin>Jo. Scotus</margin>, explaining Aristotle's *Categories*, supports our opinion, saying that if "good" is taken as it is convertible with "being," then "evil" is nothing, and thus is not contrary to "good." For since it is beyond controversy that both contraries must be something positive, it is necessary that what is "nothing" in the nature of things—which is what evil is—cannot be pronounced a contrary. 

And although you have denied that evil is nothing, appealing to Thomas, he himself not only supports your opinion but also abundantly refutes it—which the uncle [Giovanni Pico] also sufficiently showed in the margin of the third letter. However, we think it would not be out of place to briefly touch upon even a few points in passing in favor of the uncle's opinion, and to show that not only was Thomas of the opinion that evil was nothing, but a whole crowd of many illustrious philosophers and theologians "descended into this opinion with hands and feet" <note>original: "pedibus manibusque decessisse"; a Latin idiom meaning to agree totally and enthusiastically.</note>. We find Augustine <margin>Augustine</margin>, in his discourse on the *Morals of the Manichaeans*, said that no nature is evil; and a little later, lest there be any ambiguity about what he meant by "nature," he added: "and nature itself is nothing other than that which is understood to be something in its own genus." 

We have seen that Aegidius Romanus <margin>Aegidius</margin>, in his first book of commentaries on the *Sentences* of the Fathers, left written that evil, insofar as it is evil, is pure privation and not "something"; and it can be pronounced to be "something" only in the way that "nothing" itself can be called "something"—when both can be named by a name. Also, in the second book of those same commentaries, he affirms that evil does not have (to use his words) "quiddity" <term>Quiddity: the "what-ness" or essential nature of a thing.</term>, and for that reason the question "what is it?" cannot be answered. He also interprets the words of Aristotle concerning the opposition of evil and good according to the uncle's mind, and agrees with the dogma of Simplicius <margin>Simplicius</margin> and other worthy interpreters of Aristotle... namely, pronouncing that they are not their own genera, but rather [the genera] of other contraries...

<summary>Gianfrancesco Pico defends his uncle's view that "evil" is not a positive existence but a "nothing" or "privation" of good. He argues that this view is supported by a wide range of authorities, including Aristotle, Simplicius, Thomas Aquinas, Augustine, and Aegidius Romanus.</summary>

...that they ought to be called genera, since one has the nature of a positive while the other does not, and none of the contraries in itself is "non-being," but rather possesses some nature and existence. Gregory of Rimini <margin>Gregory of Rimini</margin> testifies to this very thing in his commentaries on the second book of the *Sentences* <note>original: "sententiarum"; The *Sentences* of Peter Lombard was the standard theology textbook of the Middle Ages, upon which all scholars wrote commentaries.</note>: namely, that evil itself is not some entity (to use his own word <note>original: "entitatem"</note>), but a pure privation. Robert Holkot <margin>Robert Holkot</margin> <note>Robert Holkot (d. 1349) was a prominent English Dominican theologian and philosopher.</note>, a man of most sharp-sighted genius, felt this same way in the first question of his commentaries on the second book of the theological *Sentences*. Many others have judged the same, whom to bring forward at present might perhaps cause weariness to me in writing and to you in reading later.

It will be enough for the present business to have numbered these especially, since in dissolving other objections it will be necessary to speak of this again when mention is made of evil in those places. But to return to where we digressed: you seem to cite only Boethius <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 477–524 AD), a Roman statesman and philosopher who was a primary bridge between Classical and Medieval thought.</note> from among all the Latins against Simplicius and the other illustrious interpreters. If you deign to count him among the Latins, he will be but one of the Latin expositors—not "the Latin expositors" in the plural—who will seem to support your opinion. Add to this that even he, if his mind is properly examined, does not protest against our opinion, since he neither ponders this question exactly nor searches it out with final judgment; rather, he only declares what Aristotle’s words, strictly and narrowly grasped, demand. This was his most familiar custom in his first editions, leaving the various opinions of the Greek interpreters to the second edition to be scrupulously and anxiously examined.

Furthermore, I think he not only proved but demonstrated that whenever it is granted that good and evil are contraries, it can be pronounced without any controversy that a Chimera <note>In logic, the "Chimera" is a standard example of a non-existent thing that can be discussed but has no reality.</note> is something in the nature of things. To his arguments against you, you respond only this: that he did not perceive the reason why you called good and evil contraries. You offer nothing else for yourself, wherefore I shall do nothing against you except to say that he both saw and perceived everything you had written, and when it pleased him, he reviewed many things you had said about contraries. For my plan in this business <margin>Solution of the twelfth objection</margin> is to dissolve your final objections against my uncle, but to pass over in silence those to which he himself responded in some way. Nevertheless, if anything seems to you not fully explained by him, which you might both hope for and demand to be opened by me, we shall attempt to satisfy your desire, through which we shall wander by both dissolving and responding to your arguments according to our strength. For he did not judge it inconsistent for even the smallest details of your words to lack a response. <margin>Solution of the thirteenth objection</margin>

He confesses in his first letters that certain things were omitted to which no response was given, lest he spend words on trivial matters, and certain things were treated lightly, as one who thought such matters should be indicated rather than explained to a philosopher. I would wish these words to be interpreted by you in such a way that several points of controversy—noted even among the Greek philosophers—were not worth being brought forward by you, a noble philosopher, against a man most celebrated in both doctrine and fame, who was holding discourse on the highest things and who would not descend to discuss these lowest matters without a loss of the contemplations conceived concerning the most difficult things. Concerning this contrariety of yours, however, we shall say something in the following response when words are spoken about "half-full" privations <note>The critic apparently used the term "semiplenas priuationes" to describe evils that are not total absences of good but partial ones; Gianfrancesco finds this terminology absurd.</note>.

He had said against you: "Evil is nothing; therefore, it is not a half-full privation." But you pursue his argument in this way: "Sickness is evil, therefore it is nothing. Therefore, it is not a half-full privation." Or, "Sickness is a certain privation; therefore, it is not a half-full privation of either health or some good, but rather a full and perfect one," which cannot happen. Therefore, you argue that imperfect privations are "half-full," such as sickness, rarity, baseness, and blindness; vision is the perfect good, and these are the imperfect—this you [addressed] to...
