<meta>This page continues Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola’s defense of his uncle, Giovanni Pico, regarding the nature of evil. The debate moves into a technical refutation of a critic named Antonio, specifically addressing whether evil is a "partial" or "total" absence of good.</meta>

-> # **OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA** <-

...word. Truly, my dear Antonio, I would say freely that these words of yours either do nothing against him <note>Pico della Mirandola, whom Gianfrancesco is defending.</note>, and so that you may see this more clearly, I shall review them one by one. You say first, based on his own words: "Evil is nothing; therefore it is not a partial privation." You are on the right track. Again: "Sickness is evil, therefore it is nothing; thus it is not a partial privation." Thus far you also proceed well, because sickness, insofar as it is evil, is to that extent nothing. Again you say: "But sickness is a certain privation, therefore it is not health," and so on until the end. By these words—if you will allow me to say so—a falsehood is constructed in my judgment, which we shall endeavor to demonstrate. 

For blindness is not only a "perfect" <note>In this context, "perfect" means "complete" or "total."</note> privation of sight, as you say, but it can also be called a perfect privation of a good, because it takes away all that good which it is naturally meant to take away—namely, sight. This is not what <term>ophthalmia</term> <note>A general historical term for various inflammatory eye diseases.</note> does, even though it also destroys the good it is naturally meant to take away. However, it cannot be called a privation of that which it is not suited to destroy, whether you call it "partial" or "full." 

<margin>Privation</margin> For <term>privation</term> <note>The absence or lack of a quality that should naturally be present.</note> is considered either <margin>can be</margin> absolutely—that is, as it regards a <term>habit</term> <note>original: "habitum"; in Scholastic philosophy, a *habitus* is a stable quality or state of being, like health or knowledge.</note> in general—or as it is restricted to a certain and <margin>considered in a twofold way.</margin> limited kind of being, such as the health of the whole body, or the eye, or beauty, and other things of that sort. Accepted in the first way, it does not deprive one of any particular "habit," because an all-encompassing privation, as <margin>Dionysius</margin> Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a 5th-6th century Christian philosopher whose works on the names of God were central to Medieval theology.</note> says in his book *On Divine Names*, fails entirely in its powers. 

Taken in the second way, which is called "singular" by Dionysius (distinguishing it from the universal), it deprives the specific "habit" it regards. In this way, this kind of habit—which the privation is naturally suited to hinder—is a "full" privation for that specific thing and not for another; for the whole thing, it is "partial." For who would dare to say that blindness is a "partial" privation of a human, or of any other good that might be in a human? Therefore, an absolute privation regards an absolute "habit," while a proper and particular privation regards a proper and particular "habit," and it does not exceed those limits. 

For this reason, sickness is a full privation, not a partial one, whether you ascribe it to the whole body or to a particular limb. For a fever is the perfect privation of that temperature which it is naturally suited to corrupt. Likewise, ophthalmia, even if it is not a privation of every good in the eye, is nevertheless a perfect and proper privation of *some* good, because it destroys all that good which it is naturally suited to destroy—namely, the perfect health of the eye—even if it does not take away sight, provided that the ophthalmia does nothing else. 

Ugliness, too, is a perfect privation because it takes away all that good which it can take away—namely, the perfect composition of parts which is called beauty—and so you may consider it in other things. We might also say this in abundance: blindness, insofar as it is blindness, is an evil; insofar as it is an evil, it is nothing; insofar as it is nothing, it is not a "partial" privation, because if it were partial, it would leave something positive behind, which evil does not do. 

Furthermore, no privation in itself actually deprives one of *every* good; if that were so, all privations would be "partial" privations. This would be against your own argument, for you contend that some are full and some are partial. This is an excellent and necessary connection, and we prove what we have assumed by this argument: no good could ever be found if a certain total and universal privation were discovered in the nature of things, as we hinted a little earlier from the words of Dionysius. For evil deprives a particular good since evil exists *within* a good; a universal evil would destroy universal good, if such a thing could be found (which is impossible). Thus, you may conclude that privations of their own proper "habits" are always found to be full, not partial.

<margin>Solution to the fourteenth objection.</margin> To the fourteenth objection, which contains several questions, I respond individually: first, that not every evil leaves something of good behind, unless you understand "in some subject" which the evil itself does not regard, or you take that subject whose "habit" is destroyed by the evil itself. Nor should you impose that "habit" which is opposite to it upon him, catching him in a premise he did not assert. For he has abundantly testified that some evil can be found which utterly removes every good naturally intended for it, as seen in the response to the second letter...

<summary>Gianfrancesco Pico argues that evil is a "perfect" (complete) privation of a specific good or state, rather than a "partial" one. Using examples like blindness and fever, he contends that while an evil may not destroy every good in a person, it completely destroys the specific good it is meant to oppose.</summary>
<keywords>privation, habitus, Dionysius the Areopagite, nature of evil, blindness, health, Scholastic philosophy, Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the technical philosophical defense of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola by his nephew, Gianfrancesco. The discussion focuses on the definition of "evil" as a lack of being and whether purely imaginary things (like Chimeras) can be considered "good" or "existing" simply because God has the power to create them.</meta>

-> # **DEFENSE** <-

He was moved concerning this matter, writing in this manner: you certainly ought to have considered that what is granted regarding certain imperfect evils—on account of the mixture of goodness they still retain—must not be transferred to the unmixed and absolute nature of evil itself. <margin>Evil is understood in two ways.</margin> And so that you may perceive the truth more clearly, it will not be a burden to explain the force of this distinction. Evil can be considered in two ways: first, absolutely and under the proper definition of evil, which is to say, insofar as it is nothing; and second, insofar as it is a <term>privation</term> <note>The absence of a quality that should naturally be present, like blindness being the absence of sight.</note> of a certain good—this is "particular evil." Evil accepted in this second way leaves behind some good as its subject; however, that other kind of evil, which is entirely non-being and nothing, does not do this. We call a <term>Chimera</term> <note>A mythological creature used here as a standard philosophical example of something that exists only in the mind and has no reality in the physical world.</note> such an evil, since it does not correspond to any subject or <term>habit</term> <note>In scholastic philosophy, a "habit" (habitus) is a positive quality or state of being, the opposite of a privation.</note>. For this reason, he calls it "entirely evil" from its absolute and unmixed nature. 

<margin>Dionysius</margin> This kind of evil—to use the words of Dionysius in his book *On Divine Names*—is nowhere and is nothing at all, because it lacks a subject. <note>original: "quia subiecto caret nullo modo nusq̄ & nihil existens est." Dionysius the Areopagite was a highly influential Christian theologian and philosopher.</note> Even if a Chimera could be called "potentially good" because of the power to produce it which exists in God, it still cannot be named as either "being" or "good." For if this connection were valid—namely, that "something is potentially good, therefore it is good"—a man of strength could turn that blow back against the author of the idea, leading him to admit that all things which ought to be created by God are created by the force of nature, and even that things which are corrupted both "are something" and "are not something." 

For if, according to him, they both "were" and "were good" by the power of the Creator, then they would also necessarily "be something"; since "something" and "good" are interchangeable and cover the same territory. <note>Scholastic philosophers held that Being and Goodness are "convertible"—whatever exists is good simply by virtue of existing.</note> I shall argue as follows that such a thing could not "be something": nothing can be made from nothing before it is created; a Chimera, according to you, cannot exist unless it is created; therefore it is created from nothing; therefore, before it was created from nothing, it was not "something." Therefore, on account of the power of goodness which is in the Creator, the thing cannot be named "absolutely good." Otherwise—to use the speech of our logicians—one would be committing the <term>fallacy of the qualified to the absolute</term>. <note>original: "fallatia secundum quid ad simpliciter." This is the logical error of arguing that because something is true in a specific, limited sense (it is potentially good), it is true in a general, absolute sense (it is good).</note>

I deliberately set aside those arguments which might be brought against that opinion regarding "eternal quiddities" <note>The essential "what-ness" or nature of a thing.</note> and "objective potentiality," even if your opinion could perhaps be weakened by those very same reasons. For it satisfies our desire if I have proven that a Chimera cannot be called good. <margin>Averroes</margin> Add to this that, following Averroes in this part, we can say that "being in potentiality" is not "being," as he said in the fifteenth division of his commentaries on the fourth book of the *Metaphysics*: that which is not in act is not being. 

Regarding what you add—namely, that a Chimera is "being" because, although the power of producing the Chimera is in God, the power of God and the being of the Chimera are distinct—I respond first that I can deny that God's power and the Chimera to be produced are of different natures. Second, even if I freely granted you that those powers were different, what would your reasoning prove? Since a Chimera can in no way be called "being" on account of the power to produce it being in God, and since that power is absent, neither the Chimera nor anything intrinsic to the Chimera can be proclaimed; they remain infinitely distant. 

You add, furthermore, that if God’s power and our thought were excluded, the Chimera would not be "evil," since evil is a privation that exists in a subject participating in goodness. I would answer this with the same distinction as before: since the Chimera does not correspond to any subject but is absolutely evil, we can pronounce that the notion of the Chimera which we carry in our minds is "something" and thus "good," but the Chimera itself is neither something nor good.

<margin>Solution to the fifteenth objection</margin> Furthermore, you seem to take pleasure in the fact that your argument was not disproved, and that the only response was that "the simple" do not say such things. Likewise, you say that you did not claim Aristotle felt that every being is so either essentially or accidentally, nor did you ascribe anything false to Thomas [Aquinas] because of it. Truly, even if so many things have been said on this matter by the man we are defending <note>Giovanni Pico.</note> that it does not seem necessary for me to speak further...

<summary>Gianfrancesco refutes the idea that non-existent things like Chimeras can be called "good" or "being" just because God has the power to create them. He distinguishes between particular evil (a lack of a specific good in a subject) and absolute evil (total non-existence).</summary>
<keywords>evil, privation, Chimera, potentiality, Dionysius the Areopagite, Averroes, logic, being and goodness, scholastic philosophy</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the technical defense written by Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola on behalf of his uncle, Giovanni Pico. The text focuses on reconciling Aristotelian logic with the theological definition of evil as "nothingness" or "non-being."</meta>

-> # **GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA** <-

And although I have once proposed not to retract those things discussed by him in any way, I say these things out of an abundance of caution for my uncle: namely, that Simplicius <note>A 6th-century commentator on Aristotle often cited in Renaissance debates.</note>, whom you have so often summoned to judgment, has more often borne witness against you, as my uncle noted more than once in his responses. Again, I would like to know whether you have undertaken to defend the view that not every being is either **by accident** <term>per accidens: occurring by chance or as a non-essential property</term> or **through itself** <term>per se: existing by its own nature or essential properties</term> according to the mind of Aristotle.

For he, in the fifth book of *First Philosophy* <note>Aristotle’s *Metaphysics*.</note>, divides "being" into being *per se* and *per accidens*. Then they divide being into **substance** and **accident**, which were contained in the first part of the division, since that which is *per se* is divided into ten categories; one of these is substance and the others are accidents. I would now most gladly be taught by you what kind of being that would be which is neither *per se* nor *per accidens*.

For if you should say that this division into being *per se* and *per accidens* is a classification of "complex being" <term>ens complexum: a being composed of multiple parts or a proposition, rather than a single simple entity</term>, as you put forward in your first objections, I would not hesitate to reply that you truly cannot show this. You cannot support your opinion by any sentiment of Aristotle or by suitable reason, since in that place Aristotle divides being *per se* into ten categories—of which one is substance and nine are accidents—which no one believes to be "complex beings," since they are distinguished from complex ones. 

In that same passage, Averroes <note>The 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were central to University life.</note> says that being *per se* is divided by terms signifying the categories; however, a single term is not a complex being. Also in the sixth book of the *Metaphysics*, the same Averroes says that the first division of being is into *per se* and *per accidens*. But it could not be the "first" division if a division of "complex being" preceded it; nor is it found in Thomas Aquinas <note>The influential 13th-century theologian.</note>, in the fifth book of his commentary on the *Metaphysics*, that complex being is divided as you asserted.

Indeed, it cannot be believed—since being is first partitioned into being *per se* and *per accidens*, and that *per se* being is sub-partitioned into ten categories which we have shown to be simple <note>original: "incomplexa"</note>—that a division of "complex being" is assigned there. This is because it is necessary that what is divided be predicated of the members that divide it. 

These things are said even if they pertain little to the business at hand, since that dogma of yours seems to me at first glance to be consistent neither with the opinions of the Aristotelian interpreters nor with reason. But if you should prove the contrary, it will be most welcome to have learned something from such a weighty philosopher as I truly think you are.

Furthermore, he [my uncle] said that evil is a **privation** <term>privatio: the absence of a quality that should naturally be present, like blindness in an eye</term> insofar as privation was formally a **negation** <term>negatio: a simple "no" or the absence of a thing where it is not required to be</term>. <margin>The tenth [point]</margin> To this you object, saying it is not established that there is one opposition for affirmation and negation and another for privation and **habit** <term>habitus: the presence of a quality or state of being</term>. <margin>Sixth objection</margin> Nor, you say, would it be necessary for "evil" and "non-good" to be interchangeable <note>original: "conuerti" (convertible), a logic term meaning two terms cover exactly the same things.</note> simply because evil was a privation of good. <margin>Solution.</margin>

To these points, I would reply that the opposition of privation is one thing and that of negation is another; nor did he maintain they were the same. But it still follows that if evil is opposed to good as a privation, then "evil" and "non-good" must be interchangeable. For privation—as Albert the Great <note>Albertus Magnus, a 13th-century scientist and philosopher</note> says in the first book of the *Physics*—insofar as it is privation, does not exist of itself or *per se*, because of itself it consists of "non-being." <margin>Albert the Great</margin> 

Nay, it is even asserted by Aristotle in *First Philosophy* that privations belong to the category of non-beings, since privation of itself becomes the other extreme of a contradiction. And therefore, since evil is a privation of good and consequently non-being, insofar as evil is evil, the terms "evil" and "not-good" are interchangeable. For "evil" and "nothing," as has been proven, are the same; "nothing" and "non-being" are the same; "non-being" and "non-good" are the same because "being" and "good" are the same. 

Therefore, my uncle most correctly said that negation is a privation insofar as privation is formally a negation. For even if they differ in this—that one of them, namely contradiction, has no middle ground, as the Philosopher [Aristotle] says in the first book of the *Posterior Analytics*, while the other [privation] might have a middle ground in a certain way since it occurs along with its opposite within the same subject—nonetheless, as far as the present purpose is concerned, they would be the same, since privation of itself is a negation and...

Concerning this naming of God, just as it was held in the book on *Mystical Theology* <note>A foundational 5th-century text by Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite which argues that God is better known through negation (saying what He is not) than affirmation.</note>, he had said in another place that when, through this expression "God," you conceive only that which is signified by the name, this expression does not have the nature of a **predicate** <term>praedicatum: the part of a sentence or clause containing a verb and stating something about the subject</term> but of a **subject** <term>subiectum: the entity about which something is being asserted</term>. For it is that about which one asks what exactly could or should be enunciated concerning it, rather than being that which is enunciated about another. 

Wherefore, this was not unknown to Simonides <note>A reference to the Greek poet Simonides of Ceos, who famously requested more time to answer the Tyrant Hiero's question "What is God?", eventually concluding the subject was beyond human understanding.</note> or to the Tyrant who consulted him. If you conceived nothing, you would not err, because you would be saying nothing. 

If you conceived something, you would say that God is something other than what you conceive, and you would explain the concept through this expression "God," since He would be above everything that could be conceived by us—these were his words. # **OF GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA**

...in whatever way anything is stated about God. However, His nature is not explained by these statements, since it differs from those human concepts by an infinite degree. This was taught quite clearly in the fifth chapter of the book *On Being and the One* <note>original: "de ente & uno"; This is one of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola's most famous works, attempting to reconcile Plato and Aristotle on the nature of existence.</note> by that uncle of mine <note>The author is Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola, the nephew and biographer of the famous Giovanni Pico.</note>. Furthermore, [John] Damascene <note>An 8th-century monk and theologian.</note> writes in the first book of the *Sentences* of his theology <note>The *De Fide Orthodoxa*, often referred to as the "Sentences" in this period.</note> that there are certain things said affirmatively about God which actually have the power of a "super-excellent negation." For example, if we speak of "darkness" in God, we do not understand a lack of light, but rather that He is not light <note>Meaning He is not "light" in the limited, physical, or conceptual way humans understand it.</note>. Truly, we say He is "above light" and is "light" only in the sense that darkness is absent from Him. The most learned and devout Chancellor of Paris <margin>Jean Gerson</margin> <margin>Chancellor of Paris</margin> <note>Jean Gerson (1363–1429), a prominent reformer and mystic at the University of Paris.</note> treated this opinion and said: "Therefore, whatever we say affirmatively about God includes a certain negation." And a little later, for that reason, he says that Dionysius denies that God is **being** <term>ens: a thing that exists; Gerson argues God is "above" the category of existence itself</term> but affirms that He is "above being." 

Giles <margin>Giles</margin> <note>Giles of Rome (Aegidius Romanus), a 13th-century philosopher and student of Thomas Aquinas.</note> says in the first book of his *Sentences* that God is "wise," but not in the way that we understand wisdom. In their manner, the things we understand are indeed in the objects themselves, but not in the same way that we understand them; just as we understand a "line" which exists in physical matter, yet we do not understand it by the same logic of the matter it is in <note>A geometric line is perfect and abstract; a physical line is messy and material. Jesus Christ himself—the power of God, the wisdom of God, and the Truth—as witnessed by the Gospel of John, says: "God is spirit." Dionysius, speaking about God in the book on *Mystical Theology*, says He is ineffable... <note>The text cuts off here at "ieffabil," likely "ineffabilis."</note>

->## **APOLOGY**<-

Again, that letter "a" will hold the position of the subject, not the predicate. If you were to conceive that which is enunciated about Him, you would wander far astray, since God Himself is infinitely greater than everything you can conceive. Even the Platonist Apuleius <note>original: "Platonicus Apuleius"; a 2nd-century philosopher and author, best known for *The Golden Ass*, but also a noted writer on Platonic philosophy.</note>, in his book *On the Doctrines of Plato*, calls Him "unspoken" and "unnamable." The words of Plato himself on this matter were translated into Latin by Apuleius as follows: "To find God is indeed not easy; to understand Him is impossible." <note>This is a famous passage from Plato’s *Timaeus* (28c), which was a cornerstone for "negative theology"—the belief that God is beyond human description.</note>

Therefore, let us say that all affirmations made about God are "improper" <note>In a technical sense, meaning the words do not literally or fully fit the reality of God.</note>, because whatever we might wish not only to say but even to conceive, He exceeds it by an infinity. Furthermore, it is not only while we are held in this earthly prison of ignorance and misery that this is true; even in the very enjoyment of God by which we are perfectly blessed when established in the heavens, the power will be granted to us not to *comprehend* God, but only to *apprehend* Him, to use the words of our theologians. <note>Theologians distinguished between *comprehending* (knowing something fully and totally) and *apprehending* (knowing or perceiving something truly but not exhaustively). Even in Heaven, God remains an infinite mystery to finite minds.</note>

Moreover, you believe these propositions contradict one another: namely, "God is above that which can be conceived" and "nothing can be affirmed about God." You say that if the definition of the name is "above that which can be conceived," then the argument...

<meta>This page continues the defense of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola’s philosophical positions, specifically addressing the relationship between God and created matter, such as gold. ->## **GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA**<-

...flows and proposes an example concerning God among other things.

Lastly, you say you believed your uncle <note>The "uncle" refers to the famous philosopher Giovanni Pico della Mirandola; the author of this defense is his nephew, Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola.</note> thought the power of gold was so great that, whether we willed it or not, it would by necessity draw God along with it, [marginal: Finally] either in reality or in the mind. But I would believe, my Antonio, that he did not think this was the *power* of gold, but rather its *impotence*—[marginal: Objection] or rather, he was made certain—that gold itself could neither exist nor be understood if God were set aside. [marginal: Solution] And although I could refer you to John of Baconthorpe <note>original: "Ioannem de bachone"; a 14th-century English Carmelite theologian known as the "Resolute Doctor," often cited in Scholastic debates.</note> [marginal: John of Baconthorpe] in whose writings we find mention of the dissolution of such a great objection; just as when you, reviewing your uncle’s arguments (by which he had asserted that "God is not" and "gold is" are mutually exclusive), you said you did not wish to reply, lest you seem to be groping in the dark in a matter clearer than light. My plan is to show (even perhaps by your judgment) that it was worthwhile for you to undertake the task of dissolving those arguments if you were able; or if not, at least to lend a hand to the work or frankly admit that his assertions were true.

These are the arguments of my uncle which I shall soon declare: it is impossible for anything to be if "Being itself" <note>original: "ipsum esse"; a technical Scholastic term referring to existence in its purest form, which theologians identified with God.</note> is not; but God is Being itself. Therefore, it is impossible for gold to be if God is not. Furthermore, if God is not, then the universe is "infinite"; if it is infinite, it is nothing. For if it is infinite, it is not "finite" <note>In this context, "finite" means having form, boundaries, and specific existence.</note>; because the infinite destroys itself, just as other things do which contain a contradiction. If "nothing" exists, then gold does not exist. It is impossible for anything to be if Being itself is not; God however, etc.

Since Being itself—which is God (as no one denies)—is that by whose participation all things not only are what they are, but also depend upon Him and are preserved at every moment; this is taught not only by all theologians—most extensively by Thomas [marginal: Thomas / Theologians] <note>Refers to St. Thomas Aquinas, the most influential Scholastic philosopher.</note>—but it was also asserted by Plato in the *Timaeus*. [marginal: Plato] It is impossible for gold to exist, which exists only by the grace of Being itself and by participation in Him. Furthermore, if God is not, then all is infinite; for all beings besides God are finite and contained within certain limits. There is no doubt that they possess and hold this limited nature by the work and grace of God. Wherefore the followers of Plato say that he called God "The Limit" in the *Philebus*, [marginal: Plato] because He limits all things by distributing forms like measures everywhere. But the Book of Wisdom also says [marginal: Book of Wisdom] that all things were constituted by Him in "weight, number, and measure." <note>A famous biblical quote from Wisdom 11:20, used throughout the Middle Ages to explain the mathematical and orderly design of the universe.</note>

If, therefore, God—the cause by which all beings are finite—were not, then nothing would be finite; therefore, all would be infinite. If it is infinite, it is nothing; for if it is infinite, it is not finite, because the infinite destroys itself just as other things which contain a contradiction. Since it has been proved that there is one certain thing from which all things receive their being and their finite existence, if that is removed, nothing remains and nothing is finite. For if something is "infinite," this means it is not terminated or made finite by that First Cause by whose help all things are both ended and bounded.

It follows that the infinite does not exist. Therefore, the infinite destroys itself. For to say that the infinite exists in the way it is accepted here is to say that nothing exists; for if it is neither finite nor God, it is beyond controversy that it is nothing at all. These, Antonio, are the points I have brought forward to defend the opinion of my uncle, which perhaps contains other doctrines as well; for it is not within everyone's reach to attain all that he had conceived. But these words move me to think that other meanings also lay hidden under the "bark" <note>original: "cortice"; a common metaphor for the literal or surface level of a text, beneath which lies the "pith" or spiritual meaning.</note> of his words, with which he concluded his response. Namely: "I believe these things are sufficient for you, a man however talented; but let us pass over the inaccessible things and hold to what we have written while performing the duty of an interpreter." Since these things are satisfactory, they shall also close my response, after first bringing forward certain points that both strengthen my uncle’s opinion and confirm as well as elucidate my own interpretation of his words which I offered before. For when the First is lacking, it is necessary [marginal: Reasons for the proposition] for all those things which proceed from it to perish: as is gathered from Aristotle’s eighth book of *Physics*. [marginal: to be shown] God, however, by the testimony of that same philosopher, is the First Truth from which all [marginal: Aristotle] other truths are; therefore, if God is removed, it is necessary that all truths perish. But if truths tend toward nothingness, then beings likewise are not saved from destruction, since they move within an equal scope. Likewise, if that which communicates both being and life to things is removed, who would not see that those same things would become like mere paintings?

He draws on Aquinas, Plato, and Aristotle to show that God provides the "limit" and "measure" that allows objects to have a finite, recognizable existence.</summary>

<meta>This page begins the famous "Oration on the Dignity of Man" by Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. While the previous page was a letter by his nephew defending the work, this is the actual primary text that sparked such controversy in the late 15th century. It sets out to explain why humanity occupies a unique and glorious place in the universe.</meta>

->ORATION<-
->ORATION OF GIOVANNI PICO OF MIRANDOLA, COUNT OF CONCORDIA<-

<note>The text begins with a large, decorative initial 'L', embellished with intricate floral patterns common in Renaissance printing.</note> I have read, Most Reverend Fathers <note>original: "Patres Colendissimi," referring to the ecclesiastical and academic authorities Pico intended to address in Rome.</note>, in the records of the Arabs, that when Abdala the Saracen <margin>Abdala</margin> <margin>the Saracen</margin> was asked what might be seen as most worthy of wonder on this, so to speak, worldly stage, he replied that nothing is more wonderful to behold than man. Supporting this opinion is that saying of Hermes <margin>Hermes</margin> <note>original: "Mercurius," the Latin name for the Greek god Hermes, here referring to the legendary sage Hermes Trismegistus.</note>: "A great miracle, O Asclepius, is man." When I began to consider the reason for these sayings, I was not entirely satisfied by those many arguments which are put forward by many for the excellence of human nature: that man is the intermediary of creatures, the intimate of the higher beings, the king of the lower ones, [possessing] sharpness of the senses, <margin>The dignity of man</margin> the searching power of reason, the light of intelligence, and the interpreter of nature. He is the interval between stable eternity and flowing time, and (as the Persians <margin>The Persians</margin> say) the bond of the world—nay, its marriage song—and, by the testimony of David <margin>David</margin> <note>A reference to Psalm 8:5.</note>, "made a little lower than the angels." These are great things, indeed, but they are not the principal ones: that is, they do not by right claim for themselves the privilege of the highest admiration. For why should we not admire the angels themselves and the most blessed choirs of heaven more? At last, I seemed to have understood why man is the most fortunate of beings and consequently worthy of all admiration, and what that condition is which he has obtained in the order of the universe—a lot that is enviable not only to the beasts, but even to the stars and to the minds beyond this world. It is a matter beyond belief and wonderful. And why not? For it is for this reason that man is rightly called and esteemed a great miracle and a truly wonderful living being. But what that condition may be, listen, O Fathers, and grant me your attention with kind ears, in accordance with your humanity. 

Already the supreme Father, God the Architect, had built this worldly home which we see—this most august temple of divinity—according to the laws of His secret wisdom. He had adorned the region above the heavens with Intelligences <note>original: "mentibus," referring to the angelic orders.</note>; He had animated the celestial spheres with eternal souls; and He had filled the excrement-filled and dregs-like parts of the lower world with a crowd of living things of every kind. But, when the work was finished, the Craftsman desired that there should be someone who could weigh the logic of such a great work, love its beauty, and admire its vastness. Therefore, when all things were already finished (as Moses <margin>Moses</margin> and Timaeus <margin>Timaeus</margin> <note>Pico cites both the biblical account of creation and Plato’s dialogue, the *Timaeus*, to show the harmony between theology and philosophy.</note> testify), He thought at last of producing man. But there was nothing in His archetypes from which He might mold a new offspring, nor in His treasures what He might grant as an inheritance to a new son, nor in the seats of the whole world where this contemplator of the universe might sit. All things were already full; all had been distributed among the highest, the middle, and the lowest orders. But it was not in the nature of the Father’s power to have failed in this final birth, as if exhausted; it was not in the nature of His wisdom to have wavered in a necessary matter for lack of a plan. It was not in the nature of His beneficial love that he who was to praise the divine generosity in others should be forced to condemn it in himself. 

At last, the best of Craftsmen decreed that he to whom nothing could be given as his own property should share whatever had been private to each individual. Therefore, He took man, a work of indeterminate image, and having placed him in the very center of the world, He addressed him thus: "We have given you, O Adam, no fixed seat, no form of your own, no gift peculiar to you alone, so that whatever seat, whatever form, or whatever gifts you yourself shall desire, these you may have and possess according to your wish and your judgment. The nature of all other beings is defined and restricted within laws prescribed by us. You, constrained by no limits, <margin>Free will in man.</margin> <margin>Will</margin> shall define your nature for yourself according to your own free will, in whose hand I have placed you. I have set you at the center of the world so that from there you may more easily look around at whatever is in the world. We have made you neither celestial nor earthly, neither mortal nor immortal, so that as if you were your own voluntary and honorary sculptor and molder, you may fashion yourself into whatever form you shall prefer. You shall be able to degenerate into the lower things, which are the beasts; you shall be able to be reborn into the higher things, which are divine, according to the judgment of your mind." O the supreme generosity of God the Father, the supreme and wonderful happiness of man! To whom it is given to have that which he chooses, to be that which he wills!

ORATION

[Main Text]
Brute animals, at the very moment they are born, bring with them from their mother’s womb (as Lucilius <margin>Lucilius</margin> says) everything they will ever possess. Supreme spirits <note>referring to angels</note> were, either from the beginning or shortly thereafter, what they are destined to be for all eternity. But at the moment of man's birth, the Father <note>God the Father</note> <margin>Note:</margin> implanted within him seeds of every kind and the germs of every sort of life. Whichever of these a man cultivates, those will grow and bear their fruit in him. If he cultivates vegetative seeds, he will become a plant. If he follows the senses, he will become like a brute beast. If he follows reason, he will turn into a heavenly animal. If he cultivates his intellect, he will be an angel and a son of God. And if, not content with the lot of any creature, he withdraws into the center of his own unity, he becomes one spirit with God, in the solitary darkness <note>original: "caligine," a reference to the mystical "cloud of unknowing" where God dwells beyond human understanding</note> of the Father who is set above all things, and he will surpass all others. Who would not admire this chameleon of ours? <margin>Asclepius of Athens.</margin> Or who could altogether admire anything else more? Not without reason did Asclepius of Athens say that man was symbolized in the mysteries by Proteus <note>A Greek sea-god capable of changing his shape at will.</note>, because of his shifting nature and his power to transform himself. Hence those transformations <note>original: "metamorphoses"</note> celebrated among the Hebrews <margin>Hebrews</margin> and the Pythagoreans <margin>Pythagoreans</margin>. For even the more secret theology of the Hebrews <margin>Empedocles</margin> sometimes transforms the holy Enoch into an angel of divinity (whom they call [blank space] <note>Pico left a space here, likely intended for the Hebrew name 'Metatron'.</note>) and at other times transforms others into different divine beings. The Pythagoreans transform wicked men into brute animals and, if we believe Empedocles, even into plants. Muhammad <margin>Muhammad.</margin> <note>original: "Maumeth"</note> imitated these ideas and frequently had this on his lips: that he who falls away from divine law becomes a brute—and rightly so. For it is not the bark that makes the plant, but its mindless and unfeeling nature; nor is it the hide that makes the beast of burden, but a brute and sensual soul; nor is it the circular body that makes the heavens, but right reason; nor is it the separation from the body, but spiritual intelligence that makes the angel. If you see someone dedicated to his belly, crawling on the ground, <margin>Note</margin> it is a shrub you see, not a man; if you see someone blinded by the vain illusions of fantasy, as if by Calypso’s <note>A nymph in Greek mythology who enchanted Odysseus; here used as a symbol of sensual distraction.</note> spells, and enslaved to his senses, it is a brute you see, not a man. If, however, you see a philosopher discerning all things by right reason, you should revere him; he is a heavenly animal, not a creature of earth. If you see a pure contemplator, unaware of the body and retreated into the secret places of the mind, this is neither an earthly nor a heavenly animal; he is a more majestic divinity clothed in human flesh.

Who would not admire man? He is, not without reason, designated in the sacred writings of Moses <margin>Mosaic and Christian letters.</margin> and the Christians sometimes by the name "all flesh" and sometimes "every creature," because he fashions, fabricates, and transforms himself into the appearance of all flesh and into the character of every creature. Therefore, Evantes the Persian <margin>Evantes the Persian.</margin> writes, where he explains Chaldean theology, that man has no single, native image of his own, but many that are foreign and external; hence that saying of the Chaldeans: <margin>Chaldeans.</margin> [blank space] <note>Pico left space for the Greek or Hebrew phrase meaning "man is a being of varied and multiform nature."</note> which means man is an animal of a varied, multiform, and changing nature. But why do we emphasize this? So that we may understand that since we are born with this condition—that we may be whatever we want to be—we must take the greatest care <margin>Note.</margin> that it not be said of us that, while we were in a position of honor, we did not realize we had become like brutes and senseless beasts of burden. Let us instead remember the saying of Asaph the prophet: <margin>Asaph the prophet</margin> "Ye are gods, and all of you are children of the most High," lest by abusing the most indulgent generosity of the Father—the free choice He gave us—we make that choice harmful instead of a means of salvation. Let a certain sacred ambition invade our souls, so that, not content with mediocrity, we may pant after the highest things and strive with all our might to attain them (since we can, if we will). Let us disdain the things of earth and despise the things of heaven <note>Pico likely means the physical celestial spheres, which are still part of the created universe, rather than the spiritual "Highest Heaven".</note>; and finally, leaving behind everything that belongs to this world, let us fly to the court beyond the world, closest to the most eminent Divinity. There, as the sacred mysteries <margin>Seraphim Cherubim Thrones</margin> hand down, the Seraphim, Cherubim, and Thrones hold the first places. Since we do not know how to yield to them, and are impatient of being second to them, let us emulate their dignity and glory. We shall be in no way inferior to them, if we so will. But by what means, or by doing what? <margin>Seraph Cherub Throne</margin> Let us see what they do and what life they lead. If we live that life (for we can), we shall then have equaled their lot. The Seraph burns with the fire of charity; the Cherub shines with the splendor of intelligence; the Throne stands firm in the steadfastness of judgment. Therefore, if we are dedicated to an active life and undertake the care of lower things with a right assessment...

# GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

...we shall be established with the steady stability of the Thrones. <margin>Throne</margin> If, resting from our actions, we are occupied in the leisure of contemplation—meditating on the Creator in His handiwork and the handiwork in the Creator—we shall flash on every side with Cherubic light. If we burn with love for the Creator alone, we shall be suddenly set ablaze in the likeness of a Seraph by that fire of His which is all-consuming. 

Upon the Throne—that is <note>original: ".i." or "id est," a common Latin abbreviation used to introduce an explanation</note>, the just judge—sits God, the judge of the ages. Over the Cherub—that is, the contemplator—He hovers, and warms him as if by brooding over him. For the Spirit of the Lord moves over the waters: those waters, I say, which are above the heavens, and which in the book of Job <margin>Job</margin> praise the Lord with hymns before the dawn. He who is a Seraph—that is, a lover—is in God and God is in him; indeed, God and he are one.

### GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

...of His saints; <note>original: "sanctoꝝ eius"</note> that death, I say—if it should be called death rather than the fullness of life—the meditation on which the sages called the study of philosophy. <margin>of the saints</margin> Let us also cite Moses <margin>Moses</margin> himself, who was diminished only a little from the fountain-like fullness of the most holy and ineffable intelligence, from which the angels are inebriated with their nectar. We shall hear the venerable judge decreeing laws for us who dwell in the desert solitude of this body: those who are still polluted and in need of moral training <note>original: "morali indigēt"</note> should live with the common people outside the tabernacle under the open sky, like the Thessalian priests <margin>Thessalian priests</margin>, expiating themselves in the meantime. Those who have already composed their character, being received into the sanctuary, should not yet touch the sacred things; but first, as diligent Levites in the service of dialectic <note>The art of logical argument and investigation of truth</note>, let them minister to the sacred rites of philosophy. Then, having been admitted to these rites, let them contemplate in the priesthood of philosophy now the multicolored (that is <note>original: ".i.", abbreviation for "id est"</note>, the starry) courtly ornament of the palace of the God above; now the heavenly candelabrum distinguished by seven lights; now the elements of skins; so that finally, through the merits of theological sublimity, being received into the inner shrine of the temple, they may enjoy the glory of divinity with no veil of images intervening. 

Indeed, Moses both commands these things to us and, in commanding, admonishes, excites, and exhorts us that through philosophy we should prepare a path for ourselves to future celestial glory while we can. But truly, not only the Mosaic or Christian mysteries, but also the theology of the ancients shows us both the benefits and the dignity of these liberal arts about which I have come to debate. For what else is intended by the stages of initiation observed in the secrets of the Greeks <margin>Secrets of the Greeks</margin>? Those who were first purified by what we called the "February" <note>original: "februales," relating to "februare" (to purify), from which the month February takes its name</note> arts—morality and dialectic—attained the undertaking of the mysteries. What else can these mysteries be but the interpretation of a more secret nature through philosophy? Then, finally, for those so prepared, that "epopteia" <note>original: "ἐποπτεία," the highest stage of initiation in the Eleusinian mysteries, meaning "direct vision" or "inspection"</note> arrived—that is, the inspection of divine things through the light of theology. 

Who would not long to be initiated into such sacred rites? Who would not desire, setting aside all human things, despising the goods of fortune, and neglecting the body, to become a guest of the gods while still dwelling on earth, and, drenched in the nectar of eternity, to be gifted with the prize of immortality as a mortal creature? Who would not wish to be so inspired by those Socratic frenzies <margin>Socratic frenzies</margin> <note>original: "furoribus," referring to the divine madness or poetic inspiration described by Plato</note> celebrated by Plato in the *Phaedrus*, so that, by the rowing of wings and feet, fleeing from here—that is, from the world which is set in wickedness—he might be carried in a swift course to the celestial Jerusalem? 

We shall be driven, fathers, we shall be driven by Socratic frenzies, which place us outside our mind in such a way that they place our mind and ourselves in God. We shall be driven by them indeed, if we ourselves have first done what is within us. For if, through moral strength, the powers of the affections are so tuned to the proper measures through due proportions that they sound together in an unshakable harmony; and if, through dialectic, reason has moved itself forward according to number, then, struck by the frenzy of the Muses, we shall drink in the celestial harmony with our innermost ears. 

Then Bacchus <margin>Bacchus</margin>, leader of the Muses, showing to us who philosophize the invisible things of God in his mysteries—that is, in the visible signs of nature—will inebriate us with the abundance of the house of God; in which, if like Moses <margin>Moses</margin> we are entirely faithful, the most sacred Theology, approaching, will animate us with a double frenzy. For raised to her most eminent watchtower, measuring from there that which is, which will be, and which has been in an unchanging eternity, and looking up at the primeval beauty, we shall be the winged lovers of those things, like Phoebian seers <margin>Phoebian seers</margin> <note>original: "Phœbei uates," referring to the prophetic followers of Apollo</note>; and finally, struck as if by a gadfly <note>original: "æstro," a Greek-derived word for a stinging fly or a goad, used to describe divine inspiration or passion</note> with ineffable charity, like burning Seraphim, placed outside ourselves and full of the divine power, we shall no longer be ourselves, but He Himself who made us. 

The sacred names of Apollo, if one scrutinizes their meanings and the hidden mysteries, show clearly enough that this god is no less a philosopher than a seer. Since Ammonius <margin>Ammonius</margin> <note>Ammonius Hermiae, a Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on the names of Apollo</note> has sufficiently pursued this point, there is no reason for me to treat it differently now. But let the three Delphic precepts <margin>Three Delphic precepts</margin> come to mind, fathers, which are exceedingly necessary for those who are about to enter the most holy and august temple of the true Apollo (not the fictional one), who illuminates every soul coming into this world. You will see that they admonish us of nothing else than that we [should strive for the three-fold...]

# ORATION

Having divided this philosophy about which the present discussion is held, let us embrace it with all our strength. For that saying, "nothing in excess" <note>original Greek: "μηδεν αγαν"; Latin: "neque quid nimis"</note> correctly prescribes the norm and rule for all virtues through the principle of moderation, which moral philosophy treats. Then that saying, "know thyself" <note>original Greek: "γνωθι σεαυτον"; Latin: "cognosce te ipsum"</note> excites and exhorts us to the knowledge of all nature, of which the nature of man is, as it were, the link <note>original: "Cynnus," referring to a mixture or marriage-bond</note> and the meeting point. <margin>Zoroaster, Plato</margin> For he who knows himself, knows all things in himself, as Zoroaster first, and then Plato in the *Alcibiades*, wrote. Finally, illuminated by this knowledge through natural philosophy, being now very close to God, and saying to Him with a theological salutation "You are" <note>original: "es," referring to the divine presence</note>, we shall call upon the true Apollo familiarly and thus happily. Let us also consult the most wise Pythagoras, <margin>Pythagoras the wise</margin> who was wise especially because he never thought himself worthy of the name of "wise" <note>Pythagoras famously coined the term "philosopher" (lover of wisdom) because he believed only God is truly wise</note>. He will first command that we do not sit upon a bushel-measure <note>original: "per modium," a Pythagorean symbolic precept</note>, <margin>Explanation of Pythagoras's precepts</margin> that is, that we do not lose the rational part by which the soul measures, judges, and examines all things, by letting it relax in idle sloth. But let us continually direct and excite it with the exercise and rule of dialectic <note>The art of logical investigation</note>. Then he will signal two things for us to avoid: either to urinate against the sun, or to trim our nails while sacrificing. But after we have, through moral philosophy, passed off the flowing appetites of overflowing pleasures, and have trimmed away the nail-clippings—the sharp prominences of anger and the stings of the soul, as it were—then at last we may take part in the sacred rites, that is, the mysteries of Bacchus of which we made mention; and we shall begin to devote ourselves to the contemplation of Him who is rightly called the father and leader of our sun. Finally, he will advise us to feed the cock <note>original: "gallum"</note>, that is, that we may feed the divine part of our soul with the knowledge of divine things, as with solid food and heavenly ambrosia. This is the cock at whose sight the lion—that is, every earthly power—is terrified and shows reverence; this is that cock <margin>The cock of Job and Socrates</margin> to whom we read in the book of Job that understanding was given. When this cock crows, the wandering man comes to his senses; this cock, in the morning twilight, daily sings along with the morning stars as they praise God. Socrates, when dying—when he hoped to join the divinity of his soul to the divinity of the greater world—being now placed beyond all danger of disease, said he owed this cock to Aesculapius <note>The god of medicine</note>, the physician of souls. <margin>Chaldeans</margin> Let us also review the records of the Chaldeans, and we shall see (if they are to be believed) that the way to happiness lies open to mortals through these same arts. <margin>Chaldean interpreters, Zoroaster</margin> The Chaldean interpreters write that it was a saying of Zoroaster that the soul is winged, and when the wings fall off, it is carried headlong into the body; then, when they grow back, it flies back to the realms above. When his disciples asked him how they might obtain feathered wings for their souls, he said: "water the wings with the waters of life." Again, when they asked where they might seek these waters, he answered them thus by a parable (which was the man's custom): the paradise of God is washed and watered by four rivers. Draw the healing waters for yourselves from there. The name of the one from the north is *Pishon* <note>original: "pi"</note>, which denotes the Right; the one from the west is *Gihon* <note>original: "gi"</note>, which signifies Expiation; the one from the east is *Tigris* <note>original: "ti"</note>, which sounds as Light; and the one from the south is *Euphrates* <note>original: "eu"</note>, which we can interpret as Piety. Pay attention and diligently consider, fathers, what these dogmas of Zoroaster mean: surely nothing else than that we should wash away the filth of our eyes by moral science, as if by northern winter waves; and by dialectic, as if by a northern rule <note>original: "amussi," a mason's tool for straightness</note>, let us align their vision toward the Right. Then, in natural contemplation, let us grow accustomed to enduring the still-weak light of truth, like the cradle of the rising sun; so that finally, through theological piety and the most sacred worship of God, like heavenly eagles, we may bravely bear the most radiant beam of the midday sun. <margin>David, Augustine, the Ancient, Abraham, Cabalists, Moors</margin> These are perhaps those morning, midday, and evening knowledges first sung of by David and more widely explained by Augustine. This is that midday light which inflames the Seraphim to the limit and likewise illuminates the Cherubim. This is that region toward which the ancient father Abraham was always traveling; this is that place where the dogmas of both the Cabalists and the Moors have taught that there is no place for unclean spirits. And if it is lawful to bring forth anything of the more secret mysteries in public, even under a riddle:

# GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

After the sudden fall of our humanity from heaven <note>original: "causus nři hoĩs," referring to the Fall of Man</note> condemned our heads to dizziness, and—according to Jeremiah— <margin>Jeremiah</margin> death entered through the windows, affecting our hearts and vitals, let us call upon Raphael, <margin>Raphael</margin> the celestial physician. May he free us through moral philosophy and dialectic <note>The art of logical argument and investigation of truth</note> as if using healthy medicines. Then, once we are restored to good health, the "strength of God," Gabriel, <margin>Gabriel</margin> will inhabit us. He shall lead us through the miracles of nature, showing us everywhere the power and presence of God. Finally, he will hand us over to the high priest Michael, <margin>Michael</margin> who will mark those who have completed their service in philosophy <note>original: "phiæ emeritos," referring to veterans who have finished their military service</note> with the priesthood of Theology, as if with a crown of precious stones.

These are the reasons, most venerable fathers, which have not only encouraged but compelled me to the study of philosophy. I certainly would not have spoken of these things if I were not responding to those who are accustomed to condemn the study of philosophy, especially in princes or in those who live in average circumstances. For now (such is the unhappiness of our age), this whole pursuit of philosophy is held in contempt and insult rather than in honor and glory. This deadly and monstrous persuasion has so invaded the minds of almost everyone: that one should philosophize either not at all or only a little. It is as if having the causes of things, the ways of nature, the reason of the universe, the counsels of God, and the mysteries of heaven and earth thoroughly explored before our eyes and hands were worth absolutely nothing, unless one could hunt for some favor or acquire profit for oneself.

Indeed, it has come to the point where—alas! <note>original: "prohdolor"</note>—none are considered wise unless they make the study of wisdom a mercenary thing. One sees the chaste Pallas <note>The goddess Athena, representing Wisdom</note>, dwelling among men by the gift of the gods, being cast out, exploded, and hissed away. She has no one to love or favor her, unless she herself, like a prostitute, taking a small fee for her prostituted virginity, brings back ill-gotten money into her lover's chest. All of this I say, not without the highest grief and indignation, not against the princes but against the "philosophers" of this time, who both believe and preach that one should not philosophize because no wages or rewards are established for philosophers—as if they do not show by this very name <note>The word "philosopher" means "lover of wisdom," implying love for the subject itself, not for profit</note> that they are not truly philosophers. <margin>Note</margin> Since their whole life is focused on gain or ambition, they do not embrace the knowledge of truth for its own sake. <margin>Note</margin>

I will grant this to myself, and I shall not blush to praise myself in this regard: I have never philosophized for any other reason than to philosophize. I have neither hoped for nor sought any other reward or fruit from my studies and my late-night labors than the cultivation of my mind and the knowledge of the truth I have always so greatly desired. I have always been so eager and loving of this truth that, leaving aside all care for private and public affairs, I have given myself entirely to the leisure of contemplation. From this, no detractions of the envious, no curses of the enemies of wisdom, have been able to deter me before now, nor will they be able to in the future. Philosophy itself has taught me to depend on my own conscience rather than on external judgments, <margin>What philosophy itself taught him</margin> and to always think not so much of how to avoid a bad reputation, but rather how to avoid saying or doing anything bad myself.

Indeed, most venerable fathers, I was not unaware that this very disputation of mine—which I wished to honor with your most majestic presence and which would be pleasing and delightful to all of you who favor the fine arts—would be heavy and troublesome to many others. I know there is no lack of those who have condemned my undertaking before now, and who condemn it at present on many counts. <margin>Note</margin> For it is customary for those things done well and toward virtue to have no fewer (if I may not say "more") barkers <note>original: "oblatratores," meaning critics who bark like dogs</note> than those things done unjustly and wrongly toward vice.

There are some who do not approve of this whole kind of disputation and this practice of publicly debating literature, asserting it is for the display of talent and the showing off of learning rather than for acquiring erudition. <margin>The age of the author</margin> There are those who do not disapprove of this kind of exercise, but do not approve of it in my case: because at this age—being only twenty-four years old—I have dared to propose a disputation on the sublime mysteries of Christian theology, on the highest points of philosophy, and on unknown disciplines, in a most celebrated city, in a most ample gathering of very learned men, and in the Apostolic senate <note>The Roman Curia or the Pope's court</note>. Others, granting me the right to dispute, do not grant...

# GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

There are those who complain about my plan to debate nine hundred questions, <note>Pico is referring to his "900 Theses," a massive collection of philosophical and theological propositions he intended to defend in public in 1847.</note> slandering the effort as being more for the sake of vanity and ambition than a task suited to my abilities. I would have immediately surrendered to their objections if the philosophy I profess <margin>Plato</margin> had taught me to do so. Even now, with her guidance, I would not offer a defense if I believed that the discussion we are holding was intended for quarreling or bickering. Therefore, let all desire for disparagement and provocation vanish from our minds, along with that envy which Plato writes is always absent from the divine choir. <note>original: "a divino sēp abesse choro," a reference to Plato's *Phaedrus* (247a), suggesting that true scholars should be free from jealousy.</note> Instead, let us examine in a friendly spirit whether I ought to conduct a debate at all, and whether I should do so on such a vast number of questions.

First, regarding those who speak ill of this custom of public debate, I will not say much. If this practice is to be judged a fault, <note>original: "culpa si culpa cēseť"</note> it is a fault I share not only with all of you, most excellent teachers—who have frequently performed this duty with the highest praise and glory—but also with Plato, Aristotle, and the most respected philosophers of every age. To these men...

<meta>This page continues Pico's defense of his upcoming public debate. Having established that public disputation is a noble tradition, he now addresses the specific criticism regarding the sheer number of topics (900 theses) he intends to cover, arguing that a true philosopher must study every school of thought rather than being "sworn to the words" of a single master.</meta>

->ORATION<-

For a man to have failed will be worthy of forgiveness rather than accusation. Indeed, as the poet says, if strength fails, audacity will certainly be a credit in great matters, and to have willed it is enough. <note>original: "audacia certe laus erit in magnis & uoluiffe fat est," a reference to Propertius, *Elegies* II.10.6.</note> If in our age many, imitating Gorgias of Leontini, <margin>Gorgias of Leontini</margin> have been accustomed to propose—not without praise—a debate not only on nine hundred questions, but on all questions regarding all the arts, why should I not be allowed, even without fault, to dispute on many, but certainly fixed and determined, topics?

But they say this is superfluous and ambitious. I contend, however, that this was done by me not only in a way that is not superfluous, but is even necessary. If they themselves would consider the reason for philosophizing with me, they would be forced to admit this, even against their will. Those who have devoted themselves to certain "families" <note>The term "families" refers to specific schools of philosophical thought.</note> of philosophers—namely to Thomas <margin>Thomas</margin> or Scotus, <margin>John Scotus</margin> who are now most popular—can, in the discussion of even a few questions, put their learning to the test. But I have so instructed myself that, sworn to the words of no single master, I have poured myself through all the masters of philosophy, examined every page, and recognized all schools. Therefore, since I had to speak about all of them, I did so lest I should seem bound to a single private dogma while neglecting the rest. Even if only a few points were proposed about each school, it was impossible that there would not be a great many when all were asserted together.

Let no one condemn me for being carried as a guest wherever the storm takes me. <note>original: "me quocūq̃ ferat tempeftas deferar hofpes," an adaptation of Horace, *Epistles* 1.1.15.</note> This was observed by all the ancients: that in rolling through every kind of writing, <margin>Observation of the ancients</margin> they would pass over no commentaries they could read. This was especially true of Aristotle, <margin>Aristotle</margin> who for that reason was called by Plato "the reader" <margin>Plato</margin> <note>original: "αναγνώστης" (anagnōstēs). Plato supposedly gave Aristotle this nickname because of his voracious appetite for books.</note>. And indeed, it is the mark of a narrow mind to have confined oneself within a single Portico or Academy. <note>Refers to the Stoa (Stoicism) or the Platonic Academy; Pico argues against intellectual tribalism.</note> Nor can one choose from among them all, since every single family has something distinctive that it does not share with the others.

To begin with our own thinkers, to whom philosophy has most recently arrived: in John Scotus <margin>John Scotus</margin> <note>John Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), a major Scholastic theologian.</note> there is something vigorous and analytical. In Thomas <margin>Thomas</margin> <note>Thomas Aquinas (1225–1274).</note>, something solid and consistent. In Egidius <margin>Egidius</margin> <note>Giles of Rome (c. 1243–1316), a student of Aquinas.</note>, something polished and exact. In Francis <margin>Francis</margin> <note>Francis of Mayrone (c. 1280–1328), a follower of Scotus.</note>, something sharp and acute. In Albert <margin>Albert</margin> <note>Albert the Great (c. 1200–1280).</note>, something ancient, vast, and grand. In Henry <margin>Henry</margin> <note>Henry of Ghent (c. 1217–1293).</note>, as it has always seemed to me, something sublime and venerable.

Among the Arabs: in Averroes <margin>Averroes</margin> there is something firm and unshakable. In Avempace <margin>Avempace</margin> and Alfarabi <margin>Alfarabi</margin>, something weighty and meditative. In Avicenna <margin>Avicenna</margin>, something divine and Platonic.

Among the Greeks, philosophy is, in general, especially bright and pure. In Simplicius <margin>Simplicius</margin>, it is rich and copious. In Themistius <margin>Themistius</margin>, elegant and concise. In Alexander <margin>Alexander</margin>, consistent and learned. In Theophrastus, seriously elaborated. In Ammonius, clear and graceful.

And if you turn to the Platonists—to review a few: In Porphyry, you will be delighted by the abundance of things and his diverse religion. In Iamblichus, you will venerate a more secret philosophy and the mysteries of the barbarians. In Plotinus...

<meta>This page continues Pico’s defense of his 900 theses. ...private doctrine, but having devoted myself to all schools of thought, I had to bring forward many different topics so that the variety of the various sects and the multitude of their doctrines would not be hidden. Nor was I content to have merely added to those common points—which are handled by everyone—many things concerning the ancient theology of Hermes Trismegistus, many concerning the dogmas of the Chaldeans and of Pythagoras, and many concerning the secret mysteries of the Hebrews. I have also brought forward several points in which I have shown that the opinions of Averroës and Avicenna <margin>Averroës & Avicenna</margin> <note>Averroës (Ibn Rushd) and Avicenna (Ibn Sina) were the two most influential Islamic philosophers in the medieval West; Pico famously attempted to "reconcile" their often conflicting interpretations of Aristotle.</note>, which are thought by many to be discordant, are in fact reconciled.

Moreover, I have proposed many things in natural and divine matters <note>original: "naturalibus & divinis rebus"</note> which, as far as I know—and may the word be free from ill-will— <note>original: "quod sciam (verbo absit invidia)"; Pico is using a traditional rhetorical formula to avoid the appearance of arrogance while claiming originality.</note> no one has ever proposed before for public discussion. For it is the mark of a narrow mind, as Seneca says <margin>Seneca</margin>, to be kept confined within a single porch. <note>original: "ut ait Seneca." Pico refers to the *Stoa* or "porch" where the Stoics taught, using it as a metaphor for being trapped in a single philosophical school.</note> Indeed, I have not been satisfied to have learned only from the Greeks or the Latins, but I have reached for the most hidden secrets of the East.

In these [theses], I have also presented several things (as some boast) <note>original: "ut iactant quidam"</note> that pertain to the highest levels of contemplation. For it is <note>original: "est," abbreviated as "ē" in the transcription.</note> through this wide-ranging study that the truth, which has been scattered among many nations, can finally be gathered back into a single body of wisdom.

<summary>Pico explains that he has not limited himself to one philosophical "family" but has synthesized views from Islamic, Hebrew, and ancient Greek sources. He argues that true philosophy requires exploring "natural and divine matters" beyond the traditional curriculum.</summary>

...one should be kept confined within a single porch. <note>Closing the note from the previous page: Pico refers to the *Stoa* or "porch" where the Stoics taught, using it as a metaphor for being trapped in a single philosophical school.</note>

And it was not enough for me, beyond the common schools of thought, to have added much regarding the Ancient Theology of the Egyptians <note>original: "Prisca Aegyptiorum theologia." This refers to the "Ancient Theology," a Renaissance belief that a single, true theology exists which threads through all religions and was given by God to man in antiquity.</note>, the dogmas of the Chaldeans, and the secret mysteries of the Hebrews, unless I also proposed many things discovered and thought out by myself regarding philosophical matters. 

And so that those who see them might appreciate not only the number, but also the novelty and variety of my propositions, I have proposed points concerning the harmony between Plato and Aristotle <margin>Plato & Aristotle</margin> <note>original: "de concordia Platonis et Aristotelis." The attempt to reconcile these two giants of Greek thought—who were often seen as opposites—was a hallmark of Pico's "syncretism," or the blending of different beliefs.</note>, which many previously believed in, but no one has sufficiently proven.

I have then proposed seventy-two new physical and metaphysical <term>Metaphysical</term> <note>Relating to the branch of philosophy that deals with the first principles of things, including abstract concepts such as being, knowing, substance, and cause.</note> propositions, entirely new. If anyone masters these, they will be able (unless I am mistaken) <note>original: "ni fallor." Pico uses this modest phrasing even while making an extremely bold claim about the power of his system.</note> to resolve any proposed question concerning natural or divine matters by a far different and much more certain path than the one taught in the common schools <margin>The Schools</margin> <note>The "schools" refer to the Scholastic universities of the time, which Pico often criticized for being too rigid or focused on logic-chopping rather than universal truth.</note>.

Nor should anyone wonder, Fathers <note>Pico is addressing the "Fathers" (the gathered clergy and scholars at Rome) who were meant to judge his public debate.</note>, that I—at such a young age, at which it has been permitted to few to even read the works of others—wish to bring forth a new philosophy <margin>A New Philosophy</margin>. 

Furthermore, I have proposed a new way of philosophizing through numbers, and I have brought back into the light the ancient and secret mysteries of the Hebrew Kabbalah <margin>The Kabbalah</margin> <note>The Kabbalah is a body of Jewish mystical and esoteric teachings. Pico was a pioneer in "Christian Kabbalah," believing these Jewish secrets could provide "proof" for the divinity of Christ.</note>, which I was the first among Latins <note>original: "primus ego ex Latinis." Pico claims to be the first Western/Latin scholar to bring these specific Hebrew traditions into the academic sphere of the Church.</note> to study.

<summary>Pico explains that his 900 theses are not just a collection of old ideas, but include his own "new philosophy" and a synthesis of Plato, Aristotle, and the Jewish Kabbalah. He claims his method offers a more certain path to truth than the traditional university education of his day.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's defense of his 900 theses. Having established his right to study diverse traditions, he is now defining "Natural Magic"—the legitimate, scientific, and spiritual exploration of nature—distinguishing it from "Goetic Magic" (dark or demonic magic).</meta>

->ORATION<-

This [natural magic], having more deeply scrutinized the consensus of the universe—which the Greeks more meaningfully call **sympathy** <note>original: "$\sigma\acute{\upsilon}\mu\pi\alpha\theta\epsilon\iota\alpha\nu$" (*sympatheian*). In Renaissance thought, this refers to the "universal sympathy" or the hidden, organic connections that tie all parts of the cosmos together.</note>—and having gained a clear perception of the mutual knowledge of natures, applies to each thing its own inherent attractions. These attractions, which the magi call **charms** <note>original: "$\iota\upsilon\gamma\gamma\epsilon\sigma$" (*iynges*). In Neoplatonic and Chaldean traditions, these were "wheels" or spiritual "links" that bind the material world to the divine.</note>, allow the magus to bring into the public eye the miracles lying hidden in the recesses of the world, in the lap of nature, and in the storehouses and secrets of God, as if magic itself were the craftsperson.

And just as the farmer marries elms to vines, so the magus marries earth to heaven—that is, he marries the lower things to the gifts and virtues of the higher. Consequently, while the former [goetic magic] appears as monstrous and harmful, this latter [natural magic] appears divine and salutary. This is especially true because the former, by enslaving man to the enemies of God, calls him away from God; whereas natural magic excites that admiration for the works of God which is most certainly followed by a ready charity, faith, and hope. <margin>Note</margin> <note>original: "Nota." This marginal note likely served as a reminder to a student or reader that this section contains a vital defense of Pico’s orthodoxy.</note> For neither toward religion nor toward the worship of God...

<summary>Pico defines Natural Magic as a legitimate science that uncovers the hidden "sympathies" of the universe to connect the earthly realm with the celestial, contrasting it with forbidden demonic magic.</summary>
