### GIOVANNI PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

...it was revealed, it was called **Kabbalah** <note>original: "Cabala." From the Hebrew word *Qabbalah*, meaning "reception" or "tradition." Pico is explaining that this wisdom was received through oral transmission rather than writing.</note>, which among the Hebrews is the same as "reception" among us. It is called "Kabbalah" because that doctrine was not received through written records, but through a regular succession of revelations from one person to another, as if by a right of inheritance. However, after the Hebrews were restored from the Babylonian captivity by Cyrus, and the temple was rebuilt under Zerubbabel, they turned their minds to the restoration of the Law. Ezra, then the head of the Church <note>Pico uses "ecclesiae" (church) to refer to the religious leadership of Israel, framing the Jewish past in Christian terms.</note>, after correcting the book of Moses, clearly recognized that because of the exiles, slaughters, flights, and the captivity of the Israelite people, the custom established by the ancestors of passing down the doctrine by hand could not be preserved. He saw that the secrets of the heavenly doctrine granted to them by God would perish, for their memory could not long endure without the intervention of commentaries. 

He therefore decreed that the wise men then remaining should be called together, and each should bring into the open what he remembered by heart concerning the mysteries of the Law. Notaries were employed to record these into seventy volumes (for there were approximately that many wise men in the **Sanhedrin** <note>original: "ſinedrio." The Sanhedrin was the supreme judicial and religious council of ancient Israel.</note>). Regarding this matter, do not merely take my word for it; listen to Ezra himself speaking: "After forty days had passed, the Most High spoke, saying: 'Make public the first things you have written, that the worthy and unworthy alike may read them; but you shall preserve the newest seventy books, so that you may hand them over to the wise among your people. For in these is the vein of understanding, the fountain of wisdom, and the river of knowledge.' And so I did." <note>Pico is quoting from the apocryphal book of 2 Esdras (or 4 Ezra) 14:44-47. In the Renaissance, this was often cited as proof that the Kabbalah was a divine secret tradition.</note> These are the words of Ezra, word for word. 

These are the books of the science of Kabbalah. In these books, Ezra rightly proclaimed with a clear voice that there is a **vein of understanding**—that is, an ineffable theology of the supersubstantial deity; a **fountain of wisdom**—that is, a precise metaphysics concerning intelligible and angelic forms; and a **river of knowledge**—that is, a most firm philosophy concerning natural things. 

<margin>Sixtus</margin> These books Pope **Sixtus IV** <note>original: "Syxtus quartus." Pope from 1471–1484. He was a patron of the arts and sciences and showed interest in Hebrew studies.</note>, who most recently preceded this **Innocent VIII** <margin>fourth</margin> under whom we happily live, took the greatest care and zeal to ensure they were <margin>Inno. VIII</margin> committed to Latin letters for the public benefit of our faith. Already, when he died, three of them had reached the Latins. These books are cherished among the Hebrews today with such great religious awe that no one is permitted to touch them unless they are forty years old. 

When I had purchased these books for myself at no small expense, and had read them through with the highest diligence and untiring labor, I saw in them (God is my witness) a religion that was not so much Mosaic as it was Christian. There I found the mystery of the Trinity; there, the incarnation of the Word; there, the divinity of the Messiah; there, I read about original sin, its expiation through Christ, the heavenly Jerusalem, the fall of the demons, the orders of the angels, purgatory, and the punishments of hell. I read the same things there that we read every day in Paul and Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian mystic highly regarded by Pico.</note>, in Jerome and Augustine. 

Truly, in those parts which look toward philosophy, you may clearly hear **Pythagoras** and **Plato**, <margin>Augustine</margin> whose decrees are so allied to the Christian faith that our Augustine gives immense thanks to God that the books of the Platonists came into his hands. In short, there is almost no point of controversy between us and the Hebrews about which they cannot be so refuted and convinced out of the books of the Kabbalists that not even a corner remains in which they might hide themselves. 

<margin>Antonius</margin> Of this matter, I have a most weighty witness, **Antonius Chronicus** <note>A learned contemporary and friend of Pico.</note>, <margin>Chronicus</margin> a most erudite man, who with his own ears heard—when I was with him at a banquet—the Hebrew **Dactylus** <margin>Dactylus</margin> <note>Likely refers to a specific Jewish scholar or convert known to Pico's circle.</note>, <margin>Hebrew</margin> a man skilled in this science, descend "with hands and feet" <note>An idiom meaning to agree completely or wholeheartedly.</note> into the Christian opinion concerning the Trinity. 

<margin>Zoroaster</margin> But to return to the headings of my disputation that must be reviewed: I have also brought forth my own opinion regarding the interpretation of the poems of **Orpheus** and **Zoroaster**. <margin>Orpheus</margin> Orpheus is read among the Greeks almost in his entirety; Zoroaster is read among them in a mutilated form, but is read more completely among the Chaldeans. Both are believed to be the leaders and authors of ancient wisdom. For, to say nothing of Zoroaster, of whom frequent mention is made among the Platonists—always with the highest veneration—**Iamblichus** the Chalcidian <margin>Iamblichus</margin> writes that Pythagoras held **Orphic theology** <margin>Chalcidian</margin> as a model <margin>Pythagoras</margin> according to which he shaped and formed his own philosophy. Indeed, they say that the sayings of Pythagoras are called "sacred" for this reason alone: because they flowed from the teachings of Orpheus.

<summary>Pico discusses the origins of the Kabbalah as a secret oral tradition preserved by Ezra and argues that its study reveals the core mysteries of Christianity. He also introduces Orpheus and Zoroaster as foundational figures of "ancient wisdom" that influenced Pythagoras and Plato.</summary>

->ORATION<-

From there <note>original: "Inde." Pico is referring back to the "Kabbalah" and the secret traditions of the Jews mentioned on the previous page.</note> the secret doctrine concerning numbers and whatever Greek philosophy held as great and sublime flowed as if from a primary source. But (as was the ancient custom of theologians) Orpheus so disguised the mysteries of his teachings in the wrappers of myths and a poetic veil that if someone were to read his hymns, they would believe nothing lay beneath them except the most trifling fables and nonsense. I wanted to say this so that it might be known what labor and difficulty I faced: to dig out the hidden meanings of secret philosophy from the tangled thickets of riddles and the hiding places of myths—especially since, in a matter so grave, so hidden, and so unexplored, I had no help from the work and diligence of other interpreters. 

And yet, my "dogs" <note>original: "canes mei." Pico uses this biting metaphor to refer to his critics who "bark" at his work.</note> have barked that I have accumulated certain tiny and trivial things merely for the sake of showing off a large number of propositions. As if these were not questions that are highly ambiguous and controversial, in which the principal academies <note>Pico refers to the various schools of philosophy, such as the Platonists and Aristotelians.</note> clash; as if I have not brought many things—even to those very people who carp at me and believe themselves the princes of philosophers—that are entirely unknown and untried. Indeed, I am so far from that fault of padding the numbers that I have taken care to condense the discussion into as few chapters as possible. If I had wished (as others are accustomed) to divide the work into its individual members and tear it apart, it would certainly have grown into an innumerable count. 

To say nothing of the rest, who does not know that one single doctrine from my nine hundred <note>Pico's famous "900 Theses" which he intended to defend in public debate in Rome.</note>—namely, the one concerning the reconciliation of the philosophy of Plato and Aristotle—could have been drawn out by me into six hundred chapters (if not more) without any suspicion of forced numbering? I could have done this by enumerating one by one all the points in which others think they disagree, but where I believe they agree. But certainly (I shall say this, though it is neither modest nor according to my nature), I will say it because my envious critics force me to speak. These detractors have forced me to want to prove in this encounter of mine not so much that I know many things, but that I know things which many people do not know. 

To the end that this may now become openly clear to you in fact, most worshipful fathers, and so that my speech may no longer delay your desire, most excellent doctors—whom I behold with great pleasure prepared and girded, awaiting the battle—may it be happy and auspicious. As if the trumpet were sounding the call to battle <note>original: "citante classico." A military metaphor for the start of the academic disputation.</note>, let us now join hands in combat.

END of the Oration of Giovanni Mirandola.

<note>A large decorative initial letter I, or "J," is adorned with floral motifs and vine-like patterns, marking the start of a new section.</note>

**Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Giovanni Francesco, his nephew from his brother. Greetings <note>original: "S." for *Salutem*, a standard Latin epistolary greeting.</note> in Him who is true salvation.** 

As you depart from me, my son, you should not wonder—nor should you grieve or be terrified—that many opportunities for evil have immediately presented themselves to disturb you and oppose your resolve to live well. How much more of a miracle would it be if the way to heaven lay open to you alone among mortals without sweat! As if the deceitful world and the evil demon had now for the first time ceased to exist, or as if you were not still in the flesh, which lusts against the spirit <note>A reference to Galatians 5:17.</note>. Unless we look out for our salvation with vigilant foresight, the flesh, seductive as she is, deforms us with her Circean cups <note>original: "circeis... poculis." In Greek mythology, the sorceress Circe used a magic potion to turn men into beasts; Pico uses this to represent how sensory pleasures strip humans of their dignity.</note>—drunk as we are—into the monstrous shapes of brutes. 

But as James the Apostle writes <margin>James</margin>, you should also rejoice. "Rejoice, brothers, when you fall into various temptations" <note>A quote from James 1:2.</note>. And not without cause: for what hope of glory is there if there is no hope of victory? Or what place can there be for victory where there is no battle? He is called to the crown who is called to the battle—and especially to that battle in which no one can be conquered against his will. Nor do we need other strengths to conquer than the will to conquer itself. <margin>The great happiness of the Christian.</margin> Great is the happiness of the Christian, since victory is placed in his own judgment, and the rewards to come will be greater than any desire or expectation of the victor. Tell me, I ask you, my dearest son: is there anything in this life among those things for which the lust of earthly minds is driven, for the sake of obtaining which many labors must not first be undergone, and many unworthy and miserable things endured? The merchant thinks he has done well for himself if, after ten years of sailing...

# LETTERS

...after a thousand hardships and a thousand life-threatening dangers, a man might acquire a slightly more plentiful estate. Regarding the "worldly service" <note>original: "militia saeculi." A common Renaissance metaphor comparing the life of a courtier or secular career to military service, often implying it is a struggle against one's own soul.</note>, there is nothing I need write to you, for experience itself has taught you—and continues to teach you—well enough of its miseries. In the effort to earn the favor of princes, in fostering friendships among peers, and in the pursuit of honors—what a mountain of troubles, what anxiety, and what worry is involved! I could sooner learn these things from you than teach them to you. 

For I, content with my books and my modest leisure <note>original: "ociolo," a diminutive of "otium," which refers to the productive, contemplative peace of a scholar.</note>, have learned from my youth to live within my means. As much as I am able, I dwell within myself, neither longing for nor seeking anything outside of my own soul. Therefore, though we sweat and pant for them, we barely manage to grasp these earthly things—fleeting, uncertain, worthless, and shared in common with the beasts. Yet toward things heavenly and divine—which "no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor heart conceived" <note>Pico is quoting the Apostle Paul from 1 Corinthians 2:9, a standard reference to the incomprehensible nature of heaven.</note>—we are drawn by the gods <note>Pico often uses the plural "gods" in a classical, poetic sense to refer to divine providence or the Christian God.</note> while we are drowsy, sleeping, and almost unwilling...

<summary>In this letter, Pico della Mirandola contrasts the exhausting, anxiety-ridden pursuit of political favor and worldly wealth with the tranquil life of the scholar. He argues that humans struggle immensely for fleeting earthly goals while remaining spiritually lethargic toward the eternal rewards of the divine.</summary>

# LETTERS

...lacks; for it is far more becoming that they begin to be human beings by living well with you, than that you, by abandoning your good purpose, should shamefully become a brute with them. I call God to witness that I am sometimes held in a kind of ecstasy and stupor when I begin to consider the pursuits of men—or, to speak more significantly, their extreme insanities. I know not whether I should think of them or grieve for them; whether to wonder or to weep. <margin>Note</margin> For it is indeed a great insanity not to believe the Gospel, whose truth the blood of martyrs cries out, the apostolic voices resound, miracles prove, reason confirms, the world witnesses, the elements speak, and the demons confess. 

But it is a far greater insanity if, while you do not doubt the truth of the Gospel, you nevertheless live as if you did not doubt its falsehood. For if those things are true—that it is most difficult for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven—why do we pant for the daily accumulation of riches? And if it is true that we should seek the glory that comes not from men, but from God, why do we always hang upon the judgments of men? There is no one who cares to please God. And if there is firm faith in us that the Lord will one day say, "Go, you cursed ones, into eternal fire" <note>original: "Ite maledicti in ignem aeternum," referencing Matthew 25:41.</note> and again, "Come, you blessed ones, possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world" <note>original: "venite benedicti possidete regnum paratum vobis a constitutione mundi," referencing Matthew 25:34.</note>, why is there nothing we fear less than hell <note>original: "gehennam"</note> or hope for less than the kingdom of God? 

What else can we say but that many are Christians in name, but very few in reality? But you, my son, strive to enter through the narrow gate, and do not attend to what the many do, but rather to what the law of nature itself, reason itself, and God Himself shall show you is to be done. For your glory will not be less if you are happy with the few, nor will your punishment be lighter if you are wretched with the many. There will be, however, two especially immediate remedies for you against the world and Satan, by which, as if on two wings, you may be lifted from this valley of tears <note>original: "lachrymarum valle," a common liturgical phrase from the Salve Regina prayer.</note> into the heights: namely, almsgiving and prayer. <margin>Two most healthy remedies</margin> For what can we do without the help of God? Or how shall He help one who does not call upon Him? But surely He will not hear you when you call if you did not first hear the poor man calling to you. For it is not fitting that God should not despise you, a man, when you, a man, first despised another man. It is written: "In the measure with which you measure, it shall be measured back to you" <note>original: "in qua mensura mensi fueritis remetietur vobis," quoting Matthew 7:2.</note>; and elsewhere: "Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy" <note>original: "beati misericordes quoniam misericordiam consequentur," from the Beatitudes in Matthew 5:7.</note>. 

When I invite you to prayer, I do not invite you to that which consists in much speaking <note>original: "multiloquio"</note>, but to that which, in the secret recess of the mind, in the inner chambers of the soul, speaks to God with pure affection. In the most lucid darkness of contemplation <note>original: "lucidissima contemplationis tenebra." This is a mystical paradox: the "darkness" refers to God’s nature being so bright it overwhelms the human mind, a concept central to the "Negative Theology" of Dionysius the Areopagite.</note>, it does not merely present the mind to the Father, but does so with certain ineffable words and in ways known only to those who have experienced them. I do not care how long your prayer is, but how effective, how burning, and how it is interrupted by sighs rather than diffused through a perpetual series and number of words. 

If your salvation is dear to your heart, if you wish to be safe from the snares of the devil, from the storms of the world, and from the ambushes of enemies; if you desire to be pleasing to God and finally happy, see to it that no day passes in which you do not approach your God at least once in prayer. Prostrate before Him with a humble affection of a pious mind, cry out—not from the tips of your lips, but from your deepest core <note>original: "imis visceribus," literally "from the innermost bowels."</note>—with the Prophet: <margin>Prayer</margin> "The sins of my youth and my ignorances do not remember; but according to your mercy remember me because of your goodness, O Lord" <note>original: "Delicta iuuentutis meae... memēto mei," quoting Psalm 25:7.</note>. 

Both the Spirit who intercedes for us and your own necessity will suggest to you every hour what you should ask of your God. Sacred reading will also suggest it; I ask you again and again that you always have it in your hands, leaving behind the fables and trifles of the poets. You can do nothing more pleasing to God or more useful to yourself than to never cease turning the Sacred Scriptures <note>original: "litteras sacras"</note> by hand night and day <note>Pico is adapting Horace’s famous advice to poets ("vos exemplaria Graeca nocturna versate manu, versate diurna"), replacing Greek classics with the Bible.</note>. For there lies hidden in them a certain living and effective heavenly power which, if only one handles them purely and humbly, transforms the soul of the reader into divine love by a certain miraculous power. 

But I have already exceeded the limits of a letter, drawn along by the subject matter itself and by a wonderful charity—with which I have always regarded you, but especially from that hour when I was informed of your most holy purpose. Finally, I would like to remind you of what I often spoke with you about when you were here with me: that you should never forget these two things: both that the Son of God [died] for you...

# LETTERS

...dead, and you also—even if you live a long life—will die soon. With these two spurs, as it were—one of fear and the other of love—drive your horse through the short race-course of this mortal life toward the rewards of eternal happiness. <margin>Note</margin> For we neither ought to nor can set any other goal for ourselves than that we may enjoy the infinite good without end, in the perpetual peace of both the inner and the outer man. Farewell. And fear God. May 15, 1492.

### Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Filippo Beroaldo, greetings.

<note>Large initial A</note> I have received from you, most learned Beroaldo, a letter that was as affectionate as it was scholarly, along with many verses that undoubtedly challenge antiquity itself. That gift was most pleasing to me. Therefore, I have spent some good hours of leisure on your "good business," and in no other pursuit could I have been more pleasantly or honorably occupied. I would act as a most ungrateful man, however, if I wished to repay your excellent works with my own, which are the worst—and, with the wit of Catullus, to exchange the "poisons of Suffenus" for your talent. <note>Pico is humorously self-deprecating here. Suffenus was a poet mocked by the Roman poet Catullus for writing thousands of lines of terrible poetry.</note> For in poetry I am no better than he, except perhaps in this: that I recognize I am a Suffenus, and I see what is in the knapsack on my back. <note>This refers to Aesop’s fable: people carry two bags, one in front for others' faults and one in back for their own, which they never see.</note> Yet you demand this: namely, that I send you something from my own writings. And you demand it in such a way—as if you were making a legal claim—that you seem unlikely to bear a refusal with a calm mind. Therefore, I must satisfy you, even at the cost of whatever reputation I hold with you. You shall have, then, two letters: one to Lorenzo de' Medici, the other to Ermolao <note>Ermolao Barbaro, a prominent Venetian scholar.</note> concerning the style of the philosophers. To these I have added certain verses which escaped me during these days while I was occupied with other things. You will read these with the understanding that in these humanistic studies I work with hurried care and in stolen moments, as one who has devoted his primary efforts and, as they say, "serious oil" <note>original: "seriosas... lucernas," a metaphor for late-night study by lamplight.</note> to philosophy. Among the philosophers, I hope I have made such progress as you have among the rhetoricians and poets—among whom (I speak from the heart) I see no reason why you should not rightly claim the first place. Your friend Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano, the renowned humanist poet.</note> is entirely yours; he loves you as much as possible. Regarding myself, you can promise yourself anything within my power. Farewell.

### Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Lorenzo de' Medici, sends much greeting.

<note>Large initial L</note> I have read, Lorenzo de' Medici, your verses <note>original: "Rhythmos," referring to Lorenzo’s Italian poetry.</note> which the vernacular Muses suggested to you during your tender youth. I recognized the Muses and the legitimate offspring of the Graces, but I did not recognize the work of a "tender age." For who, in your rhythms and the melodious joining of your verses, would not perceive the Graces dancing to the beat? <margin>Note</margin> Who would not hear the Muses singing in your tuneful and rhythmic style? Who—in your unpretentious charm, your cheerful wit, your honeyed jests, your fitting allurements, and your wonderful clarity; in your wise arrangement and in those most profound thoughts drawn from the inner sanctuaries of philosophy—who would recognize a young man? I know for certain that I am not on this list of great judges, nor am I one to climb to such heights of judgment. But I would wish it could be said, without suspicion of flattery, what I feel about them. I would say, indeed, that there is no ancient writer whom you have not surpassed by a long distance in this style of writing. Lest you think this is said merely to win favor, I will bring you my reasons for this opinion. 

There are among you two especially celebrated poets of the Florentine tongue: Francesco Petrarch and Dante Alighieri. Regarding them, let me preface by saying generally that there are learned men who find the substance lacking in Francesco and the words lacking in Dante. In you, however, who possess both mind and ears, neither will be found wanting; in you, one cannot see whether the subject is more illustrated by the speech, or the words by the thoughts. But let us weigh the merits of each one part by part, as if on a scale. Indeed, if Francesco were to return to life, who doubts that, as far as the thoughts are concerned, he would willingly yield the palm to you? <note>original: "herbam tibi daturum," a Roman idiom for admitting defeat.</note> For you are always so sharp, serious, and subtle; while he, mostly snatching ideas from the common stock, colors them with words and makes ordinary things extraordinary through his style of speaking—in which let us see what he provides to you, and what you provide to him. In certain parts he might appear sweeter. But to me, his sweetness—if I may put it this way—seems to fall "sweetly and pleasantly harsh."

# LETTERS

He is diffuse and evenly soothing. You strike the mind with majesty and a certain lively light of speech. In him, there is an ambitious and excessive diligence; in you, a care that is neglected rather than affected. <note>Pico is praising Lorenzo’s "sprezzatura"—the art of making difficult composition look effortless.</note> He is tender and soft; you are masculine and muscular. He is rolling and melodious; you are ready, full, firm, and rhythmic. He is perhaps more charming; you are certainly fuller and more upright. He is more artificial, but you are more sinewy. In him, there is much that you might cut away; in you, nothing is redundant and nothing is cut short. 

But perhaps I am a bit bold to say that anything should be removed from him. Yet it is certainly so; so it seems to many in whose judgment I trust. For in my view, it is common to see him erring in the way the "Asiatic" orators used to err—that is, stuffing in words as if to fill cracks, and employing full and elegant phrases not to adorn the subject, but to prop it up, like flute-players who support a song lest it limp. <note>The "Asiatic" style was a term in classical rhetoric for a flowery, verbose, and overly rhythmic prose style, often contrasted with the more restrained "Attic" style.</note> In you, all words are no less necessary for the matter than they are pleasing in their ornament, so that he who takes from you mutilates the work, while he who takes from him merely shears and purifies it. 

Even if we were to grant—though I will never grant it—that what he wrote was more charming and elegant than yours, it was easy to excel for a man who did not have to struggle with the weight of the ideas themselves. But those sharp, subtle, and—to speak in one word—Laurentian <note>original: "laurentianæ"</note> thoughts of yours can hardly be described; they reject "curling irons" <note>original: "calamistros"—a metaphor used by Cicero to describe artificial, over-processed rhetorical embellishment.</note> and do not willingly admit those artificial dyes. If that other man had been required to handle your subject matter—he whom we read as soft, bright, and pleasant—we would instead find him thorny, squalid, and unpleasing. We see this in him: whenever he attempts something sharp, intricate, or knotty, he fails in style just as much as he rises in thought. 

But when he shows off his "furniture" of words—his ointments, curls, and flowers—he reminds me of what Castritius <note>Titus Castritius was a famous teacher of rhetoric in Rome, mentioned by the author Aulus Gellius.</note> used to warn regarding the orator Gracchus: that we should not be deceived by the rounded sound and the flow of the verses. Instead, we should inspect what lies beneath: what seat, what foundation, what bottom there is to the words. If you were to do this with his work, you might see something like the "void" of Epicurus: <note>Epicurus’s physics relied on atoms moving through an infinite "void" or vacuum; Pico suggests the rival writer's words are empty of substance.</note> either no sense lies beneath them at all, or the meaning is cold and trivial. 

In that part which is of greatest importance, even if you do not surpass him, I do not see <margin>Note</margin> at all why he should be considered superior to you in the grace of speaking. For words cannot be more illustrious than they are in your work, and their arrangement is so fit that they could not cohere better, nor flow more roundly, nor fall more rhythmically in any way. 

But now let us weigh Dante against you, about whom perhaps more people will stir up a controversy. For there are many who, in comparing writers, do not so much weigh their merits as count their years. They command others to read the ancients with reverence, yet they themselves cannot read their own contemporaries without envy. In the first place, certainly, as far as style is concerned, I think no one will deny the prize to you. Dante is sometimes so rough, harsh, and lean, as to be quite crude and unpolished.

He specifically begins to critique Dante Alighieri, noting that while Dante is a classic, his style is often unpolished compared to Lorenzo's.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Giovanni Pico della Mirandola's letter to Lorenzo de' Medici, moving from a general stylistic comparison to a specific ranking of Lorenzo against the titans of Italian literature: Dante Alighieri and Francesco Petrarca (Petrarch).</meta>

# LETTERS

...they seem to be born, not arrived; necessary, not brought in; and entirely genuine, not grafted. This is what I cannot admire enough, and in this, you seem to me to have surpassed Dante. For even if he flies high, he is lifted by the wings of his subject matter; <note>Dante’s *Divine Comedy* deals with the grandest possible themes: Heaven, Hell, and Purgatory.</note> but you, even when the subject resists and pulls downward, are lifted into the heights by the wings of your own talent. You rise in such a way that you do not depart from the subject, but rather lift the subject up along with you. You have deserved as much from your subject as Dante’s subject deserved from him. 

Now one can see the difference between you, Francis <note>Pico refers here to Francesco Petrarca, known in English as Petrarch.</note>, and Dante. Regarding them, I would add this: Francis sometimes fails to live up to his promises; he has that which charms at first sight, but he does not satisfy further in. Dante has that which sometimes offends upon meeting, but he pleases more as one penetrates his depths. Your works have no less in their interior to hold the reader than they have on their surface to capture them. Add to this that those men composed their poems in retreats, in the shade, and in the highest tranquility of study; you sang yours amidst tumults, the noise of the court, the clamors of the forum, the greatest cares, and the most turbulent storms, while being most occupied. To them, the Muses were their ordinary and principal business; to you, they are a game and a certain relaxation from cares. To them, poetry was the ultimate exhaustion; to you, it is rest for the exhausted. Finally, by relaxing your mind, you reached a point which they, perhaps, did not reach even while straining every nerve of their souls.

But what shall I say of my paraphrase? <note>Pico refers to his *Commento*, a philosophical commentary he wrote on Lorenzo’s sonnets.</note> Why should I not call it mine, by the right of this name? Or why not mine, since even if I venerate it as yours, I love it as if it were my own? I truly admire both the work and you in it. From this conjunction, I realized how far I was from a true appreciation of your verses; I had not looked closely enough with my "night-owl eyes" at those things which were greatest and most illustrious. I then saw them revealed through you, which only you were able and duty-bound to do—duty-bound to yourself and to us, lest you defraud yourself of much glory and us of much pleasure. 

I read it (God is my witness), most excellent Lorenzo, not so much for delight as for doctrine. For how many things are there from Aristotle’s <margin>Aristotle</margin> *Physics*, from his books *On the Soul*, *On Ethics*, *On the Heavens*, and from his *Problems*? How many from Plato’s <margin>Plato</margin> *Protagoras*, from the *Republic*, from the *Laws*, and from the *Symposium*? All of these I have read elsewhere in their original authors, yet I read them in your work as if they were new, as if they were better, and transformed by you into I-know-not-what appearance so that they seem to be yours and not theirs, and in reading, I seem to learn something new. 

This is the greatest proof that you know these things not merely from a commentary, but from yourself. <margin>Note</margin> For many are accustomed to practice a greater <term>sophistry (original: σοφισΤεία)</term> in literature than actual work; when they are about to write, they treat philosophers like "pragmatic" assistants, suggesting certain dogmas to be shoved into their little books so they might seem like philosophers themselves. But you can easily catch these people. For you will see those ideas are neither rightly arranged nor coherent, and they are not explained by the authors, but rather entangled. Men who are otherwise eloquent appear like speechless infants when speaking of these things. But who would not see that you do not hold these ideas "on loan," but as if you have the right and power over them to turn, act, and treat them at your will? 

These things you have achieved (O happy genius!) in the heat of the Republic and in an active life—things which we, who are not the disciples of philosophers but merely their tenants in a shadowy and sedentary life, follow rather than overtake. 

But what shall I say of the sweetest style of your paraphrase? <margin>Caesar</margin> To me, it seems entirely like that of Caesar in the Roman tongue; for the speech is not manufactured by hand, not gilded, not twisted, but upright, candid, and square by its own talent. <note>Pico compares Lorenzo’s Italian to the "Attic" purity of Julius Caesar’s Latin, which was prized for being direct and unadorned.</note> It does not run out rashly, but keeps its pace; it is neither luxurious nor thin, neither wanton nor unpleasant. It is sweetly grave and gravely lovable. The words are chosen and not hunted for; illustrious and not fake; necessary and not sought after; not merely explaining the matter, but placing it before one's very eyes. I pass over how you always remember your own character, and how seeds and traces of your wisdom are scattered everywhere. These things I and many others have seen. 

But besides these, I saw two principal things which perhaps not many see, even those with sharp eyes. The first is that the work hides its own riches; it flees from envy and keeps its flowers in its lap, rather than showing them off. It does not lift itself up...

V iii

# LETTERS

...into plants; but let the natural quality remain so that it appears lesser <note>Pico is likely suggesting that Lorenzo's natural talent is so great that it makes any artistic "grafting" or imitation look small by comparison.</note>, I do not see what else it could be, nor am I so clever, but I see it is something—I know not what—that I might call most distinctly "Laurentian." For if anyone were to see Lorenzo’s gifts, genius, and excellence, they would see the whole Lorenzo graphically portrayed <note>original: "graphice effigiatum." This implies the poetry is a perfect visual and spiritual likeness of the man.</note>. But perhaps I have said too much, even against my will, as the very sentiment of my mind draws me "athwart," as they say, into words. I will not pass over this: I exhort you with as much effort as I can that you might occasionally steal a little leisure from governing the Republic <note>A reference to Lorenzo's role as the de facto ruler of the Florentine Republic.</note> to devote to finishing your paraphrase; it will indeed bring honor to you and your native tongue, and be of use and pleasure to your citizens and to us all.

Florence, on the Ides of July <note>July 15</note>, 1484.

### Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to his friend Hermolao Barbaro, greetings.

I, indeed, my dear Hermolao, can neither remain silent about what I feel regarding you, nor fail to feel those things which ought to be felt toward one in whom all things are found at their highest, just as if they were found in specific individuals. But would that my mind’s capacity were such that I could feel toward you according to your merits; would that I had such power of speech that I could sometimes express what I always feel. I know that what I have conceived of you falls infinitely below the heights of your learning. And you should know that whatever we speak is far less than what we conceive. Know that words are as lacking for the mind as the mind is lacking for reality. And yet, believe me to be so bold that I hope I might also imitate your works, the greatness of which I cannot even estimate. Everyone can admire you; so few can imitate you that no one can find fault. And would that I had such good fortune that what I write might reflect my Hermolao in some part. 

For your style itself—to say nothing of the rest—which you favor so little, affects and delights me more than I can say. It is so learned, grave, composed, erudite, refined, and ingenious; in it, nothing is commonplace, nothing trivial, whether you look at the words or the thoughts. Often I and our friend Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano, a renowned Renaissance poet and scholar.</note> read whatever letters of yours we have, whether to others or to us. Thus the subsequent letters always vie with the preceding ones, and new graces bloom fruitfully during the reading, so that in a certain perpetual acclaim, we have no room to catch our breath.

But it is wonderful to say how you persuade and drive the reader’s mind wherever you wish. I have experienced this both at other times and especially in this most recent letter of yours to me. In it, while you attack these "barbarian" philosophers—whom you say are commonly held to be sordid, rude, and uncultivated, and who <margin>Thomas</margin> <note>St. Thomas Aquinas (c. 1225–1274), the preeminent Scholastic theologian.</note> did not even live while alive, much less live now that they are dead; and if they live now, they live in punishment and <margin>John Scotus</margin> <note>Duns Scotus (c. 1266–1308), known for his complex "subtle" logic.</note> disgrace—I was so moved, and so ashamed and regretful of my studies. For I have already <margin>Albertus</margin> <note>Albertus Magnus (c. 1200–1280), teacher of Aquinas and a key figure in medieval science.</note> spent six years among them, so that I wish I had done no less than to have struggled so laboriously in such a worthless matter. I said, "Have I lost my <margin>Averroes</margin> <note>The 12th-century Islamic philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were central to Scholastic study.</note> best years, and such long night-watches, with Thomas, John Scotus, Albert, and Averroes—years in which I might perhaps have become something in good literature?" 

I was thinking to myself, to console myself, if any of those men were now to come back to life, whether they—otherwise argumentative men—would have nothing with which to defend their cause by some reasoning. At last, it occurred to me that one of them, a little more eloquent than the rest, might defend his "barbarism" in a way that is not at all barbarian, perhaps in this manner: 

"We have lived as celebrated men, O Hermolao, and after this, we shall live, not in the schools of grammarians and pedants, but in the circles of philosophers and the assemblies of the wise. There, the discussion and debate are not about the mother of Andromache <note>A common example of the trivial mythological questions studied by grammarians that philosophers found useless.</note>, nor about the children of Niobe, nor light trifles of that sort, but about the reasons of human and divine things. In meditating upon, inquiring into, and unravelling these things, we have been so subtle, sharp, and keen that we might perhaps seem to have been sometimes too anxious and fastidious—if indeed anyone can be too fastidious or over-curious in tracking down the truth. And if anyone in these matters should accuse us of dullness and slowness..."

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s famous 1485 letter to Hermolao Barbaro. Pico is responding to Barbaro's earlier letter which had criticized the "barbaric" (uncultured) Latin style of the medieval Scholastic philosophers. Pico adopts a persona to defend these thinkers, arguing that substance and truth are more important than rhetorical beauty.</meta>

# LETTERS

...[nobili]ty <note>This completes the sentence from the previous page: "would that I had such power of speech that I [could speak according to the dignity of your] nobility."</note>: Come then, I pray, whoever he is, let him step forward: let him clear the reputation of those "barbarians" by showing they had Mercury <note>The god of both eloquence and intelligence.</note> not in their tongue but in their heart; that wisdom was not lacking in them, even if eloquence was. Indeed, to have not joined eloquence with wisdom is perhaps so far from being a fault that to have joined them would be a sin. For who would not condemn and detest curls or rouge on a modest maiden? So great is the conflict between the duty of the orator and the philosopher that they could not fight against each other more. For what is the duty of the rhetorician other than to lie, deceive, circumvent, and play tricks? For it is your boast, as you say, to be able at will to turn white into black and black into white; to be able to raise, cast down, amplify, or diminish whatever you wish by speaking; and finally, by the almost magical powers of eloquence of which you boast, to transform things themselves into whatever appearance and form you please, so that they might appear to the audience not as they are by their own nature, but as you wish them to be—not that they actually become so, but though they are not, they seem to be. Is this whole thing anything other than pure lying, pure imposture, pure trickery? Since it always either exceeds the nature of the thing by exaggerating or falls short by diminishing, and by a deceptive harmony of words—holding up masks and phantoms as it were—it mocks the minds of the listeners with flattery. 

Will such a man have any affinity with the philosopher, whose entire study is occupied in knowing the truth and demonstrating it to others? Add to this that no trust will be placed in us if we affect the refinements and charms of words, as if, lacking confidence in the facts and not relying on the truth, we sought to draw men to our opinion with these allurements. For this reason, it is better to read sacred matters written crudely rather than elegantly, because nothing is more unseemly or harmful in any subject dealing with the knowledge of truth than this whole elaborate style of speaking. This belongs to legal disputes, not to natural and celestial matters. It does not belong to those in the Academy <note>The school of philosophy.</note>, but to those who are active in the Republic, where what is done and said is weighed on the popular scale, where flowers far outweigh fruits. Do you not know that "not all things suit all people with the same thread"? <note>original: "non omnia omnibus pari filo conveniunt." A proverb meaning that different styles are appropriate for different subjects.</note> Eloquence is an elegant thing (we admit this), full of charm and pleasure, but in a philosopher, it is neither becoming nor welcome. Who would not approve of a soft gait, expressive hands, and playful eyes in an actor or a dancer? But in a citizen or a philosopher, who would not disapprove, rebuke, and abominate them? If we see a girl with charming manners and a witty tongue, we shall praise and kiss her; but in a matron, we shall condemn and prosecute these same things. 

Therefore, it is not we who are foolish, but those who celebrate the Bacchanalia at the feet of Vesta <note>Vesta was the Roman goddess of the hearth and virginity; to perform the wild, drunken Bacchanalia in her temple is a metaphor for gross impropriety.</note>; who dishonor the gravity and chastity of philosophical matters with playthings and curling irons. Indeed, as can be aptly said regarding Synesius’s <margin>Synesius</margin> <note>Synesius of Cyrene (c. 373–414 AD), a philosopher and bishop.</note> speech about a young man, a "well-groomed speech is always a degenerate." <note>original: "comatam orationem semper cinaedam." Pico uses a harsh term for an effeminate man to argue that an overly ornate style is morally suspect.</note> Therefore, we prefer our speech to be shaggy-haired, dense, and unencumbered, rather than one beautifully groomed with either the mark or the suspicion of impurity. And though nothing else remains, this is most true: nothing is more different from the philosopher's purpose in any matter than that which tastes in any way of luxury or pride. Socrates <margin>Socrates</margin> used to say that Sicyonian shoes <note>Sicyon was famous for luxury footwear; Socrates argues that while they are comfortable, they are inappropriate for a philosopher's simple life.</note> were comfortable and fit the foot well, but that they did not suit Socrates at all. There is not the same standard for a civic dress as for a philosophical one, just as there is not for the table or for speech. The philosopher uses these only for necessity; the man of the world uses them for grace as well. If the latter neglects grace, he is not a man of the world; if the former affects it, he will not be a philosopher. If Pythagoras <margin>Pythagoras</margin> could have lived without food and spared the vegetables, or if he could have explained his thoughts by a look, or at least with less effort than speech requires, he would not have spoken at all. Far be it from him, then, to polish and adorn his tongue! Indeed, for this very reason we must take care lest the reader, enticed by the medicated skin of the prose, linger upon it and fail to penetrate to the marrow and blood, which we have often seen to be corrupted beneath a face painted with white lead <note>original: "cerusato ori." White lead (ceruse) was used as a cosmetic to whiten the face, often hiding blemishes or decay.</note>. We have seen, I say, in all these people, that it has come into use for this reason: since there is nothing inside that is not empty and vain, they detain the reader at the first appearance with various modulations and harmony. If a philosopher were to do this, Musonius <margin>Musonius</margin> <note>Musonius Rufus, a Stoic philosopher known for his emphasis on simple living and ethics.</note> would cry out that it is not a philosopher speaking, but a flute-player singing. Let it not, therefore, be imputed to us as a fault that we have not done that which...

<note>At the bottom right of the page, there are several small red ink spots, likely accidental splashes from a later reader or the printing house.</note>

<summary>Pico della Mirandola defends the "barbaric" style of Scholastic philosophers, arguing that the pursuit of truth requires a plain, "shaggy" style of speech, whereas the ornate rhetoric of the humanists is deceptive and inappropriate for serious philosophy.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s 1485 defense of the "barbarian" medieval philosophers against the criticisms of the humanist Hermolao Barbaro. Pico has just argued that the orator’s art is often based on deception, whereas the philosopher’s goal is pure truth.</meta>

-># LETTERS<-

...to have done so was a fault <note>This completes the thought from the previous page: that for a philosopher to have used the deceptive "flowers" of rhetoric would have been a moral failing.</note>. We seek *what* we should write; we do not seek *how*. Or rather, we do seek a "how," but one that is without any parade or flower of speech. We do not wish for our writing to be delightful, charming, and witty, but rather to be useful, serious, and revered; so that it may attain majesty from a certain ruggedness <note>original: *horrore*. In classical styling, this refers to a rough, unpolished quality that inspires awe, contrasted here with the "softness" of popular oratory.</note> rather than grace from softness. We do not wait for the applause of the theater, for a smooth or rhythmic cadence <note>original: *clausula*. This refers to the rhythmic patterns used by orators to end their sentences musically.</note> to soothe the ears, nor for this to be called "false" or that "charming." Instead, we look for the silence of the few, born of admiration, as they gaze deeply into something—either unearthed from the inner shrines <note>original: *adytis*. The most sacred, private chamber of a temple; here used as a metaphor for the deep secrets of the natural world.</note> of nature or brought down to men from the court of heaven. Then again, we seek something so sharp in its reasoning that there is no room left for defense, and so well-defended that there is no room for argument. Let them admire us, furthermore, as keen in inquiry, circumspect in exploration, subtle in contemplation, grave in judgment, intricate in binding an opponent <note>original: *vincindo*. This refers to the "binding" of an opponent through the inescapable steps of a logical syllogism.</note>, and easy in unravelling a problem. Adm...

<summary>Pico della Mirandola defines the ideal philosophical style as one that prioritizes logic and "rugged" majesty over the decorative, rhythmic, and often deceptive charms of popular rhetoric.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola’s famous 1485 letter to the humanist Ermolao Barbaro. Pico is speaking in the persona of a "barbarian" medieval philosopher, defending the plain, unadorned language of the Scholastics against the humanist demand for eloquent Latin. -># LETTERS<-

But Lucretius will insist <margin>Lucretius</margin> that even if philosophical treatises do not, in themselves, require the pleasantness of speech, nevertheless, by employing such beauty, the austerity of the subjects themselves should be disguised. Just as wormwood <note>original: *absynthia*. Wormwood is a famously bitter herb used in ancient medicine; Lucretius famously used the metaphor of "honey on the rim of the cup" to explain why he wrote his philosophy in verse.</note> by its own nature dispels diseases, yet doctors smear the cup with honey so that the unsuspecting age of children may be deceived into taking it. Perhaps this is what you had to do, O Lucretius: if you were writing your works for children; if for the common people, you certainly had to do it—you who were serving up <term>serving up</term><note>original: *propinaries*. This term specifically refers to the act of offering a drink or a toast, continuing the medicinal cup metaphor.</note> not just wormwood, but the most undiluted poisons <note>Pico is attacking the philosophy of Lucretius (Epicureanism), which he regarded as spiritually poisonous because of its denial of divine providence and the immortality of the soul.</note>. But we must hold to a far different reasoning: we who, as we said before, do not seek to entice the common people, but rather to frighten them away. Nor do we offer earthy wormwood; rather, we serve up nectar. 

But Lactantius will contend <margin>Lactantius</margin> that it is well enough established that truth flows more powerfully into the minds of listeners, or even of the more discerning <note>original: *feniorꝝ*, likely a transcription error or variant for *seniorum* (the elderly/wise) or *saniorum* (those of sounder mind).</note>, when it is both equipped with its own strength and adorned with the light of oratory. If you had been, O Firmianus <note>Lucius Caelius Firmianus Lactantius (c. 250 – c. 325) was known as the "Christian Cicero" for his eloquent defense of Christianity.</note>, as frequent a visitor to sacred letters as you were to fictional lawsuits <note>original: *fictis litibus*. Lactantius was a teacher of rhetoric before his conversion; Pico suggests his bias toward eloquence comes from his legal and rhetorical training rather than divine truth.</note>, you would not have said this, and our own writings would not...

<summary>Pico della Mirandola rejects the use of rhetorical "honey" to sweeten philosophy, arguing that unlike Lucretius, true philosophers do not need to deceive the masses. He further critiques the Christian rhetorician Lactantius for valuing eloquence over the plain strength of sacred truth.</summary>

--- Page 250 ---
<meta>Continuing Pico della Mirandola's 1485 defense of Scholastic philosophy. In the previous section, he argued that philosophers should prioritize substance over style, even using the metaphor of bitter medicine to describe the harsh but truthful language of the "barbarian" thinkers.</meta>

-># LETTERS<-

Your argument fails: the Arab will say the same thing, as will the Egyptian; they will not speak in Latin, but they will nonetheless speak correctly. For either the names of things are established by arbitrary choice <note>original: *arbitrio*. This refers to the linguistic theory that words are social conventions rather than having a "natural" link to the objects they describe.</note> or by nature. If names were established by a fortuitous placement—as if by a common agreement of men coming together in the same opinion, by which it was ordained what each thing should be called by name—then among those men, the thing is called correctly. What prevents these philosophers, whom you call barbarians, from having conspired in a single norm of speaking, which is held no less sacred among them than you hold the Roman <note>i.e., Classical Latin</note> tongue among yourselves? There is no reason why you should not call their style "correct" while calling your own "correct," if this imposition of names is entirely a matter of choice. But if you do not wish to deign to call it by the name "Roman," then call it Gallic, British, Spanish, or what the common people are accustomed to call it: "Parisian" <note>original: *parisiensum*. This refers to the technical, often convoluted Latin used at the University of Paris, the global center of Scholastic logic and theology which humanists like Barbaro despised.</note>. When they speak to you, it will happen that most of their words are laughed at and most are not understood; the same will happen to you when speaking among them: "Anacharsis commits a solecism among the Athenians; [likewise] the Athenians [among the Scythians]." <note>original: *αναχαρσισ παραθηναιοισ σολοικιζει. αθηναιο* (Anacharsis par' Athēnaiois soloikizei. Athēnaioi). Anacharsis was a Scythian prince and philosopher who visited Athens in the 6th century BCE. He famously remarked that while the Greeks laughed at his "barbaric" speech, they sounded just as barbaric to his people. A "solecism" is a grammatical mistake or an uncultured way of speaking.</note>

<summary>Pico argues that because language is a social convention rather than a natural law, the technical "Parisian" Latin of medieval philosophers is just as valid for seeking truth as the eloquent Latin of the Romans. He uses the figure of Anacharsis to show that "barbarism" is merely a matter of perspective.</summary>

<keywords>linguistic convention, Scholasticism, University of Paris, Anacharsis, solecism, Latin vs. Barbarism, philosophy of language</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the 1485 correspondence between Giovanni Pico della Mirandola and Ermolao Barbaro regarding the value of Scholastic "barbarian" philosophy, before transitioning to later letters from 1490 addressed to Battista Mantovano and the famous printer Aldus Manutius.</meta>

-># LETTERS<-

...knows: the one [knows] of God and nature; the other, most childlike in speaking, feels those things which cannot be sufficiently praised in speech. The one, most eloquent in his speaking, speaks of things that are unspeakable <note>original: *eloqṝ nefanda*. Pico is using a wordplay to suggest the humanist orator speaks beautifully about trivial or wicked things, while the "barbarian" philosopher speaks roughly about divine truths.</note>. These things, perhaps, dearest Ermolao, they will bring forward in defense of their own barbarism, or perhaps things that are much better in their subtlety. I do not entirely agree with their opinion, nor do I think any free-born or liberal person should. But I have willingly exercised myself in this matter as if it were an infamous subject—just as those who praise a quartan fever <note>A common rhetorical exercise in the Renaissance called *adoxography*, where a writer displays skill by praising something inherently bad or trivial.</note>—both to test my wits and with the intention that, just as Glaucon in Plato's works praises injustice <note>A reference to Book II of Plato's *Republic*.</note>, not from his own judgment but to stimulate Socrates to praise justice, so too I might hear the cause of eloquence pleaded by you. I have been led somewhat against my own sense and nature into this license of opposition; for if I thought eloquence should be neglected or held as secondary to the barbarians, I would not have almost entirely abandoned them for it, as I recently did, turning to Greek letters and to your Themistius <note>Ermolao Barbaro was famous for his Latin translations of the Greek commentator Themistius.</note>, which can never be praised enough. But I shall say freely what I feel: certain grammarians stir my stomach, who, when they have grasped two origins of words, show themselves off so much and go about so boastfully that they think philosophers are to be held as nothing compared to themselves. "We do not want," they say, "these philosophies of yours." And what wonder? Neither do dogs want Falernian wine <note>A famous high-quality wine from Roman antiquity; Pico is calling the grammarians "dogs" who cannot appreciate the vintage of philosophy.</note>. But let us close this letter at this point. If those barbarians earned any honor or name for themselves by the knowledge of things alone, it is not easily said. What a place! What praises you might claim for yourself, since you are the most eloquent among philosophers and, to speak in Greek, the most philosophical <note>original Greek: Φιλοσοφωτατοσ (*philosophōtatos*)</note> among the eloquent. Florence, June 3rd, 1485.

<note>A large, decorative initial 'S' is penned in red ink at the start of this section.</note>
Hail, most beloved father. Concerning Apollonius of Tyana <note>A 1st-century Neopythagorean philosopher and reputed miracle worker; Pico was often interested in such figures for their "natural magic."</note>, I feel nothing more than what you feel, about which I shall write more to you when there is leisure and things that will perhaps not be ungrateful to you. Concerning the diversity of our translation from the Hebrew text in the third chapter of the book of Genesis, where it treats of Eve and the serpent, I judge thus: it is in the Hebrew, as you write, "He shall crush your head" <note>original: *ipsum conteret caput tuum*. This refers to Genesis 3:15. The Hebrew pronoun is masculine (*hu*), referring to the "seed" of the woman.</note>, and it refers to the seed of Eve, of which it had said, "I will put enmity between your seed and her seed." However, the Seventy <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> and Jerome <note>The translator of the Latin Vulgate.</note> translated it as "She shall crush your head" <note>original: *ipsa conteret*. The Vulgate used the feminine pronoun, often interpreted as referring to Mary.</note>. In both cases, however, the sense is the same: for when it says "He shall crush," it regards not so much the person of Eve herself as the posterity of Eve. Since it says she will do what she will do in her seed. But as to why they preferred to translate "she" rather than "he," I think the reason was to signify that since from Eve not only females but males were to be propagated, that which was said of the seed should be referred to the female seed alone. These are the things that come to mind at present on this matter. I am constantly working on the harmony of Plato and Aristotle. I give to that study its due every morning; after the midday hours, I give time to friends, to health, and occasionally to poets and orators; and if there are any studies of lighter labor, the night is shared with you and the sound of the Sacred Letters <note>The Bible.</note>. I beg you, do not let me lack your company for too long. Greet Beroaldo. Your Politian <note>Angelo Poliziano, the famous humanist poet and Pico's close friend.</note> is entirely yours. Farewell, and pray to God for me. Florence, March 20, 1490.

To the Reverend Father in Christ, Brother Battista Mantovano <note>Battista Spagnoli (the "Mantuan"), a famous Carmelite poet and theologian.</note>, of the Order of Carmelites, distinguished poet, philosopher, and theologian, etc. His son, Giovanni of Mirandola.
Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Aldus Manutius <note>The renowned scholar-printer of Venice.</note>, greetings.

<note>A large, decorative initial 'M' is penned in red ink, with a smaller 'm' nestled inside its curve.</note>
I send the Homers which you desired, though later than you wished and I owed. I am so distracted, my Aldus, by occupations that there is no room even to breathe. I have long since bound myself (as you know) in service to letters. They demand a task of reading and dictating so severely, according to their own impious law, that I can scarcely redeem my health. As for what you write that you will do: gird yourself for philosophy, but on this condition: that you remember there is no philosophy which calls us away from the truth of the mysteries. Philosophy seeks the truth; theology finds it; religion possesses it. Farewell. Florence, the eleventh day of February, in the year of grace 1490 <note>Historically 1491, as the Florentine calendar began the year in March.</note>.

**Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Marsilio Ficino, greetings.**

**Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Angelo Poliziano, greetings.**
<note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494) was a brilliant poet and scholar; this letter famously discusses his Latin translation of the "Enchiridion" (Manual) of the Stoic philosopher Epictetus.</note>

<note>A large initial E is decorated with red ink.</note> My "Loves" <note>term: *amores* — refers to Pico's early Latin elegies and poems, which he eventually attempted to suppress or burn in his later religious fervor.</note> declare they have never been received more urbanely or more cheerfully than in these last few days at your house, and how as friends they were indeed "pierced" <note>A joke referring to Poliziano's sharp scholarly edits and corrections.</note>. While they congratulate themselves, they also owe you the most. For who would not wish to die by that sword of yours? They grieve, however, that it was done more indulgently than was proper; and they are at the point where they doubt whether Love himself made you blind toward my "Loves." And thus they doubt so much that they do not trust your judgment (otherwise most grave) in their own case. They trust nonetheless, and now they claim their chains, for they do not know how to be free at home, and they securely demand a public appearance. 

But what shall I say of the playfulness of your Epictetus? O, what a humorous thing, worthy of a <term>Catonian laugh</term> <note>Referring to Cato the Elder, known for his extreme gravity; a laugh from him would be a rare and significant event.</note>. He was hardly at the threshold when, spreading open his robe, he said, "Look, here are critical marks! Look, here are arrows!—if you do not know Greek." <note>original: "en obelos en sagittas si nescitis græce." Who could have restrained themselves from loud laughter when a Stoic man joked so charmingly? We certainly abstained from his weapons, as he had threatened he would repay any injury, and his skin had grown so thick that he would not admit such light blows. 

Therefore, we treated the old man with the veneration we owed him. When he finally sat down among us, he began to philosophize about morals. And he did this in Latin—not so much because he was among Latins (for there were those in the assembly who knew Greek), but because he himself tasted more brilliantly in Latin by your favor <note>Referring to Poliziano's high-quality Latin translation of the Greek original.</note>. Nor did he waste his effort, since he did not stop speaking until he had made us Stoics instead of Peripatetics <note>term: *Peripatetics* — followers of Aristotle's school of philosophy.</note>. We all approved of that <term>apatheia</term> <note>term: *apatheia* — the Stoic ideal of being "unaffected" by passion or external suffering; freedom from emotional disturbance.</note>. One could see that people who were delicate just a short time ago have now become the most tolerant of all things. Indeed, we can be provoked by others, but harmed only by ourselves if we struggle against fate; and we wish that things which are not our own finally happen just as God wills. We shall never blame nor accuse them; we shall grieve for nothing, demand nothing, and we shall not know how to be enslaved or defeated. Let us philosophize in action, not just in speech: and because we are novices, let us observe ourselves as if we were our own adversaries. Let us neglect, rather than reject, the opinions of others about us and other things of that kind which are external. Let us take care that we act as travelers at an inn for a day; in short, let us not possess those things. Let us love silence, lest the mind vomit up what it has not digested. Let us rarely cause laughter for others, and never for ourselves. 

And to embrace it in a single word: we have abundantly learned all of Epictetus—to endure hardships and to abstain from pleasures. <note>original: "sustinere aduersa & abstinere uolptatibus." This is a paraphrase of the famous Stoic motto "Sustine et abstine" (Bear and forbear).</note> See how point by point we have modeled our life after your Epictetus. See how quickly we did so, lest in this part too we should not be Stoics; for they wish to warn us that a man fails for as long as he does not make progress. Although I have admired this in others, I admired it most in myself alone. Though I have always spent my time in the Lyceum or the Academy <note>The schools of Aristotle and Plato, respectively.</note> and never in the "Porch" <note>term: *Porticus* (Stoa) — the school of the Stoics.</note>, I was so conquered by the speech of the old man that I moved over to his opinion not only with my feet, but with my hands and my whole body. <note>A Roman idiom for giving one's total and enthusiastic support to a proposal.</note> The index of Greek books that are staying here with me, along with the letter of Manuel which your letter...

->LETTERS<-

(if any occasion is given) I shall not neglect any kind of service toward you: since you yourself acted first toward me in the vestibule of friendship. Farewell.

**Giovanni Pico of Mirandola, Count of Concordia, to his Niccolò Leoniceno, greetings.** <note>Niccolò Leoniceno (1428–1524) was a celebrated Italian physician and humanist, famous for correcting errors in ancient medical texts.</note>

**I** have already spoken with you through letters quite often and at great length, my sweetest Niccolò, if only it had been known to me where on earth you were, either by messenger, or letters, or by rumor. Indeed, I have anxiously inquired after this from many people, but I received only an uncertain response from all of them. At last, in recent days, there fell into my hands the letters of Antonio Faventino, a most serious philosopher, written to Thomas Frignanus; from those letters I learned that you were in Florence, which was then most pleasing to me. As soon as I understood this, I gave letters to a courier to take to you in Florence. The journey was in vain, for he did not find you there. I grieved exceedingly. Today, Thomas indicated that you had departed Florence and were in Bologna; I immediately ordered these letters to be delivered to you.

In these, I shall strive neither to reveal my benevolence toward you nor my singular love at great length; for you ought not to doubt even a little bit regarding my goodwill toward you, unless you thought me one who has forgotten both your excellent virtue and your services toward me—which is not my nature. However, I could not help but marvel greatly that when you snatched yourself away from the tumults of the city to seek a seat in which you could live both tranquilly and joyfully, you either certainly forgot this little town of ours, or certainly looked upon it with disdain. You seemed, Niccolò, to lack confidence either in my will or in my resources; yet while the latter may be less than your merits, the former is greater than your opinion of it. It will be pleasing to me if you would inform me of your plan; it would be the most pleasing of all things if you would not disdain to share my hearth <note>original: *lares*; the household gods of a Roman home, used here to mean "home" or "fireside."</note> with me, and take your leisure with me while others are negotiating with Mars <note>An allusion to war; Pico is inviting his friend to the safety and quiet of his estate during a time of conflict.</note>.

The remainder of *Joannes Grammaticus* <note>Referring to the commentaries of John Philoponus, a 6th-century scholar known as "The Grammarian," whose works on Aristotle were vital to Renaissance philosophers.</note> I am sending to you; it was not found for many days, but has now been recovered. I am yours, and I wait for you. Farewell. At Mirandola, the 20th day of July, 1482.

If you love me, see with all diligence that you obtain an index of all the books found in the library of Saint Dominic <note>The Dominican library in Bologna, one of the most important collections of the era.</note>. Send it or bring it with you. Farewell again.

I have built a suburban villa, pleasant enough considering the condition of the place and the region. I have composed a long poem about it; the home will be sweet to you, and the poem will not be unpleasing. Farewell once more.

**Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to his Angelo Poliziano, greetings.** <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494) was the preeminent poet and classical scholar of the Medici circle in Florence and a close friend of Pico.</note>

**B**ecause you praised me so greatly in your recent letters, I owe you as much as I am distant from being worthily praised. For that which is given freely is owed to each person, not that which is paid as a debt. Therefore, I myself owe you all that you write about me, since there is nothing of the sort in me. Since you owed this to me in no way at all, it was entirely the result of your kindness and your singular benevolence toward me. For the rest, if you examine me, you will find nothing except what is thin, humble, and narrow. We are novices and mere recruits <note>original: *tirunculi*; a term for young soldiers or beginners in a field.</note> who have only just moved a foot out of the shadows of ignorance; we have advanced almost nothing. It is a kind dealing with us if we are numbered among the ranks of the studious. The name "learned" has a certain other quality which is peculiar to you and those like you; such grand things do not suit me. Since of those things which are foremost in the study of letters, I have nothing not only fully explored, but have not even seen anything yet except through a screen <note>original: *per transennam*; meaning a glimpse through a lattice window or a partial, obscured view.</note>. 

I shall indeed try (which is what I am doing now) to be at some time the sort of man you now proclaim me to be, and judge me to be—or at least wish me to be. Meanwhile, I shall imitate you, Angelo: you who excuse yourself to the Greeks because you are Latin, and to the Latins because you "Graecize" <note>Speak or write in the Greek style.</note>. I shall use a similar refuge, so that I may be approved by the poets and rhetoricians because I am said to philosophize, and by the philosophers because I play the rhetorician and cultivate the Muses. Although, it happens quite differently for me than for you. Indeed, while I wish to sit on two chairs <note>original: *geminis sellis sedere*; a proverb for trying to hold two positions at once. Pico is humbly suggesting that while Poliziano excels in both poetry and philosophy, Pico fails at both.</note> (as they say), I am excluded from both.
