...and it results finally (to put it briefly) that I am neither a poet, nor a rhetorician, nor a philosopher. You, however, so fulfill both <note>Pico refers here to the mastery of both Greek and Latin literature</note> that it is not sufficiently clear which you embrace more beautifully, the Greek or our own Minerva <note>Minerva was the Roman goddess of wisdom; Pico uses her name here to represent Latin scholarship</note>. You are like a swan of both languages, so that what is adopted and what is genuine cannot easily be discerned. For, to say nothing of the Latin authors (concerning whom you yield to no one), who would believe—as was said of Hadrian <note>The Roman Emperor Hadrian (reigned 117–138 AD) was a famous "Philhellene" or lover of Greek culture</note>—that a Roman man could speak so well in Greek? Our friend Emanuel <note>likely the scholar Manuel Chrysoloras or a contemporary Greek teacher</note> swore while he was reading your work that Athens itself was not so "Attic" <note>Attic refers to the refined, classical dialect of Athens, the gold standard for Greek prose</note>. You are such a man, my Angelo (let all flattery be cast aside), that among our people only one or two—not to say no one—can be compared to you. If there were more such men, these ages would have no reason to envy antiquity. Apply yourself, I pray, and rescue literature from neglect as much as you can, lest that brilliance of the Roman language utterly fade away through the injury of time. Always forge something new that may assist and illuminate Latin affairs. And those works you have at home, let them finally come forth for the common benefit of students. I indeed love you and all your works, and I desire them all the more because I have set you before me as a model to be shaped by—even if you are one whom all ought to follow, yet few can overtake. Farewell.

**Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to his friend Paolo Cortesi, Greetings.** <note>Paolo Cortesi (1465–1510) was a Roman humanist known for his strict adherence to Ciceronian Latin style.</note>

**B**enevolently <note>The OCR indicates a large red initial 'B' for 'Bene'</note> you think, Paolo. Let us send letters frequently so that we, who are divided by the distances of places, may certainly be joined by the exchange of letters. It is customary to lighten the longing for those who are absent: perhaps if you have a statue or an image of that person at home. To me, however, there seems to be this difference between an image and a letter: the former shapes the body, the latter the mind. The former outlines only the outermost parts; the latter clearly expresses and shapes the innermost parts. That one represents as it were the tunic and clothing of a friend; this one represents the true friend to us. That one emulates the colors and figure of the flesh as best it can; this one represents thoughts, counsels, sorrows, joys, cares, and finally all affections. And those secrets of the soul which one hardly speaks even to oneself when present, a letter transmits most faithfully to an absent friend. This, finally, is a living and effective image; that other is a dead and mute likeness. Let us therefore send these images of our souls to one another: you indeed send what you can—golden and silver ones—while I send either bronze or clay ones <note>Pico is using a common humanist trope of humility, calling his own writing "clay" compared to Cortesi’s "gold"</note>. Thus we shall be beyond every injury of places and times, just as the power of the soul itself knows neither the intervals of space nor the delays of time.

But truly, how much do I owe you, most dutiful Paolo, since you were the first to call me to this duty with such a letter—one which held and delighted me so much that I do not remember being delighted by any reading more for many days now. For it is full of eloquence, full of grace, full of love and benevolence; perhaps you were expecting me to say it was full of my own praises. Indeed, I was going to say this as well. For I am not so iron-hearted—or if you prefer it said this way, I am not so much a philosopher—that I am not delighted by the praises of friends. If they are true, they commend me to myself; if false, they commend the love and goodwill of my friends to me. I shall easily obtain permission from my philosophy to read your letters frequently and with pleasure, even in the parts where they praise me. But it is not so easy to appear sufficiently civilized or not ungrateful in repaying this duty of letters. For my mistress <note>original: "imperiosa dña" (imperiosa domina). Pico refers to his obsessive study of philosophy as a demanding mistress.</note> so distracts me, so demands her daily task, and finally so occupies all of me, that there is hardly anything of me left even for myself. But such is your humanity that you will even prefer the bad letters when we write, and you will take our silence in good part when we are quiet. Poliziano, our mutual delight, greets you. Farewell.

**Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Troilo Malvezzi, Greetings.** <note>Troilo Malvezzi was a Bolognese nobleman and scholar.</note>

**L**ittle book of yours regarding the brave <note>original: "Libell9 tu9 de fortib9" referring to his work 'De fortibus' or 'On Fortitude'</note> affected me with as much pleasure as usually affects one to whom the best fortune has befallen. I give you immense thanks for making me a participant in your late-night labors <note>original: "lucubrationū". This refers to scholarly work done by lamplight at night.</note>, especially in such works where both the subtlety of disputation and a manifold and varied knowledge of things easily appear. Of these, one holds the praise of intellect, the other of diligence. My trifles <note>original: "Nugas nostras". Pico often referred to his own poems or early writings as 'trifles'.</note> which you desire, I shall give to you shortly. It is uncertain, however, which is more unworthy: your occupation with the reading of them...

...whether a most distinguished legal consultant should be detained, or if I have kept a most dear friend in suspense for too long by my longing. Farewell and love me. Ferrara, May 29, 1482.

[Large red initial G] **Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Thadeo Ugolino, Greetings.**
I received your very welcome letters, full of love, faithfulness, and charity; not only because you remembered me, but because in them you friendly advise me to remember myself—that is, to remember the study of good things and the expectation I have given for my future work. Indeed, being conscious of my own weakness, I dare promise nothing even mediocre about myself. But He from whom all good comes, the most merciful Father of lights <note>original: "pater luminum," a reference to James 1:17</note>, just as He has previously given cause for men to hope for something from us, so He will give in the future, so that we do not hold such a well-conceived opinion in vain. I hasten to Rome, where we shall make trial of our studies, even if it brings danger. If we achieve anything, it is God's gift; to Him be the praise and thanks. If we fail, it is our own weakness; let it be attributed to us. For the rest, I am yours, as one who, because of the integrity of your life and character, has hardly granted the first place in loving you even to our friend Jerome <note>likely referring to Girolamo Savonarola, a close associate of Pico</note>. Farewell, from Fratta.

**Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Tommaso Mezzo, Greetings.**
[Large red initial S] I do not remember being more solidly delighted than recently, while I was reading your *Epyrota* <note>A Latin comedy written by Mezzo around 1483, modeled on classical styles</note>; it is undoubtedly a most witty little tale, challenging even the ancient comedies with its festive plot and learned style. For what shall I say of these modern works—plainly inept and tasteless—which easily reveal the ignorance of their authors? It was truly worthy to be dedicated to Hermolao Barbaro <note>A famous Venetian humanist and diplomat known for his translations of Aristotle</note>—I know not whether more to your name or mine? To him alone I think all literate men owe as much as they owe to antiquity itself. In that you did not deprive me of it, you acted according to your benevolence toward me, which has been well-perceived before. There is nothing I possess of such value that, if I were to send it to you as a gift in return, I would consider the favor fully repaid. As for the new comedy you promise me, I am already waiting with open mouth <note>original: "inhio," literally "to gape," expressing eager anticipation</note>. Nor is there anything I desire more than its arrival, except for your own visit to us. If I did not have to leave here within ten days (as I think you have learned from our location), I certainly would have obtained it from you by persistent entreaty. For one can gather from what you have written what future pleasantness there would be in your company, in your conversation, and in your living voice—which possesses a certain hidden energy <note>The term "energia" in humanist rhetoric refers to the power of language to vividly represent reality and move the listener</note> that affects the mind more deeply and delights it in wonderful ways, far outweighing all writings. But since this is not permitted, do not expect the material for a comedy from me in return. I prefer you to produce both from your own storehouse, so that Tommaso Mezzo tastes not like a "middle" man, but a whole one <note>Pico puns on the name "Mezzo," which means "middle" or "half" in Italian and Latin</note>. For I fear that by obeying you, the dullness of my talent would cause a loss. And from what I might add, the work would degenerate from the hand of the craftsman. In my own work, there is nothing that is not exposed, tasteless, foolish, or common. But these comedies require I know not what secret things: something biting, elegant, and sharp—qualities peculiar to your pleasant genius. Therefore, let the finished work be most welcome to me, so that since I cannot enjoy your presence in person, I may enjoy it in this way while you are absent. If, as I said before, my departure from here were not so swift, we would have surely cultivated both our guiding spirit and our intellect together for some days. Farewell.

**Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Marsilio Ficino, Greetings.**
[Large red initial N] You could not have asked for your Latin Mahomet <note>Referring to a Latin translation of the Quran or a related Islamic text which Ficino had lent to Pico</note> back at a more opportune time than now, when I hope soon to hear "Mahomet" himself speaking in his native tongue. For after I watched over the Hebrew language day and night for a full month, I have turned myself entirely to the study of Arabic and Chaldean <note>In the 15th century, "Chaldean" was the common term for Aramaic or Syriac</note>. I have no fear that I shall make less progress in them than I have in Hebrew, in which I can already compose a letter—not yet with great praise, but certainly without fault. See what the impulse of the soul can do! See what labor and diligence can achieve even where one's strengths are somewhat weak! Certain books in both languages have compelled me to learn the letters of the Arabs and Chaldeans...

...not by rashness or by chance, but by God’s design and through the favor of the divine power toward my studies, they have come into my hands. Listen to the titles—you will surely be stunned! These are Chaldean <note>original: "Chaldaici," referring to Aramaic or Syriac texts which Renaissance scholars often associated with ancient "Chaldean" wisdom</note> books. If they can be called books and not treasures! Among them are the oracles of Ezra, Zoroaster, and Melchior the Magi, in which those same works that are circulated among the Greeks in faulty and mutilated forms are here read in their complete and absolute state. 

Then, there is an interpretation by those Chaldean wise men—brief indeed and rugged, but full of mysteries. There is also a small book on the dogmas of Chaldean theology, as well as a divine and most rich commentary on many Greek and Chaldean matters. See, Marsilio, what unexpected riches have crept into my lap! Why should I not think that I have now obtained the Horn of Plenty <note>original: "Cornucopiae," the mythical horn of abundance</note>? 

But what of the Arabic works? Among these are the letters of Muhammad of Toledo <note>original: "Maumet Toletini"; likely referring to the 12th-century translator or a specific Islamic text known in Spain</note> and Abulgalé <note>Abu al-Ghalib</note>, who heard Averroës <note>the famous 12th-century Islamic philosopher from Cordoba</note> speak; and (something that will touch you more) many questions by a certain Adelard <note>likely Adelard of Bath, a 12th-century scholar who brought Arabic science to the West</note> who studied philosophy in Egypt under Ammonius <note>Ammonius Saccas, the legendary teacher of Plotinus</note>, the master of Plotinus.

->LETTERS<-

->Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Brother Battista of Mantua <note>Battista Mantuanus (1447–1516), also known as Spagnoli, was a famous Neo-Latin poet and Carmelite monk, later canonized as a saint. He was often called the "Christian Virgil."</note>, Carmelite. Greetings, etc.<-

**S**alutations, excellent father. For some time I have not written to you, but in the meantime I have read those divine and most holy poems which you have written. In them, there is such royal majesty and such splendor of eloquence that the words and the thoughts seem to contend with one another for the palm <note>original: "palmam," the classical symbol of victory or excellence awarded to the best competitor</note>. Happy are you, who are able to achieve the very best things you desire. Happy are we, to whom it has been granted not only to read what you have written, but also to love you, to see you, and to speak with you. 

Here is a rich subject for me, and one that would fill not just a letter but a full volume, if either my own weakness or your modesty <note>original: "pudor," referring to Battista's humble nature despite his widespread fame</note> would allow me to wander at length in praise of your poems. This one thing I will say: I am so delighted by the reading of your verses that almost daily, when either weariness or exhaustion takes hold of me, I am accustomed to withdraw into them as if into a garden.

I value a single [letter of yours] more than the entire library of either Sunadius <note>original: "Sunadii." This likely refers to a legendary collection or is a corruption of Eumenes of Pergamum, whose library rivaled Alexandria's.</note> or Ptolemy <note>A reference to the Great Library of Alexandria, founded by the Ptolemaic dynasty.</note>. For I am so far from neglecting the friendships of learned men that nothing is more a matter of concern or closer to my heart. I know indeed what place you claim for yourself among men of letters; since your letter was the clearest proof to me of your learning, erudition, and humanity <note>original: "humanitatis," referring to the 'studia humanitatis' or liberal arts that defined the Renaissance man.</note>. Wherefore, if I did not love you greatly, I would surely have forgotten my own nature and would act quite differently than I am accustomed.

I love you, therefore, uniquely, although I have never seen you. I love you so much from my soul that I love few others more deeply; so that, in short, while [meeting in person] might add to our familiarity, it could not add to my love for you. And if anything can be added, it will all come from your arrival here. You promised this arrival of your own accord in your letters, and I seek it as ardently as I desire it impatiently.

If you would procure for me John the Grammarian <note>John Philoponus (c. 490–570), a Byzantine philologist and theologian whose commentaries on Aristotle were highly sought after by Renaissance scholars.</note> on the *Physics* and Aristotle’s *Metaphysics*, you would bind me to you in perpetual service...

->LETTERS<-

...they come to be corrected and to be beaten, so that they may pay the penalty for their errors with both the fingernail <note>original: "ungue," referring to the classical 'test of the nail' (ad unguem), meaning to polish a work to perfect smoothness.</note> and the daggers <note>original: "obeliscis," the editorial marks used by ancient scholars to denote suspect or redundant passages.</note>. Therefore, show yourself to be a fair judge to them, not an unfair one—that is, be severe, not indulgent. For what is more unfair than to deceive a friend who expects everything from you? I am not of such a delicate spirit that I loathe another’s erasures; I do not seem so handsome to myself that I would either ignore or blame a censor. Indeed, perhaps neither you nor anyone would believe how much these works of mine do not satisfy me; for even in those things which please me more, I fear lest I be like that fellow Suffenus <note>A character from the poet Catullus, famous for being a terrible poet who was nonetheless convinced of his own brilliance.</note>. We are all too easily deceived and do not see the knapsack on our own back <note>A reference to Aesop’s fable: people carry their own faults in a bag behind them and others' faults in a bag in front, where they are easily seen.</note>. Therefore, do not deny your effort in this honorable and noble matter to a very dear friend, especially one who asks with such great zeal and from the bottom of his heart. If I were the kind of man who could return the favor in such a matter, I would not remain silent about that Greek proverb: that Lysippus used the work of Apelles, and Apelles that of Lysippus <note>Two of the greatest artists of antiquity—the sculptor Lysippus and the painter Apelles—who were said to have assisted one another to achieve perfection.</note> in turn. Farewell.

->Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Angelo Poliziano, Greetings.<-

**C**UM <note>Large red initial C</note> When I was in Florence in previous years, I left four love elegies with you which, as happens, I had fashioned almost as a boy for the sake of exercising my mind. They were indeed tasteless, unlearned, and light, easily showing the age and ignorance of the author. You, however, approved of them—not because of their merit, but because of your kindness, or even indulgence. And for that very reason, to prove you approved, you asked for copies; surely you were not unaware that such things are sharp stimulants to the minds of young men toward virtue, so that, enticed by the desire for praise, having tasted a little glory, they soon strive for higher things. For just as strength lies flat and cold in despair, there is no one who doubts that it is lifted up and set on fire by hope. But now, the defense of my age is taken away; and those errors which were previously signed off on <note>original: "subsignabatur," meaning endorsed or excused due to his youth</note> will now be turned into a fault against me, because I have not yet, in my more mature years, either cleaned them up better or deleted them. Therefore, if you love me, either send back to me those poems of mine which are with you, or tear them up, or give them to the fire. All those, worked on more carefully, and many others which have slipped from me during my leisure since I left that place, will soon be entrusted to your file <note>original: "limæ," a common metaphor for the painstaking polishing or refining of a literary work.</note>. Meanwhile, let those which cannot live without harm to a friend be condemned by a fatal vote <note>original: "capitali dānentur calculo," literally 'condemned by a capital pebble,' referring to the ancient practice of using black pebbles for a guilty verdict in a death penalty case.</note>. Furthermore, I would very much like your Epictetus, and what you have translated from Homer up to this day, and likewise what you have composed about Giuliano de' Medici in our native tongue <note>Italian</note>, and whatever else you have written in the Latin language, to be sent to me. I ask this of you most earnestly, for I desire it most impatiently. There is no reason for you to refuse because they are perhaps not yet brought to the 'navel' <note>original: "ad umbilicum," a Roman expression meaning 'to the end' or 'finished,' referring to the wooden rod at the center of a papyrus scroll.</note>; since, if this is your wish, I now announce and promise you that all these things will remain secret with me. Farewell.

->Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Marsilio Ficino, Greetings.<-

**M**EI <note>Large red initial M</note> It has always been my judgment, most learned Marsilio, that one should labor in no matter more than this: that we do not in any way degenerate through laziness or sloth from the nobility of the soul, by which (as Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary figure to whom the Hermetic corpus is attributed; a major influence on Renaissance Neoplatonism.</note> testifies) we are considered next after Jupiter <note>In the syncretic language of the Renaissance, "Jupiter" here refers to God or the highest Divine Mind.</note>. This has always been my chief concern: to acquire for myself the cultivation of the mind and the disciplines of the noble arts from wherever I could. Although this intention of mine has been most constant since childhood, your exhortations greatly excited and inflamed me when I was with you in previous years; never have I more ardently addicted myself entirely to letters from that day to this. I have now spent three years, Marsilio, among the Peripatetics <note>The followers of Aristotle.</note>, nor have I omitted anything, as far as I was able, so that I might be admitted into the Aristotelian house as one not unworthy of their family. Although I have not achieved this in abundance—since I am barely in the vestibule—I have nevertheless proceeded far enough that I would not hesitate to claim for myself the name of a student, if not of the learned and erudite (which my age does not yet allow). But since...

It has always been your opinion, as well as that of the most learned men, that whoever blends Academic <note>The "Academic" school refers to the teachings of Plato, named after the Academy where he taught in Athens.</note> thought with Peripatetic <note>The "Peripatetics" were the followers of Aristotle, so named because Aristotle was said to have walked (*peripatētikos*) about the Lyceum while lecturing.</note> philosophy would hold both sects more correctly and more richly. I have come to believe that I should undertake this province <note>original: "provinciam," here meaning a specific field of duty or a scholarly mission.</note> myself, so that now, through the strength of my own natural talent, and with as much assiduity and diligence as I can manage, I might compare Plato with Aristotle, and in turn, through alternating studies, compare Aristotle with Plato.

But just as I previously needed you as a guide, so now I have need of you as a helper. It will be a mark of your kindness and your goodwill toward me not to fail my purpose—especially one so honorable and noble. I believe you will have fulfilled this most abundantly if you send me your book *On the Immortality of Souls* <note>original: "de immortalitate animorum." This refers to Ficino's monumental work, the *Theologia Platonica* (Platonic Theology), which was a key text of the Renaissance attempting to prove the soul's immortality through Platonic philosophy.</note>. With that work acting as a kind of pathfinder, I am confident that I shall make progress in the Platonic discipline as I hope. For who is superior to Ficino? In whom, if true...

<note>A large, decorative red initial M contains a smaller letter 'm' within its body, featuring an ornamental flourish extending to the left margin.</note> **I** remember when I was deliberating which of Italy’s schools <term>schools (gymnasiis): referring to universities or centers of higher learning, styled after the classical Greek gymnasion.</term> I should choose as my home for the study of philosophy <note>original: "phiæ studia," an abbreviation for "philosophiae studia."</note>. ### ->MIRANDOLA<-

Would it not be ungenerous <term>ungenerous (illiberale): in the classical sense, this refers to behavior that is "un-free" or beneath the dignity of a nobleman or a free citizen.</term>, or not at all befitting a prince, to make the study of wisdom <note>original: "studium sapientiae"</note> anything but un-mercenary? Who could bear or hear of such things with a calm mind? Certainly, he is never a philosopher who is a philosopher only so that he might one day either be able to, or choose not to, philosophize. Such a man has practiced trade <note>original: "mercaturam," referring to commerce or business conducted for profit.</note>, not philosophy. 

You write that the time is approaching for me to give myself over to one of the highest princes of Italy. You do not yet know the opinion that philosophers hold of themselves: following Horace <note>Pico references the Roman poet Horace (65–8 BCE), specifically his *Epistles* (I.1.106–107), which describe the wise man as a "king of kings," second only to Jupiter.</note>, they consider themselves the **kings of kings**; they do not know how to endure the whims of others or to serve. They dwell within themselves, and content with their own tranquility of mind, they are sufficient unto themselves. They seek nothing outside of themselves; those things which are held in honor by the common crowd are without honor to them. And they utterly neglect and despise whatever human lust thirsts for or ambition sighs after. 

This is something that must be done without doubt by everyone, but especially by those to whom Fortune has so indulged herself that they might live not only elegantly and comfortably, but...

## Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to his nephew Gianfrancesco, Health.

Your letter was most pleasing to me: not only because I had heard nothing of you for a long time: but also because it signified things to me in which I am wonderfully delighted: because I do not doubt those same things are pleasing to you and most pleasing to God. You also should not doubt, if only you proceed in the way you have begun, that your reward will be plentiful in heaven. I do not yet have it sufficiently explored whether I should go to Rome or not. And as much as I can follow by conjecture, I believe it will rather be the case that I must go there; you know the cause. As soon as I have this for certain, I will make you more certain, lest if you happen to come here (which otherwise I would greatly desire) you either do not find me here, or I departing immediately, you must return to your homeland. In the meantime you can be at home, unless you think otherwise. But remember also that you have a wife to whom you owe your body no differently than you owe your soul to God himself: Her desire must be satisfied in some part: and you must consider what she, from the habit of the body and from age, either desires or is able to desire; and what from shame or virtue she does not ask. For why should one be ashamed to write these things which Paul the Apostle also writes? <note>Pico alludes to 1 Corinthians 7:4: "The husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife does."</note> There is almost no matter in which I suspect you could err more: And indeed our men are very much deceived who think their wives are bound and devoted to them, but they owe nothing to their wives: But they think they can decide whatever they judge fit about themselves at their own discretion. Finally, you cannot be entirely your own, since once subjecting yourself to the laws of marriage, you wished to be your wife's; you can nevertheless be entirely God's, whom you also deserve while you obey his law for yourself...

Once I have untangled myself from these bundles of Greek books, I will come to Ferrara immediately. In the meantime, I am applying myself to sacred literature, and especially to the reading of the Gospels, which repeatedly draws the soul toward God; from whom both the world and that demon do not cease, day and night, to lead it away with allurements here and deceptions there. **Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to his dear Jacopo Antiquario, greetings.**

<note>A large red initial **I** begins this letter.</note> **Among** the pleasures I most enjoyed when I was in Florence from the company of Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), a brilliant Renaissance poet and scholar who was a very close friend of Pico.</note>—a man, in my opinion, the most learned of our age—it was no small thing that he would immediately give me your letters to read, those grave and always elegant ones, as soon as he received them. I was greatly delighted in them by a certain singular wisdom, for which you are commended by the most prudent men even in handling great affairs and business, and by the refinement and restraint of your speech. Furthermore, because in some of them you made honorable mention of us, your letters not only pleased me, but in them I also pleased myself. That is, with my conscience giving way to the testimony of such a man, thinking that he was not at all hiding what he felt; even if my conscience betrayed itself, it was not fighting very hard and was almost willing to be deceived.

Thus I was bound to you by a double name: on one side by your virtue, and on the other by the kindness, not just duty, so often bestowed upon us. I thought more than once of giving you thanks by letter, lest perhaps I should be thought ungrateful or unrefined toward you. But since you and our Poliziano were carrying out a most beautiful exchange of letters between you, I did not want the intrusive Magpie <note>original: "Pica." A play on his own name, Pico, and the "Pica" or magpie, known for its harsh chattering.</note> to screech at the Muses, or like a poorly singing Goose, to disturb the swans singing to one another. Otherwise, I knew my mind was open to you through our Poliziano; then, conscious of my own speechlessness, I used him as a most eloquent interpreter.

Now your letters have been sent to us by him, which you recently gave to Riccio, a youth of exceptional talent; in these you attribute so much to me that I would not dare to hope for it, much less believe I deserve it. The magnitude of your kindness has broken my silence—which until now was perhaps uncivil, though certainly not proud—nor could I fail to give you immortal thanks. This is not because you overwhelm me with immoderate praise, which I do not recognize as my own, but because you love me so much that your judgment, otherwise constant and robust, has wavered so greatly under the weight of love for us. I owe you, therefore, more than I could pay, or you could easily believe; nor is there anything so arduous or difficult that I would not do for your dignity as I would for my own safety. You who until now possessed me through Poliziano, now indeed, with nothing changed in the matter, you will find the name of Pico, which was underneath, revealed for your own reasons. Farewell. From the territory of Ferrara, 28 June 1494.

**To the excellent and most learned man, Master Jacopo Antiquario, as if to a father.**
**Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to Andrea Corneo, sends many greetings.**

**Giovanni Pico of Mirandola to the Reverend Cardinal [S.]**

<note>A large red initial **M** (though the OCR reads A, the context of "Mattheus" suggests a large initial for the start of the paragraph) begins this letter.</note> **Our** Mattheus, a most dutiful man, has given me your warmest greetings in your name, and has most aptly declared with what love and goodwill you regard me. Therefore, how much I rejoice for myself, or how much I owe to you, I cannot explain, nor even fully conceive. Certainly, I owe you all the more because you owe me nothing at all. 

Nor are those things so great or so many which Mattheus and my other friends have reported, estimating me out of affection rather than judgment. But such as I am, or however great, allow me also to be among all those who—to say nothing of the rest—cultivate and admire your virtues, through which one may see in you both that which surpasses antiquity and that which cannot be surpassed by posterity. I would say this deservedly, since in you nothing is found wanting that is placed in honor, or prudence, or learning. This one thing ought to be desired by all: that through you someday, according to Plato’s wish, supreme power may be joined with supreme wisdom. <note>A reference to Plato's *Republic*, which argues that the world will only know peace when "philosophers become kings or kings become philosophers."</note> But these things come from God. In the meantime, I seek and ask this of you: that you provide me an occasion—not for returning thanks (for there is no place for that, either because of your greatness or my own smallness)—but for testifying to my spirit toward you, and for witnessing my loyalty and devotion. You will find Giovanni Pico a man devoted and dedicated to you beyond all opinion. You cannot promise yourself more from him, but you can use all those things, such as they are, which are in him; when you use them, you will bring something of your own splendor to them. They will become great when they begin to be yours, for while they are mine, they cannot be great. Farewell.

**Giovanni Pico della Mirandola to Andrea Corneo, greetings.**
->[Large red initial E]<-ven if I have sent letters to you either rarely or never, I have nevertheless thought of you and your affairs either often or always. But I do not wish to sell you hope, nor will I write to you what I might do for your benefit until I can write what I have accomplished. But if that should never happen, through your misfortune or mine, I prefer you to believe that I have labored at nothing more than your affairs, even if in vain. But perhaps fortune will be more joyful for you than either hope itself or fortune is accustomed to be. There is no reason for your Laura to wait for our poems; for they have been called back to the anvil to be more closely reshaped, nor do they dare to go out into public with the face they now have. However, the pressing and urgent reason for a new work I have in hand at the urging of **Lorenzo de' Medici** delays their correction. In this work, I am not only illuminating the Davidic hymns <note>The Psalms.</note> with a longer interpretation, but since those which the Church chants were translated by the Seventy <note>original: "a. lxx. uersi sunt," referring to the Septuagint, the Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note>—and the Hebrews prove that translation to be unfaithful in more than six hundred places—I, relying on the properties of **Hebrew and Chaldaic** <note>Aramaic.</note> literature, both assert and defend them against every calumny of the Jews for the integrity of their meanings. There is nothing else to write, except that you should commend me in no ordinary way to Hermolao <note>Hermolao Barbaro (1454–1493), a famous Venetian humanist.</note> as often as you see the man. Likewise, see that the learned and grave man Jacopo Volaterrano <note>Jacopo Gherardi of Volterra (1434–1516), a papal secretary and historian.</note> understands that he is vehemently loved by me; if I ever obtain from him the letters of **Symmachus** <note>A late 4th-century Roman statesman known for his refined Latin correspondence.</note> for a few days until they are transcribed, he will bind me to him by a perpetual favor. Farewell. 1489.

### PICO DELLA MIRANDOLA

...hence it might well inaugurate our friendship. I wanted to signify to you what I was feeling. I would certainly do this much more richly if I had here those friends of mine above all other men—I mean my books—whom I might consult; but they have already preceded me to Rome, like forerunners going before their master. And I myself, now wearing my traveling hat <note>original: "petasatus" — referring to the *petasos*, a broad-brimmed, low-crowned hat worn by travelers in antiquity.</note> and boots <note>original: "caligatus" — wearing the *caliga*, a heavy military or traveling boot; here used to signify he is ready for the road.</note>, being fully prepared for the journey <note>original: "in procinctu" — a Roman military idiom for being girded and ready for immediate action or departure.</note>, have sent these words to you as familiarly as they were written in haste. 

As to what you ask regarding Josephus <note>Flavius Josephus (c. 37–100 AD), the Romano-Jewish historian whose works were vital for Renaissance scholars.</note>, you should know that the true Josephus is not found among the Hebrews. Instead, there is an "epitome" of Josephus—that is, a certain abridgment—in which many things are fabricated. And regarding what is read there concerning the ten tribes <note>The "Lost Tribes of Israel" who were exiled by the Assyrians.</note> who did not return by right of recovery <note>original: "postliminio" — a legal term regarding the restoration of rights to those returning from exile or captivity.</note> after the Babylonian captivity, several Hebrews <note>Pico frequently consulted with Jewish scholars and rabbis during his studies of Hebrew and Kabbalah.</note> have confessed to me that those accounts are spurious and adulterated. 

Therefore, no credit at all should be given to their version of Josephus. In the Greek Josephus, I know there are certain passages that make honorable mention of Christ and the faith; but whether these are entirely the same as those read in the Latin manuscripts, I do not...

<meta>This page continues the philosophical and spiritual counsel of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. Following his previous discussion on scholarly pursuits and his journey to Rome, he now addresses the spiritual trials of the scholar and the Christian, specifically how to handle public criticism and the "folly" of the cross.</meta>

**EPISTLES**

...in heaven, when men have spoken evil of us and said all manner of evil against us falsely for his sake. If you do not know it, this is apostolic dignity: to be held worthy of being defamed by the impious for the sake of the Gospel's name. When we read of the apostles in Luke <note>Refers to the Book of Acts 5:41, attributed to the Evangelist Luke.</note> rejoicing as they departed from the presence of the council because they were considered worthy to suffer insults for the name of Jesus. Therefore, let us also rejoice if we are worthy of such great glory before God: that his glory might be made manifest in our disgrace. 

And if we suffer anything harsh or troublesome from the world, let that most sweet voice of the Lord console us: "If the world hates you, know that it hated me before you." <note>original: "Si uos mundus odio habet scito te quia priorem me uobis odio habuit." — John 15:18.</note> If the world hated him through whom the world was made, how much more should we, the most vile of little men? <note>original: "homuntiones" — a diminutive used to emphasize human insignificance compared to the divine.</note> And if we consider our own crimes, we are most worthy of all insults; even if someone disparages or speaks ill of us, we should bear it so poorly that we do not begin to act wickedly ourselves simply because he speaks ill of us. 

Let us rather receive these insults eagerly; and if it is not our good fortune to endure lashes, chains, prisons, and swords for the sake of virtue and truth, as our heroes <note>A reference to the early Christian martyrs.</note> once did, let us consider it a job well done if we suffer at least the taunts of wicked men, their detractions, and their hatred. Let it not be that, with every opportunity for merit taken away, no hope of a reward remains. If men praise you for living well, then this virtue of yours—insofar as it is virtue—makes you like Christ; but insofar as it is praised, it makes you unlike him, who received from men as the reward for his virtue the death of the cross. Because of this, as the Apostle says, God has exalted him and given him a name that is above every name. 

It is therefore more desirable to be crucified by the world so that you may be exalted by God, than to be exalted by the world so that you may be judged by God. For the former is crucified unto life, while the latter is exalted unto glory; the former exalts unto a fall, the while the latter judges unto Gehenna <note>term: Gehenna — a historical valley in Jerusalem used as a metaphor for a place of fiery torment or Hell.</note>. Finally, if the world applauds you, it can hardly happen that virtue—which, being directed entirely upward, ought to have only God as the one it pleases—does not incline itself for a moment toward the favor of men who are applauding it. And even if it does not lose its integrity, it nonetheless loses part of its reward; for when the reward begins to be paid on earth, where all things are small, it will be less in heaven, where all things are immense. 

Fortunate are the insults that keep us safe, lest the flower of justice wither by the poisonous breath of vainglory, or our wages for eternity be diminished by the empty contract of popular rumor. Let us embrace these insults, my son, and with a most holy ambition let us, as faithful servants, take pride in the sole ignominy of the Lord's cross. "We preach," says Paul, "Christ crucified: a stumbling block to the Hebrews and foolishness to the Gentiles; but to us, the power of God and the wisdom of God." <note>1 Corinthians 1:23-24.</note> This wisdom of the world is foolishness before God, and that foolishness of Christ is that which conquers the wisdom of the world, through which it pleased God to save those who believe. 

If you do not doubt that those who disparage your virtue are insane, and that they call the Christian life—which is to say, wisdom—madness, then consider how great your own madness would be to be moved from the path of a right life by the judgment of the insane. Since every error should be removed by correction, not increased by imitation, let them gape, let them bark, and let them yap; you, proceed on the journey you have begun without fear. Consider how much you owe to God because of their wickedness and misery—He who illuminated you while you were sitting in the shadow of death, and translated you from the company of those who, in the thickest darkness, wander here and there like raving madmen without a leader, and associated you with the children of light. 

Let that most sweet voice of the Lord sound always in your ears: "Let the dead bury their own dead; you, follow me." <note>Matthew 8:22.</note> For they are dead who do not live for God, and in this space of temporary death, they most laboriously acquire eternal death for themselves. If you ask them where they are going, to what end they direct their studies, works, and cares—in short, what goal they have set for themselves in the attainment of which they will be happy—they will either have nothing at all to answer, or they will speak words that are self-contradictory and at odds with themselves, like the ravings of fanatics. For they do not know...

He encourages his correspondent to follow the "folly" of the cross rather than seeking the fleeting approval of the world.</summary>

# **EPISTLES**

...I urge you to turn your mind to this: ponder day and night how much you owe to Him who has enriched you to such an extent that you will never be able to repay or even calculate the value of what you possess. Consider how powerful He is, He who willed that you should be capable of such things; consider how much He loves you, He who chose you for Himself out of so many thousands—you, who as a mere boy almost surpassed old men, and who, not yet a youth, turned circles of learned men to admiration of your learning. <note>Gianfrancesco, like his uncle Giovanni Pico, was a child prodigy whose intellect astonished the older humanists of the Italian Renaissance.</note> Unless you see this, and unless you value it, I affirm to you right now and openly proclaim: you are not yet as great as you truly are. What I long ago promised myself about you, and still promise, is immense and infinite; but neither speech nor public praise can keep pace with my preconceived opinion of you. 

I act as people usually do: the more they admire someone and wish to explain what they feel, the less they achieve what they desire; so that although they conceive something great in their mind, words fail them, and they seem to have been able to struggle with the thought rather than express it. Therefore, do not listen to these words which I write about you and put forth publicly; rather, understand those things which I speak of you inwardly, alone and in silence—things so much greater (by Hercules!) than this speech, just as thought is greater than words. 

Greet Marsilio <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the priest and philosopher who led the Platonic Academy in Florence and translated Plato's works into Latin.</note> and your friend Salviati. Regarding Poliziano, <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), one of the greatest poets and scholars of the age.</note> there is no need for you to trouble yourself, for I hear he will be with me shortly. Nothing more pleasant could have happened to me in this whole embassy. I am so glad that the library there <note>The Laurentian Library in Florence, which Lorenzo de' Medici was aggressively expanding with rare manuscripts.</note> is being built up every day to be larger and more ornate that nothing could surpass my joy. Literature owes much to the Florentines; and among the Florentines, it owes much to the Medici; and among the Medici, it owes much to Lorenzo, <note>Lorenzo de' Medici, "the Magnificent" (1449–1492), the de facto ruler of Florence and a legendary patron of the arts.</note> who fosters this ancestral glory of his family with no less care than he does the republic, which he has the right to administer and establish. Farewell. From Milan, on the Kalends of January [January 1st], 1488. <note>original: "Mcccc lxxxxyii" — likely a transcription error for 1488 or 1489, years when Barbaro served as the Venetian ambassador to Milan.</note>

<meta>This page continues the correspondence of the Venetian humanist Ermolao Barbaro. # **EPISTLES**

...you will equip all the volumes of that philosopher <note>referring to Aristotle, whose works Barbaro spent much of his life translating and correcting</note> according to my manly ability. For there are some things in the *Problems* and in the *History of Animals* that desire clarity and light; I am prepared to pass through those matters cursorily, by the light of a brief annotation. Furthermore, I intend to undertake nothing new for my whole life; for I must suppress this greed—or rather, this persistence of my intellect—lest it wish to be held as rectifiable and fertile, appearing daily to be more laborious and ambitious. I daily experience more truly than is usually said that to embrace all things and to embrace nothing are equal. Farewell. From Milan, October 21, 1488.

**Ermolao Barbaro to Giovanni Pico, Greetings.**

**I** read your *Hexameron* <note>original: "Exameron"; Pico's work is actually titled the *Heptaplus*, a seven-fold narration of the six days of Genesis</note> three days ago, delivered to us by the effort of Salviati, so greedily that I swallowed it whole on the very first day, and that not entirely without catching my breath. Three things in it delight me wonderfully: first, that your speech teaches and moves; a quality which it is agreed the ancient theologians observed in the sacred rites of Isis, and the Pythagoreans and Platonists in natural philosophy, while more recent scholars <note>original: "recentioribus," likely referring to the dry style of the medieval Scholastics</note> merely sweat in their teaching. The second is that in such a great abundance of matter and such impunity for plundering, you have such chaste and innocent hands that in this genre of writing, you seem to have followed yourself and no other. This is now common neither with the ancients nor with the moderns, but is peculiar and your own; in which (to open my feeling to you) I am so affected that, since those predecessors did not say what you have said, they seem to me to have said almost nothing. The third is that I see you are initiated into the mysteries not so much of Aristotle as of Plato and his sects, and have brought full draughts from there into this midnight study. I omit how many excellent things from Plotinus you have touched upon cursorily and elegantly, so that you seem not so much to have read but to have mastered by heart almost whatever his fifty-four volumes, arranged into six sets of nine <note>referring to the *Enneads* of Plotinus, edited by Porphyry</note>, contain. Nor can I pass over the fact that you carry yourself as a middle-man between the new and the old theologians, so that you neither hate the simple majesty of the former, nor are you carried away by the ambitious subtlety of the latter. Thus it happens that while you wish to imitate the one, and are able to imitate the other, you have plucked the best of both kinds—which we hope you will do also in your exposition of the Davidic poems <note>the Psalms</note>. Farewell. From Venice, September 4, 1489.

**Ermolao Barbaro to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, Greetings.**

**G**reetings, most refined Mirandola. Indeed, I speak of you so willingly everywhere that I do nothing with greater pleasure; not only because nothing (as Plato says) is more pleasant to hear than the truth, but also because, as Palemo says, it is much more pleasant to speak true things than to hear them. It happens that with no labor—as is often found in Aeschylus, Menander, and Euripides—the truth comes forth even when not sought; it is often expressed even against one's will, by no interrogations but by its own power alone. This is that "tyranny" <note>the "tyranny of truth," a classical concept where truth compels the speaker despite themselves</note> which you, following your own sincerity, interpret as humanity and goodness; and by Hercules, you are already so great that whoever does not praise you detracts from their own judgment and reputation. They act in their own interest, consult their own reasons, and redeem their own fame, who favor and desire yours. There are many names in your ledger that you do not know your creditors owe you; many owe the counsel of Prodicus... <note>Prodicus was a Greek sophist known for his linguistic precision and moral parables.</note>

...and living in this age, he joins himself most closely to the ranks of Dionysius, Hilary, John of Damascus, Augustine, Ambrose, Jerome <note>These are the "Church Fathers," the influential early Christian theologians whose works formed the basis of Western and Eastern doctrine</note>, and those other most holy and rare men of old. All posterity shall admire him once envy has fallen silent and the slow passage of time has established his authority.

O supreme God, what might we expect him to produce if a lifespan equal to his great spirit is granted to him? For even in "his first beard" <note>original: "prima barba"; a classical idiom referring to his extreme youth, as Giovanni Pico was famously a child prodigy and still in his twenties</note>, he has already achieved that for which antiquity marvels at Origen and Jerome: he is already most highly learned in both Latin and Greek literature, nor is he ignorant of Hebrew. Furthermore, in the sacred scriptures he is truly so capable that it is scarcely believable that any other man could achieve as much. Indeed, we await with great delight his upcoming work on the Psalms and the songs of David, which he has long been handling, interpreting, and explaining. He has searched with infinite labor through everything that the Latin, Greek, and Hebrew writers have left recorded on these subjects; toward which business...

**LETTERS**

**From the same, a little further below:**

**B**ut if there is anyone from that flock who can grasp those things which you have said—endowed with such elegance, so many rhetorical lights, and so many emblems <note>In this context, "emblems" refers to ornate or symbolic language that illustrates a deeper truth</note> that dazzle the eyes of those who approach them—add to this so many provocative <note>original: "prurientes"; literally "itching," here meaning thoughts that stimulate or prick the mind</note> sentences, so many histories and examples of more remote learning, like little flowers and <margin>wine</margin> at which if there are those among them who are little less than asses—I was going to say <term>unrefined</term> <note>original: "αμουσοί" (amousoi); a Greek term meaning "without the Muses," used to describe those lacking in culture, taste, or education</note>—they only twitch their ears; the rest flee, reject, and detest them; and so forth.

I have run through the work as much as was permitted, amidst heat and dust <note>A common humanist trope suggesting he read the work while traveling or during a busy, arduous period</note>. It is a birth truly worthy of a divine and admirable genius; indeed, the harvest and the material of the work do not demand a hurried and hastily prepared opinion. <meta>This page continues a letter addressed to Giorgio Antonio Salviati regarding Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, then transitions into a new letter from the humanist educator Battista Guarino to Pico himself. # LETTERS

...the reward of your testimony, which I judge to be more pleasing to me. I know how much I ought to value being loved and praised by that man in whom the rewards of learning and character have converged with the highest glory of our age. It is more fitting to admire his *Heptaplus* <note>Pico’s *Heptaplus* (1489) is a mystical, seven-fold commentary on the Book of Genesis. The author suggests the work is so profound it is beyond human critique.</note> than to judge it. That style of writing delights me wonderfully: for I see no more fertile crop of both doctrine and erudition than from the sacred scriptures. 

But that bold stroke is successful in very few, among whom is my Pico. Greet him in my name as much as you can; or rather, for this very reason he is most dear to me: because I love him vehemently. You, my Salviati <note>Giorgio Antonio Salviati, a Florentine scholar and diplomat who moved in the same circles as Pico and Poliziano</note>, shall promise yourself as much from me as is fitting to be provided by a most friendly and benevolent man. 

Farewell. Milan, October 25, 1489.

<meta>This page continues the letter from the humanist educator Battista Guarino to Roberto Salviati, discussing the arrival and impact of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola’s work, the *Heptaplus*. Guarino uses an extended metaphor of a mystical journey through the spheres of the universe to describe the experience of reading Pico's text.</meta>

# LETTERS

...are greater and worthy of greater admiration. For, raised up from the waters—I know not whether by swan's feathers, or by the wings of Daedalus or Pegasus—I have arrived through all the air, through all the ether, to the very highest peak of corruptible things, with that man <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</note> not so much leading me as carrying me along. It is a matter truly worthy of the utmost amazement: to have traversed this lower and elemental world. But it is a far greater thing to have reached the celestial world, and to have penetrated first the sphere of the Moon, then that of Mercury, and next that of Venus; to have seen the rays of the Sun; to have felt the heat of Mars; and finally to have known both the health-giving rays of Jupiter and the heavy rays of Saturn. Then, finally, to have observed that eighth sphere <note>The "firmament" or the sphere of the fixed stars in the Ptolemaic geocentric model</note> shining with burning stars, and to have noticed that all these heavens revolve not with a simple and uniform motion, but with a triple and triform motion; yet who is unaware that all these things fall within our senses? 

But he gave me that third world <note>In Pico’s cosmology, the three worlds are the elemental (Earth), the celestial (the planets/stars), and the supercelestial (the angelic or intellectual realm).</note> to fly through in such a way that, with all senses lulled to sleep (for these hinder rather than help such an inspection), I might have looked upon it and perceived it with the mind alone—for by the mind alone are such great spaces traversed. But its sharpness, like an owl going blind at the rays of the sun, could not endure the splendor. Therefore, whatever in this kind of pilgrimage—or to speak more truly, in this return to the homeland—either lay hidden from me or escaped my eyes, the guide himself is not to blame, if he to whom the way was being shown is easily caught in fault. For the divine genius of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola both undertakes and guarantees that he will demonstrate everything.

What is there then, my Robert <note>Roberto Salviati, the recipient of this letter</note>, that I should not confess I owe to you, having been enriched by you with such a great gift? As soon as I began to taste it, such a great greed was immediately excited in me, and such a love of feasting from the sweetness of the food, that, impatient of any delay, I did not entrust anything to be chewed by the jaws, but like a most ravenous steer, I swallowed everything whole. But when, through continued reading, I had finished the whole matter, and like that same beast, having gathered it into my stomach, I had called it back to my mouth to ruminate <note>A common humanist metaphor comparing the deep study of a text to a cow chewing the cud</note> more diligently—then indeed a wondrous sweetness appeared; then such amazement as never before stole over me. 

But you will say: Did you not admire the man's learning before? I did indeed admire it: that he was so engaged in all disciplines that he seemed to excel in each one. No topic escaped him when debating in physics or mathematics; and in metaphysics and in every kind of theology—whether you seek that which was stirred up by Mercury <note>original: "a Mercurio excitata"; a reference to Hermes Trismegistus and the Hermetic tradition</note> and brought to perfection by Plato, or our own Christian theology, the most excellent and truest of all—these our ages and several before have seen nothing more learned than him. But lest you think (a fault which many of our people have labored under) that he separated eloquence from wisdom: does he not describe everything most weightily, most abundantly, and furthermore most ornately, so that he can now, by his own best right, be joined with those ancient orators? These things, then, I admired about him until now, thinking that nothing could be added to such an invention. But having read his *Heptaplus*, I began to admire those former things even more. 

Therefore, I would believe it happened neither by chance nor by some luck, but by God’s command, that this divine man emerged distinguished by these three names. For "John" <note>original: "Ioannes"</note> is interpreted as "the grace of the Lord," or "in whom there is grace," or "to whom a gift has been made by God." Who would not see that he could not have attained the learning he has without the special and greatest grace of God? In the "woodpecker" <note>original: "pico"; Guarino is punning on Pico's family name and the Latin word for woodpecker, *picus*</note>, however, we know there is such hardness of beak and strength of head that you can find no wood so bony (so to speak) or so stony that this bird does not bore through it, and in it artfully excavate a hiding place where it may retreat and build a nest. In the same way, nothing in all disciplines is so difficult for human intellect to know that he has not, by striking the hardest parts, penetrated it, built a nest, hatched his young, and brought them forth. Since indeed all things in this man are to be wondered at, who would not think he should be called "Mirandula" <note>Punning on his title and the Latin *mirandus*, meaning "wonderful" or "to be wondered at"</note>? Therefore, just as I congratulate you, who enjoy his constant friendship, so I congratulate myself...

<meta>This page continues the praise of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, shifting from Battista Guarino's letter to Roberto Salviati into a new letter from the humanist Alessandro Cortesi to Pico himself. The text emphasizes Pico's unique ability to harmonize ancient philosophy with Christian theology.</meta>

# LETTERS

I grieve, I say, because I consider myself unhappy in this: that due to my many and necessary occupations, I am not permitted to cling to him day and night, as I most ardently desire. For if it were permitted, I would never depart from the side—not of an old man, but of a youth—of that youth, I say, in whom is all the wisdom and all the learning of old age and gray hair <note>A common humanist trope: the *puer senex*, or "old-souled youth," possessing wisdom beyond his years.</note>. You, however, to whom fortune has offered far greater leisure, and to whom nature has granted an excellent intellect—which your continuous exercise and frequent practice in all the liberal arts have subsequently increased and polished—enjoy this good that has fallen to you from heaven. Drink from this most fertile fountain, or rather, this immense ocean; and drink as much as can suffice to quench not only your present thirst, but all future thirst as well. Consider, then, calculate, and debate with yourself how few mortals such a great good has ever happened to. Alexander the Great boasted merely of having lived in the times of the philosopher Aristotle. But to you, by your most happy lot, it has been granted to live familiarly with Aristotle and Plato at the same time—and such an Aristotle and Plato that in them, besides the ancient doctrine of the Academics and Peripatetics, we see shining again our Pauls, Johns, Dionysii, Augustines, Jeromes, Thomases, and other lights of this kind <note>This refers to Pico’s famous "syncretism," his attempt to prove that the philosophies of Plato and Aristotle were compatible with each other and with Christian theology (represented here by the Apostles and Church Fathers).</note>. Therefore, conclude from these things how much you ought to love either yourself or him, best Roberto; for fortune herself has offered this to you, and you, by your own prudence, have succeeded in making yourself most familiar to this man. Farewell. November 22nd. <note>original: "x. Kalen. Decembris," the tenth day before the Kalends of December.</note>

### Alessandro Cortesi to his friend Pico, greetings.

**E**ver in my whole life have I received greater pleasure than recently from your letter; and although I had believed everything highest of you, you have nevertheless surpassed (I confess) my opinion. You have surpassed it so much that I now consider the boundaries of your glory narrow, even though it is spread far and wide. Let us speak more aptly and far from flattery, from which illustrious minds have always recoiled: What is in you that is not extraordinary? What is not worthy of admiration? Individual qualities could bring honor to anyone, yet in you they have all been gathered together. From everyone (if I may say so), you alone have snatched away all the Graces <note>original: "veneres," referring to the charms or qualities of Venus.</note>. And although your ancestors reached a height where only those born of their blood could easily arrive, you have turned out so great that you seem to return more honor to them than you received. While old age brings authority to others, youth extols your dignity, and what others conquered only by the passage of time, you have surpassed by invincible virtue. 

In my judgment, you are placed beyond all risk of genius <note>That is, his talent is so great it is beyond doubt or gamble.</note>, and though I search through Greek panegyrics, I find no one to whom I may deservedly compare you; in short, though one may imagine that some equal to you once existed, it is not possible to see one in this time. Let all men of talent forgive me: they are all greatly surpassed by this one Pico. Nature's kindness has so cherished him that it must seem a wonder to her as well that such an abundance of all praises has been gathered into one man. Why do you blush? Or do you think I am lying? I will indeed yield if you attribute this to love, which is painted blind. 

But I have more reliable witnesses than my friend Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), the renowned humanist scholar and poet who was a close friend of Pico.</note>, who is deceived only in his opinion of me. And if he, as I hear, daily increases his riches of gold no less than those of speech, I congratulate him as much as I thank him; would that he might possess the horn of plenty, since he is mindful of neither his guest nor our old friendship. Concerning Pucci <note>Likely a member of the influential Pucci family of Florence.</note>, the most affectionate of men, I shall write another time; who would not wish to be indebted to him? But I delay you too long while you are intent on higher studies. Even Marsilio Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499), the leader of the Platonic Academy in Florence and a central figure in the Renaissance.</note>, the prince of philosophers of our age, I see laughing at these trifles—and why should he not laugh, he who weighs all mortal things no less than he despises them? O, would that someone might place me in your academy and cover me with the vast shade of its branches! Especially because Mars alone possesses this sky; no honor is worthy of the plow; the fields lie neglected since the farmers have been led away; and curved sickles are turned into stiff swords <note>Cortesi is quoting Virgil’s *Georgics* (1.506-508) to describe the contemporary state of war and political unrest in Italy.</note>. But we are content with this Cato <note>A reference to a stern or virtuous figure, likely referring to Pico himself or another mutual friend.</note>. You, in turn, gather the fruit of my love from these trifles, and do not think it a small thing to be loved by me, but return the favor. For the longing for you... <note>The text breaks off here.</note>

<meta>This page continues the letter from Girolamo Donato to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. Donato is praising Pico's rare ability to combine deep scholarship (erudition) with beautiful expression (eloquence), a combination he argues is rarely found in a single individual, even among the greatest figures of antiquity.</meta>

# LETTERS

...[ele]gantly <note>original: "ganter," the conclusion of the word *eleganter* from the preceding page.</note> you draw forth the sentiments of your mind, so that the immortal gods seem to have granted to you alone what they have granted to very few indeed: namely, to think the best thoughts and to say the best things. And you encompass this no less in verse than in prose speech. Livy <note>Titus Livius, the Roman historian.</note> and Homer write, almost by divine inspiration, that the gods have not bestowed all gifts upon any one man. 

From this it follows that we often read of some who flourished by being outstanding in eloquence, while others were endowed with erudition; but very few have emerged as both eloquent and erudite at the same time. On this account, the two summits of the Roman language, Terentius Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BCE), celebrated as Rome's greatest scholar.</note> and Marcus Cicero <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BCE), Rome's most famous orator and statesman.</note>, are cited: from the former, the knowledge of things was sought; from the latter, the knowledge of words. The one is called "most learned" from every side by Terentianus <note>Terentianus Maurus, a grammarian and poet who wrote on Latin meter and style.</note>; the other is called "most eloquent" by everyone. 

As Seneca excellently says, that felicity of genius failed Virgil <note>The great epic poet of the *Aeneid*.</note> in prose; while Cicero wrote poems with no grace and no charm—the Muses, of course, being unwilling and resistant <note>original: "musis scilicet invitis atque repugnantibus." A classical idiom suggesting that one is attempting an art form for which they have no natural talent.</note>. But you indeed, being both most learned...

# LETTERS

Indeed, through your kindness, I have achieved what I most desired. I thank you for such a gift, and I offer him <note>Pico</note> my warmest congratulations for having published a work of such magnitude that it ought to be celebrated by all of Christendom. In this work, I am truly uncertain which to admire more: the discovery of so many and such great things, the incredible order maintained within such variety, or the great elegance of speech found in such laborious descriptions. For why should I mention the *Heptaplus* <note>original: "heptaplo." Pico’s famous work, a seven-fold commentary on the first chapters of Genesis.</note>, which especially commends the author’s efforts? There is no wordiness, no "swelling" <note>original: "tumor," referring to a bombastic or arrogant literary style.</note>, and in everything there is a singular modesty, free from any suspicion of malice. I truly wish I could have returned a similar gift for this most sweet and welcome favor of yours, so that you might more clearly see my heart's affection for you. But for now, I have sent you the speech I recently delivered at Buda <note>The capital of the Kingdom of Hungary.</note> before King Matthias Corvinus <note>Matthias Corvinus (1443–1490), King of Hungary and a great patron of the Renaissance.</note>. When you have read it yourself, you will also give it to your friend Pico to read. I judge him to be the most outstanding in every branch of learning of all those whose writings I have seen in our age. Farewell, and continue to love me in return, as you do.

<note>A large red initial letter N containing a smaller n inside it marks the start of a new letter.</note> Battista Guarini to the most learned prince Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, greetings.

I do not yet concede that the dispute should be settled in your favor. For I can easily turn those clever arguments of yours **back upon yourself** <note>original: "ἀντιστρέφοντα" (antistrephonta), a Greek rhetorical term for an argument that can be reversed to prove the opposite point.</note>. If I am your teacher, why do you not obey me? If I am not, why do you call me teacher? Nor do I refuse this name because I scorn you as a pupil—you whom I claim as my own teacher—but because I both venerate and proclaim your learning. In this learning, I am conscious that neither my own talents, nor the marks of a pen held sideways, nor little wax marks, nor finally the obelisk <note>A horizontal line (−) used by ancient grammarians to mark suspected or spurious text.</note> or the asterisk <note>A star-shaped mark (∗) used to highlight noteworthy passages.</note> have moved you very much. But we seem to have fallen into a new kind of judicial case, while you strive to grant me that "possession" which I am trying to grant to you. What case of the rhetoricians ever had a plaintiff or defendant of this kind? My dear Pico, I will never **stretch out the grass** <note>original: "herbā porrigā," a classical Roman idiom meaning to admit defeat, as a defeated soldier might offer a handful of grass to the victor.</note> to you in this fight unless we first settle the matter with good grace: since you will not yield otherwise, let each of us be judged as both teacher and pupil to the other simultaneously.

But jokes aside, let us discuss serious matters. Both your *Heptaplus* and you yourself can rightly be pleased with your work. You have achieved all the goals of learned men so thoroughly that not even a trace of envy appears in your writing. It is to be hoped that the same success will be granted to you even more easily in your other writings, since that best master of writing, practice, will be added to them. As for what concerns me, I rejoice greatly that I am in the thoughts of that praised man—one who should be praised by everyone and everywhere—Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo de' Medici (1449–1492), the "Magnificent" ruler of Florence.</note>. This is especially true when added to the judgment of Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), the preeminent poet and scholar of the Medicean circle.</note>, whose copious and secret reading of manifold disciplines I so embrace that I admire it, and so admire it that I never cease to commend it. Thus it happens that I consider being placed by him outside the "risk of learning" <note>original: "extra doctrinæ aleā," likely meaning being beyond the reach of criticism.</note> to be like a triumph.

As for your request for a list of my books, that is laborious and useless for me. It will be enough if you assist my needs as time allows. Currently, I desire Martianus Capella <note>A 5th-century author of an influential encyclopedia on the seven liberal arts.</note> and Seneca's *Natural Questions*, provided the copies are free of errors. For the works of the Sibyl <note>Prophetic books of the ancient world.</note> we have here are in need of repair. If I could buy them in printed form, it would be more pleasing to me; if not, they will return to you after no long "right of recovery" <note>original: "postliminio," a legal term for the restoration of rights to a person returning from abroad.</note>. Farewell, my hope and the hope of good disciplines, and continue to love me. Ferrara, the Nones of December, 1489.

<note>A large red initial letter Q containing a smaller q inside it marks the start of a new letter excerpt.</note> From a letter of Hermolao to Giovanni Pico.

Although I love these letters of yours because they flow, because they are not affected, and because they—I will not say do not know care, but rather—reject it: that is, they do not receive it **by design** <note>original: "de cōposito."</note>, and they exclude it when it approaches and wishes to be brought in. Thus, there are indeed traces of diligence in them, but they are in a way suppressed and repudiated. I am not so skillful that I can look into your genius and estimate its magnitude and fruitfulness. But this is how it seems to me—and perhaps I am not mistaken—whither you are directing your aim, and where you will end up, and what you will soon become. Nothing is more liberal than that talent of yours, nothing more delightful; and let it be said once, even if a bit harshly, it produces nothing...

# LETTERS

...more intense—if such a natural talent is even to be so called—which has produced fruits that would not be despised even in mature ages or by any well-practiced learning. Consider how great you are, as I hear, in poetry: what spirit, what happiness of expression, what vigor, and finally what nobility and splendor in every act of literature. What of when you act the philosopher? What memory, what subtlety, what speed of mind agreeing with the vigor of the whole body! But I am carried away into your praises against my will. Nay, rather, most willingly; for everyone desires most that which turns them toward itself even when they are unwilling and reluctant. That ambition of being praised by your peers in learning will be granted to you. A time more suited to this duty will surely be given. Now I come to the rest.

From a letter of Hermolao <note>Hermolao Barbaro (1454–1493), a prominent Venetian scholar and diplomat.</note> to Giovanni Pico.

I have congratulated this age on a life of such learning that it knows almost nothing <note>The author likely means the age is so learned that "ignorance" is almost unknown.</note>; with such care that it seems to know nothing at all <note>Likely referring to the ease and lack of pretension in Pico's scholarship.</note>. I see that Greek literature—the only thing that could have been found lacking in you, and without which you would have achieved nothing—you have not merely learned, but drunk deep; and with such ease and speed that neither do you remember, nor can you persuade others, that you were ever once ignorant of Greek. This is what I declare no less gladly than truly regarding my friend Girolamo Donato. I would exhort you, and so forth.

Yesterday and almost always (perhaps too immodestly), I have burned with a desire for perpetual fame, such that anything else was considered as nothing compared to surviving glory. Why then should I seek Glaucus’s herb <note>original: "glauci gramen." Posterity will one day tell that there was once a certain Poliziano whom even Pico himself, the light of all learning, valued so highly that he did not hesitate to dedicate to him his most beautiful book on the highest matters. Therefore, I give you thanks for immortality—immortal thanks. Farewell.

You wish to be more certain about the death of Pico della Mirandola, which seems still uncertain to you; you wish, Germain, to grieve more heavily. For since you have grieved heavily thus far over this ambiguous loss, once you are made certain, I think you will soon grieve most heavily. It was perhaps better to mourn a doubtful loss than to be tortured by a certain one. Alas, what do you ask, my most beloved Germain? I would indeed prefer to remain in doubt. Nor can I, at present, make you more certain without tears. Last November, on the day when Charles, the great King of the French <note>Charles VIII of France, whose invasion of Italy began in 1494.</note>, entered our city of Florence, our Mirandola left us. He affected the learned with almost as much grief as the King meanwhile brought joy to the city; thus did the provident genius of the place balance the groans of the scholars with the joy of the people.
