<meta>This page transitions from the praises of Pico's living mind to a poignant reflection on his death in 1494. It details the loss of both Pico and his contemporary Angelo Poliziano, and discusses the efforts of Pico's nephew, Gianfrancesco, to preserve his uncle's unfinished intellectual legacy.</meta>

# LETTERS

...in place of the extinguished philosophical light, a royal light is meanwhile kindled, lest Florence should perhaps see a darker day. The Mirandolan light is extinguished on earth and returned to heaven. For Pico migrated from this shadow of life with such cheerful security that he seemed undoubtedly about to return from a kind of exile to his heavenly fatherland. You desire, moreover, to know what Pico once composed, or what he was recently composing: he wrote the *Hexameron* <note>original: "Exameron"; a commentary on the six days of Biblical creation titled *Heptaplus*.</note>, the *Apology*, and a treatise *On Being and the One* <note>original: "de uno & ente"; a work attempting to reconcile the philosophies of Plato and Aristotle.</note>, as well as several letters. Whatever he had composed regarding love during his formerly fervent youth, he later condemned with a more mature judgment and wished to be entirely destroyed; it cannot be published without doing him an injustice. 

Indeed, I knew the final will of that pious man. For in age, Pico was a son to me; in familiarity, a brother; and in love, truly another self. He was daily toiling at three works: the harmony of Aristotle with Plato, commentaries on the sacred scriptures, and the *Confutations of Astrologers*. All these were disputed with as much eloquence as subtlety. But though they were brilliant in style, they were sketched in such strange and obscure handwriting <note>original: "characteribus"; Pico was known for using a personal shorthand and having difficult script.</note> that they could scarcely be read even by him. Therefore, they have not yet been completed or revised by him, nor can they be transcribed by others, unless perhaps by someone with the gift of prophecy. For if they could perhaps be transcribed, we would not miss our Pico so much as if he were absent, nor would we ever suspect him to be extinguished. But his pious nephew, Gianfrancesco, a man powerful in letters and intellect, strives daily to rescue them from the darkness into light, and he is writing the life and deeds of his uncle.

Accept, finally, this epitaph of ours for him: "The High Priests rarely permit the more secret mysteries to be seen, and they hide them away immediately; so God showed to mortals the divine philosopher Giovanni Pico of Mirandola, ripe in his thirtieth year."

Furthermore, so that you may know the rest of the loss to literature suffered this autumn in Florence: our Angelo Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), a renowned poet and humanist scholar.</note>, most learned in the Latin and Greek languages, migrated from this life this past September before Pico’s death, in the fortieth year of his age. He had already published his *Miscellanea*, his *Silva_e* <note>A collection of occasional poems.</note>, and certain declamations and several letters—all things composed with both sharp insight and elegance. He also daily noted down many things necessary for elegance in uncertain handwriting, just as Pico did, so that in both men a grave loss to literature has occurred. 

Dated the 23rd of March, 1494 <note>The Florentine year began on March 25, so this date corresponds to 1495 in the modern calendar.</note>.

<note>A large red initial E marks the beginning of the following letter from Marsilio Ficino.</note>

->Marsilio Ficino the Florentine sends greetings to Giovanni Francesco, Count of Mirandola.<-

I sent a short letter to Gaul concerning the death and praises of Pico after your departure. However, one may collect long and singular praises of Pico from my many writings scattered here and there, especially from the later books of my letters. There are now twelve of them printed. From the preface to Plotinus, from the *Book of the Sun*, and from the commentaries on the *Timaeus* and the *Parmenides*, accept this epitaph for him: "The High Priests rarely permit the more secret mysteries to be seen, and they hide them away immediately; so God showed to mortals the divine philosopher Giovanni Pico of Mirandola, ripe in his thirtieth year." Let the epitaph end here. 

God seems to have given all things to Giovanni Pico: the most abundant goods of the soul, the body, and fortune. If only He had granted a longer span of life. But it is not right to accuse Providence in this matter. For if God had led him, in a very short time and beyond the powers of nature, to the very summit, he perhaps could not have proceeded toward anything better. Indeed, the mobility of nature does not allow one to remain in the same state, and perfected virtue does not permit a relapse into something worse. But you yourself have written these and other things of that kind better and more extensively in the *Life of Pico*—not so much to add luster to him (for who could add light to the sun?), but rather to clear away the clouds so that his hidden works, which are most worthy of the light, might shine clearly. Mortals will therefore wonderfully commend your great piety toward your uncle, and God will judge you worthy of no small rewards.

Dated the first of November, 1495.

### The Twelve Rules of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, partly rousing and partly directing men in the spiritual battle.

<summary>This page contains letters from Marsilio Ficino mourning the deaths of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola and Angelo Poliziano, while discussing the preservation of Pico's unfinished philosophical works. It concludes with the introduction to Pico's "Twelve Rules" for spiritual life.</summary>

--- Page 289 ---
<meta>The previous page concluded the biographical introduction regarding Pico della Mirandola's death and his unfinished manuscripts. This page begins a specific spiritual text titled "The Twelve Rules of Spiritual Combat," which Pico composed as practical advice for a Christian life.</meta>

# LETTERS

**The first rule:** if the path of virtue seems harsh to a man because we must continually fight against the flesh, the devil, and the world, let him remember that whatever life he chooses—even one according to the ways of the world—he will still have to suffer many adversities, sorrows, inconveniences, and labors.

**The second rule:** let him remember that in worldly matters, the struggle is longer, more laborious, and more fruitless; in these things, labor is the only end of labor, and its final result is eternal punishment.

**The third rule:** let him remember it is foolish to believe that one can reach heaven except through a struggle of this kind, just as Christ, our head, did not ascend into heaven except by the cross; nor should the condition of the servant be better than the condition of his master.

**The fourth rule:** let him remember that this struggle is not only to be endured with difficulty, but is to be desired, even if no reward were to come to us from it, solely so that we might be conformed to Christ, our God and Lord. Every time you resist a temptation or do violence to one of your senses, think of which part of Christ’s cross you are being made to conform. When you resist gluttony and afflict your sense of taste, remember that he was given gall and vinegar to drink. When you pull back your hands from stealing <note>original: "rapina"; referring generally to taking what is not one's own.</note> something that pleases you, think of his hands nailed to the wood of the cross for your sake. If you resist pride, remember him who, though he was in the form of God, took on the form of a servant for you and humbled himself even unto death on the cross. When you are tempted by anger, remember him who was God and the most just of all men, yet when he saw himself treated like a thief, mocked, spat upon, scourged, afflicted with every insult, and counted among criminals, he never showed any sign of anger or indignation; instead, bearing all things with the greatest patience, he answered everyone with the utmost gentleness. Running thus through every single instance, you will find that there is no suffering that does not make you, in some part, conformed to Christ.

**The fifth rule:** trust neither in those "twelve arms" <note>A reference to Pico's own work, *The Twelve Weapons of Spiritual Warfare*.</note> nor in any other human remedy, but only in the power of Jesus Christ, who said: "Have confidence, I have overcome the world"; and elsewhere: "The prince of this world is cast out." Therefore, let us trust in his power alone both to conquer the world and to overcome the devil. For this reason, we must always seek his help and that of his saints through prayer.

**The sixth rule:** remember when you have conquered one temptation, another is always to be expected, because the devil always circles about looking for someone to devour. Therefore, it is necessary to always serve in fear and to say with the prophet: "I will stand upon my watch."

**The seventh rule:** strive not only to avoid being conquered by the devil when he tempts you, but to conquer him himself. This happens when you not only do not sin, but take the very thing he tempted you with as an occasion for some good. For example, if he offers you some good work of your own so that you might fall into vanity, you should immediately think of it not as your own work but as a gift from God; humble yourself and judge yourself to be insufficiently grateful to God for his benefits.

**The eighth rule:** when you fight, fight as if you are winning, as one who will thereafter possess perpetual peace; for perhaps God will give you this by his grace, and the devil, confounded by your victory, will return no more. But when you have won, behave as if you are about to fight again, so that in the struggle you are always mindful of victory, and in victory, you are always mindful of the struggle.

**The ninth rule:** though you may feel yourself well-fortified and prepared on all sides, nevertheless always flee the occasions of sin, because as the wise man says: "He who loves danger will perish in it."

**The tenth rule:** always meet temptations at the very beginning, and "dash the little ones of Babylon against the rock." <note>A metaphor based on Psalm 137:9; in mystical tradition, the "infants of Babylon" represent the first stirrings of sinful thoughts, and the "Rock" is Christ.</note> For the Rock is Christ; medicine is prepared too late once the illness has taken hold.

& i i i

--- Page 290 ---
<meta>This page continues Pico della Mirandola's practical guide to spiritual life, moving from the general rules of struggle to the specific psychological "weapons" of the soul and a mystical comparison between human love and the love of God.</meta>

# LETTERS

**The eleventh rule:** remember that although in the very conflict of temptation the battle may seem bitter, it is nevertheless far sweeter to conquer the temptation than to go toward the sin to which you are inclined. In this, many are deceived, because they do not compare the sweetness of victory to the sweetness of sin. Instead, they compare the struggle [itself] to the pleasure; and yet a man who has experienced a thousand times what it is to yield to temptation should, at least once, experience what it is to conquer temptation.

**The twelfth rule:** because you are tempted, do not believe yourself abandoned by God, or to be little pleasing to God, or little just and perfect. Be mindful that after Paul saw the divine essence <note>A reference to St. Paul's mystical vision of heaven</note>, he suffered a temptation of the flesh, by which God allowed him to be tempted lest he be tempted by pride. In this, man should also take note that Paul—who was a chosen vessel and caught up even to the third heaven—was nevertheless in danger of becoming proud of his own virtues. As he says of himself: "lest the greatness of the revelations should exalt me, there was given to me a thorn in my flesh to buffet me" <note>original: "stimulus carnis meæ qui me collaphizet"; quoting 2 Corinthians 12:7.</note>. Therefore, above all temptations, a man should most of all arm himself against the temptation of pride, for pride is the root of all evils. Against this, the only remedy is to always think how God humbled himself for us even to the cross; and death, even against our will, shall humble us to the point that we are food for worms.

**Twelve weapons of spiritual combat** which ought to be kept ready at hand when the desire for sinning subdues the mind.

| | |
| :--- | :--- |
| Brief and small pleasure. | Eternal reward: eternal punishment. |
| Companions: disgust and anxiety. | The dignity and nature of man. |
| The loss of a greater good. | Peace of a good mind. |
| Life is a sleep and a shadow. | God's benefits. |
| Death is imminent and unforeseen. | The cross of Christ. |
| The suspicion of impenitence <note>The fear of dying before having the chance to repent.</note>. | The testimonies of martyrs and examples of saints. |

**Twelve conditions of a lover.**
1. To love one alone and to despise all things for him.
2. To think him unhappy who is not with the beloved.
3. To suffer all things to be with him—even death.
4. To adorn oneself so as to please him.
5. To be with him in whatever way one can: if not in reality, at least in thought.
6. To love everything that pertains to him: all his friends, houses, clothes, and images.
7. To desire his praise and to be unable to endure any of his disgrace.
8. To believe all the highest things about him, and likewise to desire that everyone else believes the same.
9. To desire even to suffer some inconvenience for him, and for that inconvenience to be sweet.
10. To weep with him often; if he is absent, out of grief; if he is present, out of joy.
11. Always to languish, always to burn with desire for him.
12. To serve him without thinking of reward or payment. We are usually led to this [service] especially for three reasons. The first is when the service itself is desirable for its own sake. The second is when he whom we serve is in himself very good and lovable, as we are accustomed to say "we serve him because of his virtues." The third is when he, before you began [to serve], bestowed many benefits upon you. And these three things are in God: because for his service nothing is newly received that is not good for us, both as to the soul and as to the body; for to serve him is nothing other than to strive toward him—that is, toward the highest good. Similarly, he himself is the best, the most beautiful, and the wisest; and he has all the qualities that usually move us to love someone and serve him freely. Furthermore, he has bestowed the greatest benefits upon us, since he created us out of nothing and redeemed us from hell through the blood of his Son.

# LETTERS

**Preserve me, O Lord.**

If anyone who has reached a state of perfection wishes to examine his own condition, he faces one particular danger: that he might become proud of his own virtue. Therefore, David—speaking in the persona of a just man concerning his own spiritual state—begins with this word: "preserve me." When rightly considered, this phrase removes every occasion for pride. For someone who can acquire something by their own power can also preserve it for themselves by their own power. He, therefore, who asks to be preserved by God in a state of virtue, signifies by this request that he did not acquire that virtue from himself in the first place. 

Furthermore, he who remembers that he obtained virtue not by his own strength, but by the power of God, cannot be proud of it; rather, he is more deeply humbled before God, according to that saying of the Apostle <note>Referring to St. Paul</note>: "What do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you boast as if you had not received it?" <note>original: "Quid habes quod non accepisti? et si accepisti quid gloriaris quasi non acceperis?"; quoting 1 Corinthians 4:7.</note> There are, therefore, two phrases which we should always have on our lips: one is "Have mercy on me, O God" <note>original: "miserere mei deus"</note> when we remember our sins; the other is "Preserve me, O God" <note>original: "Conserva me deus"</note> when we remember our virtues.

**Because I have hoped in you.**

This is the one thing that allows us to obtain from God what we ask: namely, when we hope that we will receive it. If we observe these two conditions—that we never ask anything from God except those things which are beneficial to our salvation, and that we ask for what we desire ardently with a firm hope that God will hear us—our prayers will never be in vain. 

Therefore, when we do not obtain what we ask, it is either because the thing is harmful to us (for we do not know what we should ask for, as Christ says), or it is as Jesus said: "Whatever you ask in my name will be given to you" <note>original: "quicquid petieritis in nomine meo dabitur vobis"; referencing John 14:13.</note>. This name "Jesus" signifies "Savior"; and therefore, nothing is truly asked "in the name of Jesus" unless it leads to the salvation of the one asking. Alternatively, He does not hear us because, though we may ask for good things, we do not ask *well*—that is, we ask with very little hope. He who hopes timidly asks coldly. Therefore James said: "But let him ask in faith, wavering in nothing" <note>original: "postulet autem in fide nihil haesitans"; quoting James 1:6.</note>.

**I said to the Lord: You are my God.**

After he has fortified himself against pride, he begins to describe his state. The whole condition of a just man consists in this phrase: "I said to the Lord: You are my God." Although this phrase seems common to almost everyone, there are few who can say it truly

Therefore, those things which we have said concerning the resurrection are understood primarily in regards to Christ, as Peter the Apostle declared <note>Referring to Acts 2:25–28, where St. Peter quotes this Psalm to argue that David was prophesying Christ’s resurrection rather than his own.</note>; and secondarily, they can be understood regarding us, insofar as we are members of Christ. # LETTERS

->Junianus Maius to Roberto Salviati sends greetings. <note>original: "S.D." stands for *Salutem Dicit*, a formal Latin greeting meaning "he says health" or "he sends greetings."</note><-

<note>The text begins with a large red initial **Q**.</note> **Q**uod <note>original: "Quod," meaning "Because" or "In that."</note> you have taken care to print the divine work of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494) was a celebrated Italian Renaissance philosopher and nobleman known for his vast erudition and his attempt to harmonize all schools of thought.</note> with no less care than he himself used in composing it, I believe much gratitude is owed both to your diligence and to his divine teaching. 

Gratitude is owed to you, because you did not permit such a sublime work to lie hidden in the darkness of oblivion; for by this single effort, you have both immortalized your friend and served the common benefit of all. 

Gratitude is owed to him, however, because he was deterred neither by the authority nor the holiness of the ancient men who previously recounted these same matters, nor did he simply follow in the footsteps of others, but rather illuminated those same things with a certain light of his own. 

For as soon as this work—so profound <term>recondite</term> <note>original: "reconditū"; refers to knowledge that is hidden away or requires specialized study to understand.</note> and removed from the understanding of many—reached my hands, I began to read it with greater diligence. It brought me not only pleasure mixed with admiration, but it also lifted my contemplating soul to such a height of sublimity that nothing seems more admirable or more thoroughly explained...

<summary>This page contains a dedicatory letter from the scholar Junianus Maius to Roberto Salviati, praising Salviati's meticulous printing of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola's works. Maius celebrates Pico's original intellectual light and Salviati's role in preserving this "sublime" knowledge for the public good.</summary>

# LETTERS

...so that the Jew can no longer object or cast it against us in his greeting, that we sing things in the temple every hour which even we ourselves do not consider to have been translated faithfully enough. <note>original: "Ne iam in salutare iudæus..." This refers to a common Renaissance humanist concern that Latin translations of the Bible used in liturgy were philologically inaccurate compared to the original Hebrew.</note>

Also from chapter 90 of the same work:

Such also is this friend of mine, Giovanni Pico, of the princes of Mirandola; a most perfect work of nature, from whom I believe philosophy—now meditating on how to speak in Latin—will receive its highest pinnacle.

Also from chapter 94 of the same work:

Sometimes I and this Pico of Mirandola—a man who can never be praised enough—spent our leisure hours running through the ancient commentators of the sacred Old Instrument <note>original: "instr̃i sacri ueteris," referring to the Old Testament.</note>, especially the Greeks: Diodorus, Philo, Gennadius, Aquila, Origen, Basil, Didymus, Isidore, Apollinaris, Severianus, and many others of that kind. Just as he does with the opinions of the Latins, he most diligently compares all these with the opinions of the Jewish and Chaldean <term>Chaldean</term> <note>In this period, "Chaldean" usually referred to the Aramaic language and the Targums (Aramaic paraphrases of the Hebrew Bible).</note> interpreters. He sifts and examines everything, so that from there, truth may be drawn out, obscurity removed, faith strengthened, or impiety refuted.

From the book *On Ecclesiastical Writers* by John, Abbot of Sponheim <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), a famous German abbot, scholar, and occultist.</note>:

Giovanni Pico, an Italian by nation, Count of Mirandola and Lord of Concordia; a man most studious of all good literature. Just as he is most noble by his illustrious blood, so he is most distinguished by his truly divine genius. Surrounded by a great company of all kinds of arts, he is worthy and most deserving that the Muses should follow his progress. He is the most learned philosopher of our age and a most sharp debater. He wrote several things in a most elegant style, which our age will both approve of and greatly admire; by these works, he has rendered the memory of his name and glory everlasting, and not unworthily.

From the *Compendium of Revelations* of the most learned and holy man, Brother Girolamo Savonarola of Ferrara, of the Order of Preachers <note>Girolamo Savonarola (1452–1498) was a Dominican friar and influential preacher in Renaissance Florence who was eventually executed.</note>:

Count Giovanni of Mirandola, a man singular in our times for his genius and manifold learning.

From the second commentary on Propertius <note>Sextus Propertius was a Latin elegiac poet.</note> by the most learned and eloquent man Filippo Beroaldo of Bologna, regarding that verse: *Not so many Achaemenians,* and so forth. I read the word *fusa* written instead of *ethrusca* in the codex of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. He is a man worthy of the memory of the ages, who, endowed with wide-ranging disciplines, adorns the glory of our age. To him can be applied what Terentianus wrote of Varro: "Pico, a man most learned from every side." He not only esteems you, my dear Minus—as a most learned man esteems one who is learned, and as a most noble man esteems one who is noble—but he loves you vehemently; he speaks of you with honor and thinks most highly of you. After his more serious studies, he is accustomed to rest in the reading of Propertius as if in a most pleasant lodging; and he agreed with me as I was reading this passage, showing me that in his own manuscript, it was written as *fusa* and not *ethrusca*, and so forth.

THE END.

->These small works of Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, Count of Concordia, were diligently printed by Bernardinus Venetus. Skill and diligence were applied to the best of his ability so that he would not wander from the original manuscript. In Venice, in the Year of Salvation 1498, on the 9th day of October.<-
